# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature. 367

...and finally the firmament, adorned with an innumerable multitude of stars, each moving in its many paths, governed by most constant laws, exact periods, and the most diverse qualities of influence, displayed to the world the immense riches of harmonic arrangement. These riches were hidden under a "consonant-dissonance"—that is, under the light and shadow of day and night—which are so necessary for the world. But so that the Supreme Organist <note>original: "Organædus"; Kircher depicts God as a master musician playing the universe like a pipe organ.</note> might vary and increase the equipment of this worldly harmony:

The **Fifth Register** <margin>Register or prelude of the fifth day.</margin> was unlocked and sounded forth by the word of His power and the cooperation of the Spirit. From the waters themselves, as if from pre-existing matter, the Water led forth an innumerable variety of animals, creeping things, and serpents, endowed with the most diverse qualities, powers, and properties. Since all of these follow different laws of agreement and disagreement, of hate and love, there soon emerged a most skillful web, a song and symphony of consonant and dissonant parts. To this day, we "hear" this music with our eyes in wonder, and "watch" it with our ears, utterly astonished. <note>The author uses synesthesia here—swapping the roles of eyes and ears—to describe the overwhelming sensory experience of nature’s complexity.</note> Finally, so that the eternal wisdom of God might demonstrate the even greater riches of His glory:

The **Sixth Register** <margin>Register or prelude of the sixth day.</margin> was unlocked and sounded, and behold! The Earth produced an immense variety of animals and four-legged creatures, distributed into various genera and species as if into certain classes. From such a great diversity of species, a new and wonderful Music arose, as if from dissonances and consonances; its most pleasant resonance even now wonderfully ravishes the ears of all who listen to it attentively. You have here, then, the preludes of the six "registers" of created things, beautifully corresponding to the six days of creation <term>Hexameron: a theological term for the six days of creation</term>. However, just as organists, after the preludes of the individual registers have been properly performed, arrange all the registers together to display the universal consonance of all the pipes; so too that eternal Master Musician <note>original: "Archimusicus"</note>, after the six preludes of created things, produced the most excellent of bodily creatures, Man. Unlocking all the registers of the worldly organ, He played the prelude of universal harmony in Man, as if in the measure and end of all things. For besides his soul, which is heaped with so many and such great gifts of grace and nature, God also fashioned his body with such symmetry and proportion that the songs divided among the individual classes of created things seem to be collected in a single human being, as if in a summary and recapitulation <note>original: "anacephaleosi"</note> of the greater world. 

We have seen, therefore, curious reader, the construction of the world-organ; we have considered the arrangement of the registers, the paths of the winds, and the variety of the pipes; we have listened to the Organist’s inimitable skill in playing and his wonderful song. Nothing further remains except that we examine the harmonies and songs hidden in each class of created things a little more deeply. To proceed in harmonic order, we shall follow the order of the ten registers—that is, the ten distinct types of beings which represent for us nothing other than a certain **Ten-Stringed Lyre** or **Ten-Piped Instrument** of nature. We shall clearly demonstrate that in each of these, God and His art, Nature, looked toward harmonic proportions and forms.

->### REGISTER I.<-
->### OR THE<-
->### SYMPHONY<-
->### of the Four Elements<-

Since the four elements hold the lowest place in this world-organ, we must rightly discuss their Symphony first, as it is "below all else" <note>original: "ὑποκάτω" (hypokato); Greek for 'underneath' or 'at the bottom'.</note>. Beginning therefore from the harmony of the habitable Earth, as if from the *Proslambanomenos* <term>Proslambanomenos: The lowest note in the Ancient Greek musical system; here it represents the Earth as the base of the cosmic scale</term>, we shall then follow the symphonies of the rest in their following order.

The harmonic arrangement of the climates clearly teaches us that the mass of the Earth was established harmonically. Every region has a certain ratio and comparison to the Sun, who is like Apollo...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between cosmic harmony and the physical world, specifically focusing on how geography and climate influence human physiology and vocal pitch, citing the Roman architect Vitruvius.</meta>

368 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance* <note>Original title: Artis Magnæ Consoni & Dissoni.</note>

A certain celestial Apollo <note>A personification of the sun as the god of music.</note>, through the varied striking of his plectrum—that is, the beating of his rays—stirs up different harmonies in the lower world. These things are so true that Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the 1st-century BC Roman architect whose theories on proportion and nature influenced centuries of design and science.</note> himself thought this contemplation should be left to posterity as the greatest secret of nature; indeed, he asserted that the diversity of human voices arises only from the different constitution of the climate, in these words:

*For in those places where the sun pours out vapors moderately, it preserves bodies in a balanced state; but where it burns fiercely in its close path, it snatches away and dries up the balance of moisture. Conversely, where vapors are cooled because they are far from the midday sun, the moisture is not exhausted by heat, but the dewy air of the sky pours moisture into the bodies, creating larger frames and higher-pitched sounds of the voice. For this reason, in the North, nations are nourished with massive bodies, fair complexions, straight red hair, bluish-gray eyes, and much blood, because they are shaped by the fullness of moisture and the coolness of the sky. Those, however, who are closest to the southern axis and subjected to the path of the sun are produced with shorter bodies, dark complexions, curly hair, black eyes, weak legs, and thin blood by the force of the sun.* <note>original: "Namque sol quibus locis..." This passage from Vitruvius's "De Architectura" (Book 6) reflects the ancient theory of humorism, where climate dictates the "humors" or fluids in the body.</note>

*And a little later, he says: Therefore, since we hold this certain in our minds, by drawing a line from the edge in the Northern region to that which is above the southern axis, and another oblique line at its height to the highest pole, we will undoubtedly perceive the schema of the world's triangle <note>original: "schema trigoni mundi"</note>, just like the instrument the Greeks call the sambuca <note>original: "σαμβύκην"; an ancient triangular stringed instrument, likely similar to a small harp.</note>. Thus, the space closest to the lowest part of the strings from the axis line in the southern borders, being under that place where the nations are because of the short altitude relative to the world, produces a thin sound of the voice, like the highest-pitched string in an instrument near the angle; following this, the rest of the nations toward middle Greece produce lower scales of sound. Likewise, from the middle in increasing order toward the farthest North, under the height of the sky, the voices of the nations are expressed by nature with deeper, heavier sounds. Thus, the whole conception of the world seems to be composed most harmoniously through the sun's temperature, in accordance with its inclination. Thus far Vitruvius; but so that these things may be better and more clearly perceived, I have decided to demonstrate that triangle or "harmonic sambuca" at somewhat greater length.*

So that Vitruvius may show the differences in the sounds of voices among various nations, having now established the horizon, he creates a certain diagram in the likeness of an instrument which the Greeks call the *sambuca* <gloss>a triangular instrument</gloss>, namely triangular and tuned with strings, shaped almost like our harps <term>Harp: A stringed instrument where the strings run at an angle to the soundboard, here compared to the geometry of the Earth's axis.</term>. The essence of it is this: those for whom the northern pole or axis of the world is raised less above the horizon have a higher and more delicate voice than those for whom the same pole is higher; for these latter have a deeper and lower sound of the voice.

->The Vitruvian Seven-Stringed Instrument<- <note>original: "Heptachordon Vitruuianum." A "heptachord" is a seven-stringed scale or instrument.</note>

[A geometric diagram of a semicircle with a triangle FHE inside. The arc is marked with degrees from 10 to 80. A line within the diagram is labeled "Heptachordon Vitruuianum."]

We demonstrate this according to the mind of Vitruvius as follows. Let the meridian circle be ABC, the center of the world E, the horizon AEC, and the north pole F, from which a perpendicular line FH <note>A line falling at a 90-degree angle.</note> falls to the horizon AC; and let the line FE be drawn from F to the center E. Thus, the triangle FHE will be formed. Again, from the pole...

It explains that people in northern climates have deeper voices and larger bodies due to moisture, while those in southern climates have higher voices and smaller frames due to heat.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Decachordon Naturae" (The Ten-stringed Lyre of Nature), specifically focusing on how the geography of the Earth and its climates affect the musical pitch of human voices.</meta>

Book 10. The Ten-stringed Lyre of Nature, 369

From the pole raised at G, let a perpendicular line GI descend to the horizon AC, and let another line drawn from G to E close the triangle GIE. I maintain that those for whom the height is greater at F have a higher-pitched voice than those for whom the same pole is at point G. Let a line EH be drawn within the larger triangle GIH, and let it be called MH there; it is certain that line GI is longer than line MN. If, therefore, the line GI were the string of an instrument, it would produce a lower and deeper sound than the string MN, which, because it is closer to the angle and therefore shorter, will also produce a higher sound. Thus, the individual sines of the polar elevations, fitted within the triangle, represent the strings on a <term>Sambuca</term> <note>original: "Sambuca"; an ancient triangular stringed instrument, often associated with a high, shrill sound.</note>; the voices of men born under various climates are entirely in harmony with these, according to the mind of Vitruvius; see the figure added here.

You see in the harmonic triangle, from the <term>Proslambanomenos</term> <note>The lowest note in the Ancient Greek musical system.</note> all the way to the <term>Nete</term> <note>The highest note in the Ancient Greek musical system.</note>, nine decades of polar elevations, denoting the depth or height of the voices of different nations.

However, when I considered this ingenious invention of Vitruvius a little more deeply, I saw that while it holds a great deal of agreement with reality, for the most part it cannot stand. Experience teaches us that within one and the same climate, high, low, and moderate voices are found. Indeed, under the equator (where Vitruvius placed the *Nete* of voices—that is, the maximum height of harmonic voices), experience in New Spain <note>Modern-day Mexico and parts of Central America.</note> and other parts subject to the Torrid Zone teaches that men mostly have very thick and dull voices. In contrast, under the Frigid Zone, men generally have very high voices, as is apparent among the Laplanders, Icelanders, and <term>Scrikfinni</term> <note>original: "Scrikfinnis"; a historical term for the Sami people of northern Scandinavia, referring to them as "skiing Finns."</note>. For although the aforementioned cold regions possess humidity, as Vitruvius well notes, the cold there has joined to it a certain parching power—I know not what—by which bodies are not only constricted but also thoroughly dried out; a high voice necessarily follows this drying. But the Torrid Zone, along with maximum heat, is known to have maximum humidity due to frequent rains, rivers, vast lakes, and the proximity of the ocean; certainly, it is so far from producing high voices that it instead produces dull and deep ones. Truly, this error is easily forgiven in Vitruvius (seeing as he had no knowledge of the aforementioned zones in his time), and he is to be greatly praised for correctly attributing the cause of the height and depth of voices to dryness, heat, cold, and humidity. Let us therefore arrange this harmony of the terrestrial world differently.

I say, first, that all places on earth imbued with moderate humidity and cold generate deep and low voices, while those prevailing in dryness and heat generate high and sharp voices, regardless of the climate. Thus, the Portuguese, despite being further south, have a deeper voice than the Castilians, for no other reason than that Portugal is more humid than the mountainous region of Castile. Similarly, sulfurous and dry lands, such as Sicily and Calabria, produce much higher voices than the humid Roman territory—not because they are further south, but because of the dry and hot condition of the soil. Thus, the diverse constitution and unique properties of horizons are the sole cause of the diversity of voices, if indeed it is to be taken from the four elemental qualities. <margin>The cause of the diversity of voices in different Regions.</margin>

But since enough was said in the first book about the combination of these qualities in the generation of the voice, we refer the reader there. In this way, through eight combinations, we can derive eight different pitches of the voices of the earth's inhabitants, which indeed correspond perfectly to the degrees of one <term>diapason</term> <note>An octave.</note>. 

1. First, those born in the most humid and simultaneously coldest places—such as those born and living near lakes and stagnant marshes within mountain enclosures—acquire a thick and deep voice, such as is the <term>hypate</term> <note>The lowest string/note in the Greek lyre.</note> in the eight-stringed scale; for cold in a humid environment is the greatest expander of the limbs. 
2. Second, those born and raised in the hottest and driest places have a very high, shrill voice, similar to eunuchs, such as is the *Nete* in the eight-stringed scale. 
3. Those born in the most temperate places acquire a perfectly tempered voice from heat, dryness, humidity, and cold, corresponding to the <term>Mese</term> <note>The middle note, considered the "key" or centering tone.</note> in the eight-stringed scale. 
4. Those born in places approaching more toward heat and dryness, yet retaining some degrees of cold and humidity, acquire a voice corresponding to the <term>Parhypate</term> and <term>Hypomese</term>. 
5. Likewise, those who approach more toward cold and humidity, while still retaining some degrees of heat and dryness, acquire a voice corresponding to the <term>Hypoparanete</term> and <term>Paranete</term>. 

See the following diagram.

<note>These terms refer to the strings or notes of the ancient Greek musical system. Nete is the highest note, and Hypate is the lowest.</note>

And in this manner the organ of Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect who famously described the "hydraulis" or water organ</note> can be constructed; where it must also be noted that the individual climates of the temperate zones have this property: they sharpen or dampen voices according to whether they have a greater or lesser latitude. Thus, in Germany, because of the cold, the *hypate* <note>the lowest note</note> in human voices is generally a whole tone deeper than the Italian *hypate*; and consequently, this affects the entire system of the octave, or *diapason*. The same is to be understood for the rest. Indeed, for the stated reasons, this system undergoes change according to the different seasons of the year, since it turns out much deeper in winter than in summer.

For as Vitruvius rightly observes, this kind of variation is noted even in the instruments themselves; for two earthenware vessels, one of which is baked less than the other and consequently possesses more moisture, also allow for a notable variety in sounding—a fact which experience compels us to admit in the case of strings and sinews as well.

<margin>
Variation of the pitch <note>original: "Toni"</note> which the Choir-leader <note>original: "Chorista"</note> commonly calls [the tone] in different regions.
</margin>

Why we experience the exact opposite in artificial sounds, however, is most worthy of admiration. For it is well known that here in Rome, organs and harpsichords are tuned a whole tone deeper than in Naples; in Florence, they are a semitone deeper than the Roman instruments; but in Venice, they are tuned a whole major third <note>original: "ditono"</note> higher than the Neapolitan ones. We attribute the cause of this matter in places so near to one another not so much to the nature of the locations as to long-standing custom. For this business can depend on the temperament of the people, some of whom are moved by higher melodies, others by deeper ones; as is clearly evident among the ancient peoples of Greece—the Aeolians, Dorians, and Ionians—who, just as they differed in customs and temperament, also disagreed in the quality of their music. The Dorians maintained a deep style of singing, the Lydians a cheerful and sharp one, and the Phrygians a softer style, as was explained at length in the preceding books. Having thus seen the harmony which the various arrangements of the earth bring to things, we must now also see what Symphony the Elements obtain when breathing together.

### THE SYMPHONISM
### of the 4 Elements.

Various authors explain the harmony of the four elements in different ways. The Alchemists <note>original: "Alchimistę"</note> report it by this example: they extract the spirit from wine, then the oil which is innate to the spirit, thirdly the phlegm <note>the watery residue</note>, after which the dross remains, which they call the "dead head" <note>original: "caput mortuum," the useless solid remains after distillation</note>. When these are enclosed in a hermetically sealed glass, they are continuously distinguished into five regions, as it were. Of these, the lower black part represents the **Earth**; the next, an aqueous or extracted substance, represents **Water**; the subtle and spirituous part represents **Air**; and finally, the fourth, oily and flammable, represents **Fire**. Over all of these finally floats a certain "fifth essence" <term>Quintessence: the purest, celestial element in ancient physics</term>, far removed from all impurity and the dross of earthly contagion, representing **Heaven**. These indeed, by a certain harmonic analogy, surpass one another according to the degrees of being proper to each, so that they closely express harmonic intervals; and they maintain that the created world was made according to this model of art and nature, as will be shown more fully later.

Others compare the whole world to a harmonic monochord <note>a single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical musical ratios</note>, in which the spirit or soul of the world—or better, God Himself—placed outside the monochord, produces all the consonances. He makes the voices sharper in those creatures that are nearer to Him, and deeper in those that are more remote from Him. Thus, the deepest voice, approaching more toward silence, darkness, and the dread of matter because of the excessive density of the air and the resistance of the spirit, can represent the **Earth**. For they wish for light to act upon the matter of the world in the same way that the spirit of a man acts upon the air. They say the string is the matter of the world, but the instrument is the "macrocosmic monochord," in which the harmonic degrees perfectly reflect the arrangement of the musical scale. Thus **Robert Fludd** <note>original: "Robertus de fluctibus," a 17th-century physician and mystic known for his "World Monochord" theory</note> places cold, thickness, and weight in the earth; these relate to the cold and matter of the lowest region (extending as far as the Moon) in a ratio of 4 to 3, which is the proportion...

...the four-to-three ratio <note>original: "portio sesquitertia," the mathematical ratio of 4:3</note>, because in this region a fourth part of light and color is present; and let a perfect fourth <term>diatessaron: a musical interval spanning four notes of the scale</term> be made from water, air, and fire. In this arrangement, Earth holds the position that the Gamma <note>The Greek letter Γ, used to denote the lowest note in the medieval musical scale</note> holds on the monochord, or what the number one is in arithmetic, and the point is in geometry. To better explain these proportions, he imagines a double pyramid: one of light or "formal," and one of shadow or "material." These are inserted into one another in such a way that the pyramid of light has its base fixed in the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, thought to be composed of pure fire or light</note>, while its tip reaches down to the Earth. The pyramid of shadow, however, fixes its base on the Earth and its tip in the Empyrean. They intersect one another around the sphere of the Sun, establishing a wonderful mixture and equality of light and darkness through a continuous harmonic progression. It works in this way: from the Earth to the water is one whole tone; from the water to the air is another; from the air to the fire (which is nothing other than the highest peak of the air) is the place of a semitone. From the fire to the Sun are three other tones. Furthermore, from the Moon to Mercury <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note>, from there to Venus <note>represented by the symbol ♀</note>, and finally from there to the Sun, it constitutes a minor third <note>original: "semiditonum"</note>. Thus, the interval between the Earth and the Sun consists of five whole tones and two semitones. In this sphere of equality, just as a string divided in half produces an octave <term>diapason: the interval of an eighth, or a full octave</term>, this harmony is born from the combination of a fourth and a fifth. From the Sun to the Empyrean, he imagines another spiritual octave; and so he composes the entire world from a double octave, both material and formal. These are subordinated to each other so perfectly that they represent the system of the musical scale, or the ten-stringed lyre <note>original: "pentedecachordon," though the title uses "Decachordon" (ten-stringed), this term implies a fifteen-stringed system</term>. When this is struck by the hand of God, it stirs up certain wondrous harmonies of both worlds. Contemplate the figure of this placed in the final Index.

When the ancients looked upon the elemental world and saw it was constituted by a certain "discordant concord" <note>original: "concordi quadam discordia," a paradox where harmony arises from conflicting elements</note>, and when they perceived a wonderful tempering of diverse qualities, they compared the elements to a tetrachord <term>tetrachord: a scale of four notes</term>. For Orpheus, as Briennius testifies, constructed a four-stringed Lyre based on the example of these elements. He established all its sounds according to the steps of a musical fourth, in which the first string, the *Hypate*, represents Earth; the second, *Parhypate*, represents Water; the third, *Paranete*, Air; and the fourth, *Nete*, Fire, as is clear in the diagram.

Highest String ________________________________________________ Fire
Next to Highest _____________________________________________ Air
Next to Lowest ____________________________________________ Water
Lowest String ______________________________________________ Earth

Indeed, the first and lowest-pitched string corresponds to Earth, while the fourth and highest-pitched corresponds to Fire; the second to Water, and the third to Air. Just as among the elements there are two heavy and two light, and one is heavier or lighter than the other, so in the said tetrachord, there are two low sounds and two high sounds, one being lower or higher than the other. Again, just as the four elements—changed one into another in different ways—acquire various thicknesses, temperaments, and qualities from which different species of things emerge; so in the said tetrachord, the sounds, when changed and compared to one another in different ways, produce various differences in sound. Furthermore, just as three intervals are recognized in the four elements, from which the changes and qualities of physical forms are born, so too in a tetrachord of four tones, various forms of consonances arise. This is evident in the four seasons of the year, in which this elemental tetrachord—struck by the plectrum <note>A tool used to pluck a stringed instrument</note> of Apollo—provides that harmony and symphony which we experience with wonder every year in the generation of things and the production of other effects. For although this tetrachord is discordant in itself and devoid of harmony, as soon as those radiant fingers of Apollo strike and stir it, it immediately exhibits a wonderful harmony, joining the consonant with the dissonant so that entirely disparate and contrary things nevertheless run together into one composition with a marvelous concord and friendship.

Furthermore, when Pythagoras searched a little more deeply into this harmonic secret, he finally discovered that nature had hidden it with truly wonderful skill in the five regular solids. For he found the harmony of the Earth in the harmonic cube; for the cube has six flat faces.

372 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

<margin>An amazing comparison of the cube to musical proportions.</margin>

[The cube has] 8 solid corners; 24 flat angles, and twelve lines, in which 12 to 6 create an <term>octave</term><note>original: "diapason"; the interval where the frequency of one note is double another (2:1).</note>; 8 to 12 a <term>fifth</term><note>original: "diapente"; a 3:2 ratio.</note>; 6 to 8 a <term>fourth</term><note>original: "diatessaron"; a 4:3 ratio.</note>; 24 to 6 a <term>double octave</term><note>original: "disdiapason"; a 4:1 ratio.</note>; 24 to 8 an <term>octave plus a fifth</term><note>original: "diapason cum diapente"; a 3:1 ratio, also called a twelfth.</note>; indeed, the entire series of harmonies is found in this one body. Nor should this seem strange to anyone. For in the Earth, as if in a foundation and base, the harmonic seeds of all things to be generated lie hidden as the <term>lowest note</term><note>original: "proslambanomena"; in the Ancient Greek musical system, this was the lowest note of the scale, the foundation of the system.</note>, as will be said later. And just as on a <term>polychord</term><note>A multi-stringed instrument used for demonstrating musical ratios.</note> all strings acquire a certain relationship when tuned to the first, so do the remaining elements relate to the Earth.

Furthermore, he <note>Referring to Plato or the ancient philosophers who associated geometric shapes with elements.</note> finds Fire in the Pyramid <note>A tetrahedron.</note>; for it consists of 4 sides and 4 solid corners, but 12 flat angles, from which a certain simpler nature arises, which we note in fire. For 4 to 4 constitutes a <term>unison</term>, and 4 to 12 an <term>octave plus a fifth</term>, through which the sharpness or subtlety of this harmony is understood. In the <term>octahedron</term><note>An eight-sided solid.</note> he finds the harmony of the Air; it consists of 8 solid corners, as many sides, and 24 flat angles. Finally, in the <term>icosahedron</term><note>A twenty-sided solid.</note> of 20 sides, 12 solid corners, and 36 planes, he finds the nature of Water, as will be discussed in what follows. And the harmonic proportions of these bodies are gathered together in this way: the Octahedron compared to the Pyramid is a double proportion <note>2:1 ratio</note> in sides; a <term>one-and-a-half</term><note>original: "sesquialtera"; a 3:2 ratio.</note> proportion in solid corners, and double in planes, from which emerge the double and one-and-a-half harmonies—that is, the octave and the fifth. The proportion of the Pyramid to the Cube in sides is one-and-a-half, and double in corners, again constituting an octave and a fifth. The Cube compared to the Icosahedron has a triple proportion in sides, a <term>one-and-one-third</term><note>original: "sesquitertiam"; a 4:3 ratio.</note> proportion in its bases, and a one-and-a-half proportion in its corners, from which emerge the octave, fifth, and fourth in the bases, and the fifth in the corners. You see, therefore, that the closer they approach the Earth, the greater the harmony that is born in those appropriate bodies. Thus you see the Cube and the Icosahedron, which represent Earth and Water, female and male, swelling with harmonic seeds—the "couch of the Nymphs," most fit for the generation of things. Hence the inscription of the Icosahedron within the Cube represents the most fruitful marriage of water and earth for the generation of all things.

We have shown the harmony of the elements according to a certain analogy of the proportions shining forth within them. Now there remains to be declared that "sensible" <note>Meaning "perceptible to the senses."</note> symphony of the elements, by which they truly and really harmonize with one another. For it is certain that from the various agitations of the elements, a perceptible harmony is born, depending on the condition of the bodies colliding. For what else does the Earth represent to us but a kind of organ equipped with hidden channels, like pipes? Through these narrow passages, that "fiery spirit" <note>Refers to the geothermal gases or heat Kircher believed moved through the earth.</note> diffused throughout the entire body of the earth rushes with force. It produces the same effect as wind in our artificial organs—namely, deep sounds mixed with high ones, according to the looseness or narrowness of the passages. I first became aware of this kind of music during those wonderful earthquakes of Calabria in 1638. From the violence of the trapped spirits shaking the sides of the mountains and escaping wherever a "gate" was opened, we heard at times the sound of a trumpet, sometimes the murmur of Resonating waters, sometimes like heavy thunder, and then again like the cries of wailing men and the whistling of winds. The <term>Catadupae</term><note>Great waterfalls, often used to refer to the cataracts of the Nile, but here meaning internal subterranean falls.</note> of waters in the bowels of the mountains are also the cause of that prodigious harmony which, as was said above, history records being perceived at certain openings in the mountains. We shall assign the reasons for these things at length in our *Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's famous 1664 work *Mundus Subterraneus*.</note>.

Furthermore, the perpetual agitations of the earth and water establish another kind of harmony. As they perpetually strike the shores, they create a harmony based on the size of the caverns and channels, which histories say various sea coasts exhibit. Thus the shores of the Aegean Sea, according to Pausanias, give off the sound of a <term>Cithara</term><note>An ancient Greek stringed instrument similar to a lyre.</note>. The banks of certain islands produce the symphony of organs and all kinds of pipes. The shores of the Baltic Sea <note>original: "Botnici maris"; the Gulf of Bothnia.</note> give back the wailing of men, according to Olaus <note>Olaus Magnus, the 16th-century Swedish cartographer and historian.</note>. For as we have shown elsewhere, the hollows of coastal caves and grottoes establish all kinds of harmonies. If their capacity is as 1 to 2, they will necessarily return an octave when struck by the waves and floods as if by a <term>plectrum</term><note>A pick used to pluck strings.</note>. If as 2 to 3, a fifth; if as 3 to 4, a fourth; if as 8 to 9, a whole tone; and so on for the rest. Thus it is no wonder that the murmur and noise of things containing hidden seeds of harmony within themselves is pleasing.

->Book 10. The Nature of the Ten-Stringed Lyre: 373<-
<note>The "Decachordon" or ten-stringed lyre is a mathematical and mystical symbol of universal harmony.</note>

Furthermore, the Air—interacting now with the earth, now with the water—gives birth to various distinctions of harmonious sounds. When it is mixed through violent agitation with mountains, rocks, caves, narrow passages, trees, and the waves of the waters, it produces a certain wondrous concert, as if composed of consonant and dissonant, or deep and high-pitched voices. 

This is first evident in the narrow passages of mountains of varying sizes, where the wind, striking them in different ways, displays a marvelous variety of sounds. For this reason, on Mount Etna, near certain cavernous cliffs, when the south-east wind <note>original: "Euronotho," a wind from the south-east</note> blows, a perpetual and harmonious whispering is perceived, just as if one were listening to strings stretched and played at intervals of the third, fifth, and octave. 

I remember observing this same phenomenon in the sounds of trees of different sizes moved by the wind. For if one tree is double the size of another—as is most clearly seen with Cypresses and Poplars—their whispers will express an <term>octave</term> <note>original: "diapason," the interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency</note>. If the ratio of one tree to the other is one-and-a-half <note>original: "sesquialtera," a 3:2 ratio</note>, they express a <term>fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente"</note>; and so on for the rest...

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature. 375

Furthermore, Pythagoras, Plato, Cicero, Pliny, Macrobius, Proclus, Chalcidius, and countless others—even the Holy Fathers <note>The "Holy Fathers" refers to early Christian theologians and saints who integrated Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>—were so astonished by this wondrous arrangement of things that they believed the heavens emit a true and most sweet sound.

Cicero, in *The Dream of Scipio*, perceiving this most sweet song of the heavens with his ear and meditating upon it in his mind, spoke thus: *What is this sound, so great and so sweet, that fills my ears? It is that which is produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves, joined at unequal intervals, yet nonetheless divided according to a fixed proportion; by tempering high notes with low, it produces various harmonies equally. And further below: For this reason, that highest, star-bearing circuit of heaven, whose revolution is swifter, is stirred and moved with a sharp and high-pitched sound.* <note>original: "Quis est qui complet aures meas, tantus & tam dulcis sonus? ... Quam ob causam summus ille cœli stellifer cursus... acuto excitatur, & mouetur sono."</note> Thus says Cicero: upon which Macrobius, in Book 2 of his commentary on *The Dream of Scipio*, <margin>Words of Macrobius.</margin> Chapter 1, comments in this way, bringing Pythagoras and Plato into the same opinion.

Therefore he says: *It is necessary that sound is born from the very revolution of the spheres: because the air, struck by the intervention of the blow itself, emits the force of a crashing sound from within itself, as nature itself compels a violent collision of two bodies to end in sound. And immediately after: From these things it is gathered by irreproachable reason that musical sounds proceed from the revolution of the celestial spheres: because it is necessary that sound is made from motion, and the Reason that dwells in divine things is the cause of the sound's modulation.* <note>The "Reason" (Ratio) here refers to the mathematical proportions that govern the universe.</note> Pythagoras, the first of all the men of the Greek nation, <margin>Pythagoras</margin> conceived and understood this in his mind: that something composed of the spheres sounds out because of the necessity of Reason, which does not depart from celestial things. These are his words, which he proves and explains from the same philosophers in the following chapter. And in Chapter 3, he begins thus: Hence Plato, in his *Republic*, when <margin>Plato</margin> he was treating the volatility of the celestial spheres, says that individual Sirens sit upon individual orbits. He means that by the motion of the spheres, a song is offered to the divine powers: for a "Siren" <margin>A single singing Siren dwells in each of the Heavens</margin> singing to GOD, in the Greek understanding, is what it signifies. <note>In this context, "Siren" does not mean the dangerous sea-creatures of Homer, but rather divine messengers or celestial voices.</note> And presently: *Therefore, even the Theologians, confirming that the heaven sings, employed musical sounds in their sacrifices, etc.* These things are there, along with others which I bypass for the sake of brevity.

And that a single Siren dwells in each of the heavens was reported by Giorgio Veneto in Volume 5, Problem Section 5, number 321, drawing from Plato’s *Republic*, Proclus in his commentary on the *Cratylus* and the *Republic*, and Chalcidius in his commentary on the *Timaeus*. Toward this looks the half-line of verse by Angelo Poliziano:
->*To each, their own harmless Siren.*<-

Pliny, in Book 2, Chapter 3, says the same: *Is it indeed with a sweet and incredibly pleasant harmony that the world glides along in silence, day and night, for us who act within it?* <margin>Pliny on the same subject.</margin> Caelius Rhodiginus in Book 5, Chapter 25, speaks thus: *How can it be that the rotated whirling of such great orbits is carried along in a quiet and still circuit, even if the wonderful pleasantness of the sounds passes by us, who are less able to hear it?* Plato asserted this; all who followed him approved it; nor did it displease Boethius.

Philo the Jew, most eloquent of men, <margin>Philo the Jew on the same, most elegantly.</margin> describes this music in Book 1 of *On Dreams* with words most worthy of note: *The heaven, by the perpetual harmony of its motions, renders a most sweet melody: which, if it could reach our ears, would stir in us uncontrollable loves and an insane desire; stimulated by which, we would forget the things necessary for our sustenance, not feeding on food or drink passed through the throat, but—just like candidates for immortality—on the divine songs of perfected music. Such songs, it is said, Moses heard when he was caught up out of his body, and for forty days and as many nights he tasted neither bread nor water. And that which follows is divine: Therefore the heaven, the archetype of musical instruments, <margin>Heaven is the instrument by which GOD is sung to</margin> seems to me to have been fashioned for no other reason than that hymns might be skillfully and musically sung to the Parent of all things.* These are the words of Philo. St. Ambrose harmonizes with this in his preface to the Psalms, saying: *The Angels praise the Lord, the Powers of the heavens sing psalms to him. A more expressive discourse says that the very axis of heaven turns with a certain sweetness of perpetual harmony, so that its sound might be heard in the furthest parts of the earth, where there are certain secrets of nature; nor does this seem foreign to the custom of nature.* <margin>Boethius also.</margin> These are the words of Ambrose. Anicius Severinus Boethius, in Book 1, Chapter 2 of *On Music*, says thus: *How can it be that so swift a machine of heaven is moved in a quiet and silent course, even if that sound does not reach our ears?* And other things in the same place. St. Isidore in Book 3 <margin>Fr. St. Isidore.</margin> of the *Etymologies*, Chapter 16, says: *The world itself is said to be arranged with a certain harmony of sounds, and heaven itself revolves under the modulation of harmony.* But also a certain Licentius, whom Sixtus <margin>Licentius, a Christian poet.</margin> records in Book 5 of the *Library*, annotation 105, speaking of GOD, sang this very thing elegantly, saying:
->*He fitted numbers to the heavens: and commanded them*<-
->*To practice sounding modes, and to lead equal dances.*<-

<margin>The marvelous proportion of the Celestial Bodies.</margin>

...parts of the whole sine <note>In trigonometry, the "whole sine" refers to the radius of the circle used for calculations, here divided into 10,000 units.</note> divided into 10,000 parts, 183 are assigned. This number doubled gives 366, which is the number of days in the Sun's annual revolution; you see, therefore, that the solar diameter of 100 parts (where the orbital radius is 10,000) is the square root of its average distance from the Earth; while the Earth, consisting of 10 parts of that same radius, is the cube root. Furthermore, the diameter of the Moon is considered to contain as many minutes of its own orbit as the Sun does of its own. Yet another marvel shines forth here: namely, that the average distance of the Moon from the Earth contains as many Earth diameters as the number of days the Moon takes to complete its monthly period around the Earth—namely, about 29 days—and the Earth is distant from the Moon by that same number of Earth diameters. Finally, the 365 days of the Sun’s annual motion, when measured in parts of its orbital radius divided into 10,000, reveals the Sun's <term>eccentricity</term> <note>the distance by which the center of a celestial body's orbit deviates from a perfect center relative to the Earth</note> to be that very same number of parts of the same radius. You see here a beautiful harmony.

# Book 10. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature. 381

And all these things follow necessarily, if—as I have said—they rest upon a faithful foundation of observations. Truly, some are not content with these, but rise even higher in their assumed proportions, trusting that by this means they can uncover the distance not only of the Sun, but also of Saturn, the fixed stars, and even the Empyrean <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest part of heaven in pre-modern cosmology, believed to be composed of pure fire or light.</note>. For when a proportion is founded and propagated in the nature of things, it is necessary that the symmetry of the rest be assigned. If you take 10,000 as the radius of the Sun's orbit and multiply it by 10, the result will be the semi-diameter of the furthest Saturnian sphere from the Earth, which is 100,000 parts. For just as the diameter of the Earth is contained a thousand times in the radius of the solar orbit, so the diameter of the Sun is contained a thousand times in the radius of Saturn's orbit. Thus, just as the Sun is the square root in its diameters to the distance from the Earth, so too it is the square root to the distance of Saturn in terrestrial diameters. <margin>A wonderful arrangement of celestial proportions.</margin> By a not dissimilar reasoning, they say the diameter of Saturn is the square root (measured in solar diameters) to the semi-diameter of the firmament; so that the semi-diameter of the firmament consists of 1,000,000 solar diameters, or 10,000,000 diameters of the Earth. Proceeding at the same pace, the entire diameter of the firmament in the diameters of Saturn's sphere is the square root of the semi-diameter of the Empyrean heaven, so that the distance of 10,000,000,000 diameters of the region and the wandering system of Planets <note>original: "systematis vagi Planetarum," referring to the solar system as then understood.</note> is utterly inconceivable; so much so that if anyone were to measure out a space in the Empyrean every single day equal to the circumference of the entire Earth, he would not actually traverse the circumference of such an Empyrean heaven in ten thousand million years.

Here, then, you have the proportion of the worldly bodies according to the conjecture of Rheita <note>Anton Maria Schyrleus of Rheita (1604–1660) was a Capuchin friar and astronomer who proposed a system of cosmic proportions based on his telescopic observations.</note>. If these should prove to agree with nature, I would certainly say that God, the Most Wise Architect, ordered the entire world and the disposition of the bodies within it according to the degrees of algebraic powers. But since we treat these matters professionally in our *Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Arte Lucis & Umbræ," referring to Kircher's own book, *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* (1646).</note>, we refer the reader there.

## §. II.
->What the music of the celestial bodies is, and in what it consists.<-

That there is a certain harmonic concord of the celestial bodies—one most worthy of that eternal and infinitely sweet <term>Harmostes</term> <note>From the Greek word for "joiner" or "tuner," referring here to God as the Harmonizer of the universe.</note>—is a truth received by the unanimous consent of the Sacred Scriptures, theologians, and all philosophers. Yet it is scarcely explicable by numbers, since the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> that unspeakable concord of the celestial bodies; for those things are reserved by that eternal and supramundane <term>Organist</term> <note>original: "Organædo," meaning one who plays the organ or an instrument.</note> for His elect alone, in the sweetness of eternal life. However, as much as the weakness of our human talent and the dim intuition of our minds can grasp, I would say that this harmony of the heavens consists not in the periodic numbers of their motions, nor in that sensible "clashing" of celestial bodies, but in nothing other than their admirable disposition and a certain ineffable proportion breathing together into a union. By this union, these worldly bodies correspond to one another in such a way that if one were removed or changed, the harmony of the whole would deservedly perish. Thus the Sun, exercising its command over the entire economy of the Planets subject to it like a <term>Choragus</term> <note>The leader or conductor of a Greek chorus.</note>, awakens all into harmony with the <term>plectrums</term> <note>A small tool used to pluck the strings of an instrument; here, a metaphor for the Sun's rays.</note> of its rays. This harmony, as we have said, consists partly in a certain admirable disposition and a most proportionate distance <margin>In what the true harmony of the world consists.</margin> from one worldly body to another, and partly in the most exact analogy of the quantity or magnitude appropriated to each for obtaining its end. Thus the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth hold such a distance from one another, and such a necessity of magnitude, that without it, it would be necessary for the world to perish. For by these intervals, the worldly things are able perfectly to help and preserve one another by their mutual influences.

To understand this, it must be noted that with fiery bodies (of which kind we say the Sun is, being indeed the fire of all nature), they are so arranged that they produce different temperaments in bodies removed at different distances. This is taught to us not only by nature but clearly by the empirical art. First, the rays of the Sun reflected upon the Earth in different ways teach us this clearly: they produce one effect under the Frigid Zone, another under the Temperate, and yet another under the Torrid—

Therefore, the distance of the Earth from the Sun, with such and such a magnitude of its body, produces this specific disposition of the earth and no other, this specific temperament and no other, and this harmonic variety and no other. Again, this distance, combined with the specific size of the earth, produces an extremely equal portion of light and shadow in all places, as we have shown in many ways in the cited *Anacamptic Art*; for if the distance were greater or smaller, the entire harmony would be reduced to a most confused dissonance. Just as musical strings of a certain length are consonant, but as soon as they deviate from the length proper to them, they produce something—I know not what—composed of consonance and dissonance instead of melody. So too if the Earth, while maintaining the same size, were closer to the Sun or more remote from it than it truly is; being closer, it would be struck by more powerful solar rays, or being more remote, by weaker rays. Besides causing the greatest inequality of light and shadow, this would produce a temperament not only harmful to human life, but utterly unsuitable for it. Here Kircher refers to alchemy or experimental chemistry, which relies on controlled fire.</note>. What previously lay confused in a single, seemingly homogeneous mass, is now, by the help of fire, separated into various natures, as it were, and exhibits various bodies of different quality through varying fermentation, coagulation, fixation, dissolution, composition, softening, and hardening. Therefore, just as the Sun is established in perfect harmony with the Earth, so too the Moon, Venus, and Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn <note>Kircher uses the astrological symbols: ☽ ♀ ☿ ♂ ♃ ♄</note> have their own harmonic ratios of intervals and magnitudes required by nature, both in relation to each other and to the earth and sun. And indeed the Moon received such a distance from the Sun and Earth, with a due proportion of magnitude, that if by divine power its distance from either the Sun or the Earth, or its magnitude, were changed, the whole harmony would necessarily be thrown into confusion, and the Earth would inevitably perish. For at its specific distance it can aptly nourish the earth with its influence, and at no other; at this specific distance, and no other, it can break the fervor of the Sun; and conversely, the Sun so tempers the moisture and coldness of the Moon with the mixture of its own rays that it produces the effect intended by nature to be bestowed upon the earth. For if the Moon were closer to the Earth, it would produce entirely discordant and incongruous effects on the earth by its excessive moisture; on the other hand, if it were closer to the Sun, the Sun acting more effectively upon the Moon would consume its moisture and destroy everything in the terrestrial world with its excessive heat. This was done by the hidden counsel of nature so that the lower world might be preserved in its perfection by this exact variety, as if by a certain "consonant-dissonant" mixture.

Yet because the most burning Sun, together with the most moist Moon, could not establish a perfect harmony of humors in the terrestrial globe (as if under a perpetual octave <note>original: *diapason*</note>) without the intervention of other bodies, Divine Providence established two other worldly bodies between the Moon and the Sun: namely Venus and Mercury. These bodies excel with diverse powers, in which the vehemence of the solar rays is refined—as if blunted—and from there, with increased strength necessary for the Lunar moisture, they might bless the earth with greater variety. For the fecundating power of the body of Venus <note>represented by the symbol ♀</note>, communicated to the influence of the Moon, similarly fertilizes its moisture. Mercury <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note>, however, acting as the separator of the consonant from the dissonant, tempers that which is harmful and excessive in both the Sun and Venus by drawing it into itself. Thus, it finally pours forth another kind of harmony necessary for the lower world. All these things, in the course of time, produce various combinations of effects according to their various aspects and the eccentric positions of the said stars. 

<margin>Why Nature established the dissonant bodies of Saturn and Mars in the world.</margin> Furthermore, because no instrument is so perfectly constructed that it does not, in the course of time, incur dissonance—either from the strings being too loose or stretched beyond measure—so it is impossible that the lower world should not occasionally fall into an imbalance <note>original Greek: *dyskrasian*, meaning a disharmony of the bodily humors</note>, due to both the distance or proximity of the said bodies to the earth and their various configurations. This state is not unlike a body filled with various humors over time and seized by a fever, which is finally restored to health through the subtraction of moisture and subsequent evacuation.

And for this purpose, GOD, through Nature—His own art—placed two entirely dissonant bodies in the heavens: Mars <note>♂</note> and Saturn <note>♄</note>. From their pestiferous evaporation, all the evils of the sublunary world take their origin. Lest these lead to an open disaster <note>original Greek: *kakodorian*, meaning an unfortunate distribution or "bad gift"</note> in the management of the entire lower world, He placed the benign star Jupiter <note>♃</note> between them. By Jupiter’s health-giving influence, the deadly and utterly ruinous force that both planets exhale is restrained and held back. And lest the earth, attacked by the virulence of Mars, be exposed to manifest ruin, nature willed it to be placed in the largest eccentric orbit of all, so that it might be coerced from its savagery for a time—restrained from below by the Sun and Venus, and from above by Jupiter. Yet, Nature should not be accused of being a "Wicked Stepmother" for creating such ruinous bodies; rather, she should be judged to have disposed them thus by a supreme and hidden plan, as one without which the world could not be preserved. 

For these planets seem to perform the same function in the "Greater World" <note>the Macrocosm or universe</note> burdened by a great mass of vicious humors, as is performed in the "Lesser World" <note>the Microcosm or human body</note> during dangerous fevers and an abundance of the worst humors by Spanish Fly <note>term: *Cantarides*; a toxic beetle used in historical medicine to create blisters and "draw out" sickness</note> and caustic medicines. By the power of these things, the flow of morbid matter is attracted and dissipated from the center to the circumference, freeing the person in danger. Thus, there is no evil in the nature of things that does not eventually yield to the good and the conservation of the whole universe. 

For what else are Mars and Saturn but certain dissonances? Yet, when tied and suspended by the perfect consonance of Jupiter, they provide not only a sweetness to the Music, but also its greatest ornament. What else is Mercury but a certain dissonance between the Moon and Venus? It acts like two tied consonances in a suspension, so that, having gained no liberty and being bound to nothing, it does not defile the earth itself with the unbridled influence of the Sun, Venus, and Moon.

In this harmony, the dissonant elements are joined with the consonant ones with such skill that they provide the world with a most pleasant harmony. So that the curious reader might have an example of this celestial four-part harmony, I have seen fit to show the idea of our speculation here in musical notes.

In this way, they bind him with harmonic measures so that they render him entirely consonant, as can be seen in the musical notes for the *Hypatodon*. The Earth, however, lying beneath all things, receives a mixture of consonance and dissonance so perfect that it constitutes the most flawless music with the planets—a music such as we might imagine here in this underlying world.

Yet, because Nature is perpetually fond of variety, she does not always offer the same harmony to the lower world over the course of time. Instead, through the individual planets—both by their rotation around their own centers and by their movement closer to or further from one another in their <term>eccentric orbits</term>, as well as by their various positions and relationships under the signs of the Zodiac—she continually establishes new and varied genres of harmony. These always remain, however, within certain limits determined and intended by Nature. Thus, in the eccentric orbits, which are like the boundaries of planetary motions, they change their ascending or descending tones or <term>modes</term> step by step, proceeding now from the <term>Dorian</term> to the <term>Phrygian</term>, and from there to the <term>Lydian</term>, soon into the <term>Aeolian</term> <note>These are the ancient Greek musical modes, each thought to have a different emotional or spiritual character.</note>, and so on through the rest, until at last they return to the tone assumed at the beginning, the full rotation of tones having been completed. 

Furthermore, since the parts of the planetary globes or bodies are heterogeneous, and have been assigned different natures, qualities, properties, and powers due to their diverse positions and relationship to the other surrounding planets, Nature willed them to turn around their own centers. She did this so that they might always turn different faces toward the Earth, performing the same role in celestial music that the joining of dissonances with consonances performs in man-made music. You see, therefore, that the planets are arranged in such an order that if even one were to recede from its determined limit (like a harmonic interval), the entire harmony would deservedly be destroyed.

### Corollary.

From this it is clear that the Earth represents a kind of <term>bass</term> <note>original: "basin"</note> upon which the remaining harmony of the universe is built; for if this were removed, the harmony remaining in the other voices would be imperfect and subject to many dissonances. But enough has been said, if I am not mistaken, regarding the universal <term>symphonism</term> of the planets; let us now return to their specific symphonies.

## §. III.
## Concerning the Specific Symphonism of the Planets.

Lest the harmony of many voices perpetually echoing should become an offense to the ears with its continuous sounds, the <term>Musurgists</term> <note>Composers or "shapers of music."</note> took care to distribute the harmony of many voices into several choirs. Thus, with alternating choirs equipped with various classes of instruments, a greater variety and a delight or pleasure for the listeners might arise. In a not dissimilar fashion, Nature, the <term>Harmost</term> <note>A "Harmost" is an arranger or regulator of harmony; Kircher views God/Nature as the ultimate conductor.</note>, divided those celestial singers into various choirs. Though these differ in the nature of their sounds, they all conspire in a consonant-dissonant union, adorning the world with variety and commending the ineffable wisdom of that supramundane Arranger. 

I shall begin with Saturn, the highest choir of the planetary concert. In these recent times, the truly <term>Lyncean</term> <note>A reference to the *Accademia dei Lincei* (the Academy of the Lynx-Eyed), the scientific society of which Galileo was a member; it implies sharp, telescopic sight.</note> school of astronomers has discovered a wonderful fact about its constitution. It clearly appears that God, the Best and Greatest, has pulled back a new "stop" on the celestial organ to draw us into the admiration and love of His wisdom. Saturn was first observed as if it were triple-bodied <note>Early telescopes were not strong enough to resolve Saturn's rings; Galileo famously described them as two smaller bodies or "ears" flanking the planet.</note>; it was later discovered that two bodies, <margin>Saturn's two companions.</margin> like vocal attendants, perpetually surround it and crowd it closely. Since the Sun, the conductor <note>original: "choragus"</note>, could not reach Saturn with the <term>plectrum</term> of its light due to the immense distance, God most wisely provided it with two companions to act as "vicars of the Sun" and stay with it perpetually, fostering it by a mutual communication of forces. By this admirable conspiracy, they create that harmony which the Sun...

### Corollary.

From the stated harmonic constitution, it necessarily follows that Saturn, because of its excessive distance, cannot be sufficiently illuminated by the Sun, and therefore light was provided for it by its two companions. For since this planet, according to the calculation of certain modern authors, is 20,000,000 hourly leagues <note>The "leuca" or league was a variable unit of distance; here it emphasizes the vast, almost inconceivable scale of the outer solar system.</note> distant from the Sun, it is certain that an eye positioned on Saturn would perceive the solar diameter as being only 3 minutes and 11 seconds wide. From there, the Sun would appear little larger than Venus, Jupiter, or a star of the first magnitude; consequently, Saturn requires light other than the Sun's. It follows, moreover, that we, if positioned on Saturn, would have a day lasting 29 of our days. We would never see the remaining inferior planets recede more than 40 degrees from the Sun: Jupiter at 40 degrees, Mars at 12, Venus at 4, and Mercury at 2. The Moon and the Earth would be scarcely perceptible. Therefore, you would say that all the described planets are "Companions of the Sun," and you would recognize the Sun's 29-year period through the Zodiac, while you would believe Saturn itself to be submerged in the center of the universe. I could demonstrate all these things in this place, but since we have reserved that for a more extensive treatment in the second edition of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>Referring to Kircher's "Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae," a massive work on optics and astronomy.</note> following the observations of more recent thinkers, we refer the reader there. Meanwhile, let it suffice that we have demonstrated the admirable harmony of the Saturnian Chorus in this place.

### §. IV.
### Concerning the Jovian Choir.

<margin>Description of the globe of Jupiter with its four companions.</margin>

It has become known through frequent observation in these recent times that the Architect of celestial harmony has adorned this Jovian Choir with a truly unique artistry above all others. While Jupiter, mighty in size and glory, has presented himself to be seen by this lower world with an unheard-of and unseen retinue of four companions, he does so in that concert of all things which we shall describe. This globe is much larger than the Earth, yet so distant from the Sun that—just as with Saturn—the Sun seems far from sufficient to illuminate it. Lest such an immense mass, imbued with most excellent powers, should be devoid of light and, wasting away in perpetual gloom, introduce a dissonance to the rest of the worldly bodies, it happened by a wonderful counsel of nature that four <term>Choragi</term><note>Chorus-leaders or conductors of a dance.</note> perpetually strike this immense mass with the <term>plectrums</term><note>A small tool used to pluck a stringed instrument; here used metaphorically for rays of light.</note> of their rays, stirring it into a most beautiful harmony by their harmonic movements. For it has been observed that the periodic motion of the first <term>phonascus</term><note>original: "phonasci"; a lead singer or choir master who sets the pitch.</note> closest to Jupiter is completed in a space of nearly 42 hours; the period of the second in 3 days and 13 hours; the third in 7 days and 4 hours; and finally the period of the last or fourth in the space of 16 days and nearly as many hours. And if we believe the calculations of Reita, <note>Anton Maria Schyrleus of Rheita (1604–1660), a Capuchin astronomer and optician who claimed to have discovered more moons than Galileo.</note> the first is distant from Jupiter by 20, the second by 27, the third by 41, and the fourth by 69 Earth-semidiameters <note>radii</note>. Truly, see the calculation performed by Reita regarding the four Jovian Companions in the following table.

Certainly, whatever can be desired in music is hidden beneath these numbers, since the distances of each body correspond exactly and harmonically to its size. And as far as could be gathered from the frequent observations of the <term>Lynceans</term><note>Members of the Academy of the Lincei, the first modern scientific society, of which Galileo was a member.</note> and the wonderful progression of proportions, we find the first Chorus-leader to be nearly equal in mass to our Moon, the second to Mercury, the third to Venus, and finally the last to be nearly equal in its mass to the entire Earth. From this it follows again that, to us standing upon Jupiter, these chorus-leaders would appear much larger than the Sun and Moon appear to us from Earth. Indeed, the second and fourth seem to mimic the light of the Moon, while the first and third possess the splendor of the Sun. We have here, curious reader—

Reader, having seen the description, position, and size of the Jovian Leaders <term>Choragorum; the term refers to the leaders of a choir, here used metaphorically for the moons of Jupiter</term>; let us now see what harmony they effect in the Jovian Choir. In the preceding figure, the first is marked with the letter A, the second B, the third C, the fourth D, and Jupiter, indeed set as if in the center, with the letter V.

Since, therefore, that immense and incomprehensible Harmonizer <note>original: "Harmosta"</note> of wisdom, GOD, had decreed to build the world with an innumerable variety of things; he established in this mundane temple a second Choir, remarkable for the manifold power of its Leaders, namely the celestial globe which we call Jupiter. For this Jovian sphere is much larger than our sphere of the Earth, and imbued with the most excellent virtues with which it influences this lower world. Since it required a location very far from the Earth and the Sun, and could not conveniently draw light from the Sun, GOD assigned to it two "vicar-suns" (the first and third) and as many "vicar-moons" (the second and fourth); and by that ingenuity and admirable providence, he ordered them to illuminate the Jovian globe perpetually and in turns, so that what one Sun and Moon could not do, these auxiliary Suns and Moons would provide. By their harmonic motion, the Jovian sphere, struck by a continuous alternation of light and shadow, would cause a great and truly wonderful diversity of natures in said body. 

For it is necessary that days and nights occur that are very unequal, not so much in duration of time as in the intensity of light. <margin>Jupiter is illuminated by its companions.</margin> For who doubts that two, three, or four Leaders rising at once for Jupiter bring more daylight to it than one alone? Certainly, beyond what can be said, the day there is of the most intense light; but when the said four Leaders are conjoined, they cause night in the opposite parts of the Jovian body, though short because of the speed of their motion. 

Lest that harmonic constitution of the Jovian body be disturbed by too much light, He did not want Jupiter to rest, but to revolve perpetually around its own center, so that one such revolution would be as many days as its periodic revolution in its eccentric orbit—namely 12 years—and to us, if we were stationed on Jupiter, one natural day would be not 24, but nearly 268 hours. <note>The author is calculating Jovian time based on 17th-century astronomical theories which differ from modern measurements.</note> Furthermore, it was arranged so that in a most pleasant and perpetual reciprocation, as the light of the first Leader quickly withdrew, the lunar light of the second Leader would succeed it; then the solar light of the third Leader would follow, and finally, as this sets, the lunar light of the fourth would rise for Jupiter. Wherefore, to blunt the intensity of the light, most frequent eclipses necessarily follow the motion of the Jovian body, so much so that I consider those "Jovian Zones" <note>The atmospheric "belts" or stripes of Jupiter visible through a telescope.</note> to be nothing other than the shadows of the lunar bodies projected onto the Jovian disk. <margin>What is the Jovian Zone?</margin> But regarding all these things, see the thorough and detailed treatment in the 2nd edition of *The Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Artis Lucis & Umbræ"</note> in the section on Cosmometry. 

For when all these things are compared together, the reader will find a most perfect harmony tempered from dissonances and consonances with such wonderful art that nothing more harmonious could be imagined. Thus, it is necessary by this harmonic constitution that the Jovian body be rendered most beautiful and imbued with the most excellent qualities, such as we experience with admiration in its influence upon this lower world.

### Corollary I.
It also follows for the harmony of the world that Jupiter ought to have been neither larger nor smaller, nor ought it to have approached or receded closer to or further from the Sun than its eccentric orbit prescribed, without manifest detriment to the harmony of the world.

### Corollary II.
It also follows that humans could by no means live there on account of the excessive intensity of light, and because of the temperament of the place which is entirely unsuitable to human nature. <margin>Whether the Jovian globe is inhabited.</margin> As for those who wish to claim that creatures of a different nature were created there: since nothing is established for us concerning them, nor can it be established—indeed, it seems dangerous to the Faith—who does not see that this is nothing but a reckless invention, devised without any foundation by those who seek after novelties? 

But having seen the Jovian harmony, let us now proceed to other choirs.

->§.	V.<-
->*On the Solar and Martian Choir.*<-

<margin>The nature of the Martian sphere.</margin>
The Solar Choir, also called the Apollonian choir <note>Apollo was the Greek god of the Sun, often associated with music and the lyre</note>, includes beneath it Venus, Mercury, the Moon, and the Earth; it is, in a sense, parallel to the Jovian <note>related to the planet Jupiter</note> choir. Since enough was said regarding its harmony at the beginning of this work, we do not wish to repeat those things here. Between this Solar and Jovian choir, nature has ordained another arrangement in the harmony of the world: the Martian sphere. Since this planet was discordant with the others, yet necessary for the preservation of the world's harmony, it was placed in the middle, between the consonant Solar and Jovian choirs, so that it might be bound to them, as if by a musical syncopation <note>A musical technique where a note is held across a beat, creating a "link" between two measures; the author uses this to explain how the "discordant" Mars is tied into the cosmic system</note>, and thus breathe together into a most beautiful harmony.

Furthermore, so that this syncopation might occur with greater benefit, it was necessary to place Mars in the largest eccentric orbit <note>In early astronomy, an "eccentric" was a circular path where the center was not the Earth, used to explain the varying speeds of planets</note> of all. In this orbit, while it sometimes descends below the Sun itself and at other times attacks the most remote empire of Jupiter, it is kept to its duty by being seized now by the light of the Sun, now by Jupiter. This prevents it from becoming a law unto itself and turning everything upside down, which would disturb the harmony of the whole. And since it travels the path of its eccentric orbit alone, associated with no other conductors <note>original: *choragis*, refers to the leaders or providers of a chorus</note>, it is forced to beg all its light from either the Sun or Jupiter. 

Yet, because light of this kind was by no means sufficient to exercise its innate power, it was brought about by the hidden counsel of nature that the Martian sphere should be equipped, as it were, with subterranean fires. It became a fountain of darkness and of smoke, filled with pestilential, excessive, and deadly heat—and even the worst poisonous evaporations. The derivation of its virulent influence would not only infect but utterly destroy all other worldly bodies, had nature not placed it in such an opportune location to restrain its power. For since it sits in the middle between the celestial choirs, it is variously bound and "syncopated" by its companions—the Sun (☉), Venus (♀), and Jupiter (♃)—as has been said, so that it finally breathes together in a perfect harmony. This is that ingenious "synopsis" which Nature seems to have aimed for in the harmonic concert of the worldly bodies and the balanced blending <note>original: *εὐκρασία* (eukrasia), a Greek term for a healthy or well-tempered mixture of qualities</note> of their influences.
