**Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature. 389**
<note>The "Decachordon" or ten-stringed lute is a metaphor the author uses to describe the mathematical and musical harmony of God's creation.</note>

<margin>Various comparisons of an eye placed on different spheres in relation to other spheres.</margin>

I say further that if the height of the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the outermost shell of the universe where the fixed stars reside.</note> is as great as Copernicus and Rheita <note>Anton Maria Schyrleus of Rheita (1604–1660) was a priest and astronomer who improved telescope design.</note> have determined, it can be demonstrated through the discipline of Optics that if, for example, the "Eye of the Bull" <note>original: "oculus Tauri," referring to the star Aldebaran.</note> or the star in the Lyre <note>original: "Lyra," referring to the star Vega.</note> were carried in an orbit three or four times larger than the Sun's, they would nevertheless be observed by us here on Earth as completely immobile and maintaining the same distance from one another. Conversely, if our own eye were placed upon Vega, a star of the first magnitude, we would look upon the Sun as having the size of a fixed star, while the other lower planets would completely vanish from sight. Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars would appear around the Sun in the same way that the four Jovian companions or "leaders of the dance" <note>original: "choragi Iouiales," referring to the four largest moons of Jupiter discovered by Galileo.</note> appear to us around Jupiter; that is, they would be entirely imperceptible without an astroscope <term>telescope</term>. From this I conclude that the multitude of fixed stars is entirely incalculable, differing in size, distance, and intensity of light. Some of these equal the Sun in light, while some are like the Moon—that is, some enjoy their own light and some a borrowed light like the moons. Many of these are separated by a gap as high as the distance from the Earth to the firmament itself. In the constellation of Orion alone, Rheita believes he has counted more than two thousand stars using a helioscope <term>solar telescope</term>—more than the Ancients found in the entire firmament—although others have not found as many. Who does not know that the Milky Way <note>original: "galaxian"</note> is an incalculable multitude of stars heaped together? Therefore, their inaccessible distance is the reason why neither their motion nor their size is perceptible to us. Indeed, through Divine power, we could recede so far from the firmament that the Great Dog <note>The star Sirius.</note> and the Lyre, stars separated by the whole sky, would become so close that they would appear like the two horns of Aries; until, as we receded further and further, they would finally merge into one. Thus, there is no doubt that if our Sun were placed in the furthest recesses of the firmament,

<margin>The Sun, if placed in the furthest reaches of the firmament, would be invisible due to distance.</margin>

it is certain that nothing of it would appear at all. From this another point is drawn: those stars in the firmament which appear to us to be separated by the space of one pace must actually be distant from each other by as much space as the diameter of the solar heaven can occupy, if the opinion of Copernicus were true. Although these things may seem paradoxical and incredible, they can nevertheless be demonstrated without any trouble based on the foundations of optical science. From this I certainly gather that—assuming the distances of Copernicus, Rheita, and Kepler—no star in the firmament is illuminated by the Sun, as was made sufficiently clear in the preceding arguments regarding Saturn. But I deal with these matters more curiously in my *Art of Light and Shadow* <note>Referring to Kircher’s own 1646 work, *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*.</note>. And from these things said perhaps more at length than was proper, that admirable harmony of the world is clearly evident. If anyone judges these things to be incredible, he clearly puts a bridle on Divine power. For the works of the Most High are wonderful, as the witness of Ecclesiasticus <note>The biblical Book of Sirach.</note> says, both glorious and hidden, and His works are altogether immense; and in Chapter 43: *Many things are hidden that are greater than these, and we know but few of His works.*

But if someone should ask me why Divine Providence wished these things to remain hidden from men, and why He chose this Earth above all the bodies of the world as the place in which He wished to manifest the great wonders of His grace, I would in turn desire to know from him: why did God wish to hide the New World <note>The Americas.</note>, filled with an infinite multitude of men, until these latter times? And why has He not yet willed to reveal even more provinces of this terrestrial globe, such as the regions near the poles and the greater portion of the Southern Hemisphere? Why also did the Divine Goodness wish the mysteries of His Faith to be revealed to so few men? And from these, why has He predestined so few for life? These things are hidden in the abyss of the height of the wisdom and knowledge of God. *For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor?* <note>A quote from Romans 11:34.</note> These things are reserved for the knowledge not of this life, but of another, more blessed one.

<margin>Why God created such a great multitude of stars.</margin>

Therefore, to what end God created such an infinite multitude of worldly bodies, even if it is hidden from us, they are not for that reason deprived of their most powerful effects. It is enough for us to know that all things breathe together into one harmony. Certainly, if there is nothing in the nature of lower things so small or minute that it was not most wisely established for certain ends, how much more so those greatest and most massive worldly bodies, which have the greatest and most eminent uses, to be revealed only in the next life. Which of the physicians has yet indicated with certainty the number and multitude of the muscles, cartilages, small veins, fibers, and other most minute parts of the human body? Yet it is certain that if even one were separated from the whole body, the harmony of the entire body would be destroyed. We do not know the powers and effects of particular stars now, but then perhaps we shall know them, those things which... <note>Text cuts off mid-sentence.</note>

...[the stars], they lower themselves closer to the earth; now, as if sparing those below, they depart further away, and in both cases lift themselves into the heights. Sometimes, as if diligent labor were not required, they linger or hesitate somewhere; at other times, as if they might be inconvenienced by delay, they fly together swiftly; often, as if the place invites them, or indeed as if some worthy task had been interrupted, they turn back and return on their course. All these things have been most wisely ordained by **GOD** to produce corresponding effects in the earthly world. Hence, when Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who believed the universe was bound together by "chains" of sympathy.</note> observed that the heavens were full of a harmony and fitness of motions, he believed that the higher Divinities were the first to participate in the harmony proceeding from heaven; from these, man then receives a rightly ordered life, a consonance of character, and a fitness of actions. He believed that this gift of the heavens descends even to the brute animals, plants, and stones, as they are capable of receiving the aforementioned harmony. <margin>Higher things flow into lower things harmoniously.</margin> For the higher beings contain and perfect all worldly things through harmonic reason, and they adapt themselves to one another to temper the world. Hence the ancient Egyptians—while considering the harmony of the celestial bodies in the things of the lower world, and observing in sublunary <note>The "sublunary" world refers to the Earth and everything below the Moon, which was thought to be subject to change and decay.</note> materials a certain sympathy, agreement, and kinship of some things to others, and of manifest things to hidden powers—established a certain sacred and mystical Philosophy. This was exhibited under various symbols and ingenious coverings of things, which they also call "hieroglyphic." This science, lost until our day, we are restoring (God willing) in our work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* <note>Kircher's own massive study of Egyptian hieroglyphs, which he believed held secret, divine knowledge.</note>.

For they saw that the highest things lie hidden in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest; in heaven, earthly things exist in a celestial manner, but on earth, celestial things exist in an earthly manner. For why else do we think those plants which we call *heliotropes* <note>original: "heliotropias"</note>—that is, "sun-followers" (about which we have written extensively in our *Magnetic Art*)—turn toward the rising of the sun? Or why do the *selenotropes* or "moon-followers" turn toward the Moon? <margin>All things turn toward the Sun.</margin> Truly, driven by nothing else but that harmonic appetite lurking in all things, all things "pray" and sing "hymns" to the leaders of their own order; but some do so in an intellectual way, some in a rational way, some in a natural way, and others in a sensory way. Do you not see with what effort plants, even when violently pressed down, rise up to conform themselves to the sky? Branches of trees led obliquely through a hole, as soon as they have found freer air, eagerly lift their heads upward, as if impatient with their love for the heaven.

Therefore, any sun-follower moves toward the Sun in whatever way it can, so that if anyone were able to hear the vibration made by them in the air by the circular motion of the plant, he would surely perceive some such sound composed for its king—the sort of sound that plants or other things are capable of producing. In the earth, therefore, one may behold the Sun, Moon, and stars, but in an earthly condition; in the heaven, one may see plants, animals, and stones, but in a celestial condition according to a certain analogy.

Thus, there are stones, plants, and animals that are "Solar," others that are "Saturnine," or "Jovial" <note>Associated with Jupiter.</note>; others are "Martial" <note>Associated with Mars.</note> or "Venereal" <note>Associated with Venus.</note>; finally, others are "Mercurial" or "Lunar." Indeed, according to the more secret Kabbalists <note>original: "Caballistas"</note>, there is no herb on earth that does not have its own star in the firmament which says to it, "Grow."

And to begin with stones, who does not know that there is in them a great appetite for the supernal bodies, and for all those things which in any way correspond to them by nature? Proclus relates that the *Helites* stone <note>A legendary gemstone, sometimes identified as sunstone.</note> imitates the Sun with its golden rays and motion. Not unlike this was that gem which Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath.</note> writes was on the finger of Pope Clement VII; it had a small golden spot which, following the motion of the Sun, moved around daily, rising and setting. There are, therefore, solar stones, such as all Carbuncles and pyropes <note>Red gemstones like garnets or rubies that were thought to glow like coal.</note>; there are also Lunar stones, called *Selenites* for that reason; it is written that Pope Gregory X had one of this kind, which simulated the metamorphoses of the Moon, passing from a blue to a white color according to the variation of the lunar light. <margin>The agreement and disagreement of plants and stones in heaven.</margin> Furthermore, the Magnet belongs to Mars; the Sapphire to Jupiter; the Agate to Mercury—all these stones are imbued with parallel virtues.

The various motions of herbs, plants, and trees also sufficiently declare the agreement of vegetable nature with the heavens. Among these, some follow the daily motion of the Sun, like the heliotropes described in the *Magnetic Art*; some follow the proper motion of the Sun, like the leaves of the Willow, the White Poplar, the Elm, the Lime, and the Olive, which experience has shown turn completely over on the day of the Solstice itself; some of...

# CANON III. Chemical.

<margin>A secret in Chemistry.</margin>
Whoever wishes to proceed in chemical business cautiously and with the desired effect, it is necessary above all else that they possess the knowledge of the dissonant and the consonant. This dissonance and consonance consists in knowing which minerals are consonant with each other, which are dissonant, and by what intermediaries they may be bound and brought back into concord. For example, if someone wishes to produce a "Solar" effect <note>often referring to the creation of gold or a sun-like vitality</note>, they must first ensure that all Solar things harmonize through the octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>, then let the harmony be completed in all its parts through the major third or the fifth <note>original: "diapente"</note>. Keep far away all heterogeneous <note>dissimilar</note> things, as they are dissonant, such as herbs, juices, gums, and similar things not contained within the natural class of metals. However, dissonant things of the same natural order can be accepted into the most perfect harmony if they are syncopated by the prescribed method of intermediaries. If someone could divide the metallic tone into two parts using Mercury as the mediator, they would undoubtedly have found that which has been most studiously sought from ages past to this day <note>a reference to the Philosopher's Stone or the secret of transmutation</note>. Nevertheless, silver <note>original: "luna"</note> will be easily obtained if Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note> is syncopated with Saturn <note>original symbol: ♄; lead</note> by a Venusian bond <note>associated with copper</note>, constituting a musical sixth. The true harmonic pattern of nature must be proposed in all things so that you may achieve a harmonic effect. But since we have reserved this harmonic application in the chemical business for our *Subterranean World* <note>referring to Kircher’s major work on geology and alchemy, "Mundus Subterraneus"</note>, we refer the reader there, where they will find everything they could desire regarding this matter, proven by innumerable experiments. For neither time nor the sheer bulk of this work allowed us to involve everything here.

# 398 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

<margin>What has some similarity with any part of a human tends to be its medicine.</margin> ...will undoubtedly find. For just as a string moves another string that is tuned to the same tension, so any thing—whether drawn from the mineral, vegetable, or sentient order of nature—which reflects a specific limb, part, or humor through a "character of similarity" (that is, in its form, figure, color, or similar bodily habit), is believed to excite that same limb, part, or humor, either to attract good or to repel evil. Hence, fleshy things increase and nourish flesh, bony things nourish bones, blood-like things nourish blood, bilious things nourish bile, and nerve-like things nourish nerves. In this way, things that express diseases through similarity contribute to driving those same diseases away.

In this manner, the *Galgalus* <note>original: "Galgalus"; likely a reference to the Golden Oriole or a similar yellow bird traditionally used to treat jaundice</note> treats those with Jaundice; the Elk treats those with Epilepsy; for a defect of the stomach, a wolf’s stomach is used; for the diseases of serpents, serpents themselves are used; and the liver of a rabid dog is used for hydrophobia <note>The historical term for rabies, referring to the fear of water</note>, along with innumerable other examples which you may see in my *Magnetic Art* <note>A reference to Kircher’s 1641 work *Magnes; sive de Arte Magnetica*, which explores universal attractions</note>. Likewise, all stony and pebble-like things, or those which possess even a shadow of similarity to a stone, are remedies against "the stone" <note>An archaic term for kidney or bladder stones (calculus)</note>. For when a "sinning humor" <note>A "peccant" or morbid fluid within the body</note> exists unnaturally in some limb, being dissonant to it, it is pulled away, attracted, and expelled by a medicine that is consonant with that sinning humor; thus, the limb is finally liberated from its sinful humor, that dissonant guest. And so that I may more deeply explain the causes of this kind of harmonic sympathy, it seems appropriate to begin a little further back.

Hippocrates called that "nature which heals diseases" the "instrumental cause," which the soul immediately uses to exercise its chief faculties in the "vapor" <note>The *pneuma* or vital spirit</note> for the sake of restoration or preservation. You should understand this not merely as an elementary mixture of parts or a temperament of the primary qualities, but most especially as that substance composed of "radical moisture" <note>The vital fluid believed to sustain life, like oil in a lamp</note>, "primordial heat," and "innate spirit." This is the bond between soul and body, the underlying essence <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> of things celestial and terrestrial, which the more secret Philosophers call "elementary heaven" or the "celestial element." According to the mind of Hippocrates, this substance, falling as seed from the individual parts of the body, informs, ferments, and disposes that seed, and forms the body from the matter subject to it for the soul that is to enter it, creating a new harmonic mixture of offspring from those very same parts from which it flowed. For the part cut from the head forms a new head, the idea of which it retained; that from the heart, a new heart; that from the liver, a new liver; that from the lung, a new lung; and so on for the rest. Moreover, it is the office of this same essence, which formed the limb for itself in the yet unborn fetus, to preserve that limb safely in all respects once it is born, or to restore it to health if it should happen to fall away from it.

But even though that whole nature concurs for the integrity, preservation, and safety of the entire body, its diverse particles nevertheless primarily bring aid and help to the specific parts of the body in which they are innate; this is what Physicians have been accustomed to call the "disposition of the parts" proceeding from the whole substance. For although these innate particles of substance differ very little from one another in their nature, they nevertheless have a certain specific <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "συμπάθειαν" (sympatheian)</note> with the parts of the body in which they reside; for they are consonant with these parts, and they reside in, preside over, and heal these and no others. Therefore, since—according to that saying of Hippocrates—<term>natures are the physicians of diseases</term> <note>original: "νόσων φύσεις ἰατροὶ" (noson physeis iatroi)</note>, and nature itself immediately heals diseases, the Physician, as the "minister of nature," must take the greatest care to join those three things which constitute implanted nature—namely, radical moisture, innate spirit, and innate heat—in a fitting bond and a thoroughly harmonic proportion. He must ensure that the fatty moisture does not fail the heat, nor that the heat itself devastates its fuel through excess and defrauds the spirit. If he procures this harmony, let him not doubt that nature, by its own character, will soon lead our body back to perfect integrity.

<margin>What things are most to be observed by a Physician.</margin>

It remains to be investigated what that harmonic connection is and how it ought to be procured by the Physician. The Arabs and Egyptians say that Medicine is "Catholic" <note>In the sense of "universal"</note>—the preserver of nature's strength and the eradicator of morbid affections. The Chemists call it the "Life-giving Stone"; Paracelsus calls it <term>Azoth</term> <note>A legendary universal solvent or panacea in alchemy</note> or "potable gold"; Lully asserts it to be the "fifth essence" <note>The "quintessence," or the purest, most refined element</note> prepared by him from wine, which he calls "heaven." But since many have sought this, few have found it, and none have left it to posterity, it has happened that Physicians—partly out of weariness, partly deterred by the difficulty and expense—have descended from the "universal" medicine (which benefits the whole body) to the "particular" medicine (which benefits individual parts). Hence, as was said a little before, "Cephalics" (for the head), "Cardiacs" (for the heart), "Splenetics" (for the spleen), "Hepatics" (for the liver), "Pulmonaries" (for the lungs), and similar remedies are used by Physicians today, having been detected both through experiment and through their "character" and <term>signature</term> <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" held that plants or minerals that look like body parts can heal those parts</note>.

<margin>The mixture of wine with water must be harmonic in order to settle one's morals.</margin>
Plutarch certainly prescribes a harmonic proportion for the mixture of wine with water, both for health and for composing the character of the soul. For if you mix 3 parts of water with 4 parts of wine, there will be born a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>original: "diatessaron," the musical interval of a perfect fourth</note>, an imperfect consonance, separate from others and unpleasant; just as wine from this mixture is almost watery and unpleasant, and is properly suited to men who are serious and intent on matters of great importance. If, however, you mix two parts of water with three parts of wine, there will be born a <term>diapente</term> <note>original: "diapente," the musical interval of a perfect fifth</note>, a pleasant and delightful consonance, and it makes a drink of such temperament. If indeed you mix two parts of water with two parts of wine, there will be born the <term>diapason</term> <note>original: "diapason," the musical interval of an octave</note> consonance, the sweetest and most delightful of all, and the drink of this mixture will be rendered such, always having respect for the place, time, custom, persons, and quality of the wine.

But let us return to the works of nature. All species—whether inanimate, vegetable, or sensitive—unite themselves to one another by a harmonic bond, since without it they could by no means be preserved. Metallic veins draw from the bowels of the earth the humors and vapors necessary for the generation of any metal, under the proportion suitable to the metal they produce. In vegetables, each one sucks from the "breasts of the earth" that nourishment which is most agreeable to its preservation, under such and such a proportion, which if they were to overstep, they would necessarily fail.

Art follows this application of nature, which in the business of grafting never inserts trees of a dissonant nature into other trees, but rather consonant ones that are closer to each other in the likeness of their nature. A miracle of this kind is seen here in Rome, to the great admiration of all, in the domestic garden of the <note>original: "PP. Aug. discalceatorum," the Discalced Augustinian Fathers</note>, where a Citron tree, hanging in the air without a root, nevertheless produces leaves, flowers, and fruit solely from the nourishment it receives from neighboring similar trees whose branches are intertwined with its own branches. Hence, plants are so eager for the heavens that they break through all obstacles to satisfy their appetite. They also studiously avoid other things dissonant to them, just as the cabbage turns away from the vine by the flight of its stalks and leaves; the gourd so abominates a vessel full of oil placed beneath it that it seems to shrink away entirely.

In animals, too, each one seeks by natural instinct that food which is most agreeable to its conservation. It flees by every means from that which could in any way bring about some destruction. Hence, from divine providence, each thing has learned its own antidote, by which it may timely repel the evils it has incautiously incurred. And all these things argue nothing else but a certain harmonic form latent in all things, by which the excesses and defects of things are called back to a middle state. But more on these matters in the following pages. Therefore, to conclude all things briefly, the disharmony of the aforementioned things will then be called back to harmony, when according to the nature of the body—

->**REGISTER IV.**<-
->**The Harmony of the Microcosm with the Macrocosm, or on Human Music.**<-

It was once thought—though perhaps mistakenly—that the force of reason could demonstrate that the world, according to the teachings of the ancients, is a kind of living creature <note>This refers to the concept of the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, a common philosophical idea that the universe itself is alive and organized by a rational spirit</note>. In this view, a single mind or soul, endowed with one spirit, is diffused through a single body with perfect balance; this was suggested not so much by human logic as by the beauty of the whole and the shared harmony <note>original: "conspiratio," meaning a breathing together or a harmonious agreement</note> of its individual parts and actions. For we consider it appropriate that this world, which is both one and many at the same time, is divided into many worlds like the joints and limbs of a nature that is both similar and dissimilar, which from conflict [are brought] into friendship...

...noting them through a certain wonderful and magical harmony. Thus, the poppy, walnuts, peony, agaric <note>a type of mushroom</note>, and squill prepared for the head—which they resemble through a certain hidden analogy—contribute wonderfully to its health. Moss, species of maidenhair, thapsia, and similar plants correspond to the hair; *Asarum* <note>wild ginger</note> and seashells to the ears; eyebright, marigold, and cinquefoil to the eyes; wild mint to the nose; henbane, toothwort, pits and seeds to the teeth; throat-wort to the throat; liverwort, lichen, and oak fungus to the liver; citron, balm, motherwort, nard, and cardamom to the heart; lungwort to the lungs; hart's-tongue fern, spleenwort, and ceterach to the spleen; sowbread and galangal to the stomach; cassia pods and sweet flag to the intestines; bladder senna and bladder-nut to the bladder; and all species of Satyrion and Orchids correspond most perfectly to the private parts. All of these are, as it were, certain strings <margin>Those things which have a likeness to the limbs, heal the same.</margin> which, when properly tuned, vibrate through a hidden harmony (as I have said) with the corresponding strings of the **microcosm** <term>Microcosm: the "little world," a traditional philosophical concept that the human body is a miniature map of the entire universe.</term>. Indeed, the head seems to rejoice at the presence of "cephalic" <note>head-healing</note> substances, the liver at "hepatic" ones, the heart at "cardiac" ones, and so the other members seem to exult and delight in the likeness of nature. They seem to run to meet these things that correspond to them by analogy, as if with open arms, greeting them as friendly guests and preservers.

In no different a way do we arrive at the knowledge of what any substance is useful for by the "signatures" <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that God marked plants with physical signs to show their medicinal use.</note> that mark diseases, through the hidden harmony of the worlds. For just as the preceding terrestrial stars—the plants—are carried from the circumference to the centers of the marked parts and members as their presiding guardians and preservers; so the following indices of diseases and imbalances of the microcosm expel the disease-causing agent from the centers of the limbs to the circumference, attracting it to themselves by a hidden reason, and by expelling the cause, they restore the body to its former harmony. In this way, crystal, flint, citron-stone, lynx-stone, the "calculus" <note>stone</note> of the microcosm, gromwell, the pits of almost all fruits, and six hundred species of "saxifrage" <note>literally "stone-breaker" plants</note> seek out, dissolve, and break apart stony concretions in the kidneys and bladder by a wonderful consensus. Thus, the juices of herbs that resemble one of the four humors <note>blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm</note> are ordained to draw that humor out. In this way, "Cancer" <note>the disease/the crab</note> kills a cancer; a crushed scorpion heals its own wound. Earthworms kill worms; a "wolf" <note>the disease lupus, Latin for wolf</note> kills a wolf. Hemorrhoids are cured by *chondrilla*, which reflects their appearance and shape. A flow of blood is stopped by blood ground into powder; the powder of a serpent heals the bites of serpents. Time would fail me if I wished to bring forward every instance here. As many species of "meteors" <note>atmospheric phenomena</note> as there are in the elementary world, there are just as many diseases in the microcosm. Hence Galen shows that the same generation of "flats" <note>gas/wind</note> occurs in us as occurs in the sublunary world <note>the region below the moon, i.e., the Earth's atmosphere</note>. Hippocrates also, in his book *On the Nature of the Child*, traced the likeness <margin>Diseases are the "meteors" of the microcosm.</margin> we share with plants—not only in sickness and health, but also in our entire birth, death, growth, maturity, and decline. What else are catarrhs and "fluxions" <note>runny noses/drainage</note>—to use the Greek terms—than rains, snows, and hailstorms? What are epilepsies, vertigoes, inflammations, and fevers, than lightnings, flashes, chasms in the sky, thunders, and that kind of fiery deluge? What are apoplexies, comas, lethargies, and other sleep-inducing diseases, than eclipses of the lights, floods, and cataclysms? What are the pains of the kidneys and gout, than monstrous births and things seen in places where they do not belong, entirely contrary to nature? What else are the pains of colic, the womb, and the hypochondrium, than whirlwinds, the overturning of embankments, and the most savage earthquakes, tangled together within the bowels of the earth while the contrary elements of fire and water—or bile and phlegm—struggle against one another? Indeed, this admirable harmony can be compared not only between the whole microcosm and the whole **macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: the "great world" or the universe at large.</term>, but also part by part. So much so, that in the human head alone, whatever nature has gathered into the entire universe is displayed to be seen. Thus it can truly be said: <note>original Greek: ἀπάντων τέλος φύσις ἀποτέλεσμένη μεγακόσμος μικρόκοσμος</note> "The end of all things is perfected nature, the macrocosm and the microcosm." For since the things understood, the intellect, and the intelligible world are the same, surely the intellect shall be the world, and the "perfection" <note>entelecheia</note> of the human head. Therefore, the world is to be looked for within the same place; if indeed the intellect, while naked in itself, is clothed with all intelligible things, it takes the place of **prime matter** <term>Prime Matter: in Aristotelian philosophy, the pure potentiality that receives "form" to become a physical thing.</term>. It performs the duty of Form, while it so shadows the intelligible things that it differs in no way from them. Thus the soul, by its vegetative faculty, corresponds to plants; by its sensitive and motive faculty to animals; and by its rational faculty to the Angels and to GOD. But to speak a little more exactly: in the head, we have the element of Earth in the skull; of Water in the *dura mater* <note>the tough outer membrane of the brain</note>; of Air in the *pia mater* <note>the delicate inner membrane</note>; and of Fire in the substance of the brain; or if you prefer, Earth is the sense of taste...

You will note that touch and the eyes correspond to water; the ears to air; and the nostrils, with their smoky and fiery exhalations, to fire. The metals, which are secreted here and there, represent the wastes of the body; hence, the black <term>humor</term><note>The "humors" were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—believed in pre-modern medicine to control health and temperament.</note> corresponds to iron, the rusty to copper, the yellow to gold, the pale to tin, the white to silver, and the dark greyish-brown to lead and bronze. All these are produced from bile and phlegm, sulfur and mercury. The "sea" exists at the body's boundaries, scattering many streams downward into the brain; cities and houses are seen in the nodules of the ventricles, and various pathways of roads in the ducts. The hair represents the forests; lice are the wild beasts; and other insects and animals occasionally arise within the brain. Tears are like distilling dew and frost; the discharge held in the corner of the eye imitates them. Foul vapors obscuring the sight are like mist; clouds are the windings of the brain; ringing in the ears represents the winds; and a running nose represents the rain. Saliva is like foamy snow; congealed phlegm is like hail; a murmur or wind in the body is like thunder; a sudden shock to the eyes is like a flash of lightning; and a terrible gaze is like a thunderbolt. Comets and other fiery atmospheric phenomena are shown in the streaks and redness of the face and forehead.

If we move beyond the elements and their compounds to traverse the heavens, the Sun lives in the native heat of the brain, the Moon in its original moisture (the two greatest lights); Jupiter lives in the temperate parts, Saturn in the <term>melancholic</term>, Mars in the <term>bilious</term>, and Venus in the <term>phlegmatic</term> blood. Mercury, however, resides in the mouth and tongue. If we examine the "fixed stars," the structure of the brain clearly displays the circles of the celestial sphere and the images of the globe. You see, therefore, that the entire machine of the world is perfectly symmetrical—not only to man as a whole, but even to a single part of him. It is no wonder, then, that man, being composed of all parts of the world, contains all things within himself.

<margin>The analogy of the microcosm with the macrocosm.</margin>

Cardinal Hugo<note>original: "Hugo Cardinalis"; refers to Hugh of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263), a Dominican cardinal and biblical scholar.</note> beautifully describes all these things in his own way: "Every creature," he says, "speaks to us with a triple voice. The first voice is: *Receive the benefit*; the second is: *Pay the debt*; the third is: *Flee the punishment*." The first voice belongs to the serving heavens, speaking thus: "I minister light to you by day so that you may see, and darkness by night so that you may rest." The air says: "I provide you with the breath of life and every kind of bird for your service." The water says: "I give you drink, I cleanse your filth, I water the parched earth, and I provide kinds of fish for your use." The earth says: "I carry you, I nourish you with bread and wine, and I fill your tables with all kinds of fruits and animals." The second voice is the world's warning: "See," it says, "O man, how He loved you, He who made me for your sake. I serve you so that you may serve Him, who made both me and you." The third voice is the threat: fire says, "By me you shall be burned"; water says, "In me you shall be drowned"; the earth and hell say, "By us you shall be swallowed up," unless you respond to the benefits granted by God which shine forth in us. But to return to our goal: certainly the ancients, looking into the <term>microcosm</term><note>From the Greek "mikros kosmos" or "little world," the idea that a human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note> at the mass of that most perfect figure, found the diverse variety of celestial and elementary things, the elegant order of most magnificent things, and the beautiful consensus and harmony of most lovely things. From this miraculous structure, they observed the numbers, measures, proportions, and harmonies, as they noted the wonderfully proportioned consonances and measurements of all the members in relation to one another. Since these things are proper to this section, we have decided to treat them a little more extensively.

### §. I.
### On the harmonic proportion of the parts of the human body in numbers.

Architects, following Vitruvius for the most part, are accustomed to divide the stature of a man into 10 parts so that they may investigate the proportions of the remaining parts from these; others have found 7 parts, and others still other measures. We, following the harmonic architecture of nature, will first divide the measure of the human body into 9 parts, as being more in consonance with nature. For nature itself formed man such that she placed this face in the highest position to be gazed upon, and the other parts of the entire body take their measurement from it. The face itself consists of three dimensions: one shall be from the top of the forehead where the hair begins to the eyebrows; the second from there to the bottom of the nostrils; the last from the nostrils to the chin. The first is the seat of wisdom, the second of beauty, and the third of goodness. These, when increased, will yield the entire stature of the human body, nine...

408 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

<margin>The members of the microcosm are compared with the political world.</margin>
The dwelling [of the body], like a certain seven-stringed instrument <note>original: "heptachord"</note>, contains a wonderful consonance of all things. For if you compare this space to the visible and invisible world, the **spleen** represents the earth, the **gallbladder** represents fire; the **intestines** with their phlegm represent the sea, and the **air** <note>within the lungs</note> represents the heavens with their double motion of contraction and expansion <note>original: "systole & diastole"</note>, moving as if from sunrise to sunset, and conversely. 

If indeed we compare it to a **Republic**, **Reason** shall be called the King, the **Will** the Queen, the **Intellect** the Counselor, and finally the **heart** represents the Nobles <note>original: "Primores"</note>; for when the heart fails, all things fall into ruin. The heart, with its perpetual contraction and expansion, beats the drum; at one moment it sounds the retreat, at another it sounds the clarion call to arms. 

Nor is it unsuitable to compare the body to a **private household** <note>original: "Oeconomiæ priuatæ"</note>, in which the **legs** act as the carriage, the **brain** as the counselor, the **liver** and **stomach** represent the kitchen, the **spleen** and **kidneys** the sewers, and the **veins** show the way for the food. The **arteries** supply heat, the **nerves** prepare the seasoning; **melancholic juice** <note>black bile</note> produces the lean person, **phlegmatic** the fat, **bilious** the hot, and **sanguine** the tempered person. The **imagination** provides the paintings, the **memory** narrates those paintings, the **eyes** represent the candelabras, and the **heart** moderates all things, with the remaining members surrounding it like servants. 

The **heart**, therefore, is the seat of the irascible soul <note>the part of the soul associated with courage and anger</note>, the source of vital power and spirit, the hearth of natural heat, and the **sun of the microcosm**, by whose perennial influence all things are preserved. Hence, to preserve this heat, it consists of a very dense and hard substance, woven together with every kind of defensive wall. Furthermore, one may not improperly compare the **four vessels of the heart** to the **four rivers of Paradise**; for there are 

<margin>The use of the members in the human microcosm.</margin>
in the right side two veins: the **vena cava** brings the blood in, while the **arterial vein** <note>now known as the pulmonary artery</note> carries it readily from the heart into the lungs. In the left part are situated two arteries: the **Aorta** distributes the vital spirit and blood to the whole body, and finally the **venous artery** <note>now known as the pulmonary vein</note> carries inspired air into the heart, carries back the smoky vapors <note>original: "fuligines"</note> of the vital spirit, and supplies the lungs with arterial blood. The bellows of this most perfect organ are constituted by the **spongy lung**, visible with its five lobes; for while this is dilated like a bellows, it draws in air, and when pressed and constricted, it distributes that air through innumerable channels to all the members as a necessity, and fans the heat of the heart. 

Next follows the **stomach**, the workshop of chylification <note>the process of turning food into chyle, a milky digestive fluid</note>, and the steward of the larder. When this is poorly affected, it undermines the entire harmony of the body; it is a troublesome collector of debts, causing much business for a man. To keep it in its duty, lest everything turn into dissonance, two bodies are established around it, the **liver** and the **spleen**, like a cauldron between two hearths; for by their warming, it is preserved in natural heat. The **liver** nourishes the entire family of the body at its own expense, so to speak; it is the seat of love and desire, and upon its **good or bad temperament** <note>original: "ευκρασία vel ακερασία"</note> both the color of a man and all vital faculties depend. It is connected to the **brain** through the nerves, to the **heart** through the arteries and the vena cava, to the **ventricle, intestines, and spleen** through the splenic and rare mesenteric vessels, and to the other parts of the body through its own and common ligaments. 

The **gallbladder** purges the liver by drawing away the thinner bile; the **spleen** frees and purges it of melancholic humor; the **kidneys** of the drawn-off watery humor; and the **intestine** thrusts out the drawn-off earthy and dregs-filled matter. The **mesenteric veins** prepare the chyle and contribute the first rudiments of blood, to which the liver gives form and redness; the **vena cava** distributes it, and the other parts purge the royal house of **blood-making** <note>original: "αἱματώσεως" (hematosis)</note>. If these are compared with the starry world, they are found to agree most exactly.

<margin>Where the kingdom of generation and corruption is in the microcosm.</margin>
The third region follows: the **kingdom of generation and corruption**, filled with meteorological impressions <note>a comparison of bodily functions to weather and atmospheric changes</note>, the belly containing within itself the **intestines**, the **bladder**, and the **spermatic parts**. The **intestine**, which in a man is seven times his length, is marked with different names according to its different effects. The first part after the stomach is called the **pelorus** or **duodenum**. ### §. III.
### *Concerning the sensible harmony and music of the Microcosm in relation to the Celestial and Elemental world.*

In the preceding sections, we have shown that the distances of the stars are like certain strings, and the globes of the stars themselves are like weights attached to those strings. These are ordered by the harmony of the world in such a proportion that, just as strings tensioned by different weights produce different sounds—and if the proportions of the weights are in a harmonic proportion to one another, the strings extended and struck by them will produce consonant intervals in equal measure—so I say, if by divine power the worldly bodies were hung from material strings, those struck strings would necessarily produce the same most perfect and most harmonious sound. All of this is clearly evident from the proportions of the worldly bodies to one another, as presented above.

By a not dissimilar reasoning, in the elemental world (about whose sensible symphonism <note>The inherent "sounding together" or agreement of elements.</note> much was said in the preceding pages), a certain sensible harmony lies hidden, which would shine forth most greatly if Divine Wisdom were to strengthen the weakness of our auditory faculty. Indeed, motion, as was said in the first book, causes the striking of bodies against one another; from the striking of bodies, with air or water intervening, a sound is made. And if indeed the movements were harmonically proportional, a harmonic sound will be excited; if not, dissonances will be born. Furthermore, if the movements are fast, high-pitched sounds are born; if slow, deep sounds. With these things supposed, a triple sensible harmony can be considered here. The first is from the motion of flight and pursuit, which we see most especially in the family of dissonant and consonant strife and friendship among plants and animals. <margin>The sympathy of one palm tree for another.</margin> This wonderful concord appears first in the male and female palm tree, which love each other so much that one completely perishes without the other; nor does it wish to be watered, so that it might grow, unless with water extracted from the other sex. The Cocoa tree of America completely wastes away without the Ebony tree shading it; and to embrace many things in a few words, there is no herb that does not either sound in harmony or dissonance with another. Thus the fern detests the reed, and the vine hates the cabbage with a natural hatred; yet in a very damp place, the fern begins to harmonize with the reed, while it frees the reed—which is almost suffocated by too much moisture—by diverting into itself what is superfluous. Thus the cabbage...

But in sadness, with a heavy heart, the languishing spirits cause slower motions, whence an effect entirely contrary to the first occurs.

The motion of the spirits in the brain harmonizes with the heart in a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>A Perfect Fourth (ratio of 4:3).</note>, and so on for the rest. Therefore, in a perfectly healthy man, there is a perfect consonance of all members—not only by analogy, but truly "sensible" <note>Capable of being perceived by the senses.</note>, if the weakness of our ears could reach that far. For the muscles and the blood, agitated by the spirits, are necessarily moved, and from motion, a striking <note>original: "illusio," here referring to the physical impact or vibration.</note> is necessarily born, which some sound necessarily follows. Since the motions of the vital organs were ordained by nature under these harmonic proportions (as has been said elsewhere at length), they will necessarily exhibit some harmony.

If, however, by an imbalance of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</note>, the motions of the animal spirits in any vital member are stretched or slackened more than is proper, disharmony is immediately introduced, which we say is nothing else than disease. This disease will be more severe the more members are dissonant to one another with graceless motions. The same happens in us: for while we hear beautiful music, we are immediately moved to produce similar songs and modulations. This would not happen unless the said harmony, through the air affected by a similar harmony, imbued our spirit with a similar harmony as well. Since, therefore, the motions of the spirits in the vital members—heart, brain, lung, liver, spleen, kidneys, etc.—are different according to the natural constitution of the members, they will harmonize beautifully with different motions, provided they are harmonic.

414 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

<margin>The ratio of pulses in motion.</margin>
The nature and condition of the pulse is not simple, nor does it consist of simple elements; rather, it is composed of several factors. If any of these are lacking, the motion does not occur. Furthermore, there are as many differences in motion as there are parts that constitute it. In pulses, there are five factors especially necessary for the complete perfection and nature of motion.

<margin>The space through which motion occurs.</margin>
**First**, the space through which the mover effects the motion, or through which the artery is moved. If this space is large, it will produce a **large** pulse; if small, a **small** one; and finally, if it is middling, it will produce a **moderate** pulse. From this, a triple difference of pulses—large, small, and moderate—immediately arises.

<margin>The measurement of time in pulses.</margin>
**Second**; the time which the mover consumes in the motion is required. From this, another difference immediately flows, which is determined by the measure of time. For if the mover consumes a small amount of time in the motion, it will produce a **fast** pulse; if it takes much time, a **slow** one; and if the time is middling, a **moderate** pulse will arise.

<margin>What is the upward and downward motion in pulses?</margin>
**Third**. Since motion of this kind is composed of motion *upward or downward* <note>original: "ἄνω vel κάτω" (anō vel katō)</note>, it will necessarily require an intervening rest. From these rests, a third difference of pulses arises: for either the artery lingers for a short time in rest, thus producing a **frequent** pulse, or for a long time, producing a **rare** <note>In historical medicine, a 'rare' pulse refers to one with long intervals between beats, the opposite of 'frequent.'</note> pulse, or a middling amount, causing a medium pulse between the two.

<margin>What is the motive force in pulses?</margin>
**Fourth**, a Mover <term>Motor: the active force or "engine" behind a movement</term> is required, which we say is nothing other than the **vital faculty** <note>The 'vital faculty' was believed to be the life-force residing in the left ventricle of the heart, responsible for involuntary movements like the heartbeat.</note> residing in the left ventricle of the heart, as we indicated above, as if stationed in a center. From this faculty, the entire harmonic craftsmanship of the pulsation is completed. If this faculty is robust and strong, it renders a **vehement** pulse; if languid and dejected, a **feeble** one; if middling, it renders a **moderate** pulse between the vehement and the feeble.

<margin>The artery is the instrument of the pulse.</margin>
**Fifth**. The instrument of the Artery is required, by which the entire craftsmanship of motion is performed. Based on the condition of this artery, another difference of pulse is born. For if the artery is hard, dense, solid, and tense, it will produce a **hard, dense, and tense** pulse; but if it is soft, flaccid, and loose, it will render such a pulse (that is, a **soft** one); or if it is of a middle condition, the artery will likewise exhibit a moderate pulse.

From these factors, fifteen differences of simple pulses flow, created by the multiplication of the three simple variations <note>Large, small, and moderate</note> across the five requirements, as is clear in the following table.

<margin>How the motive force produces the pulse.</margin>

The vital faculty, therefore, aware of its duty and excited by the use it naturally understands, moves the instruments committed to it with whatever strength it possesses. First, it agitates the arteries with unceasing motion according to their quality and condition, distending them as much as it can. By this faculty, motion is produced through the aforementioned instruments and space, in such a condition as necessity demands. From this it is clearly evident that magnitude or smallness must be taken from the space traversed; the state of the faculty is judged by the strength of the stroke or the percussion of the artery against the fingers; and the hardness or softness is perceived in the pulses. Whoever perfectly masters these will understand not only the physiology of motions and pulses, but also—

And from these beats, the machinery of the microcosm <note>A common Renaissance concept that the human body—the "microcosm"—reflects the laws and structures of the "macrocosm," or the universe.</note> is stirred whenever it encounters an imbalance or a disharmony of the humors. Physicians describe these using many different names according to the various conditions of diseases: equal and unequal, as well as ordered unequal and unordered unequal. For when a pulse is unequal in its magnitude, yet always maintains a consistent manner of inequality, following the same parity in its order and circuit, it is called "ordered unequal"—as when every third or fourth beat is larger or smaller than the rest, while always keeping to that same pattern. A "deficient" pulse is when the artery seems almost destitute of motion due to the weakness of the beat. It is called a "reciprocating deficient" pulse when it returns to motion again after some interval of time, as is evident in the notes for intermittent and deficient pulses.

A "wavy" pulse occurs when certain parts of the pulse are elevated more and others less; some parts move slower and others faster, like waves pushing against each other. Some people confuse this with the "worm-like" and "ant-like" pulses. The difference, however, is this: the worm-like pulse imitates the progressive and wavy motion of earthworms, while the ant-like pulse imitates the crawling step of ants.
<margin>What worm-like and ant-like pulses are.</margin>

The "goat-leap" pulse <note>original: "caprizans"; from the Latin *capra* for goat.</note> is taken from the category of unequal pulses and named after the behavior of fighting goats. For when a goat attacks another, it first rears up, then restrains itself slightly from the impact, and immediately rushes in with a second motion that is much faster and stronger. If the pulse produces a similar motion, it is called "goat-leap."

...of these movements for forming a solid judgment about the state of the body and its health; only he shall truly excel who has rightly understood **Rhythm**—that is, the knowledge of harmonic concord and modulation, and of the equality and inequality maintained between the expansion <note>The "dilation" or swelling of the artery, known as systole.</note> and contraction <note>The "compression" or shrinking of the artery, known as diastole.</note> of the pulse. Therefore, in this context, Rhythm is nothing other than the proportion of the timings found in the pulse relative to one another. <margin>What is the rhythm of the pulses?</margin> Since proportion is the relationship of two quantities of the same kind to each other, and time belongs to the category of quantity, it follows that if you compare the quantity of the artery's expansion to the quantity of its contraction, you can perfectly judge its excess, its deficiency, and its equality. <margin>Twofold rhythm</margin> Furthermore, Rhythm is twofold: **equal** and **unequal**. The former occurs when the time of expansion is equal to the time of contraction, or when one time does not exceed the other; the latter proceeds in the opposite order.

**Equal Rhythm**, which Galen also calls harmonious <note>original: *eurythmon*</note>, or the natural and best pulse, <margin>Deviation from rhythm and harmonious rhythm</margin> is properly suited to those enjoying the best health. However, when the pulse changes due to age, region, or temperament, it is called *pararhythmos* <note>A rhythm that is slightly "beside" or altered from the natural state.</note>. If it is outside of nature, it is called <insert>unequal</insert>. **Unequal Rhythm**, which Galen calls erratic <note>original: *ekrhythmon*</note> or non-natural, exceeds Equal Rhythm either by a manifest or a hidden excess. Or it may be with a **superparticular proportion** <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one part of it (e.g., 3:2).</note>, such as the **one-and-a-half** <note>original: *sesquialtera* or *hemiola* (3:2 ratio).</note>, the **one-and-a-third** <note>4:3 ratio.</note>, the **one-and-a-fourth** <note>5:4 ratio.</note>, the **one-and-eighth** <note>9:8 ratio.</note>, etc.; namely the **fifth** <note>original: *diapente*</note>, the **fourth** <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>, and the **whole tone**. If the latter—that is, by a hidden excess—it is then called "Well-Rhythmed" <note>original: *Eurythmus*</note>; if it can be expressed by any musical note outside of nature, which need not be discussed here. But we must discuss that manifest excess which shows us clear traces of health or infirmity. If this changes into the rhythm of youth, it acquires a rhythm of longer time and a more vigorous nature. But changed into the rhythm of manhood, it becomes most tempered and most fit for performing actions worthy of a man. Until, changed into the rhythm of old age, it finally becomes flaccid in its ruin. Truly, so that we may apply this harmonic speculation to some use, it remains to be said how this kind of rhythm may be examined in all circumstances, and how we may divine the health of the sick from them.

### On the Harmony of Pulses by reason of the four temperaments, the air, the region, and the seasons of the year.

Since it is clearly evident to us that men are variously tempered, it is certain that any temperament provides various, diverse, and entirely different pulses. For bodies prevailing with a **hot** temperament are found to necessarily have a large, fast, and frequent pulse, but not a violent one; which constitution <note>original: "complexio"</note>, as it admits various degrees of intensity and relaxation, so it also has different pulses.

Bodies of a **cold** temperament are allotted pulses entirely contrary to those mentioned: small, slow, and frequent. **Moist** temperaments are allotted a pulse entirely equal to the pulse of women, as will be taught shortly. **Dry** temperaments produce a larger, hard, and quite rare pulse, somewhat more violent, such as we experience in slender bodies—the harmony of which we show in the following notes.

| Cold | Hot | Moist | Dry |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Whole Tone | Dissonant | Octave | Whole Tone |
| Dissonant | Fourth | Fifth | Octave |

In this scheme, you see the difference of pulses in the four temperaments shown by musical notes, together with the combinations made between them. Thus, just as the **cold** and **hot** temperaments are contraries, so also their pulses differ entirely in time; they produce the same effect in music as a <term>whole tone</term> <note>original: "tonus"</note>, which is the most dissonant among the consonances. By a similar reasoning, the pulses of **moist** and **dry** temperaments differ from each other, and it is impossible for them to sound together, just as in music a whole tone cannot be consonant.

But **cold** and **moist** temperaments, as they are joined, can agree, though with difficulty; when joined together they produce the same effect as a **fourth** in music, which, according to its different position, is sometimes consonant and sometimes dissonant. The **hot** and **moist** temperaments, however, because the moisture is friendly to the heat, are very sociable; thus they produce the same effect as an **octave** in music.

Book 10. The Decachord of Nature. 419
<note>The "Decachord" refers to a ten-stringed musical instrument, used here as a metaphor for the harmonious laws of nature.</note>

<margin>The pulse is changed by the different constitution of the air.</margin>

Furthermore, you will undoubtedly find very similar pulses resulting from the temperament of the air, inasmuch as either the seasons of the year or the diverse nature of regions changes it entirely. According to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his theories on the pulse dominated medicine for over a millennium.</note>, the seasons of the year are divided by an excellent system into hot, cold, dry, and moist. He established that their temperament is so effective that they change not only the pulse, but also the actions and almost all the duties of the body. In temperate bodies, the pulse becomes greatest and most vehement; but if the bodies are less temperate, they will differ from the aforementioned pulses to the same degree that the temperament of the body whose pulse you are touching differs from the middle (or balanced) temperament. The reason is that the <term>faculty</term><note>The "vital faculty" or "virtue" refers to the innate power of the soul or body to perform biological functions.</note> is not equally robust in intemperate bodies, nor are other things as they should be. Indeed, bilious bodies fare better in winter, phlegmatic bodies in summer, and temperate bodies in spring. In summer, pulses become small, swift, frequent, and weak; the reason for this is the dissipation of the innate heat, which renders them weak. However, since the "use" <note>In this context, "use" refers to the body's need for cooling and ventilation.</note> is increased at that time, it follows that the pulses must be swift and frequent. Furthermore, in winter, pulses are small, slow, rare, and weak according to Galen; but we assert that they are large and moderate in other respects, and not as vehement as in spring. For since the internal parts grow hotter in winter through <term>antiperistasis</term><note>An ancient physical theory where a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as internal body heat increasing to resist external cold.</note>, it is necessary that large pulses follow. In autumn, the pulses are rendered weak and unequal for a twofold cause: the first is that autumn is similar to diseases arising from corruption; the second is because of the sudden inequality of the weather at this time, which nature cannot endure without harm. For nature bears it very poorly to be chilled and then suddenly warmed at the same time, because it is distracted by different things at once; and as the artery accommodates itself to the sensation of the weather—now toward larger, swifter, and more frequent pulses, and now toward the opposite—it is necessary that both debility and weakness of the pulse follow from this very fact.

<margin>The diversity of the pulse in the four seasons of the year.</margin>

<margin>Autumnal pulses.</margin>

The nature of the air and the region corresponds in every way to these four seasons of the year; for if the air of a region has a summery constitution, it will produce a pulse similar to summer; if it has the disposition of springtime, it will return spring-like pulses; if autumnal or wintery, it will manifest such pulses. Following this wonderful analogy is the fourfold division of the day: Dawn, Midday, Sunset, and Night; Dawn corresponding to spring, Midday to summer, Sunset to autumn, and Night to winter, producing corresponding pulses in each.

### Corollary I.

<margin>Why the diversity of pulses was established by nature.</margin>

And from what has been said, the wonderful, hidden harmony of pulses in bodies is clearly evident, ordained by divine counsel so that without this variety, no perfect health could subsist in its time, as the harmony of the pulses affects the harmony of the seasons. For just as the elementary world could least exist without the variation of the seasons of the year (which is necessary for the generation of things, as was said above), so the pulses—now vehement, thick, and hard, now soft, slow, and weak, and now maintaining a middle course—are absolutely necessary both for drawing in ever-new air and for expelling the <term>sooty vapors</term><note>The "fuligines" or sooty vapors were believed to be the waste products of the blood "burning" in the heart, which needed to be exhaled.</note> of the blood. Since all these things were touched upon in the preceding sections, we shall not dwell on them longer.

### Corollary II.

<margin>The harmony of pulses in people of different ages.</margin>

It is also clear from the preceding discourse that if it were granted to us to hear the pulses of different times and ages, it would happen that we would perceive a certain harmonious symphony or <term>concordant harmony</term> <note>original: "σύμφωνον" (symphōnon)</note> composed of thirds, fifths, and octaves. Since the pulse of a child to an old man is in a double or even quadruple proportion, an <term>octave</term> <note>original: "diapason"</note> or <term>double octave</term> <note>original: "disdiapason"</note> would necessarily be perceived. And since the pulse of a child to a youth is in a ratio of five-to-three <note>original: "superbi partiente tertias" (likely superbipartient thirds)</note>, a <term>minor third</term> <note>original: "semiditonus"</note> would be manifested to us; again, since the pulse of a child to a man is in a <term>sesquialterate proportion</term> (3:2), soon a <term>fourth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron"</note> would be felt, and so on for the rest; provided, however, that each is established in the best of health.

In a not dissimilar way, the pulse of a healthy man in winter, when compared to the pulse of the same man in summer, would be found to exist in a **double proportion** <note>original: "dupla proportione"; a 2:1 ratio, equivalent to an octave in music</note>; Autumnal pulses compared to summer ones are in a **four-to-three ratio** <note>original: "sesquitertia"; the musical interval of a perfect fourth</note>, and these compared to spring pulses are in a **three-to-two ratio** <note>original: "sesquialtera"; the musical interval of a perfect fifth</note>. This was most wisely established by nature, both as a necessity for preserving the balance of the temperament and for ordering it according to the laws of the seasons. But if, through an imbalance and *akrasia* <note>original: "ακρασίαν"; a Greek term meaning a "bad mixture" or lack of self-control over the humors</note> of the humors, the pulses are worn down—just as when a melody is confused and the steady rhythm of the pulse is changed—the union of harmony must necessarily perish. You see, therefore, how the pulses perfectly measure harmonic time, while the animal spirits <note>In historical medicine, "animal spirits" were fluids or gases believed to transmit sensation and movement through the nerves</note>, like voices, exactly complete the harmony.
A similar harmony is carried out between the pulses of a man and a woman.

### Corollary III.

<margin>What dissonance is.</margin>
From this it follows: that whenever the harmonic proportion of the pulses is disturbed, disease necessarily rushes in. Disease is nothing other than a certain **dissonance of the humors**; and since these humors are so diverse, so too do different humors cause different diseases. In this way, there is one pulse for those with fever, another for those with dropsy, another for the consumptive, another for the epileptic, and so on for every other individual disease. This is why nature struggles so much; for disharmony tortures the soul and body and inflicts manifest violence upon nature.

### Corollary IV.

If, therefore, there were a physician who possessed such knowledge of this great harmony that he could distinguish the pulses of every disease, he could undoubtedly—through contrary means applied harmonically, both by adding and subtracting—soon lead the body back to perfect harmony. And since nature has willed that few be conscious of this secret science of pulses, it is no wonder that so few physicians are found today who perform anything extraordinary in the cure of diseases. However, if any physician understands our mind well and has a disposition for the aforementioned things, and has practiced himself duly in this secret teaching of Science, I do not doubt that he, aided by these things, will perform wonders.

### *Music of the five external senses.*

<margin>The physician must be skilled in music.</margin>
The external senses in man also have their own harmonic union, perfectly joined together from consonances and dissonances. Before we prepare to describe the harmony of the inner man, or the "pathetic symphony" <note>An emotional or moving symphony; "pathetic" here refers to the *pathos* or passions of the soul</note> of the internal senses, we wish first to explain this here, so that we do not seem to have omitted anything in this "Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance."

Since we have already treated the harmony of sight and colors extensively in the fourth part of the preceding book, as well as in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>Refers to Kircher's 1646 work, *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*</note>, and since this entire work is concerned with the object of hearing (which is music), nothing remains but to follow the harmony of the remaining senses: Smell, Taste, and Touch.

<margin>The music of flavors.</margin>
Thus, musical proportion, says Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath who wrote on medicine and music</note>, can be considered in flavors in two ways: simply, and by comparison. Simply speaking, the highest sweetness is referred to the **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note>: for it is the sweetest concord among flavors, therefore "sweet" corresponds to it as a simple [consonance]; for what can be sweeter in either genre? But a "fatty" flavor, such as in well-prepared meats and eggs, is referred to the **fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note>, for it is itself the sweetest after the sweet and perfect in its own kind. The **fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>, however, best suits the "salty"; for this is inherently harsh and unpleasant, just as a salty flavor is. Now, a fourth with a fifth completes an octave, but it is entirely dissonant with the octave itself; likewise, a salty flavor brings the greatest delight when combined with a fatty one, but it accords so little with the sweet that it is better paired with bitter things, such as well-salted olives. Therefore, the salty flavor matches the fourth to a hair's breadth; again—

<meta>This page continues the author's complex analogy between the "harmony" of musical intervals and the "harmony" of flavors, a common theme in Renaissance and Baroque natural philosophy where the laws of music were thought to govern all of nature.</meta>

# Book X. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature. 431

Again, the <term>minor third<note>original: "semiditonus"</note></term> corresponds exactly with the **insipid**, and the **astringent** with the <term>major third<note>original: "ditonus"</note></term>; for both are not unpleasant and harmonize with the **sweet**, just as the minor and major thirds harmonize with the <term>octave<note>original: "diapason"</note></term>. Both of these flavors also move the senses only slightly; and they are, as it were, similar to one another, which is also the case with the major and minor thirds. However, neither of these harmonizes with the **fat** or oily, nor does the major or minor third agree with the <term>fifth<note>original: "diapente"</note></term>, for such a composition results in no small discord. Again, they are similar in this: just as the <term>fourth<note>original: "diatessaron"</note></term> harmonizes greatly with the major and minor thirds, so too do the **insipid** and the **astringent** harmonize best with the **salty** <note>The text uses "falso" here, likely a variation of "salso" (salty), as confirmed by the later discussion of salt.</note>. For a fourth combined with a major third creates a **major sixth**, and with a minor third it creates a **minor sixth**; both of these are consonant, yet they are not particularly sweet in themselves because they lack the "sweet" and "fat" elements, just as the major or minor sixth do not complete an octave or a fifth.

The **sharp** flavor is similar to the major sixth, while the **acidic** is like the minor sixth. The **sharp** harmonizes naturally with the **insipid**, and the **acidic** with the **astringent**, just as the major sixth is joined with the minor third, and the minor sixth with the major third, both of which complete an octave. However, these are less "sweet" because the fifth is absent, just as the "fat" element is missing there. The **harsh** <note>original: "austerum"</note> flavor, moreover, harmonizes with a moderate **sharpness**; therefore, both are well-joined with the **insipid**, according to that saying:

->*So that the tasteless chard of the laborers' lunch may have flavor,*<-
->*O, how often does the cook call for wine and pepper?*<note>A quote from the Roman poet Martial (Epigrams 13.13), suggesting that bland food needs the "sharp" kick of pepper and the "harsh/astringent" quality of wine to be palatable.</note><-

For pepper is **sharp**, and wine is **harsh**; both flavors harmonize with the **sweet** and the **fat**, just as both the major and minor sixths harmonize with the octave and the fifth. Yet neither harmonizes with the **salty**; for the fourth cannot be joined with either the major or minor sixth. 

The **bitter** flavor is similar to the <term>whole tone<note>The interval of a major second.</note></term>. It is always discordant by itself, just as the bitter is unpleasant on its own. The whole tone is the origin of all consonances; likewise, all fruits—whether sweet, astringent, acidic, or sharp—are **bitter** before they ripen. Furthermore, a whole tone combines more poorly with an octave than with any other consonance; in the same way, a **bitter** flavor is joined more unhappily with the **sweet** than with anything else. The **bitter** flavor also harmonizes with nothing better than the **salty**; just so, a tone added to a fourth completes the fifth, the sweetest of consonances, as is seen in **salted olives**. 

A light **bitter** flavor does not shrink from the **fat**, though it makes it somewhat worse, as in cakes made from wormwood, eggs, and cheese, and in grapevines where the foliage of wormwood has been cooked in; that flavor deviates only slightly from the **fat**. Similarly, when a tone is added to a fifth, it becomes a major sixth—not quite as sweet as the fifth, but not entirely unpleasant. Likewise, if a tone is added to a minor or major third, a fourth is made from both, which is not particularly consonant; but the <term>tritone<note>An interval of three whole tones, famously known as the "Devil in Music" for its extreme dissonance.</note></term> is the harshest of all. Therefore, the same thing happens when **bitter** is joined with the **insipid**, and even worse with the **astringent**, as in **bitter acorns**, than which nothing more dismal can be tasted. It is manifest, therefore, that this division of flavors corresponds perfectly with musical proportions.

Therefore, among flavors that harmonize in any way, if the proportion of the best flavor to the inferior is **double** (2:1), while the middle to the inferior is **one-and-one-third** (4:3), and the best to the middle is **one-and-one-half** (3:2), that best flavor will certainly be the most excellent. And first we see this in the **fat** compared to the **sharp** and **insipid**; for it is clear that of these, the **insipid** is the best because it can be endured by itself, the **salty** is the middle, and the **sharp** is the worst. Therefore, the insipid will exceed the salty by a ratio of 3:2, and the sharp by a ratio of 2:1, while the salty exceeds the sharp by 4:3. Again, if we couple the **sweet** with the **sharp** and the **insipid**, or with the **acidic** and **insipid**, the sweet will prevail, so that it exceeds the insipid by a double (2:1), quadruple (4:1), or eightfold (8:1) proportion—that is, by an **octave**, a **double octave**, or a **triple octave**. The **acidic**, meanwhile, will exceed the **insipid** by a ratio of 4:3.

Another reasoning regarding the combinations of flavors must be referred to the individual's own senses. Those flavors which provide the greatest pleasure to the taste can rightly be established as the **octave**. Half of that—as far as the ears are concerned—is the one-and-one-third (4:3) ratio from the less pleasant, and the 3:2 ratio from the middle. For example, let us suppose that for someone, **harsh** flavors are the most pleasant; for **salty** flavors are pleasant to no one, because no animal except man—indeed, not even plants, except for a very few of their own kind—can be nourished by salt. Since the salty is a part of the bitter, it is worse because it is sharp, which is why no animal is born in salt; whereas in wormwood, although it is very bitter, a small species of flies... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the comparison of life-sustaining properties of bitter vs. salty substances.</note>

What has been said of tastes ought to be said by exactly the same reasoning regarding smells and touch, since the logic is the same in all things. I truly marvel that no one until now has been found to assign individual names to these various smells, tastes, and touches, <margin>How individual names might be assigned to tastes and odors.</margin> since I see no difficulty in this; for a taste could be named after the things themselves, so that besides sweet, bitter, salty, sour, pungent, astringent, and fatty, there would be the "taste of such-and-such a fruit," the "taste of such-and-such a meat," the "taste of such-and-such a bread or cheese."
