If these things were done, something more exact could be established regarding the nature and harmony of these senses. But let others look into this. For us, it is enough to have demonstrated in some way that a certain wonderful harmony lies hidden under all things, as well as under the five senses.

# REGISTER IV.
## The Emotional Symphony, or on the Music of the Soul's various Affections toward one another.

That divine Harmonizer <note>Kircher uses "Harmosta," a Greek-derived term for a regulator or arranger, to describe God as the ultimate composer.</note> of things, after he had formed man from clay with a certain harmonic proportion of members, so that there might be some use for members so beautifully ordered; and so that he might turn out to be an instrument most perfect in every part, He placed within him the breath of life—I mean the spirit, or rational soul—rendered perpetually movable by a twofold appetite, as if by two wind-reservoirs or bellows. The first of these, on the side of the **sensory** <note>original: "αἰσθητικὸς"</note> faculty, <margin>The twofold appetite in man.</margin> is the origin of **disturbances and passions** <note>original: "παθημάτων"</note> of the soul; the other, on the side of reason, is the author of good habits, both natural and supernatural. Thus, a most beautiful organ soon shone forth in this worldly temple, whose foundations are the structure of the human body. The **Registers** are the principal organs of life: the heart, the liver, and the brain; the **bellows** are the sensory and rational appetites; the **spirit or air** is the vital faculty; the **keys** <note>original: "palmulæ siue tasti"</note> are the various "pathemata" themselves, which they call the passions of the soul. The **Organist** acts through the power of reason or the rational appetite; but the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note> or the sensory appetite, blind and headlong in its passions, strikes the keyboard of the passions through various apprehensions of evil or good. This is the same as an unskilled person in the art: when he does not know how to rightly arrange consonant keys with dissonant ones, instead of harmony, he produces a certain ridiculous, ill-sounding, and intolerable noise for the ears...

§. I.
*On the Music of Love.*

<margin>The Music of Love.</margin> 
**L**ove, insofar as it is a certain disturbance of the soul, has such power over the change of the pulse that many, following the example of Erasistratus <note>An ancient Greek physician who famously diagnosed "lovesickness" by watching a patient's pulse</note>, have convinced themselves that the arteries pulse in an "amorous" way. ## § II.
## On the harmonic enchantment of Love.

<margin>The enchantment of lovers.</margin>
That wondrous effect of reciprocal love has twisted the minds of almost all philosophers. We see it bind two people together so tightly—sometimes at first sight—that they can hardly be pulled apart. A person may frequent the company of beautiful youths or other people and cast their eyes over everyone; yet there is only one who strikes them, only one who pleases, only one whose friendship is sought. One person, even if unknown and never seen before, wounds the anxious mind above all others. There may be many in the same company, many in the same <term>academy</term> <note>original: "phrontisterio"; a place for study or reflection</note>; some may be beautiful and graceful, others physically deformed; some may be well-mannered and of high character, others rude and dissolute. Yet it happens that out of all these, only one pleases, only one is desperately longed for, and no other—even if that other is more beautiful or possesses better character. This "pleasing" is often mutual, though sometimes, without being returned, it exerts its force even upon one who resists. I say that while everyone has sought the cause of this,
<margin>How the Platonists explain enchantment.</margin>
hardly anyone has correctly assigned it. The Platonists, in their fashion, attribute it to a certain "enchantment." <note>original: "fascinum"; a spell or binding gaze</note> Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a famous Renaissance philosopher who merged Platonism with Christianity</note> declares all this beautifully through the example of Lysias and Phaedrus falling for one another: *Lysias,* he says, *gapes at the face of Phaedrus; Phaedrus fixes the sparks of his own eyes into the eyes of the other, and together with those sparks, he transmits his spirit. The ray of Phaedrus is easily joined to the ray of Lysias, and spirit is easily joined to spirit. A vapor of this kind, generated in the heart of Phaedrus, immediately seeks the heart of Lysias; by the density of Lysias's heart, the vapor becomes more compact and turns back into the original blood of Phaedrus, so that Phaedrus’s blood is now in the heart of Lysias. From this, both immediately burst into outcry: Lysias to Phaedrus, "My heart, Phaedrus, my dearest vitals!" and Phaedrus to Lysias, "O my spirit, O my blood, Lysias!" Lysias follows Phaedrus because his heart demands its fluid; Phaedrus pursues Lysias because the bloody fluid demands its own vessel and requires its own seat.* But Lysias pursues Phaedrus more ardently, for a heart lives more easily without a tiny particle of its fluid than the fluid itself lives without its own heart; for the stream delights more in the fountain than the fountain in the stream, etc.
<margin>Enchantment does not happen through the eyes.</margin>
The Platonists therefore think the enchantment of love is caused through the eyes. If they mean "visual rays" <note>the ancient theory that the eyes shoot out beams to see</note>, this is completely false, since according to the principles of Optics, rays are not emitted *from* the eyes, but are sent *from* the objects themselves into the visual faculty. Let us explain, therefore, how an enchantment of this kind actually happens.

It must be understood, then, that there is a certain remarkable similarity in the temperament of humans,
<margin>How love is born between similar people.</margin>
founded on a specific agitation of the spirits and the more subtle blood. This gives a corresponding form to each person's body; from this follows a similarity of character and actions. Since, by a natural appetite, like seeks the company of like, the same thing happens in humans that happens in **musical strings tuned to unison**: when one is struck, the other soon sounds in harmony. Thus, when someone in a general social gathering looks at another, the reason they are immediately captured by one person and not another is that the "pulses" in the agitation of their spirits are equal. Since the exact same actions and manners proceed from this, and their traces exhibit themselves in the eyes and in the conformity of outward actions, it is no wonder that another person endowed with a similar temperament, a similar pulse, and a similar agitation of spirits is moved—as if by a unison—at the very first sight, and takes fire in love as if toward a thing most identical to themselves. Add to this that in this effervescence of mutual love, the spirits, always agitated more and more vehemently and dilated, break out through the hidden channels of the eyes located near the corners [of the eyelids]...

...and there occurs a mutual communication of the most refined blood and <term>vital spirits</term> <note>In early modern physiology, "vital spirits" were believed to be subtle, air-like substances that moved through the blood to sustain life and transmit emotions.</note>, which produces certain behaviors in inseparable friends and the most discordant effects. ### §. III.
### On the Harmony of the Rational Appetite.

Having explained at length the Music of the sensitive Appetite and its effects in men in the preceding sections, it remains for us to discuss the Music of the rational soul with equal pace. The Appetite, being subject to frequent and turbulent passions, produces such dissonances that we might not inappropriately compare it to an unskilled Organist. Therefore, so that the organ may produce music that is perfect in every measure, a skilled organist must be summoned: namely, the **rational appetite**, or the dictate of right reason. For when reason tames the discordant and disordered <note>original: *ἀτάκτους* (ataktous)</note> passions, and when it throws the reins upon the lower appetite to subjugate it to the rational will, what else is it doing but reducing the strings—which are either tighter or looser than is proper—to a middle ground, binding the dissonant with the consonant with such dexterity that it forms a beautiful concord from them? However, for this to happen, the soul’s consensus with itself is necessary. For just as we feel the <margin>With what things the soul's dissonance is to be cured.</margin> torment of immense pain from the breaking of continuity and the tearing apart of our frame, so too does the soul suffer when it falls into a lack of moderation in the virtues due to the rebellion of the lower appetite. Indeed, when the framework of rational movements is loosened, the soul endures great punishments and torments; all the senses and all the limbs feel the punishment of this disorder <note>original: *ἀταξίας* (ataxias)</note> as if they were languid, though they ought to be ruled by the soul. Therefore, the Soul must be cured through true philosophy and the assiduous contemplation of virtue, through sacrifices, and the application of suitable expiations. Thus restored to health, strengthened by truth, and protected by such safeguards, it may fear nothing of the force of surging shocks; but being in agreement with itself, it may harmonize with all other things and receive friendly support for its growth from everyone. Where, however, the soul disagrees with itself, it is impossible for it to feel the harmonious symbols of others; for every soul disordered by passions is, as Saint Augustine witnesses, a punishment unto itself. Indeed, when uprightness is put to flight, order is disturbed and true peace—which is the "tranquillity of order"—goes into exile. In its place, harsh and unpleasant dissonances arise, such as perturbation, restlessness, inconstancy, affliction, and various kinds of torments; by these, the temperance of the soul, which is the best harmony of all virtues, is utterly destroyed.

Since, therefore, the virtues of the soul are its delights and the remedies for its diseases, it is necessary that they be harmonious, since health and delight are born only from things that are consonant; indeed, beautiful things...

But let us apply these things to the mystic Lyre: Man, therefore, ascending from the foundation of the civil <note>The "civil" or "political" virtues are the basic social ethics required to live in a community.</note> virtues and raised up to the purgative virtues, is seen to complete the first interval of the **octave**; but being carried up from this to another **octave** of the heroic virtues, he produces a most finished harmony through the mediation of the remaining virtues. To be sure, the civil virtues—through discretion, prudence, and deliberation—temper the motions of the sensory appetite so that nothing is committed against the right dictate of reason. The Purgative virtues—Temperance, Chastity, Patience, and Humility—do not merely restrain these motions, but utterly exterminate them, so much so that the mere presence of reason (the empress of the appetites) is sufficient to suppress them. By these virtues, the soul is freed from disturbances and renders itself a most well-tempered instrument. 

Indeed, the Political virtues compose the exterior of men—that is, they establish the first steps of the harmony. The Purgative virtues, through the first **octave**, cleanse the spirit, and so that the whole might emerge harmonious, they render it tuneful. The Heroic virtues, however, <margin>Harmony of the virtues.</margin> elevate the mind to the supreme concert; they unite and identify man with the Intelligences <note>In this context, "Intelligences" refers to angelic beings or higher spiritual realities.</note> and thus with GOD himself. For as the Philosopher <note>Usually referring to Aristotle.</note> rightly says, men are made Gods through the excellence of virtue. And Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher whose ideas heavily influenced Christian mysticism.</note> says: *The study and the vow of the Heroic person is not only to be free from sin, but to be GOD, and to return to that place from whence he proceeded.* Moreover, when we return to where we proceeded from, we then complete the perfect **octave**, in which the tone returns to the same step and key from which it had departed, as is well known to musicians. 

You see, therefore, in the present diagram, how the Soul—beginning from Justice or conversion—reaches the **double octave** by little steps through harmonic degrees, all the way to that uniting love, which is the goal and center of the entire harmonic system. But having now examined the symphony of the soul with the virtues, nothing remains except that we show how, and by what means, we can compose this harmony in the soul, so that we may finally attain that end of harmony, which is peace, tranquility, and a certain blessedness of the soul on this earth. For through this harmony, joined to the archetypal harmony, one is made happy in oneself, blessed, and a sharer with the children of GOD. 

For since GOD is the first rule and moderator of all contingent things, <margin>How we are united to GOD.</margin> He is necessarily always in tune; indeed, He is that "One" and the harmonic power through which all things agree and are made tuneful. For this reason, the Sacraments were ordained as signs of sacred and Divine things and as if they were the producing causes—namely, as tokens <note>original: "τεκμήρια" (tekmēria)</note> of divine grace and heavenly favor, by whose help man is led to the proper concert with GOD.

Order is therefore necessary in all things, as Boniface beautifully stated, as recorded by **Gratian** <note>original: "Gratiano"; referring to the "Decretum Gratiani," the fundamental collection of Canon Law in the Catholic Church.</note>: "By <margin>The order of the world is necessary.</margin> this promise of divine dispensation," he says, "He established that there be distinct degrees and orders, so that while the lesser show reverence to the more powerful, and the powerful bestow love upon the lesser, a true concord might be made, a texture woven from diversity, and the administration of individual offices might be rightly carried out." Indeed, because every creature cannot be governed or live in one and the same quality, the example of the heavenly hosts instructs us: for while there are Angels, there are also Archangels, who, though they are not equal, differ one from another in power and order, as is well known. Thus, a Republic could not possibly consist if all were equal. For what kingdom is safe where the guardian of the people is fear? What city is secure in which a multitude lives suppressed by force and arms? Therefore, for the Republic to harmonize perfectly with itself, the **tritone** <term>tritone: a harsh musical interval of three whole steps, historically known as "the interval of the devil" for its dissonance</term> must be removed; the tritone with the **fifth** <term>diapente: the musical interval of a perfect fifth</term> must be avoided; the **fourth** <term>diatessaron: the musical interval of a perfect fourth</term> with the **minor third** <term>semiditono</term> or **major third** <term>ditono</term> must be utterly eradicated; the **octave** <term>diapason</term> with the fourth, and similar monsters of maximum dissonance must be fled from by all means. This is to say: dissensions, riots, the prevalence of the worst morals, and the splitting of the established Religion into various heresies should by no means be permitted; for these have at all times been the greatest seeds of huge calamities and the overturning of Kingdoms and Empires.

And from these things, perhaps declared more extensively than was proper, it is sufficiently clear in what true harmony in the Republic consists. Nothing remains, therefore, except that we now show what proportion belongs to each of the three states of the political world—Monarchical, Aristocratic, and Democratic—as well as the Economic, so that they may coalesce into perfect harmony.

### On the three proportions fitting the triple state of the world:

Three types of proportions are considered by Geometers: Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic. When equal amounts are added to some numbers without considering their magnitude, then it is an **arithmetic proportion**.

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of how mathematical proportions—arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic—serve as the underlying fabric of human society, shifting from pure theory to practical applications in governance and law.</meta>

436 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

<margin>Aristocracy requires geometric proportion.</margin>
...is perhaps obtained by chance, as by a lot; where in place of a lot, other means of acquisition can also exist. Conversely, just as in **geometric proportion** the differences between numbers are matched to the numbers themselves (so that a large number has a large difference), so too in a **Republic of the Best** <note>The "Optimates," referring to an aristocratic form of government.</note> persons are distinguished, and burdens, rewards, offices, and duties are likewise distinguished. The most excellent roles are reserved for the Best, while the remainder are left to the common people. In such a state, it is necessary that an **arithmetic proportion** be admitted separately within each faction; for regarding those things which belong to the people, all who are among the people shall decide by lot; and regarding those things which belong to the Best, all the Best shall decide. Unless this is done, there will be permanent ranks within the people reaching down to the very dregs of the populace, and permanent ranks among the Best reaching up to the Prince of the Republic, by which reasoning it would not be a Republic, but a certain royal kind of City.

<margin>The Monarch loves harmonic proportion.</margin>
The **Royal state**, truly, even if it is most especially likened to geometric proportion—because all rights of the Magistrate are reserved for the King, just as he himself excels all others either by noble lineage, or by arms, or by virtues—nevertheless, the method of governing in this state can be most rightly tempered from both types of proportion. For one King, the arbiter of all, dispenses everything between the Best and the common people, not by blind impulse like a lot, but by the reasoning of virtue, merit, order, and rank. He executes all parts of **distributive** and **commutative justice**; the joining of both these proportions is sufficient to constitute a **harmonic proportion**. Thus, from justice, which embraces all methods of governing, a triple form of justice results: **commutative**, which consists in arithmetic proportion; **distributive**, which consists in geometric; and **musical**, which consists in a mixture of both. To these correspond the three daughters of Themis: *Eunomia* (Good Law), *Epieikeia* (Equity), and *Eirene* (Peace) <note>original Greek: εὐνομία, ἐπιεικεία, & εἰρήνη</note>, serving as the tutelary guardians of the three proposed proportions.

<margin>A rare example of commutative justice.</margin>
A clear example of these proportions is found in the *Education of Cyrus* <note>Referring to Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*, a semi-fictional biography of Cyrus the Great.</note>. When Cyrus was a boy, he saw a tall man wearing a short tunic and a small boy nearby wearing a loose, long tunic. He judged that they should swap tunics so that what was suitable might fall to each. His Master, however, declared that what belonged to each should be left to each. But if the tall man had been ordered to pay some money to the small boy, and only then the exchange was made, the Master might have seemed to have advised his pupil excellently. Here, Cyrus urged **geometric proportion** by measuring the clothes to the bodies; the Master urged **arithmetic** by protecting the possessions of each. But a third way would have looked at both at once: both the physical need and the safety of each person’s property. Thus, one chooses a **harmonic** mixture of the two previous ways; in this manner, the common advantage of both is compared to the sweetness of a musical harmony. A father also uses this tempering—

<margin>Example from a surgeon.</margin>
—in giving rewards. For a doctor <note>original: *Lithotomo*, literally a "stone-cutter," refers to a surgeon who specializes in removing bladder stones.</note> often demands 500 gold pieces to remove a bladder stone, but from a poor man he asks for nothing but small scraps of bread. If he were to follow arithmetic or geometric analogy strictly in every case, one patient would die of the stone and the other of hunger; but by **harmonic reasoning**, wealth is provided to the doctor and health to the poor man. 

<margin>Harmonic proportion in the laws of marriage.</margin>
The use of these proportions is also seen in the laws of marriage. For example, if patricians <note>The hereditary noble class.</note> are ordered to marry patrician women and plebeians to marry plebeians, this is a **geometric similarity**. But if marriages were sought indiscriminately by lot, or if one contended as much as possible for beauty, wealth, or virtue without respect for lineage, and no condition was forbidden, this would be an **arithmetic condition**. Truly, in the former case, the minds of the citizens are torn into factions; in the latter, the social orders are confused; both are ruinous to the Republic. Whence legal experts persuade us to occasionally permit wealthy plebeian marriages for the poorer patricians, and for wealthy plebeians to marry impoverished patrician women. This is advantageous to both orders: to the Nobles, so that increased wealth may protect the status they hold and their women may be married; and to the common people, so that with an entrance to honors opened, they may apply themselves to virtue. Finally, it benefits the Republic, so that the orders may embrace one another with mutual charity. 

<margin>Harmonic proportion must be observed in the laws of the banquet.</margin>
The same must be observed in the **law of banquets**, in which not geometric alone, nor arithmetic alone, but a harmonic proportion mixed from both holds a place. Indeed, an arithmetic equality in banquets is inept if people take their seats indiscriminately without any consideration of sex, condition, age, or status. A geometric arrangement is also tasteless; for if everyone is learned, how will they benefit the unlearned? If the loud are with the loud, who will be the author of modesty for them? If the melancholic are with the melancholic, what [joy] in that place...

<margin>In the laws of friendship, harmonic proportion must be observed.</margin>

...in the place of delights, is there not pleasantness? Therefore, the law ought to be tempered according to <term>harmonic proportion</term> <note>Harmonic proportion is a mathematical relationship often used in music to create pleasing chords; here, the author applies it to social balance.</note>. This harmonic proportion and concord is also observed in the entire scope of human life as love, which is the foundation of friendship. For if a mere equality of duties is introduced by <term>arithmetic law</term> <note>Arithmetic equality means everyone gets exactly the same thing, regardless of their status or needs.</note>, there will be no friendship except among equals. If, however, between unequals there is a mere and exquisite similarity of duties according to <term>geometric proportion</term> <note>Geometric proportion provides rewards or duties based on a person’s status or merit, rather than giving everyone the same amount.</note>, there will be friendship in neither case, but rather a perpetual business transaction and a "market-day" of duties for the sake of one's own advantage. From this arises the necessary

<margin>comparison</margin>

association of patron and client, without which there is no freedom to demonstrate love, and nothing spontaneous. Thus, this arithmetic equality is most beautifully likened to an iron ruler, which does not know how to bend; geometric similarity is likened to a <term>Lesbian rule</term> <note>original: "regulae Lesbiæ"; a flexible lead ruler used by ancient masons to measure curved surfaces, symbolizing adaptable but potentially inconsistent standards.</note> made of lead, adaptable to all angles. But the harmonic proportion is likened to a wooden ruler, which, when bent, immediately returns to its shape. In

<margin>The office of the Judge corresponds to Arithmetic proportion.</margin>

the governance of all kinds of states, the rigor of the laws and the office of the judge are compared to arithmetic equality. This not only grants to each person exactly what is theirs, but also imposes punishments on delinquents equally without respect for their person. By this, judges are bound to the laws and to the evidence and proofs, so that they may judge according to them, even if the laws seem unjust. In turn, equality and the pure will of the magistrate—provided he

<margin>Geometric proportion is appropriate for the Magistrate.</margin>

is good and acts according to conscience—takes on the nature of geometric proportion. Others, following the example of harmonic tempering, place the duty of either the higher courts or the supreme magistrate between these two. These are not permitted to act out of pure whim, and yet they are allowed to bend the laws according to the reason of the circumstances, in the manner of a wooden ruler, without breaking them, and to interpret those laws in judgments according to <term>equity</term> <note>Equity refers to the principle of fairness that looks at the spirit of the law rather than just the literal text.</note>.

<margin>In sumptuary laws, geometric proportion must be observed.</margin>

Furthermore, in <term>sumptuary laws</term> <note>original: "legibus vestiarijs"; laws intended to restrain luxury or dictate clothing based on social class.</note>, much is held regarding geometric proportion: that the higher the rank of dignity a person holds, the more precious the adornment of clothing permitted to them. Here, arithmetic equality is intolerable. However, because it is not only the variety of ranks that demands distinction in dress, but also some account must be taken of wealth and some of merit, and since all ranks cannot be constrained by a single law, a tempering of both proportions is usually inserted into the laws themselves, or is partly

<margin>In penal laws, harmonic proportion must be observed.</margin>

left to the judgment of the governors. This harmonic proportion is also preserved in penal laws according to the requirement of vindictive justice, namely, that punishment be inflicted on delinquents according to the gravity of the crime. Indeed, the law of retaliation <note>original: "poena talionis"; the "eye for an eye" principle.</note> favors arithmetic proportion, while the law of fines favors geometric proportion. In this way, in other laws—such as those of voting, the restitution of creditors, interest, rewards, wages, and inheritances—just as a triple proportion can always be seen, so the harmonic is the best of all.

<margin>Geometric proportion is appropriate for an Aristocratic state.</margin>

In a Democratic government, arithmetic equality holds the greatest place. In an Aristocratic state, geometric similarity prevails, though in this case a method of tempering is often used. For example, when the people themselves, though holding power, voluntarily entrust honors, magistracies, and priesthoods chiefly to the Patricians; or when the Nobles make the common people partakers of some honors, giving the most profitable offices to the commoners alone, and most severely avenging injuries done to them by the Nobles. They grant the freedom of enjoying pleasures, which in itself

<margin>How harmonic proportion is disturbed in the Republic.</margin>

tastes of a popular state, and they permit the commoners a certain right of voting in naming a certain number of candidates from the Noble class, from which number the Nobles themselves afterwards entrust the magistracies to whomever they wish. Indeed, as long as this communion stands by the will of that order which holds supreme power, the sweetest harmony of concord among citizens endures. But if it is revoked, first the complaints of the penalized party emerge, then discords follow as if the harmony were disturbed, and finally, either the power is transferred, or the entire city falls to its enemies.

<margin>In a monarchical state, arithmetic equality cannot exist.</margin>

The same must be held in a Royal or Monarchical state, to which the harmonic ratio is familiar. In such a state, as much as one person stands above all others, so much does he alone possess the supreme right of empire; the rest live under him in arithmetic equality.
Therefore, in the form of politics, there can be three types of governing: For if a King communicates all duties equally, with no distinction between the nobility and the commoners, the moderation will be popular and similar to the arithmetic style. This is not becoming to the Supreme Majesty, since the Sovereign himself would be joined with the lowest commoner with no middle rank interposed. Indeed, citizens of noble character...

Finally, the **Body** of the Republic consists of the princes subject to the King, the Magistrates, and the People. # Book X. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature. 441

<margin>How the nature of the soul is understood to be formed from numbers.</margin>

For the **triad** <note>The number three.</note> is simple, insofar as it is indivisible and incapable of any expansion or contraction; yet it is composed of the even and the odd. However, it is composed of nothing but itself, for according to **Plato**, nothing can be conceived before the existence of number. If anyone were to conceive of three "units" before the triad itself, those units would not constitute a triad unless he conceived of them as united; but three units joined together is properly what a triad is. Therefore, it is composed of itself. And because it is composed of itself—of the one and the other, the same and the different, the even and the odd, the divisible and the indivisible—it must be so composed. 

Now, a number composed in this way is conceived as if it were moving itself. For this reason, the **Ancients** beautifully compared the rational soul to number: for the soul is both simple and composite. Yet, it is composite in such a way that it does not arise from something else; rather, since the soul exists only as an immediate creation of **GOD** (who is simplicity itself), it is a "composite simplicity" flowing from that pure simplicity. Thus, just as number is a "living thing" composed of even and odd, divisible and indivisible, the soul—insofar as it is life—can be conceived as a **numbering number** <term>numerus numerans: a philosophical concept where the mind acts as the active force that counts and organizes reality, rather than just being a passive symbol.</term> composed of the sensible (the divisible) and the intellectual (the indivisible).

Hence, the soul beholds harmonies within itself. It measures external harmony against its own internal, intellectual harmony via a "corruptible ray" <note>This likely refers to the visual or auditory senses which are "corruptible" compared to the eternal mind.</note>. And since it possesses within itself the number that counts all things, it contains the harmonic proportion of all things within its own beauty. 

<margin>Which number is understood here.</margin>

We are speaking here not of **mathematical number**, but of **symbolic and rational number** which proceeds from the Divine Mind. Mathematical number is merely a certain image and likeness of this. Just as our mind stands in relation to the Divine Mind, so the number of our mind stands in relation to the number of the Divine Mind. But let these things be demonstrated more clearly.

<margin>What the first originated principle is.</margin>

It must be understood that there can be only one infinite principle <note>The Creator.</note>, and this is infinitely simple. However, the **first originated principle** <term>primum principiatum: the first thing brought into being by God, often identified by these philosophers as the World Soul or the Primordial Light.</term>, as the philosophers call it, cannot be infinitely simple. Nor can it be composed of other parts that make it up, for if the parts preceded it in nature, it would not be the "first" originated thing. 

Therefore, it must be conceded that the first originated principle is composite in such a way that it is not made of "others," but is **composed of itself**. It is impossible to assign this kind of "self-composition" to anything other than **number**, or to the number of our mind. 

The whole matter is placed beautifully before our eyes by the **equilateral triangle**, whose rationale and essence cannot be conceived unless three equal lines are joined into a triangle. 

                      a
                     / \
                    /   \ [A diagram of an equilateral triangle with vertices labeled a, b, c]
                   /     \
                  b-------c

Considered separately, lines **a**, **b**, and **c** are not united, and thus they cannot represent the essence of a triangle. Just as a triangle cannot be conceived without three equal straight lines being united, so the **triad** cannot be conceived without three units being united. This union creates a certain "composite"—not made of matter and form, but as has been said, a union of the one and the other, the even and the odd, the divisible and the indivisible. In a similar way, the **Soul** is formed, as will be declared shortly.

Furthermore, when we look precisely at "unity" within a number, we see nothing other than an **uncomposed composition**; or to speak more clearly, a *coincidence* <note>original: ὁμόπτωσιν (homoptōsin) — a falling together or overlapping.</note> of simplicity and composition, or of unity and multitude. For when we behold a composite unity within a number, we immediately contemplate a **perfect harmony**, such as we find in the harmonic unities of the **Octave**, the **Fifth**, and the **Fourth** <note>original: diapason, diapente, & diatessaron.</note>.

<margin>Harmonic and Geometric comparisons.</margin>

For a harmonic relationship is a unity that cannot be conceived without number. Anyone who searches deeply into the relationship of the parts of a **tone** and an **octave** divided in two will find that they relate to one another in exactly the same way as the **side of a square relates to its diagonal**. <note>This refers to the "irrational" ratio of 1 to the square root of 2. The author is noting that geometry and music both lead to numbers that the human mind finds mysterious or "transcendent."</note> We find this number to be "simpler" than the reason of the human mind can grasp. For since there is no [rational] proportion there, it cannot be a [standard] number—yet number cannot be conceived without relationship, and such a number would have to be even and odd at the same time. Who does not see how difficult this is to conceive? 

We have, therefore, what the **first originated principle** is and how it comes to be. Number bears the "type" or pattern of this principle, and it is nothing other than **symbolic number**. For number is the subject of proportion, and proportion is the "seat" of form; and just as proportion cannot exist without number, so a form cannot shine forth without a fitting and congruent proportion...

<margin>The exemplary unity cannot exist without number.</margin>
cannot shine forth. For the eternal mind acts in the manner of a Musician who, in order to bring his internal concept out into the world to be met by the senses, brings many voices into a congruent proportion of harmony and adapts them; thus it happens that in that harmonic proportion, when it is there as if in its own place, it shines forth most sweetly and perfectly. 

<margin>How the divine mind conceives.</margin>
Therefore, in the mind and from the mind come number and all things; indeed, the plurality of things is nothing other than the number of the divine mind. 

<margin>How number exists in the mind of the Creator.</margin>
For because the divine mind is one, and understands one thing in one way and another in another, there arose a multitude of all things, which we assert to be nothing other than a certain intermediate "reason of understanding" of the divine mind. 

<margin>How number becomes one and all things.</margin>
Hence the first exemplar in the mind of the Creator is necessarily number. The delight and beauty that exist in all things bear witness to this; for beauty consists in proportion, and proportion consists in number. Consequently, number is the most fit instrument for investigating wisdom more deeply. 

<margin>Solution to the proposed difficulty.</margin>
Since our own mind is such a likeness and a perfect image of the divine mind, the exemplar for our mind's conceptions can be nothing other than number. For without number, there is no distinction, no comparison, no notion, and no measurement. For who could define? Who could distinguish? Who could discern and divide without number? Since one thing is substance, another is quantity, and another quality, who could comprehend these as distinct things without number? Since, therefore, number is the "reason of understanding," nothing can be conceived without it. But let us explain how this number is both "one" and "all things."

<margin>The One, the peak of many things.</margin>
If, then, the "one" is in every way nothing but one, how can all things be in it, or how can it be all things? For if all things are in it, the one will be a multitude; if it itself is all things, it will also be a multitude. Therefore, the one will be both one and a multitude; and insofar as it is one, it will produce a multitude within itself, and insofar as that multitude is produced, it will produce itself, and it will be the thing produced rather than the source. Or, as the "one" is the principle (the source), and as the multitude is the result, the question and the reasoning fall into the same absurdity. What then should be said? What way can be found so that the one is only one, and yet is likewise all things?

<margin>All things can be taken in a threefold way.</margin>
I say, therefore, that all things are not everywhere distinct in their multitude. For since "multitude" implies number, and every number is necessarily distinct by its individual species and proceeds from its own unity repeatedly folded into itself, every unity will necessarily have a respect for the multitude that follows it, and being derived from the "one," it will depend on that same one. 

<margin>How multitude exists in the one.</margin>
The one, however, is a certain peak of many things, just as unity is the peak of numbers. But so that these things may be better understood, it must be known that "all things" can be taken in a threefold way: namely, all things **unitarily**, all things **united**, and all things **distinct** and thus multiplied. 

We explain that first, more hidden concept in this way: In the One all things exist, but in its own way, just as in another way all things exist in unity, and in a third way proper to itself, all things exist in a multitude. In the One, I say, all things are in their own way and—if it is permitted to speak thus—<note>original: "ἑνιαίως"</note> *unitarily*, which is to say: as one, indiscriminately, indistinctly, indivisibly, and "onely." That is, so that although they are "all things," they are yet "one" rather than "all." For the "one" exists through itself and by its nature and primarily; it is "all things" only insofar as it holds them within itself indistinctly and unitarily, and insofar as it is the cause of all things. 

Therefore, that first "One," on which all other things depend as one, is necessarily either truly one or not truly one. If it were not truly one, it would be either many or nothing. Since this is absurd, the former cannot be asserted; therefore, it is neither nothing nor many. Consequently, it will be truly one, and nothing other than one—simply one. Indeed, it is the supreme simplicity and, as a result, the extreme absolute. If it is the supreme absolute, it is therefore the supreme perfection, or rather the most perfect; if it is the most perfect, it is the most sufficient; if it is the most sufficient, it is therefore the best and the supreme good. 

But who does not see this multitude emerging from the One, shining forth in simplicity, absoluteness, perfection, sufficiency, and goodness, as if they were so many attributes of the One, as we descend from the "one" to the "senary" <note>The number six. Kircher often associates the number six with the attributes of God or the days of creation.</note>? Truly, he who has well understood what preceded will clearly see that this "senary" (this group of six), considered in itself, is truly and properly one, and is only divided by our own mind. For if someone asks us: "What is the one?" We answer immediately: "One." "What is the one?" "Simplicity." "What is the one?" "Absoluteness." "What is the one?" "Perfection." "What is the one?" "Sufficiency." "What is the one?" "The Good." And conversely...

### §. II.
### On the harmony of the [mental] power toward objects.

It has already been shown many times that when a string is struck, it causes another similar to it to vibrate, even if the second is untouched. Our mind is like a **multi-stringed instrument** <note>original: "polychordum"</note>, bringing forth the forms of things from itself by the power of assimilation. In sight, it assimilates itself to visible things; in hearing, to things heard; in taste, to things tasted; in smell, to things smelled; in touch, to things felt; in sense, to things sensed; in imagination, to things imagined; and in reason, to things reasoned. <margin>The mind conforms itself to objects through **species**. <note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental "images" or "forms" that represent objects to our senses.</note></margin> For an image exists in the absence of sensory things, just as a sense exists without the discernment and distinction of sensory things. In the presence of non-sensory <term>species</term> <note>Mental representations of things.</note>, our mind is carried and excited by the "vehicle of the spirit." By meeting the species represented by objects, the mind conforms itself entirely through these species, so that it may form a judgment about the object through assimilation. Whence that vital spirit, animated by the mind, is shaped into the likeness of the presented species by the movement of the spirit—just as flexible wax is configured to a shape by the application of a craftsman. <margin>How the mind sees, hears, etc.</margin> In a similar way, the mind creates various configurations in the organs according to the varying agitation of the spirits, and according to the condition and quality of those organs. In the optic nerve, it is conformed not to sounds, but to the species of colors; in the auditory drum of the ear, it is conformed not to color, but to the species of sounds; and so on for the others. In the "phantastic" <note>imagination-related</note> organ, it can be configured to the forms of all sensory species in an indistinct way, whereas in the "noetic" or reasoning organ, it is configured to all sensory things in a distinct and clear way. These configurations, because they occur by means of corporeal spirits, are the assimilations of sensory things. After these, our mind—not as it is immersed in the body which it animates, but as it is a mind capable of being united to the body in itself—looks toward its own immutability. <margin>How the mind abstracts.</margin> It performs an assimilation of forms, not as they are in and of themselves and immutable; it conceives the "whatness" <note>the essence or "quiddity"</note> of things, using itself as an instrument without the need for any organic spirit. For example, when it conceives a **circle** to be a figure in which all lines drawn from the center to the circumference are equal, it is occupied with a truth that is free from matter. It is impossible for radii to be precisely equal in physical matter, and much less can a mathematical circle be described upon a material subject. Therefore, the circle in the mind is the **model** for the circle that can be drawn on paper. And when the mind performs these assimilations as it exists in itself and abstracted from matter, it is by this very act that it assimilates itself to abstract forms. Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature. 445

In the Angel, God conceived all creatures; He then brought them forth visibly, created them in substance, and completed matter. You will understand this better through a musical example: <margin>Harmonic comparison</margin> an organ player <note>original: "Organædus"</note> first conceives a most beautiful organ in his mind, then leads his concept into a physical work, and thirdly produces harmony, which is the ultimate goal of his art. The first conception of God corresponds to the first stage of the musician. The second stage to the second, and the third to the third. Thus, from God—the source of all—two intellects first emanated: the Angelic and the human. <margin>Two intellects emanated from God: first the Angelic, and then the human.</margin> The former is pure, separate, and simple; the latter is joined to a body and to matter. The former was made from the beginning in the "act" of knowing all things, and thus knows everything; the latter was made from the start as a being capable of all things—possessing the "potential" for all—and is finally perfected in the "act" of knowing all through science. Hence, the Angelic intellect, being entirely a substantial unity, represents the nature of an indivisible point; the human intellect, which is perfected gradually, represents a line, which is the unfolding and flow of a point. Therefore, the Angelic intellect differs from the human just as any two opposites do: <margin>How the human and Angelic intellects differ.</margin> act and potency, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, beginning and end, the immobile and the mobile, nature and art, the consonant and the dissonant. Yet, I would not have these opposites understood as being in conflict with one another, but rather as looking toward one another from opposite sides, turning toward each other so that one might perfect the other—just as act perfects potency, light perfects darkness, knowledge perfects ignorance, nature perfects art, and the consonant perfects the dissonant. For whatever is present in the Angelic intellect from the beginning is present in the human intellect at its end. <margin>The angelic intellect exists by way of a beginning; man’s by way of an end.</margin> For the Angel is the beginning of God's Creation and the noblest creature, from whom the line of creatures began to unfold; man, however, is the end of God's Creation and the "period" <note>The author uses "period" in the classical sense of a full circle or completion of a cycle.</note> or completion of all creatures, being only slightly lower than the Angel. And just as the Angelic intellect is, from the beginning, in the being and "act" of all things, so is the human intellect at its conclusion; the Angel is perfected by nature, the man by art. Hence, while there is a supreme inequality between the two at the start, there is a maximum equality at the end; for the human intellect becomes as much through art as the Angelic is by nature. <margin>Various comparisons of both intellects.</margin> The Angelic intellect is immobile, existing in a single, simple, and indivisible state before and above all things; it is all things in its own being without needing the individual "species" <note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental images or forms of things.</note> of things. The human intellect, however, is mobile through all things, becoming all things by running through the individual forms and actions of them all.

From this it is clear that only three things were created by God: the two extremes—the Angelic and human intellect—and the medium, which is the sensible creature, or the "Greater World" <note>The Macrocosm or the physical universe.</note>. Each of these is a whole and a totality, and each is in each. The first extreme, the Angelic intellect, is the "being" of all things and the universal act of all; the other extreme, the human intellect, is the "possibility" of all things and the universal potency of all. <margin>Both intellects are the boundaries of the entire sensible creation.</margin> Whatever sensible creatures are left between these two intellects are all composed, according to their substance, of act and potency. Therefore, both intellects are the natural boundaries and goals of all worldly and sensible things. The Angelic is the beginning of every creature; the human is the completion and end of every creature. All things exist in a higher way in the Angelic intellect before they exist according to their own forms; they exist in the human intellect after they have existed according to matter and substance. And just as in the lowest order of things both extremes are one, so also must the medium be one. First, He made the Angelic intellect before all things; the medium He made as all things in all things and as individuals within themselves; and finally, or after all things, He fashioned the human intellect. Both intellects are directed toward the same object: the Supreme Good, which is the uncreated Truth, by whose natural light they are both illuminated.

Thus, the Angelic intellect proceeds from God immediately through the circuit of sensible creatures, and man—having been procreated as man and imbued with the forms of all things—finally ends in God. You see, therefore, a certain admirable circle in the creation of all things.

Furthermore, the Angelic intellect is "impassible" <note>Meaning it cannot be changed or affected by external things.</note>, while the human is "passible"—not indeed of itself, but <margin>The angelic intellect is impassible; the human is passible.</margin> because of Memory, in which the images of things and intellectual forms are received. As soon as the intellect has captured these from the world and from sensible substances, it is accustomed to entrust them to the internal storehouse of memory for future true turnings and <margin>Comparison of Memory with the Intellect.</margin> cyclical movements of contemplation and speculation within itself. Indeed, it is so much the case that the intellect is like an eye, memory is like a mirror, and the intellectual form is like an image shining in the mirror...

**Book 10. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature. 447**

They possess and obtain access to being itself; therefore, the soul is not a **blank slate** <note>original: "tabula rasa"</note> void of all notions, but rather, as Proclus <note>A fifth-century Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced medieval and Renaissance thought</note> testifies, it is a **tablet always written upon**, and she herself writes upon herself and is filled with writings from the mind. The mind, or intellect, is a certain thing that is fertile within itself, revolving according to the prior intellect as an image of it, and it is a figure or **type** <note>A symbolic representation or pattern</note> made externally. For if that higher intellect is all things intellectually, then the soul will be all things "animally" <note>Livingly, or in the manner of a soul</note>; and if that is all things in an exemplary way, the soul will be in the manner of an image; and if that is contracted and united, the soul is divided. When Plato understood this, he constituted the soul out of all things, and divided it according to numbers, and bound it back together by analogies and harmonic ratios, and brought into it the first principles that produce shapes, and he moves the circles existing intellectually within it. <margin>The soul becomes all things through understanding.</margin> Therefore, all **mathematical things** are first in the soul: numbers moving themselves exist before the numbers we see, vital figures exist before apparent figures, and the very ratios of concords or harmonies exist before things are tuned or arranged.

We can, however, consider two faculties existing here regarding harmonic proportions: first, that which acts through mental discourse, and second, the operative faculty. The mental is again twofold: it is either the **inventive** faculty of proportions from abstract qualities, or the **recognitive** faculty of chosen proportions in sensible things. Therefore, the faculty that investigates harmonic ratios is the same one that embraces the rest of the sciences and arts—namely, the superior part of the human soul. But that faculty which notices and recognizes noble proportions from sensory things, or even in other things established outside itself, is a lower faculty of the soul. It informs the senses most closely, or is an even lower **vital faculty** which neither reasons nor exists in humans alone, but also in the irrational soul <note>The "anima irrationalis," or the soul of animals which lacks human reason</note>. But if it is incapable of reasoning, and cannot grasp the science of harmonic proportions, it is asked: from where does it obtain the ability to recognize them when they are presented from the outside? <margin>How the soul knows things presented from without.</margin> For to recognize is to compare an external sensory object with internal ideas and judge it to be fitting. I respond that the ideas or formal ratios of harmonies are present in all those things that possess the said faculty of recognition; even if they are not received within through reasoning, they instead depend on a **natural instinct** and are born with them—just as the number of leaves is born with the forms of plants in a flower, or the proportionate disposition of colors in feathers, flowers, and birds. <margin>Examples from natural things.</margin> This experience in plants produces something similar to harmonic proportions; indeed, I would not easily deny that even the vegetative faculty in plants themselves has its own way of recognizing harmonic proportions latent in their "plastic and chromatic virtue" <note>The natural power to shape matter and create color</note>. Thus it happens that uneducated boys, farmers, barbarians, and even wild beasts themselves perceive the sweet harmonies of voices. If you ask where this instinct comes from, I shall either flee to **GOD**, who forms and presides over all these forms in bodies as images of Himself according to His mastery; He inserts harmonic proportions into the plastic and chromatic virtue and makes them carry these with them, just as He Himself embraced them in His mind from eternity and expressed them in creation. <margin>The reason why the soul is delighted by harmony.</margin> Or, what comes to the same thing, I will cite the kinship indicated above of these souls (even the lower ones) with the **circle**, according to which they are composed and shaped as if by a norm and law; and with the circle and its demonstrability, they have put on the idea of harmonic proportions depending therefrom.

Furthermore, the means used by these lower faculties of the soul to perceive the harmonies of external things are the same as those by which they receive the external objects themselves: if they are sensible, they are perceived by the senses. All of this will be explained most fully in *Hieroglyphic Theology*, God willing. <margin>Imperceptible harmony.</margin> Namely, that the faculties of the soul informing the senses are themselves no less involved in the comparison of certain things than the superior faculty, although by instinct rather than discourse. Thus, consonant sounds are distinguished from dissonant ones by the **acoustic faculty**. In this way, architectural proportions are perceived by the eyes; by the virtue of sight, they are judged as fitting or unfitting. If, however, the things themselves in which the harmonic ratio exists are not sensible, but perhaps perceivable by another faculty, those same proportions of things reflect within the soul.

Nonetheless, in the lower faculties of the soul, this perception of harmonies is dull, obscure, and in a way material, hidden as if under a cloud of ignorance: so it is, when seeing...

When we see something, we do not notice that we are seeing it; such are those movements and terrors celebrated by the **Stoics**, which are natural, occurring without deliberation and beyond the will. <note>original: "motus illi & pauores à Stoicis celebrati". The author refers to the Stoic concept of *propatheiai*, or involuntary emotional "pre-reactions" like flinching or blushing that happen before the mind can process them.</note> Such also is the natural affection of hate or love, which is of a primary and wondrous nature, and which we have discussed extensively above. When the soul, through the harmony of the limbs, the similarity of spirits, and the qualities of the voice and temperament, senses a goodness or likeness to its own in another soul, it breaks out into a wonderful flame toward that person. Thus, someone may love another and not know why, or what it is in that person they love most, which no one else could provide. 

But the <term>physiologist (in this historical context, one who studies the inner workings of nature and the body)</term>, coming upon the scene and understanding the hidden characters of the harmony or disharmony operating within, finds in both people a similarity or dissimilarity of certain habits. If these are dissonant, they will generate natural aversion and strife; if they are consonant, they will generate friendship. To this we must also refer that entire <term>physiognomic instinct (the intuitive ability to judge character from physical features)</term>, which, although it is mute and unreasoning, is the sole interpreter and arbiter of human affairs. For a person obtains only as much prosperity (speaking naturally) as their face, the proportions of their body, their gait, and the movement of their limbs find favor with those in power, and as much as they creep into their favor as if by a hidden force, even when those in power have used no deliberation on the matter. Indeed, they often testify that they love or hate someone without knowing for what reason. Such, I say, is the sense of proportions within the lower faculties of the soul, which occurs without conscious awareness. It is also clear from this why humans are naturally delighted by music; but since we have dealt with this at length in the seventh book, we refer the reader there.

<margin>Why and from where sudden love [arises].</margin>

### Corollary.

It is also clear how, according to **Plato**, the various kinds of all things are mixed together in the fabric of the soul by a certain fixed ratio, and how these are mixed by a *harmonic* ratio, not an *arithmetic* one—otherwise the distribution of said things would be in vain somewhere—nor by a *geometric* proportion alone—otherwise there would be such equality in the mixture that it could not closely harmonize with the external diversity of bodies. <note>The author is arguing that only "harmonic" ratios allow for the perfect balance of similarity and difference required to link a spiritual soul to a physical body.</note> But the harmonic ratio, consisting of the similarity of various things, makes dissimilar things similar and connects unequal things by a certain common equality. Furthermore, the quality and duty of the soul is to be blended both with itself and with bodies; for whether it acts within itself by the identity of intelligence (if I may speak so), it mixes the "otherness" of certain things with a certain "identity" by reason of that otherness. It does the same in the imagination and the senses. Truly, he who desires more on the harmonic composition of the soul should read **Marsilio Ficino** on Plato, page 1158. <note>Ficino was a key Renaissance philosopher who translated Plato and sought to reconcile Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note>

<margin>In the concepts of the soul, all things are mixed.</margin>

### §. IV.
### On the Tetractys, or the harmonic quaternary of the soul, or on the four Virtues.

It is well known that at all times the number four was sacred to the **Pythagoreans** because of the great mysteries of nature hidden within it. <note>The <term>Tetractys (a triangular figure of ten points arranged in four rows)</term> was the most sacred symbol of the Pythagorean school.</note> Let us see now how it exists in GOD, in an Angel, in man, and in animals. It is established that one, two, three, and four joined together produce the number ten, the symbol of the entire universe, the goal and boundary of all things, and they explain the natural power of simple unity. From this very ten (the "denary"), which is a kind of second unity, the explanation of the square root is reached by an equal progression of four: for 10, 20, 30, and 40 joined together constitute 100, the square of the root of ten. Likewise, the hundredfold unity brings forth the thousand by an equal movement: for 100, 200, 300, and 400 joined together constitute 1000, which is the cube of the second unity (the root of ten). Therefore, by natural influence, there are no more than 10 numbers, which are bounded by a fourfold progression. Nor does any other variation of repetition occur beyond the thousand (the cube of the root of ten), since the quaternary, repeated three times in progression, then rises in the order of the denary. You have, therefore, in the quaternary of unity, the explanation of the entire number.

...contains power. For the general Unity is distinguished by four units, which are arranged here in a fitting order. However, all things in GOD are GOD; in intelligence, they are intellect; in the Soul, they are soul; in the body, they are body. And indeed, in the first unity, you will behold all the remaining units, though they are folded together in an indivisible, indifferent, and indistinct way. Certainly, if anyone should penetrate this simplest unity alone, having rejected all multiplicity—so that he proves it to be simple rather than not simple, and one rather than not one—let him know that he has penetrated all secrets. <margin>One skilled in mystical arithmetic can penetrate all secrets.</margin> For through this unity, you will see the unity of the mind stripped of all multiplicity, and you will find that its life is not corruptible in its absolute unity, in which it is all things. Moreover, the certainty of this absolute unity is most precise, so that the mind acts in it and through it; for it is the entity of all entities, the essence <term>quiddity; the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> of all essences, the cause of all causes, and the end of all ends. You also see a certain admirable harmony lying hidden beneath these four units, representing that highest harmony in the archetypal world. <margin>Harmony under the number four.</margin> For what else does the first unity denote to us, if not the unison <note>original: "vnisonum"</note> which enfolds all sounds and all consonances within itself? What else does 1 to 2 denote, if not the octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>? This is clearly the angelic being; for just as the octave is closest to the unison, so too it participates most greatly in that unison of divinity. What else does 1 to 3 denote but the octave combined with a fifth <note>original: "diapason cum diapente"; a musical interval of a twelfth</note>? Since this consonance is a composite, what else does it denote but the sensible world or the world of substances? Finally, what does 1 to 4 denote but the double octave <note>original: "bisdiapason"</note>? This is clearly the other, the human intellect, which is closest to the angelic octave.

### Book X. The Ten-Stringed Harp of Nature. 451

...you will behold the orderly arrangement of the parts, and finally the harmony of all nature in one most pleasant synopsis.

As we have shown at length above, every number is comprised within the ten; <margin>Every number is comprised within the ten.</margin> but the progression of all numbers is completed by the four, for four times ten make 40. <note>Kircher is referencing the Pythagorean idea that the sum of the first four numbers (1+2+3+4) equals ten, and expanding this to a cosmic scale of forty.</note> Hence, we have distributed the entire harmonic diagram into 40 circles. In this distribution, we have used the numbers 1, 3, 9, and 27. This sequence is highly mystical and was established by Plato in the *Timaeus* as the symbol of the soul, as will be discussed shortly. For these numbers, when collected together, constitute 40, a number most suitable for our purpose. <margin>Explanation of the mystical numbers</margin> For just as 1, 2, 3, and 4 represent the most orderly progression of the universal number—since if you multiply the two by itself, you produce 4, and if you add one to 3, that same four comes forth—so there is no progression more orderly toward the "ten of the four" (namely 40) than 1, 3, 9, and 27. Just as the former simple numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 added together make 10, and this multiplied by 4 makes 40, so 1, 3, 9, and 27 joined together make 40.

Following these principles, we illustrate the following diagram, in which a simple Unity—by which we denote **GOD**—touches four circles: <margin>Explanation of the figure.</margin> namely, the greatest circle of universal nature, the highest circle of the world, the highest of the order, and finally the highest circle of the choir. From this Unity, they participate step by step in light and being: first the universe, after this the highest order, and in the fourth and final place, the highest choir. Consequently, you see how choir communicates light to choir until it reaches the last one; you will also observe how that which is found in the universe and in any world is found in an orderly fashion. For the unit of ten signifying the <term>Intelligence</term><note>In this context, an "Intelligence" refers to a purely spiritual being or angel that governs a celestial sphere.</note>, the unit of a hundred the soul, and the unit of a thousand (as has been said) the body, exists in one way in the highest world—according to that world's sublime, simple, and noble nature—in another way in the middle world, and in another way in the lowest, shadowy world. For you will see that the lowest part of a higher world coincides in all things with the highest part of the lower world; for the sense-perception of the higher world is simpler than the intellect of the middle world, and the sense of the higher order is more perfect than the intellect of the one following it.

You see, therefore, how fittingly the whole Universe is distributed with a triple series of worlds: nine tens, nine hundreds, and just as many thousands, all comprised within the smallest circles. <margin>All things in all things.</margin> <note>original: "Omnia in omnibus." This is a Neoplatonic maxim meaning that every level of reality reflects every other level.</note> To these ninefold triads, if you add the same number of units indicated by the three larger circles, you will finally find the thousand signified in a simple unity by the greatest circle encompassing and unfolding all things. And you will see how everything exists in any world, and how the law and constitution of progressions are the same in each series of worlds. For if the first ten of the higher world is as two, the second as three, and the third as four, you will have a perfect progression; the second world, marked by the ten, will keep the same law of progression (as follows: 20, 30, 40), and the third world, marked by the hundred, the same (as follows: 200, 300, 400). For if you join these correctly, a mixture of the ten will emerge in each.

From which it is clearly evident how the unity of the intellect of the lower world—even if it is not of the nature of the higher or middle worlds, being further removed from their simplicity—nevertheless reaches out to touch their nature through a certain analogy in a wonderful way, as appears in the grades of being of the three worlds. <margin>Further explanation of the figure.</margin> See the following archetypal diagram, in which the lowest sphere, marked by 1000 or the <term>cube</term><note>Kircher uses 1000 (10x10x10) to symbolize the three-dimensional, material world.</note>, comprises corporeal nature, constituted from the temperament of the four elements; it is therefore immersed in darkness the further it is from the peak of light. The second sphere contains the celestial world, holding a middle seat between light and darkness, full of the Intelligences that move the spheres, who both illuminate and fertilize the lower world (wrapped in darkness) through a perpetual derivation of light. The third sphere contains the Angelic world, the dwelling-place of light, in which those celestial armies of blessed minds are distributed in harmonic order, dispensing and distributing the various ministries of the lower worlds. <margin>Orders of angels.</margin> <margin>Seraphim.</margin> The **Seraphim**, burning with divine love, inflame all lower things, inciting and attracting them toward divine love through the harmony of their works and a certain perennial and divine motion. <margin>Cherubim.</margin> The **Cherubim**, absorbed in the immense ocean of divine knowledge, illuminate the minds of men and the lower orders toward true science and cognition. <margin>Thrones.</margin> The **Thrones**, of the world and of the things existing in...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of "Musica Mundana" (World Music) from Kircher’s *Decachordon Naturae*, transitioning from the metaphysical structure of light and darkness to the literal and metaphorical "Music of the Spheres" and the Divine Trinity.</meta>

**Book 10. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature. 451**

Just as the highest world abounds in light, so the lower world abounds in a wealth of darkness; the middle world participates in an equal portion of light and darkness from both, although the higher is not entirely without darkness, nor is the lower entirely without light. It is as if light in the lower world, and darkness in the higher world, seem in some way to be absorbed. If, therefore, you look more deeply into the diagram <margin>All things tend toward one.</margin> <note>Kircher likely refers to a "pyramid of light and shadow" diagram common in his works.</note>, you will discover through the descent of unity into multiplicity, and the return of multiplicity into union, how in the highest Heaven all things that belong to multiplicity proceed into unity itself. That is to say: the divisible into the individual, darkness into light, the composite into the simple, the mortal into the immortal, the changeable into the immutable, potential into act, the part into the whole, and so on with the rest. You will find the opposite process in the [lower] world. If you investigate these things with a sharp mind, you will behold the greatest things, though through a most obscure light, clearly, even down to the most hidden secrets of nature. You must, however, conceive of the unity of any particular thing in its perfection, and imagine the quality of darkness according to that intensity of light. Among the graduations of unities, you should consider that one "lesser" which possesses more darkness, more multiplicity, more potentiality, and more divisibility; but that one is "greater" which possesses more light, more unity, more action, and indivisibility. For the less a unity is in "act" <term>Act: In Aristotelian philosophy, 'act' or 'actuality' refers to the fulfillment or realization of a thing's potential.</term> and the more it is in potential, the more changeable it is. For a unity that unites is more perfect than a unity that can be united, just as the unity of the Soul is more perfect than the unity of the body; because the end of the body's unity is the unity of the soul, upon which the bodily unity depends as if from its own starting principle. Time would fail me if I wished to explain every detail at greater length.

But who can express in words that admirable order of the heavenly choirs and the harmony of beauties; the concord of blessed minds? That inexplicable and super-mundane concert, in which those supreme voices—the sweetest instruments of the unceasing praises of God—resound perpetually with the lowest and middle choirs in that great house of eternity? Where the Conductor <note>original: *Choragus*</note> and Master Musician <note>original: *Archimusurgus*</note> is God the Father himself; the Son is the Incarnate Word, the eternal wisdom; and the Power that Harmonizes <note>original: *Virtus ἁρμόζουσα*</note> <margin>Music of the Holy Trinity.</margin> and adapts all things acts as the organist; where the Spirit of holiness will perpetually animate the organs with the bellows of divine air. Who can express the number of these musicians? In comparison to them, the sand on the seashore is nothing. There, a symphony not of three, four, or five, but of innumerable voices will sound forth eternally and without fail; there the Saints will rejoice in their chambers, the exultations of God in their throats <margin>Music of the Heavenly Homeland.</margin> <note>A reference to Psalm 149:5-6.</note>. There, there is no labor in performing musical praises, no fatigue, no satiety; rather, the more they are perceived, the more they flood the soul with a greater desire to perceive them continuously. *O how beloved are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul faints for the courts of the Lord. Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord; they will praise thee forever and ever,* etc. <note>Psalm 84:1-4.</note>

Inspired by even a thin whisper of this divine music, certain holy men of God, as if snatched outside of themselves, sent a divorce-notice to the love of fleeting things and betook themselves to the solitudes and caves of the mountains, so that, separated from the noise of worldly affairs, they might acquire ears more fit for perceiving this music. For if it is true, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, in 1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> (that instrument of divinity) says, that *eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love him*; no one should doubt that the powers of human genius can in no way reach this super-eminent symphony of the celestial choirs. Our ears, as it were, are growing deaf at the waterfalls of earthly confusion. But when that day of eternity dawns for us, then the ears of the deaf shall be opened. For as Saint Augustine rightly says, then the souls of the faithful will be immediately animated into the instruments of the living God; then the concert of divine minds will be revealed—not merely Music, but something more excellent above all Music; where there is sweetness and pleasantness, not merely harmonic, but something most sweet above all harmony. Thus says Augustine. Let these things said concerning Angelic Music suffice; nothing remains, therefore, except that we now say something concerning the music of the Divine Essence, which enfolds all the music of worldly choirs.
