# REGISTER X.
## Concerning Divine Music or the Choir of Choirs, which is the Symphony 
## of GOD with All Nature.

### To the Most Illustrious and Noble Lord, Lord Lazarus Henkel,
### Free Baron of Mount St. George, etc.

Since I have known you, Noble Sir, to be always a supreme admirer of worldly harmony; and being mindful of the benefits which you once conferred upon me in Rome with a liberal hand; and further incited by the distinguished honor of your virtue, it has pleased me to inscribe this final Register of the world to your honor. You will find here much to marvel at and much to truly desire, wherein, as if in the final center of all things, you may at last rest eternally blessed in happiness.

# §. I.
## On hierarchical harmony compared to GOD and man.

The Heavenly Father, having constructed this mundane organ, <note>Kircher uses the "organum" metaphor throughout; he views the universe as a complex musical instrument with many "registers" or stops.</note> through His wisdom and by the blowing of the Spirit, has drawn out the registers of the entire mundane organ described thus far. He has exhibited a symphony—not only most absolute in all its numbers, but altogether admirable and incomprehensible to human minds—both in Himself and in the universe. Of what nature this is, and in what it consists, must now be told.

<margin>How unity agrees with multitude.</margin>

That the Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the number one, representing God or the singular source of all things in Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy.</note> is diffused into the multitude has been clearly shown from what preceded; but how the nature of unity agrees with multitude, and dwells within it without discrepancy, is that which racks the intellect and places a barrier to the fragility of our comprehension. You will grant me pardon, O inaccessible light hidden in the darkness of eternity, if I, who am but smoke and dust, should somewhat presumptuously approach the abyss of your immensity. We have shown in various places that what the Monad is to Arithmeticians, the Unison is to musicians. And just as the Monad is the fountain and origin of all numbers, so the isophone <note>original: "isophona," meaning "equal-sounding" or unison.</note> Monad is the source of all consonances. Therefore, the Monad diffused into a multitude cannot agree in any other way except through the harmony of the unity that exists within that multitude. Hence Plato, imitating Timaeus of Locri <note>A Pythagorean philosopher whom Plato used as a character in his dialogues.</note> as we showed previously, describes the fabric of the soul and the world through the received Monad; he arrives at the number 27 (the cube of the triple Monad) through doubled, tripled, and quadrupled proportions. For the first and supreme Monad is diffused into the first triple number, which will be taught later; this square completes the number nine, by which number the orders of separated intellects <note>Likely referring to the nine choirs of angels.</note>, the Heavens, and all elementary things are distributed in the highest harmony. The triple number, again cubically multiplied (that is, multiplied by nine), produces twenty-seven. Because this number is exceedingly mystical—and though we explained it more than enough in the preceding diagram—nevertheless, because it is full of divine harmony, we think it should be discussed here at somewhat greater length. There are, therefore, twenty-seven primary genera of produced things, distinct in three enneads <note>Groups of nine.</note>: the supercelestial, the celestial, and the elementary. Their harmonic concord is seen united by GOD in a certain admirable connection. For from the Archetype to the Angelic orb or to the spheres, and from there to the orb of earthly habitation, that unity descends, rendering all things most consonant; so that whatever is in each one likewise responds in the others with a most sweet proportion of voices, as if by the melodic energy of life. For it is GOD in whom we live, move, and have our being <note>original: "in quo viuimus mouemur & sumus," a reference to Acts 17:28.</note>, by the mediation of that Spirit which nourishes from within, and the Mind which moves the mass of created things—that true "Soul of the World" intended by the Platonists—which, by vivifying the members of the world and binding them with harmonic concord, gives back the concerts of the mundane decachord <note>A ten-stringed instrument, here symbolizing the ten-fold harmony of the universe.</note>.

**Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature. 455**

<margin>What Pythagoras thinks about the order of things.</margin>

...produced the most harmonious results. Pythagoras, that most skillful investigator of natural order and harmony, first noticed this; Anaxagoras agreed with him when he contemplated "everything in everything," <note>original: "quodlibet in quolibet." This refers to Anaxagoras's theory that every substance contains tiny parts of every other substance.</note> not indeed finding a donkey in a fly, or a camel in a earthworm, but seeing the species of each represented in the other with a wondrous affinity. Just as all things live by a single universal life, so too are they joined to one another in a friendly society, held by what we might call "Heracleote bonds," <note>Heracleotic bonds: A reference to the "Heracleote stone" or magnet, symbolizing the invisible forces of attraction that bind the universe together.</note> from which that wondrous harmony of things is born. This more hidden secret the aforementioned Anaxagoras did not fully explain. Pythagoras, however, did so with a clearer light, having been illustrated by those who had drawn that spirit from the divine Oracles—first from the Egyptians, and they in turn from the Hebrews, who handed it down more aptly. The Prophets themselves, raised up to the divine banquet, perceived that harmony of all things most clearly.

<margin>How the Prophets knew all things in God.</margin>

In that divine realm, the forms, models, and patterns of things are exhibited with a fitting sweetness in a single sound and a single Word. Yet we, pressed down by the weight of our human frailty, cannot perceive this harmony diffused through the vastly different members of this worldly "ten-stringed lyre," <note>Kircher uses the "Decachordon" (ten-stringed lyre) as a metaphor for the ten categories of being or the completeness of the universe.</note> unless we take up now one tone, now another, and collect them all within the organic system of the mind. Only then can we perceive, with some small sweetness, that harmonic concord of created things with one another and with their Creator. It remains, therefore, to be said and explained how that "equal-sounding monad" <term>monad: from the Greek 'monas,' meaning unity or the number one, representing God</term> of divinity descends into all the parts of the worldly ten-stringed instrument to arrange the harmony of things.

<margin>How uncreated unity diffuses itself into a multitude.</margin>

Not only Christian theologians but also Gentile philosophers have recognized the admirable power of the "ternary" <note>ternary: the number three or the Trinity.</note> flowing forth from the monad. Aristotle says at the beginning of his books *On the Heavens*: "We have the number three from nature, and we uphold it as a law according to which all things are arranged." Hence, by this number, we are bound to celebrate God, the Maker of all things. For all things, whether spiritual or corporeal, consist of three parts: a beginning, a middle, and an end. They certainly draw this ternary from that ineffable Trinity of the supra-celestial world, from whom all things, in whom all things, and through whom all things exist, as the Apostle <note>The Apostle: St. Paul (referencing Romans 11:36).</note> testifies. For nature has placed before our eyes the most lucid signs of those things which "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man."

<margin>The Trinity shines forth in all things.</margin>

If we believe that all nature is perfect, it is necessary to confess that it is also "triune," since in every natural thing the number of the Divine Triad shines and is expressed. Since everything triple is perfect, and we assert that God is the Maker, Author, and Creator of all, we are necessarily compelled to assert that He is also triune and perfect. For every creature is a "divine something," or as the poet said, *a small particle of divine breath*, <note>original: "divinae particula aurae." A quote from Horace (Satires 2.2.79), suggesting the soul is a spark of the divine.</note> and every creature, as an image and very likeness of divine goodness, must carry the traces of divine perfection and unity. Let us therefore discuss the steps of all nature, let us search the universal nature of things deeply, and we shall gaze with admiration at the traces of this wonderful Trinity impressed upon individual things.

<margin>The trinity in Adam. The trinity in the soul.</margin>

The first production of man began in Adam as a monad; this, diffusing itself into a "dyad" <note>dyad: the number two.</note>, produced Eve; and from both was born Abel, who completed the "triad" of human origins. God preserved this pattern in the subsequent propagation of the human race in the form of father, mother, and son. Furthermore, the rational soul is one indivisible substance, yet it is triple without being divided: it is fruitful and manifold, distinguished into intellect, memory, and will. The intellect is not the memory, nor the will; the memory is neither the intellect nor the will; the will is neither the intellect nor the memory; yet they are one and the same substance of the soul, distinct in their three-fold relation. Again, every soul is three-fold: rational, sensitive, and vegetative. The intellect is three-fold: divine, angelic, and human—the first we call Mind, the second Intellect proper, and the last Reason.

<margin>The trinity in a tree.</margin>

A tree is one, joined in its trunk, but divided in its branches, in which it brings forth only three things: leaves, flowers, and fruit. There are three intervals of magnitude: length, breadth, and depth, which correspond to the line, the surface, and the body—the common measure of all perceivable bodies. There are three primary and chief units of numbers: the linear, the superficial...

He provides examples of this three-fold nature in human reproduction, the faculties of the soul, and the physical growth of plants.</summary>

§. I.

### On the Music of the Triune GOD with the Angelic Orders.

<margin>All things in number, weight, and measure.</margin>
GOD arranged the world in three ways: by number, weight, and measure, through which all things bear the imprint of the most high Trinity <note>original: "Triadis"</note>. For they derive their number from that supreme <term>monad</term><note>In Pythagorean and Neoplatonic philosophy, the Monad refers to "the One," the indivisible source of all numbers and, by extension, all existence.</note> and source of all numbers; they derive their weight from that wisdom which balances all things; and they derive their measure from that spirit of the Creator <note>original: "Artificis spiritu," meaning the "spirit of the craftsman" or "divine architect."</note> who distributes a fitting portion to each. Hence, according to the doctrine of the Magi <note>Kircher likely refers here to the "Hermetic" or ancient mystical philosophers thought to possess primordial wisdom.</note>, three things rule the world: GOD, Mind, and Soul. Unity, or the monad, properly belongs to GOD; order or weight belongs to Mind or wisdom; and measure and motion belong to the Soul or spirit. This is beautifully explained by the enigmatic statement made by Plato to King Dionysius: "All things are around the King of all; all things exist for his sake; he is the cause of all beautiful things."
<margin>Plato's enigma.</margin>
For all things are connected around the King by his unity, and all things are weighed by his grace, and all things are ordered toward him; he indeed, by numbering and proportioning all, is the cause of all beautiful things.

# Book 10. The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature. 457

...leads to harmony and the strengthening of all virtues; and since the Triune <note>The author refers to the Holy Trinity.</note> communicates himself in a threefold manner, he willed to govern man and all things he had produced for man’s sake through a threefold scale. Among the **Principalities**, he established the rule of Empires, Kingdoms, and Provinces. Among the **Archangels**, he placed the care of Kings and Princes themselves. Among the **Angels**, he decreed the care of individual human beings. Thus it happened that just as God, through that fruitful monad <note>original: "monade"—referring to the divine unity or the "One."</note> of his, descends to us through the tripartite order of Angels, so we might ascend through them to God as if by a certain **Jacob's Ladder**. 

<margin>How we are united to God through the steps of the angelic orders.</margin> For it is certain, according to the testimony of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian philosopher who wrote "The Celestial Hierarchy."</note>, that we can be purged, illuminated, and perfected not only by the lower intelligences but also by the higher ones. Through the diligent practice of all virtues, we may become companions of the hierarchical minds according to the degree of virtue that flourishes most within us. This occurs if we rightly tune the <term>decachordon</term> <note>A ten-stringed musical instrument, used here as a metaphor for the soul's moral and spiritual state.</note> of our own mind to the angelic decachordon. If we stretch the string of virtue corresponding to a hierarchical string until they sound in perfect harmony, we—already conforming to the minds of that specific order—will obtain from God, the Great Harmonizer, the virtues proper to that order. 

<margin>The greatest secret in Kabbalah.</margin> This is the greatest of all secrets in the **Kabbalah**; the masters of secret theology report that by this means alone, the holy men of God have emerged as performers of miraculous works. For if we strive to conform ourselves to any order through the study of similar virtues, being purged of dissonances by the harmony of those virtues, we shall easily ascend into that rank. 

<margin>How we are made like the Angels.</margin> Hence, certain holy men of God, through the fire of divine love, have blossomed into **Seraphim** <note>The highest order of angels, associated with burning love.</note>; some, through the study of divine contemplation, have become **Cherubim** <note>The second order, associated with wisdom and knowledge.</note>. There have even been those who, by perpetually enduring divine things, were taken up into the **Thrones** <note>The third order, associated with God's justice and steadfastness.</note>. Since many angels fell from each of these orders, it was necessary for others to be admitted to restore them—none other than humans, according to the degree of virtue God bestowed upon them while on earth.

It is also clear from this why God struck the fear of Princes into the hearts of peoples and subjects. <margin>Why subjects naturally fear their princes.</margin> Is not a King a man similar to other men? Yet we see everyone submit to him with the greatest reverence and fear. This could happen by no reason unless God had impressed upon him the "character" <note>An indelible mark or spiritual seal of office.</note> of His own fear. Once a Prince is marked and elevated by this, others—compelled by a certain reverential fear and a hidden force—submit. All of this is executed through the order of those supreme **Principalities**. 

However, if Kings and Princes, through a life that is unworthy and contaminated by crimes, place a barrier against the influence of both God and the Principalities, <margin>The source of the ruin and transfer of kingdoms and empires.</margin> behold! Immediately, as if the character of the fear of God has been erased in the Prince by public sins, the people turn from harmony to dissonance. Rebellions are stirred up, and the Prince is cast down as one unworthy of the character of the fear of God. Thus, the changes of empires, the transfers of kingdoms, and the uprooting of principalities and commonwealths have no other origin than what we have stated. Let the Prince, therefore, remember to order his life and to cultivate justice and piety so that he may always find the Archangels—the overseers of his own principality—favorable to him. Without their perpetual protection and assistance, neither the kingdom nor the Ruler can endure. For the same reason, God impressed the character of fear even upon the fiercest animals, so that they would be subject to and obey man, for whose sake they were created...

<margin>What the Virtues influence in humans.</margin>
The Angels of the **Principalities** indicate the sovereignty of the world by the omen of the prince bird <note>original: "principis volucris augurio"; Kircher is likely referencing the Roman tradition of augury, where the flight of birds signaled divine will regarding leadership</note>. But because earthly sovereignty is dissonant in itself and deformed unless it is consonant within itself and with others, and acquires beauty and comeliness through this harmony, the ministry of the superiors is necessary for the Prince. This is achieved by the order of **Virtues**, by whose favor—having prepared us with constancy and strength—we are made strong against the inducements of vice and pleasure. 

<margin>The influence of Powers.</margin>
But so that we may also prevail against these airy powers full of envy and malice, the protection of the supercelestial and divine **Powers** is necessary for us. 

<margin>The influence of Dominations.</margin>
Lest we also be hindered by worldly affections, but instead dominate ourselves by subjecting those affections harmonically to the rational appetite, the assistance of the **Dominations** was necessary for us. Once dominion over all lower things is obtained, it remains that we, having turned toward GOD, may be free for Him alone. This happens if we retain the memory of supercelestial things through the aid of the **Thrones**, and contemplate those same things by **Cherubic** illumination, until at last we are united to our kin and supreme parent, the divine unity <note>original: "monadi divinae"</note>, through **Seraphic** ardor. From this, just as the Maker of things descends into us with His power through the Angelic steps, so through those same steps we may return to Him from whom we proceeded. We do this as if through certain steps of virtues: the first step of rational nature joins us to **Angels** through the senses; imagination joins us to **Archangels**; fear to the **Virtues**; sorrow for sins to the **Powers**; and reason to the **Principalities**—for just as the latter preside over spirits, so reason presides over the senses and affections. Furthermore, Love joins us to the **Dominations**; the intellect to the **Thrones**; intelligence to the **Cherubim**; and finally, let Hope unite us to the **Seraphim**, for these lead most closely to GOD, who is the hope of all the ends of the earth.

<margin>Angels, the musicians of the celestial song.</margin>
You see, therefore, how these ministering orders, the supreme <term>Harmostae<note>From the Greek "Harmostai," meaning tuners or those who bring things into right proportion.</note></term> assisting at the divine tribunal, strive to lead all things into consonance with their prince. For joined together, they anticipate those singing psalms and are themselves <term>in unison<note>original Greek: ὁμοφωνοῦνtes (homophonountes)</note></term> as musicians of the celestial Song, adapting all strings and voices in that supreme <term>monochord<note>A single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical musical ratios; here Kircher uses it as a metaphor for the singular, unified harmony of God's creation.</note></term> of GOD, so that they may render it elegant and most sweet. If there be any useless strings or dissenting melodies, they cast them out, cut them away, and reject them, lest anything dissonant be found in the worldly, celestial, or human <term>polychord<note>A multi-stringed instrument; here representing the complex, multi-layered harmony of the universe.</note></term>. Therefore, all things rejoice as the Father moves them, as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine orders of angels used here.</note> testifies; for being moved by GOD, they move the sphere, and they dispose our bodies and other lower things toward that consonance which the first Mover of all things himself commands.

### §. III.
### *Concerning the harmony of the celestial Nine, which it forms with the Hierarchical Nine.*

<margin>Hierarchical music with the celestial bodies.</margin>
So that the Author and Maker of all nature might preserve the <term>microcosm<note>original: "mundum minorem" (the lesser world), a common Renaissance term for a human being as a reflection of the universe.</note></term>, for whose sake all things were made, in the most absolute harmony, He moved another <term>Ennead<note>A group of nine.</note></term>; namely the systems of the celestial world, by whose influence the lower world might be governed: the first Empyrean Heaven, the Starry Heaven or firmament, and the globes of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. But since these bodies were by themselves and their nature inanimate and incapable of motion, He attributed to each its own **Intelligences**. By the power of these Intelligences, the bodies are agitated in various motions to produce various effects according to the needs of the sublunary world; thus, the constitution of corporeal nature depends on the influence of the superior bodies. The Intelligences assisting the Heavens have the care of arranging souls, while GOD, the supreme <term>Choragus<note>The leader or conductor of a choir or dance.</note></term>, binds the lowest things to the highest and the middle to the supreme in one most perfect harmony. But let the harmony of each be made more clearly manifest.

<margin>The Empyrean Heaven corresponds to the Seraphim.</margin>
First, Note that there are nine heavens: the Empyrean heaven, the court of the eternal King above that worldly home of the Mover of all, which—due to its order and infinite light—corresponds not incongruously to the order of **Seraphim**. From this heaven, all illuminations of souls proceed as if from a most abundant fountain.

...not only in nature, but also in the intellectual **ennead** <note>A group or set of nine. Kircher uses this to structure the hierarchy of the universe.</note>, and indeed in **GOD** himself in his own way, so that the musical concept of the world might be more clearly revealed alongside the **Archetype** <note>The divine "blueprint" or original model of the universe in the mind of God.</note>. The Ennead contains the four elements along with the five grades of corporeal nature; these joined together constitute nine levels, as follows: Earth, Water, Air, Fire; then stones or metals, plants, **zoophytes** <note>term: Zoophytes (literally "animal-plants"). In the 17th century, these were organisms like corals or sponges thought to be the bridge between the plant and animal kingdoms.</note>, brute animals, and Man, of which the inferior world consists. Although these are corporeal, the most wise Creator and **harmonizer** <note>original Latin: "harmosta," meaning one who joins things in harmony.</note> has linked them with such harmony to the remaining two worlds that each individual thing exists in its own way in every one of the worlds. In the Angels, it is a teaching and cleansing force, according to the scripture: *Who covers its higher parts with waters* <note>original: "Qui tegis aquis superiora eius" — a reference to Psalm 104:3.</note>. *Epilogue of the entire work.*

**H**itherto, therefore, I have dealt with the wonderful works of the Creator, the Greatest and Best, in the musical structure of the world, as far as the powers of my intellect permitted. It remains now that, having removed my eyes and hands from the table of demonstrations and lifted them up to heaven, I should pray as a devoted suppliant to the Father of Lights: O eternal Wisdom, the founder and maker of all things, who by the light of nature promotes in us a desire for the light of grace, so that through it You may transfer us into the light of Your glory; I give thanks to You, because You have delighted me in Your creation, and I have rejoiced in the works of Your hands. I give thanks that You have introduced me into the hidden music-room <note>original: "odæum," a small ancient Greek or Roman building used for musical performances</note> of Your divinity, where You have so ravished my heart with even the slight whisper of Your infinite sweetness, and so filled my ears, that I have nearly become deaf to all the delights and joys of earthly corruption, as if to the tumultuous cataracts of a falling world. Behold, I have now finished the work of my profession, using such powers of intellect as You have given me. I have manifested the glory of Your works to the men who will read these my nocturnal studies, as much as the narrowness of my mind could grasp of Your infinite greatness. I have completed this sacred discourse, this hymn to God the Creator, judging this to be true piety: not to sacrifice hecatombs of bulls to Him, nor to burn incense and cassia; but first to learn myself, and afterwards to teach others, how great He is in wisdom, how great in power, and of what kind of goodness. For I have always held that the desire to spread what is good, and to envy it to no one, is the proof of the most perfect goodness. My mind has always been ready to philosophize as accurately as possible; if anything unworthy of Your counsels has been uttered by me—a little worm born and nourished in the wallowing-place of sins—may You deign to inspire me to correct it, if You wish men to know it. If I have fallen into rashness because of the admirable beauty of Your works, or if I have sought my own glory among men while proceeding in a work destined for Your glory, I earnestly pray that You forgive me according to Your infinite mercy. Finally, may You deign to be favorable, so that this work of musical meditations may serve solely for Your glory and the salvation of souls.

### ON WONDERFUL MUSURGY

->PREFACE.<-

[Decorative initial I] **SO** in all arts and sciences **Practice** and **Theory** <note>original: *Praxis & Theoria*</note> seek a union, so that if one lacks the other, both deservedly fail. Practice does not gain its reputation without Theory, nor does Theory alone find its worth without Practice. This principle applies in all disciplines, but it holds a special place in the field of **Music**. For although Musical Theory, content with the love of truth alone, might be said to achieve its purpose in some way—that is, in its own intellectual pleasure—it is simply impossible for a Musician who lacks all practical experience to produce anything of value in this art. ## 2 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

...so that for one whose mind was set on probing more deeply into the innermost secrets of Music, practice would not lack Theory, nor Theory practice, in the pursuit of performance. A further stimulus to carry out this proposal was the arrogant rebuke of purely practical <term>Symphonetae</term> <note>From the Greek 'symphonistae,' referring here to performing musicians or composers who work by ear or tradition rather than mathematical theory.</note>, who, while they think it impossible for a Theorist to compose a melody with the skill, elegance, and grace that modern Music rightly requires—indeed, asserting the contrary—they receive such ideas with laughter and mockery. To show that this rebuke of theirs was false and unjust, I have applied myself seriously to this task for many years, leaving nothing untried, so that I might find an Art by which anyone, no matter how unskilled in Music, could achieve in a small amount of time and without labor what practical Composers can scarcely achieve in the space of many years.

Therefore, having been taught by frequent musical experience, I noted the great power of combinations hidden beneath musical intervals and the diversity of tones. I approached the principles of the entire <term>Musurgic</term> <note>Kircher's term for the 'work of music' or the art of composition.</note> combination with the aid of the analytical art, and with truly great labor, I reduced the more excellent and necessary transformations of harmonic relations into tables. These were arranged with such secret skill that, in whatever position the <term>Melotactic</term> <note>Literally 'melody-arranging' columns.</note> columns were ordered, a new harmony would always emerge. This truly wonderful Melotactic combination—when it was achieving its first successes in simple <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>The art of combining different melodic lines; here, Kircher refers to the most basic form of note-against-note composition.</note>, still crying, as it were, in its very cradle—was not enough for me. Carried away by a heat of the mind, I applied my spirit to bringing forth a universal method of <term>Melothetic</term> <note>The art of 'placing' or 'constructing' a melody.</note> Musurgy. In this, I seem to have succeeded so well that I have exhibited every beauty and grace of harmony, together with the appropriate artistic words. Although these things at first seemed <note>original: "παράδοξα" (paradoxa)</note> paradoxical and truly prodigious to musicians, they were nonetheless convinced by experiments made by various illustrious men, and they learned to have faith in this Art, even if they did not know its principles. 

Furthermore, this new Musurgy of ours consists mostly in the skillful combination of Melotactic Tables; however these are made, a new harmony necessarily emerges. Thus, since compositions of this sort are nearly infinite, an infinite diversity of harmonic concertos is born. Whoever, therefore, knows how to adapt our Melotactic Tables according to the rules to be prescribed by us shortly, and knows how to properly transfer the harmonic numbers into the melotactic scale, will also know how to compose—with the same ease—any skillful songs: simple, complex, florid, diminished, syncopated, or interwoven with skillful ligatures and chasing each other in the manner of <term>fugues</term> <note>A complex musical form where a theme is introduced by one part and then taken up by others.</note>, in whatever tone and with whatever texts of words are given. 

For just as in <term>Algebra</term> <note>In the 17th century, algebra was often viewed as a semi-magical or 'shorthand' method for solving complex problems through rules.</note>, a calculator following the course of a rule completes the explanations of paradoxical questions with such ease that the operator himself may not know what he has done, and thus an unexpected effect comes forth with the calculator scarcely thinking about it; so here, for those following the course of the prescribed rules, the desired harmony will emerge, whether performed by those skilled in Music or those ignorant of it—even by children and women. Certainly, the vows and effective prayers of our Fathers migrating to the most remote <term>Indias</term> <note>Referring generally to overseas mission territories, including the Americas and East Asia.</note> were able to do much to bring this secret to the public. Since the attraction of people in those lands consists in the practice of music and the frequenting of divine praises, and since printed books or composers are not always present, they believed this Musurgy would be of the greatest use to them. With this, they will be able to produce not only the desired songs in the Latin language, but also in any proposed language, even an Indian one, no matter how "barbaric" the idiom, as will be discussed at length later.

Led by these considerations, I have chosen to make this "Miraculous Art of Music" <note>original: *Musurgiam hanc mirificam*; Kircher uses this term to describe his system for automated or simplified musical composition.</note> public property, lest I should seem to have omitted anything in this work that might serve to propagate divine worship and honor. ## THE FIRST PART OF THE MIRACULOUS ART OF MUSIC
### COMBINATORIAL MUSIC-MAKING

#### MUSICAL LEMMA I.
<note>A "lemma" is a preliminary proposition or auxiliary theorem used as a stepping stone to a larger conclusion.</note>

Whenever a ratio—for example, A to B—is said to be "composed" (for instance, from the ratios A, E, and I), I say that the same is composed from those same parts regardless of the order in which they are placed. That is, between two terms A and B, it is permitted to continue the stated ratios as many times as they can change places among themselves. For example: take as many numbers in a natural sequence <note>i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5...</note> as there are things proposed. Multiplied together, they produce the total sum of mutations (permutations), so that for two things there are 2; for three things, 6; for four things, 24; and for five things, 120 mutations result.

#### Paradigm.

1. Suppose there are two things proposed, A and B. I say they can be changed twice and no more, for each will occupy the first place only once, as is evident in the margin; for these numbers multiplied together produce two. <margin>AB 1 & BA 2</margin>

2. But three things can be varied in six ways. For these numbers 1, 2, 3, multiplied in order, produce six: that is to say, 1 times 2 makes 2, and 2 times 3 makes 6, etc. The reason for this is that each thing will hold the first place once, and the remaining two can be changed between themselves twice, as is evident in the following example.

| 2 | OAR | 4 | RAO | 6 | ARO |

3. Suppose there are four things to be changed among themselves: multiply the number four by the number produced from the previous multiplication (namely, by 6), and 24 mutations will be produced; for these numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, multiplied in order, produce 24. For each thing will hold the first place only once, and the remaining three can be varied among themselves six times. Look at the present example.

**L E M M A  II.**

Whenever similar things occur—or, what is the same thing, when the same items are placed multiple times among the things to be combined—the total combination number divided by the combination number of the similar items (as shown in the preceding table) will give the required number of combinations.

<margin>Permutations of a five-letter name in which two letters are similar.</margin>

Let the name MARIA be proposed. Since it has two similar letters—or, what is the same thing, one letter A placed twice—we ask how many times it can be combined. Since the name is a <term>pentagrammaton</term> <note>a word consisting of five letters</note>, if all the letters were different, they would have 120 combinations as shown in the preceding table. Let this number be divided by the combination number of two items (that is, by 2, as the table shows); it will give a quotient of 60. And so, any name of 5 letters that has two letters the same (as in the present name with the two As) can be combined that many times.

<margin>Of a three-letter name.</margin>

Again, let a <term>trigrammaton</term> <note>a word consisting of three letters</note> name be given in which two letters are placed twice, such as the name ALA. If someone wishes to know how many times it can be combined, he will achieve his wish if he divides the combination of the whole—namely, the combination of three things, which is 6—by the combination number of two, which is 2. The result will be 3, the required combination for the proposed name.

# CHAPTER I.
## Concerning the Combinations of Musical Notes.

Through several problems, we will teach here the method and reasoning by which one may determine how and how often any number of <term>Notes</term> <note>musical pitches</note> can be varied and combined among themselves.

### Combinatorial Problem I.
*To find, given a melody of any number of notes, how many times it can be changed within a certain interval.*

Let there first be a melody of three notes which ascends through a <term>third</term> <note>an interval spanning three steps on the scale, such as C to E</note> from C through D into E. It is asked how many times it can be changed within this interval so that no note is placed twice on the same step, but each is different within the same interval? I answer that this can happen six times and no more; for since according to the first <term>Lemma</term> <note>a proven proposition used as a stepping stone to a further result</note> three different things can be changed six times, and here there are three notes placed in three different steps, it follows necessarily that they can also be changed six times within the interval of a third. Indeed, for a further demonstration of this, nothing else seems to be required but a visual demonstration, which follows.

[A musical staff with six measures, each containing three notes (C, D, E) in different permutations. The measures are numbered 1 through 6 below the staff.]

You see therefore in the example how the proposed melody is changed six times so that none is placed twice on any step, but each is distinct within the same interval; thus we have performed what was proposed.

In no different a way, a melody of four notes ascending step by step from C to F through a <term>fourth</term> <note>an interval spanning four steps on the scale</note> can be changed 24 times according to Lemma I. For since the 4 positions in the interval of a fourth are all different, the melody can be changed six times beginning from the note C, six times from the note D, six times beginning from the note E, and finally six times starting the melodic mutations from the note F. Moreover, four multiplied by six gives the total number of the proposed combination. As is clear in the following example:

### Combinatorial Problem II.

### Combinatorial Problem IV.

*Given a voice of any number of notes, in which two are the same on one string* <note>In this context, "string" or "chord" refers to a specific line or space on the musical staff representing a pitch.</note>, *and three are the same on another string; find the combination—that is, the number of mutations of the voices.*

Suppose there is a certain voice of nine notes, of which two are the same on string A, three are the same on string C, and two others are again the same on string A <note>The author is describing a set of nine notes where there is one pair of identical pitches, one triplet of identical pitches, and another separate pair of identical pitches.</note>; as is clear in the present example; the question is, what is the mutation of the proposed voice? Proceed as follows: multiply the combination of three, which is 6, by the square of the <term>combination of two</term> things, which is 4 <note>The "square" here refers to having two separate pairs; (2!) × (2!) = 4.</note>. You will have 24 as a divisor. Divide the combination of nine <note>9 factorial (9!)</note>, namely 362,880, by this number; and the result will be 15,120, which are the sought-after mutations in the given voice.

->[A musical staff showing nine notes. Underneath are the labels for the pitch levels: A A C C C A A]<-

<margin>The <term>combination of 4</term> is 24 <note>4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1</note>, the square of which is 576.</margin>

If there should again occur a voice of 22 notes, of which two are repeated twice; and one is repeated thrice; and two others are repeated four times; the question is how many times can the voice be changed? One proceeds thus: you will square the combination of 2, and you will have 4. Multiply this by 6, the combination of three, so that you have 24. Then multiply this again by the square of the combination of 4, which is 576. The product, 13,824, will give the divisor. By this, the number of the combination of 22 <note>22 factorial (22!)</note>—that is, 1,124,000,727,777,607,680,000—being divided, will give 8,130,792,301,632,000 as the number of mutations of the sought-after song.

## Universal Problem V.

->**Given any number of notes in any voice—whether they are different from one another or not—to find how many times any other number of notes, chosen and determined from this set, can be changed.**<-

This proposition has something marvelous about it, which is why it seemed appropriate to begin from a higher principle; and so that we may explain our meaning more easily, we shall begin with an example of the proposition itself. Let some <term>Musurgis [music-maker or composer]</term> propose this combinatorial riddle: given 22 notes in order, first with all of them being different and ascending through a <term>trisdiapason [a three-octave range]</term>, exactly as many as there are notes in the <note>original: "scala musicali Guidonis." This refers to the Guidonian Hand or the medieval hexachord system used for teaching music.</note> musical scale of Guido, as appears in this present diagram.

It is asked, first, how many times these can be changed simply; we shall immediately satisfy this question through Lemma I and Problem I. Since all the notes are different, they will admit the usual combination of the number 22, as Table I shows: namely **1,124,000,042,171,709,440,000**.

It is asked, secondly, how many times two notes can be changed within the space of a three-octave range; then how many times 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and so on up to the number 22 (excluding 22 itself)? How many times, I say, within a determined three-octave interval can a voice consisting of any number of notes chosen from these 22 notes be varied? To find this out, proceed as follows. Since 22 notes have been chosen: first, multiply 22 by 21 (the next smaller number by one unit), and the result is **462**. This is how many times two notes can be arranged within a three-octave interval, always being different. The reason for this is that since all 22 notes are different and ascend by degrees, it follows that the order can be changed twenty-one times. For the first change occurs through 21 degrees. The second change will occur when the notes are arranged by a third ascending. The third change of notes will be by a fourth; the fourth by a fifth; the fifth change by a sixth, and so on for the rest up to 22, which is the <term>trisdiapason [three-octave range]</term>. Therefore, since in 22 notes there are 21 different changes, these being multiplied by 22 will produce the proposed number 462. Thus, two notes can be changed within a three-octave range that many times, and no more, which is what the proposition intended.

All of this should be understood regarding the 462 different permutations of two notes variously arranged within the interval of a three-octave range, as is clear in the attached examples. From here, if you wish to know how many times three notes within the inter...

### Problem VI. The most universal combinatorial method.

**Given any number of notes, to find how many changes can be made from any number of notes chosen from them, whether those notes are different, or the same, or similar, or both similar and different.**

In the preceding section, we showed the way in which, given any number of notes, we can derive different changes from any chosen number of notes. Now it must also be shown how, from any number [of notes] chosen within a certain interval, changes of notes can be made, whether they are different, similar, or partly similar and partly different.

Proceed as follows. Let the <term>Great System</term> <note>original: "Systema maximum"; the full musical scale used in Kircher's time</note> of the musical scale consist of 22 notes as an example; and suppose someone desires to know how many times individual musical intervals assumed within it permit precise changes. For example, I desire to see how many changes 3 notes, variously arranged within the musical scale, may undergo. Proceed thus: multiply 22 notes by itself, and the result will be 484; and these are the changes that 2 notes, variously arranged within the entire system, can undergo. Furthermore, multiply this number 484 again by 22, and you will have 10,648 sought-after changes of three notes within the said scale.

In this way, 22 multiplied by 10,648 will produce 234,256, the number of changes for four notes variously arranged within the scale. Thus, 22 multiplied by the recently found number 234,256 will give the changes of [five] notes variously placed within the given System; and so, by always multiplying the last product by the notes of the entire scale (that is, by 22), the number of all changes will be produced for that number of notes which follows next in the natural order. If, however, you wish to know the number of notes that are partly similar and partly different, subtract the numbers of the preceding table from the numbers of this table, and the remainder will give what is sought.

Book VIII. Miraculous Music-making. 21

You see therefore in this single example of the second series how the permutations <note>Kircher uses *mutationes* to describe what we now call mathematical permutations or combinations.</note> are always made distinct with respect to a single note up to 22; and the black notes clearly demonstrate this diversity. In the second series, however, where two notes change their placement <note>original: *filum*, literally "thread," referring here to the mathematical sequence or the line on a staff</note>, there are 231 permutations. This is because these two notes, while always remaining on the same line <note>original: *chorda*</note>, can be changed ten times in each of the 22 series of notes, and a little more, which completes the 231 permutations. You shall reason no differently concerning the remaining series, whose permutations have been recorded.

### CHAPTER II.
### On the combination of the value of notes.

In the preceding Problems, we spoke of the combinations and permutations of notes—specifically, how many times given notes can change their position relative to one another to constitute different voices. Now we will also show by what method we can know how many times notes of different <term>value</term> <note>Value here refers to rhythmic duration (whole notes, half notes, etc.) rather than pitch.</note> can be permuted, even when arranged on a single line. Thus it is:

#### Problem I.
#### Given a melody of any number of notes which are all of different value, to find how many times those notes of different value can be permuted among themselves.

We are not demonstrating here how many times the proposed notes can change their pitch <note>original: *locum*, literally "place"</note>, but only how many times notes of different rhythmic value—even when arranged on one and the same line <note>original: *chorda*</note>—can be permuted and variously arranged among themselves. To begin with small examples: let three notes of different value be proposed, and you wish to know how many times they can be permuted among themselves. You shall <term>cube</term> the number three <note>Kircher is calculating $3^{3} = 27$. In modern combinatorics, if we are filling three "slots" using a set of three possible values (allowing repetition), there are $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ possibilities.</note> placed three times, as is evident from the margin: by multiplying 3 by 3 to make 9; <margin>3 3 3 / 9 / 27.</margin> then, you multiply 3 by 9, and you will have 27. And that is how many times three notes of different value can be permuted among themselves, as is clear in the example added below.

### Book VIII. Miraculous Music-making. 23

->**USE OF THE TABLE**<-

There are 4 columns in this table. The first shows how many permutations <note>original: "mutationes"</note> any number of musical voices—up to eight—can undergo in terms of **position** <note>In this context, position refers to the pitch or the placement of the note on the musical staff</note> alone. The second shows the permutations of any number of notes—up to eight—in terms of **value** <note>Value refers to the rhythmic duration of the note, such as a whole note or half note</note> alone. The third shows the permutations of any number of notes within an octave, differing in both **position and value**. The fourth shows the entire operation through **examples**.

If, therefore, someone desires to know how many permutations five notes (which always have different positions within the scale) admit, let him look in the first column for the 5th row, "5 voices," and in the corresponding combination column he will find the 120 sought-after permutations of five notes.

If, however, you wish to know how many times five notes—differing only in value (the kind of five different notes shown in the 5th row of column IV)—can be changed, you will find in column II, row 5, the number 3,125. This represents the permutations of five notes of different value, whether they are placed within the same interval or arranged according to steps.

But if you wish to know how many times the said five notes can be changed when they differ in both **position and value**, column III will show this to you in row 5: specifically, the number 375,000. Therefore, in the fifth example, where all five notes are different, they can first be changed 3,125 times without any change in position, simply by varying the transposition of the different rhythmic values within the same fifth <note>original: "diapente," a musical interval of a fifth</note> or even on the same <term>string|chorda; here referring to a single pitch or line on the staff</term>. If, however, the change of position is added—which, according to column I, can change 120 times within the interval of a fifth—the total permutations will become 375,000, as was said and as Column III shows.

### Problem II.

**Given a musical phrase of any number of notes differing in both position and value, find how many times the given phrase can be changed under this double variety.**

In the preceding problem, we showed how many times a phrase of any number of notes of different value could be changed, without regard for changing its position. In this problem, however, we intend to demonstrate how many times a phrase of any number of notes, differing in both position and value, can be changed and transposed.

Let this be the universal rule: Whenever the notes in a musical phrase differ in both position and value, one must first multiply the combination of notes differing in position by the combination of notes differing in value, and the product will give the result sought.

Let us show this matter in the smallest numbers. If someone wants to know how many times a phrase of two notes, differing in position and value, can be changed: he will multiply the combination of notes differing in position alone—which is 2, as the first column shows—by the combination of notes differing in value—namely, the number 2, as the second column demonstrates—and the product will give the result, which is 4, as is evident.

[A musical notation diagram appears here showing four short staves with notes and numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 below them, illustrating the permutations of two notes.]

If you desire to know the permutations of 3 notes differing in both position and value, you will multiply the combination of three in the first column (which is 6) by the combination of three in the second column (which is 27), and 162 sought-after permutations will be produced.

You shall proceed in the same way for all the rest in order; always multiplying the combination of notes differing in position (shown in the first column) by the combination of notes differing in value (shown in the second table): and you will have the sought-after number of permutations for any number of notes assumed to differ in both position and value. Indeed, the preceding table teaches all these things exactly.

But if, among three notes, one differs while the other two are similar, the cube of three <note>3 multiplied by itself twice, as shown in the margin</note>, which is 27, will give the sought-after number of permutations for those three notes where one differs and the rest are similar, as the subjoined example teaches.

27

# L E M M A.
<note>A lemma is a preliminary proposition used to prove a later theorem.</note>

<margin>The marvelous affinity of Music to Algebra.</margin>

**I**F any chosen number is repeated in order—twice, thrice, four times, five times, etc., even unto infinity—the numbers repeated in order and multiplied into themselves will produce the <term>algebraic number|original: "numerum cossicum", referring to early algebraic notation where the unknown was called the "cosa" or "thing"</term> of that order, which the character of the number continued in natural order, or the exponent numbers, demonstrate. Let the number three be repeated several times, as is evident in this example. Then let 33 be multiplied into itself, and it will have a Square [Q]. If 3333 is multiplied into itself in order, it will have a biquadrate, and so on for the others as the table shows, in which you see 3 placed twice and multiplied into itself produces a square, which the algebraic character **Q** placed before the number two indicates.

| | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| R. | 1 | 3 | 3 | Root. |
| Q. | 2 | 33 | 9 | Square. |
| C. | 3 | 333 | 27 | Cube. |
| QQ. | 4 | 3333 | 81 | Biquadrate. <note>The fourth power.</note> |
| SS. | 5 | 33333 | 243 | Surdsolid. <note>An archaic term for the fifth power.</note> |
| QC. | 6 | 333333 | 729 | Square-cube. <note>The sixth power.</note> |

Those numbers continued in a natural series are called "exponents," because they "expose" how many times the chosen number must be placed and how many times it must be multiplied into itself, so that the desired algebraic power <note>original: "dignitas algebraica"</note>, indicated by the character prefixed to the exponents, may be produced. Thus, the exponent 4 shows that three ought to be placed four times, then multiplied into itself, so that 81 is produced—the biquadrate of the number three, indicated by the character **QQ**. The exponent 6, however, shows that 3 ought to be placed six times and multiplied in order into itself so that 729 is generated—the square-cube of the number three, which the character **QC** indicates. Therefore, we shall apply this preceding Lemma to the following problems.

# Problem III.

### *In Polyphonies, or melodies of many voices, of any number of notes—which are nevertheless equal in position and value—the mutations of the voices increase in the same order as algebraic powers in numbers.*

### Book VIII. Miraculous Music-making. 25

...emerge from the voices, proceed thus: let the combination of the number of notes that each voice has be set as the root of the <term>Cossic progression</term> <note>original: "progreſſionis Coſſicę." "Cossic" (from the Italian "cosa" or "the thing") was the standard term for algebra in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</note>. Since in this example the number of notes is 3, and its combination according to the first combinatorial table is 6 <note>Kircher is referring to a factorial (3 x 2 x 1 = 6).</note>, this number six will be the root of the entire harmonic algebraic progression. Thus, this six, placed twice and multiplied by itself, will produce the Square of 36, which shows the mutations of 2 voices: each of which has 3 notes equal in value, and can be changed in 36 ways. For since the first voice can be changed 6 times while the first [singer] sings one of the six, the second voice can meanwhile sing all 6 at the same time; and while the first sings the second voice out of his 6, the second will meanwhile sing another 6; and so on until the first singer has completed six mutations and the other has completed 36. This is the reason why two voices can be changed 36 times. For the same reason, three voices can be changed 216 times, because just as 6 placed three times and multiplied in sequence produces a cube, so three voices, each of which is changeable six times, multiplied by each other produce what we might call a harmonic cube, namely 216: the sought-after mutations of three voices. By this logic, 6 placed four times in order and multiplied by itself produces the harmonic <term>biquadrate</term> <note>The 4th power (6 to the power of 4).</note>, specifically 1296 mutations for 4 voices; and so on for the rest. As the following table shows, if there were 8 voices, each of which had 3 equivalent notes, there would be produced from eight sixes placed in order and multiplied by themselves the harmonic "square-of-the-square squared," namely 1,679,616 mutations for the 8 voices sought.

### Problem IV.
#### Given any number of notes for any number of voices, where the notes differ in pitch but are equal in duration, find their combinations.
Let there be, for example, 4 voices of six notes each, in which two pairs of identical notes are found in each voice; you proceed as follows: divide 720 (the number of combinations for 6 unique notes) by the square of the combination of a pair, which is 4. This results in 180, the number of mutations sought. This will be the <term>harmonic root</term> <note>the base number used for further calculations</note> for the "co-harmonic" powers of two, three, four, etc. voices—or, what is the same thing, the sought-after mutations to be investigated. I do not add an example here, as everything can be easily understood from what has already been said.

### Problem V.
#### Given 4 voices, of which the first consists of 4 notes, the second of three, the third of 4 (but with 2 identical), and the fourth consists of 5 notes, all differing in duration, find the mutations of all voices together.
Suppose we have this present <term>tetraphonium</term> <note>a composition for four voices</note>, and someone wishes to know how many times the voices can be rearranged; he should proceed as follows:

1.  Since the **first voice** [Musical notation: four notes on a staff] has 4 notes, all of equal duration and placed within the interval of a fourth, according to the previous **Problem I**, its combination is 24 <note>4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24</note>.
2.  Since the **second voice** [Musical notation: three notes on a staff] has only three equal notes arranged within the interval of a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>a musical fourth</note>, its combination is 6, according to the first Table of Combinations. Multiply 6 by 24, and you will have 144, the sought mutations of the first and second voices together.
3.  If you then desire the combinations of the **three voices**: the **third voice** [Musical notation: four notes on a staff] indeed has four notes, but two are on the same space; according to the preceding rule, you divide the combination of four (24) by 2. This results in 12, which, when multiplied by 144, gives 1,728, the sought mutations for three voices.
4.  Finally, if you desire the mutations of **4 voices**: the **fourth voice** [Musical notation: five notes on a staff] has 5 unique notes. Its ordinary combination is 120. Multiplying this by the mutations of the 3 voices (namely 1,728) will give the sought mutations for all 4 voices, which is **207,360**.

#### Corollaries.
#### Regarding the changes resulting from the 12 different modes or Tones.

Since the seven species of the octave constitute 12 different modes, and each individual mode within the octave <note>original: *διά πασῶν* (dia pason); Greek for "through all," referring to the octave</note> can be changed 40,320 times according to Problem I, these multiplied by 12 will give 483,840 changes of the 12 tones, if each octave is considered separately. If, however, they are taken as a mixture, the square of this number will give the desired result, namely 234,083,727,360 changes.

->**MIRACULOUS MUSIC-MAKING**<-
->**PART II.**<-
->**RHYTHMIC OR POETIC MUSIC-MAKING.**<-
->**CHAPTER I.**<-
->**On the power and efficacy of the Rhythmic art.**<-

I truly do not know what hidden and hitherto unpenetrated force of nature resides in motion, by which we see that possible in another which one does oneself; this occurs not only in the outward motion of the body, but most especially in that motion which, by the office of the tongue, breaks forth into words and song. For we see even a single person singing <margin>The human voice provokes imitation.</margin> excite others to do the same by a certain hidden force (whether this happens through dread, as in those struck by panic, or by an instinct of joy, as in those dancing). While this occurs in other motions, it certainly holds the greatest place in human voices. For since the human voice is nothing other than a certain artful motion of the tongue, formed according to a person's intention to signify something, we see it plainly cause in others that which it performs itself. For experience has taught that one person humming, or wailing, or whistling, or even yawning, excites others to do the same. Since this is true in sounds and voices that are even raw and unpolished, it will certainly be verified much more so in a skillful arrangement of words and voices. 

The Masters of primeval wisdom noted this hidden force of nature from the beginning. Hence, they did not compose the praises of the immortal Gods with just any haphazard arrangement of words; rather, they constrained their speeches with a certain harmonic measure, as if bonds had been cast upon them. They did this so that the very measure of the words would precisely correspond to the internal affections of the soul. From this, you may recognize the first rudiments of sacred poetry, which—just as it did then—has at all times maintained a certain divine quality in the minds of those who followed. For they believed that by this art, they could not only make Spirits and Gods stand near them through a certain sympathetic alteration, but could also change the minds of men into whatever state they wished. All these things that most learned <note>original: *πολυδίδακτος* (polydidaktos); Greek for "much-taught" or "highly instructed"</note> Horace teaches so excellently that it seems nothing else can be added to his words.

Certainly, this divine and impenetrable power—to speak with Plato—has no origin except from harmonic motion, as we have explained more fully elsewhere; especially if that motion corresponds proportionally to the internal passions of the soul. It will correspond proportionally if speech is drawn into fitting and harmonious periods through the brevity or length of syllables; or, what is the same thing, if a quick and swift measure follows quick movements of the soul, and a slow measure follows slow ones. 

And although this measure possesses a wonderful power in the Metric or Rhythmic art, it is certain that it has much greater energy in Musical poetry or Rhythm. For when the former is joined to the latter, as if complete in all its parts, it obtains truly prodigious effects in the minds of men, as almost infinite monuments of Historians testify. For there is, as I said a little earlier, a certain sympathetic connection between our soul and harmonic and rhythmic movements. As soon as metric harmony is presented to the ears, the mind—agitated by various passions—now gives signs of joy, now of love, now of sorrow, compassion, anger, groans, and other <term>affections<gloss>original: "pathematum"; the internal emotional states or "passions" triggered by external stimuli</gloss></term>. These sometimes increase so much that the mind, unable to be contained within the internal cloisters of the soul, excites the external limbs to acts corresponding to the passion. But since we have shown these things extensively in our *Magnetic Art*, Book III, on the Magnetism of Music and <term>Tarantism<gloss>A historical phenomenon where victims of a spider bite were said to be cured only by dancing to specific frantic music</gloss></term>, we refer the reader there.

Therefore, so that even those unskilled in Music might know how to join rhythms to harmonic numbers fitly and without any error, it seemed best to put forward here "Rhythmic Music" or "Poetic Harmony," so that directed by it, they might achieve their intended effect. Under this metric art of ours, we include not only poetry but also Rhetoric; that is, the creation of elegant periods of prose and applying them to musical melodies by a fitting pronunciation of syllables. Since this is so, let us begin the matter from its earliest cradle.

## CHAPTER II.
## On Accents.

<margin>What an acute accent is.</margin>

An accent is nothing other than the system of raising or lowering a syllable in terms of its tone. Among the Greeks, it is threefold: **Acute**, **Grave**, and **Circumflex**. Latin speakers enjoy only the acute and circumflex, neglecting the grave, as has been said. The **acute accent** is that by which a syllable is raised, the effect of which is <term>arsis<gloss>original: "ἄρσις"; the "lifting" or upbeat of a foot in meter</gloss></term>, that is, elevation. The **grave** is that by which the syllable is lowered, favoring <term>thesis<gloss>original: "θέσις"; the "placing" or downbeat of a foot</gloss></term>. They are called "accents" from *accinendo* <note>meaning "singing along with" or "attuning to"</note>, because they [govern] song or recitation...

...regulate the rhythmic recitation; whence they are also commonly called tones, tenors, vocalizations, and the peaks of voices. Regarding these, see Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book 3; then Quintilian, Book 1, Chapter 5; Gellius, Book 13, Chapter 6; and Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author whose work on the "Seven Liberal Arts" was a standard textbook for a thousand years.</note>, who calls the accent the "soul of voices and the seedbed of music" <note>original: "animam vocum & musicæ seminarium"</note>. Furthermore, just as an accent placed over a syllable does not necessarily show that the syllable is short or long, so too musical timings—or notes—do not strictly indicate the length or shortness of the syllable to which they are applied. Instead, what is precisely observed is the lifting or expression of the voice through a fast or slow duration. From this, a triple quantity can be considered in the pronunciation of a syllable:

The first is **time**, which is the duration we linger on the concept of a syllable before we cease its utterance; <margin>The triple quantity in the pronunciation of a syllable.</margin> and this is what authors mean when they say a syllable is short or long. To produce a short syllable, they used one beat of time; for a long one, they used two beats, as is clear in the musical notes placed here. 
[Musical notation on a staff] 
Hence the ancients, as Quintilian teaches in Book 1, Chapter 7, used to pronounce long syllables with a double vowel, such as *Maater* for *Mater* <note>Mother</note>, *deemit* for *demit* <note>He takes away</note>, *piipit* for *pipit* <note>He chirps</note>, *poonit* for *ponit* <note>He places</note>, and *puunit* for *punit* <note>He punishes</note>. 

[Musical notation on a staff]

The second quantity is the **intensive tenor**, by which the tone of the voice is lifted more intensely or lowered more gently; this is seen in the steps of the musical scale. For this reason, the same syllable—whether long or short—requires a note one step higher (at least a semitone) if it is <term>acute</term> <note>A high-pitched or sharp accent.</note> than if it is <term>grave</term> <note>A low-pitched or heavy accent.</note>; as is clear in example A. If, however, it is <term>circumflex</term> <note>An accent involving a rise and fall of the voice on a single syllable.</note>, it requires two notes, one of which is on a higher step and the other on a lower one; as seen in B.

The third quantity, arising from the accent, is **duration** <note>original: "mora"</note>. This is not so much the syllable itself, but its image propagated through the air, lasting within the space it meets. For an acute or circumflex syllable penetrates a longer interval and propagates more "copies" of itself in the air; <margin>The nature of utterance.</margin> therefore, its audible image lives longer, is perceived better by those at a distance, and is repeated by an Echo at a greater interval than a grave syllable or one uttered softly with a syllabic accent. It is no different than what happens with a string pulled tightly versus one pulled loosely. From this, it follows that an acute syllable always seems longer than a grave one—considering its lingering presence—not because it is held longer in the mouth of the speaker, but because its "species" or essence lives longer in the air.

You see, therefore, how Music gradually grew out of the nature of the accent. For the accent directs the entire business of human speech; thus, eloquence is more elegant the more it is distinguished by its accents. Hence all peoples and nations have their own accents proper to their nation, by which they are distinguished from other peoples. But since we have reserved all these matters for other treatises, we do not wish to be longer here. Just as the accent gives birth to syllabic pronunciation, so the musical accent gives birth to the harmonic. And just as <term>Rhythm</term> <note>Referring here to the poetic meter or "feet" of a line.</note> is born from syllabic pronunciation, moving now with a fast, now with a slow motion of feet, so too is harmonic Rhythm born. Having seen the nature of the accent, it now remains to inquire what Rhythm is.

**CHAPTER III.**
**On Rhythm and its accent.**

**R**hythm, insofar as it regards time and motion, is common to Poets and Orators as well as Musicians, since both the former and the latter distinguish voices and periods of voices by certain times. They differ, however, in this: among Poets, all short syllables are of the same shortness, and all long syllables are of the same length and extension. Conversely, among Musicians, the shortening and lengthening of syllables is not taken so precisely according to their nature. Instead, in three-syllable words, only the middle syllable is attended to as long or short; in four-syllable words, the penultimate is considered. This shortness and length they measure by the various values of notes, as will be shown shortly. Thus, the order of various times and measures...

...is called Rhythm, which Plato in the second book of *The Laws* defines as **the order of motion** <note>original Greek: "τῆς κινήσεως τάξιν"</note>; Aristoxenus, however, defines it as **the order of times** <note>original Greek: "τῶν Χρόνων τάξιν"</note>, so that some smallest moment of time can be the same thing in Rhythm as a sound is in Music, a point in Geometry, and <term>unity</term><note>The number one, the basic building block of mathematics.</note> in Arithmetic. From this Rhythm—which establishes the slowness and speed of time and motion as they appear in the very length and shortness of harmonic voices—comes the name **Rhythmic Music**. To declare myself by an example: if, for instance, in <term>Sapphic verses</term> <note>a specific meter used in ancient poetry and hymns</note> I place a *choree*, or an *iamb*, or a *pyrrichius*, or a *spondee*, it will always sound the same in music. ->*Iste Confessor Domini sacratus*<-
<note>This sacred Confessor of the Lord</note>
->*Pie Confessor deprecare Deum*<-
<note>Pious Confessor, pray to God</note>
->*Sanctus Confessor Oratores audit.*<-
<note>The Holy Confessor hears the Orators.</note>

In these, only the first verse, which consists of its required feet, is truly "poetic"; the other two are "musical," not preserving the quantity of the feet, but only preserving the leaps of the Rhythm accommodated to the verses. This sets aside the quantity of syllables except for the penultimate, which in this meter always requires a sharp accent.

However, let all these things be said concerning words or polysyllables that are not bound by the laws of meter; as is the case when we compose melodies upon some passage from Holy Scripture, or upon any other text of words in prose. For as I said a little while ago, prose and rhythmic speech belong no less to Rhythmics than does bound speech, as occurs in poetic meters.

If anyone applies harmony to verses and meters composed according to the laws of prosody, just as we shall professedly teach in what follows, he will make the work all the more perfect as the song or meter is more skillfully crafted and more exact in its movements.

But so that you may see how you can reduce metrical feet to harmonic feet, we shall show you the individual poetic feet in harmonic notes, after we have first set forth certain things for a better declaration of the matter.

It must be noted, therefore, that just as among Poets only one species of short and long syllables is considered, so among Musicians there are many species, according to the variety of value and the diminution of the notes. For example, *pænæ* <note>punishments</note> is a *spondee* <note>two long syllables</note> and is of one kind among Poets. Among Musicians, however, it can be manifold, since all these following notes can express a spondee.

So that it may be evident from this single example that Music extends much wider than Poetry...

**F**irstly, not all feet of this kind are suitable for metrical feet, nor can all be applied to every word. # Book VIII. The Miraculous Art of Music. 33

### §. I.
### Regarding three-syllable harmonic feet.

**First**, a triple progression can be observed in three-syllable harmonic feet: **ascending**, **level**, and **descending** <note>original: *ἀνάβατος* (anabatos), *ἰσόβατος* (isobatos), & *κατάβατος* (katabatos)</note>. An **ascending progression** occurs when the "foot" <note>a rhythmic unit of three syllables</note> moves upward, whether by steps or by leaps. A **level progression** is when the foot moves forward on the same pitch with equal steps. A **descending progression** <note>original: *katophatos*, likely a variant of *katabatos*</note> is when the foot moves downward either by steps or by leaps. This triple classification of movement is of such great importance in musical meter that without it, nothing can be correctly established in the Art of Music, as will be seen in the following sections.

**Second**, the greatest consideration must be given to the **upbeat** and the **downbeat** <note>original: *Arseos* (arsis) & *theseos* (thesis)</note> in three-syllable units. For someone who would begin a *Molossus* <note>a poetic foot consisting of three long syllables</note> on a **downbeat** would produce a ridiculous pronunciation; it would be quite different if they performed it on the **upbeat**.

**Third**, certain three-syllable feet are more suitable for **perfect time** <note>triple meter, which in early music theory was considered "perfect" as it represented the Holy Trinity</note>, while others are suited for **imperfect time** <note>duple or common meter</note>; which ones these are will be seen shortly.

**Fourth**, notes altered by a dot <note>dotted notes</note> have a great effect on the shortening of vocal sounds. But let us look closer at the matter. In order to proceed more solidly in our *Musurgia* <note>The Art of Music</note>, we will adapt poetic meters to various musical feet in different ways. Once these have been seen and examined, we will then decide which is better and more suitable for musical melodies.

**First**, therefore, one must especially consider the middle syllable in three-syllable feet; it is either short or long. Among those feet that have a short middle syllable are the **Dactyl**, **Tribrach**, **Anapaest**, and **Cretic**, which for this reason are called **middle-shorts** <note>original: *mesobrachos*</note>. Those that have a long middle syllable are the **Molossus**, **Bacchius**, **Antibacchius**, and **Amphibrachys**, which we therefore call **middle-longs** <note>original: *mesomacros*</note>. Some people adapt these to musical feet in such a way that the notes perfectly correspond to these signs of quantity ( ◡ for short and — for long), as follows:

-> **Three-syllable feet that shorten the second syllable, or "Middle-Shorts."** <-

| Tribrach | Dactyl | Anapaest | Cretic |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ◡ ◡ ◡ | — ◡ ◡ | ◡ ◡ — | — ◡ — |

[Musical notation follows, matching the rhythms above]
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

-> **Three-syllable feet that lengthen the second syllable, or "Middle-Longs."** <-

| Molossus | Bacchius | Antibacchius | Amphibrachys |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| — — — | ◡ — — | — — ◡ | ◡ — ◡ |

[Musical notation follows, matching the rhythms above]
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8

Behold, here is the method used by some who think that poetic feet should be adapted to musical melodies in such a way that short syllables correspond to notes of shorter duration, and long syllables to those of longer duration. **I do not approve of this for any reason**; it can cause huge errors in syllable harmony and entirely ridiculous pronunciations, especially regarding the rise and fall of notes...
