### Book VIII. Wondrous Music-making. 35

**Secondly, it must be noted** that in order to preserve the natural accent of individual <term>feet<note>In music and poetry, a 'foot' is a rhythmic unit made of long and short syllables.</note></term>, great consideration must be given to the ascent and descent of the notes. For if, in the case of three-syllable <term>mesobrachic feet<note>original: "pedum mesobrachorum." A rhythmic unit where the middle syllable is short (from the Greek 'mesos' for middle and 'brachys' for short).</note></term>, there is an <term>ascending<note>original: "anobatus"</note></term> motion—whether by step or by leap—the pronunciation will not be without a <term>solecism<note>A grammatical or structural error; here, it refers to a musical "clash" with the natural rhythm of speech.</note></term>. This is because the short middle syllable, through this upward progression, will cause a certain violent lengthening, which will be all the more absurd as the leap is larger, as was clear in the preceding example. Conversely, a <term>descending<note>original: "catobatos"</note></term> progression, by whatever means, will produce the natural accent of these same feet.

->Forbidden progression of Mesobrachic feet. | Permitted progression of Mesobrachic feet.<-

[Musical notation on two staves.]
[Staff 1: the word "**facere**" <note>Latin for "to do/to make." The middle syllable "ce" is short.</note> is set to three rising notes.]
[Staff 2: the word "**facere**" is set to three descending notes.]

Where you see the <term>Level Progression<note>original: "Isobaton," meaning staying on the same pitch.</note></term> moving equally, it holds a sort of middle ground of equality; the further you depart from this, the more imperfect you make the pronunciation. Thus, the best progression of all is the level one, then that which proceeds by steps; thereafter, the larger the intervals it consists of, the greater the violence it will inflict upon the ears.

In three-syllable <term>mesomacric feet<note>original: "pedibus Mesomacris." A rhythmic unit where the middle syllable is long (from 'mesos' for middle and 'makros' for long).</note></term>, or those having a long middle syllable, the progression behaves in the opposite manner. For an **ascending** progression preserves the natural accent however it is placed; but a **descending** one destroys it, affecting a certain forced lengthening in the middle syllable, as is clearly seen in the following example.

4 Forbidden progression of Mesomacric feet. | Permitted progression of the same.

[Musical notation on two staves.]
[Staff 1: "**The Plowman** <note>original: "Arator"</note> **lamented the deceased.**" The word **Arator** is set to descending notes.]
[Staff 2: "**Orator**" is set to ascending notes.]

**Thirdly, it must be noted** that just as the quantity of mesobrachic feet does not suit long and semi-long notes, so the quantity of mesomacric feet does not suit <term>quarter notes<note>original: "semiminimis"</note></term> well, and suits <term>eighth and sixteenth notes<note>original: "fusis & semifusis"</note></term> most poorly of all, because of a certain natural <term>asymmetry<note>original: "ἀμετρίαν" (ametrian)</note></term>. However, having noted these things, we will now hand down several rules by which we can give a perfect accent to harmonic melodies.

**Rule I.** Mesobrachic feet should be descending or level; mesomacric feet, on the contrary, should be ascending or level. Mesobrachic feet are conveniently applied to all notes of lesser value than a <term>half note<note>original: "minimas"</note></term>, because of the similarity of their inherent speed. Mesomacric feet, however, can be applied to all notes of greater value preceding a quarter note, in both ascending and descending progressions, because of the natural slowness that exists in both the notes and the syllables.

**Rule II.** Mesobrachic feet acquire a perfect and natural accent if the middle syllable is "elided" by a dot <note>Kircher means adding a rhythmic dot to the preceding note to shorten the middle one.</note>; this dot has enough power that, even in an ascending progression, it saves the shortening of the middle syllable. The same will happen if the first note of the Mesobrachic foot is <term>syncopated<note>A rhythmic displacement where the note starts on a weak beat or after a rest.</note></term> by placing a rest before it. It will, however, have a better effect in descent than in ascent. Mesomacric feet will acquire a perfect accent if a <term>quarter rest<note>original: "pausa semiminima"</note></term> precedes the first note. But let us give examples of each.

Behold, these are the feet which all poets use in composing meters. Some people apply the value of musical notes to these feet more superstitiously than is right. For some apply long musical notes to long feet and short notes to short feet; but in musical pronunciation, this would more likely provoke laughter than any real emotion. Hence, I wonder again why <term>Mersenne</term><note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and music theorist who was often Kircher's intellectual rival.</note>, though otherwise perceptive, thinks in his *Universal Harmony* that this comparison of notes with metrical feet is something extraordinary. For who would not laugh at musical pronunciation of this sort, where he thinks these notes [four diamond-shaped notes with stems] ought to be applied to a <term>Major Ionic</term> foot?

[Musical notation present]
You will perform miracles
<note>original: "Miracula patrabitis"</note>

It is evident, therefore, that in musical pronunciation, no account should be taken of the length or shortness of syllables, except for the **penultimate syllable** alone. Thus, all eight feet listed just above that have a long penultimate syllable can be treated as one and the same musical foot. Likewise, the eight feet with a short penultimate syllable can be accepted as another musical foot. Consequently, there are only two "musical" four-syllable feet: one that shortens the penult, and another that lengthens it. How these feet are to be applied to notes remains to be investigated.

Feet with a long penult sustain musical pronunciation whether the melody is rising, falling, or staying on the same pitch, as is clear in the following example.

# Book VIII. Wondrous Music-making. 39

### CHAPTER V.
### On the Variety of Meters.

**Meter** or verse is speech bound together in a certain kind, number, and order of feet, not without a sense of <term>harmony</term><note>Kircher uses "concentu," which implies a blending of sounds or musical concord.</note>. For verse without harmony would not be distinguished from prose speech, since the latter cannot exist without at least some degree of number and order of feet. And just as a line arises from the flow of a point, and a surface from the movement of a line, and a body from the extension of a surface, so also the **foot** is constituted from the syllable, and the **meter** from the feet. Since these feet possess infinite breadth, they can also constitute an infinite variety of meters. Of these, some take their name from the number of feet; some from the excess or deficiency of syllables; some from the feet themselves; others from the number of stanzas and "members" <note>In rhetoric and prosody, a "member" or "colon" is a distinct segment of a verse.</note>. Regarding each of these we shall speak in order.

Verses established by the number of feet are mostly **Iambic** and **Trochaic**, the first of which is the <term>dipody</term><note>From the Greek meaning "two feet." In certain meters, feet are counted in pairs.</note> or "two-foot" measure. For no meter can have fewer than two feet; otherwise, it would not be a meter, but simply a foot. One meter, therefore, is a dipody; but two meters consist of four feet, which are the kind of verses called **dimeters**, consisting of four feet. If indeed some verse consists of six feet it is called a **trimeter**, and if eight, a **tetrameter** by the Poets. <margin>Which feet are <term>catalectic</term> and <term>acatalectic</term>.</margin><note>Catalectic refers to a line of verse that is lacking a syllable in the last foot; acatalectic refers to a line that is metrically complete.</note>

<summary>Kircher defines poetic meter as a harmonious arrangement of "feet" and compares its structural evolution to the geometric progression from a point to a 3D body. He introduces the classification of verses based on the number of feet, such as dimeters and trimeters.</summary>
<keywords>meter, poetic feet, dipody, dimeter, trimeter, tetrameter, perfect time, musical prosody, geometry of music, Athanasius Kircher</keywords>

1. **Adonic**, which always consists of a <term>dactyl|a metrical foot consisting of one long syllable followed by two short syllables</term> and a <term>spondee|a metrical foot consisting of two long syllables</term> at the beginning.
2. **Glyconic**, in the first position it always consists of a spondee and a <term>choreus|also known as a trochee; a long syllable followed by a short one</term>, then of two dactyls, as in "Stars of heaven" <note>original: *Sidera caeli*</note>.
3. **Dactylic Alcaic**, which consists of a spondee, an <term>iamb|a short syllable followed by a long one</term>, and a long <term>caesura|a rhythmic break or pause in a line of verse</term>, followed by two dactyls. [See how the white mountain stands deep with snow.] <note>original: *Vides vt alta stet niue candidum* — Horace, Odes 1.9</note>
4. **Choriambic Asclepiadic**, consisting of a spondee, a dactyl, a long caesura, and two dactyls. [Maecenas, descended from ancient kings.] <note>original: *Mecænas Atauis edite regibus* — Horace, Odes 1.1</note>
5. **Euripidean Iambic** is composed of three iambs; however, in the third position, it can also admit a spondee and a <term>pyrrhic|a foot consisting of two short syllables</term>, as in [Hail, Star of the Sea.] <note>original: *Ave maris Stella*, a famous medieval hymn</note>
6. **Anacreontic** consists of three iambs and an extra syllable, such as [Cicada, when you have drunk enough of the sweet dew, you fill the pleasant fields with song.] <note>original Latin: *Roris vt sat bibisti dulci cicada cantu campos reples amænos*</note>.
7. Finally, **Archilochian Iambic**, both <term>catalectic|a line of verse lacking a syllable in the last foot</term> and <term>hypercatalectic|a line of verse having an extra syllable at the end</term>. [God powerfully rules the stars as the ancient race of mortals.] <note>original: *Deus potenter astra vt prisca gens mortalium*</note>.

To these are added the **Phalaecian** (an eleven-syllable verse) and the **Sapphic**.
And these meters are the most suitable of all for harmonic melodies, since the rhythms <note>original: *musarithmis*—Kircher’s specific term for musical-poetic rhythms</note> contained within them can be applied to melodies perpetually and without error, as we shall see later.

### CHAPTER VI.
### On the Application of Poetic Metric, or Rhythm, to Harmonic Poetry.

**I**n the preceding sections, it has been extensively declared that in poetic harmony, the strict length of syllables is not the only thing observed; rather, the "accent" is the primary consideration, which shines forth most clearly in the middle or penultimate syllable of words. However, so that even someone completely unskilled in Music might nonetheless be able to animate all kinds of meters into harmonic settings, we must first describe the meters most apt and suitable for this task. For as was also said above, not all poems are suitable for harmonic melodies, but only those which maintain a fixed and unchangeable arrangement of "feet." Such are the Adonics, Glyconics, certain Iambics, Phalaecian, Sapphic, and others of this kind. 

Hexameters and Pentameters, and Anapestic verses, because they involve a varied mixture of feet—and if you except the dactyl and spondee at the end of a hexameter, they have no fixed foot anywhere else in the remaining positions—it follows that they cannot be so easily accommodated to harmonic melodies, unless one were to preserve the exact same sequence of feet throughout, which would be a difficult task. Therefore, we judge that Hexameters and Pentameters and similar meters of "unstable feet" are to be ascribed not to harmonic prosody, but rather to the rhythms of Rhetoric or prose. How these are to be accommodated to musical melodies will appear shortly hereafter.

#### §. I.
#### On the Five-Syllable Adonic Verse.

**A**lthough, strictly speaking, any word composed of two Iambs, Chorees, Pyrrhics, or Spondees could be called a "meter" (insofar as it consists of more than one foot), poets reject the four-syllable rhythm as unfit for metrics. This is because the four-syllable count, due to its brevity, eludes the ear and vanishes too quickly, failing to provide a sufficient sense of proportion in movement. Therefore, no four-syllable grouping should properly be called a meter. The first of the meters is deservedly the five-syllable (pentasyllable); for this five-syllable rhythm exhibits to the ears the first and a certain pleasing proportion of movement. Of this kind are the five-syllable verses called **Adonics**, which consist of two feet: a dactyl and a spondee, as follows:
Cloudy- <note>original: *Nubi-* — likely the start of an example such as *Nubila soli*</note>

We have already shown the quality and condition of the Adonic meter; now it is our duty to explain the system of the Adonic <term>metrometer</term> <note>Kircher's term for a rhythmic template or "musical meter" that dictates how a poetic line should be set to music.</note>. For in the future, we shall call these not merely metric feet, but "Musurgical meters" of every kind, by which we may distinguish musical meters from poetic ones. Therefore, when we speak of a Musurgical Adonic, a Musurgical Glyconic, a Musurgical Iambic, and so on for the rest, we mean "metrometric" notes that correspond to the accents of the poetic meters, or those which measure the song itself. Indeed, these notes, when applied to the words of any meter, will measure them perfectly both in terms of time and accent. 

We have placed here 12 Musurgical Adonics expressed in metrometric notes, which can be beautifully applied to each and every Adonic line according to the subject matter and the condition of the words; from this, Curious Reader, you may learn the admirable variety in harmonies. For if you combine one of these Adonics of five notes in various ways according to their different values, 256 mutations will be produced that can be precisely made, even if you do not change the state or position of the notes. This was demonstrated at length above in the section on <term>Combinatorial Music</term> <note>Kircher was obsessed with "Ars Combinatoria," the mathematical study of how a limited set of elements (like notes or syllables) can produce near-infinite variations.</note>, so much so that a single metric Adonic can be expressed by 256 different Musurgical Adonics. However, from those 256, we have selected here only the twelve most suitable, which will be more than sufficient for the composer <note>original: "symphoniurgo," literally a maker of polyphony or harmonies.</note> to express any metric Adonics whatsoever. Furthermore, we have provided 8 Musurgical Adonics in <term>imperfect time</term> <note>Equivalent to modern duple or quadruple time (e.g., 4/4).</note> and 4 in <term>perfect time</term> <note>Equivalent to modern triple time (e.g., 3/4).</note>, so that the musician may use them at his pleasure. But concerning the explanation of these, we shall speak more at length in what follows.

## §. III.

### Concerning the Anacreontic Iambic, a seven-syllable meter.

The **Anacreontic Iambic** is a seven-syllable meter <term>heptasyllabon | a verse of seven syllables</term> and consists of three iambs and one extra syllable. It is of two types: the first always delights in an iamb at the beginning, while the latter always delights in an anapest <term>anapest | a metrical foot consisting of two short syllables followed by one long one</term>. Observe the example of both in the accompanying figure.

<margin>Metrical notation for Anacreontic verses.</margin>

O three and four times happy         Every pleasure has this: <note>This second poem is from Boethius's *Consolation of Philosophy*.</note>
Cicada, who in the high                It drives those who rage with stings
Greenery of the trees                   And like the winged bee
Having drunk a little dew             When it has poured out its pleasing honey
You rejoice to sing sweetly.           It flees, and with a too-tenacious
Anapestic verses follow                Sting, it strikes the wounded hearts, etc.

<margin>[Musical notation symbols] Anacreontic anapests in notes</margin>

From these twelve Anacreontic harmonies, any one can be adapted to individual stanzas. However, since the latter type has an anapest at the start of the stanzas, you will have **Anacreontic Anapestic Musical Settings** if you divide the first notes in each five-syllable group into two notes equal to the first. This is clear in the accompanying example, where you see the individual first notes divided into two equivalents so that you may have an Anacreontic anapest. Although the anapestic version has eight syllables, it is nevertheless the same as the seven-syllable Anacreontic, whether you look at the accent or the duration of time.

### §. IV.

### On the Iambic Archilochian eight-syllable meter.

After the seven-syllable meter follows the eight-syllable, which is a most widely sung type of verse. Indeed, there is hardly a hymn found in the Roman Breviary <note>A liturgical book containing the public or canonical prayers, hymns, and readings of the Roman Catholic Church.</note> that does not consist of this type of verse, for it is—if any other is—uniquely suited to musical melodies. Of this type are the hymns:
*The banners of the King go forth* <note>Original Latin: *Vexilla regis prodeunt*</note>
*Come, Creator Spirit* <note>Original Latin: *Veni Creator Spiritus*</note>. And also that:
*Enough for the funeral, enough for tears,*
*Enough has been given to sorrows.* <note>Original Latin: *Sat funeri sat lachrymis / Sat est datum doloribus.*</note>
The musical notes to be adapted to these are placed here; and since this kind of meter is usually a four-line stanza, one of these 12 musical metrometers <term>metrometers: Kircher’s system of shorthand musical notation used to assign rhythmic values to poetic syllables.</term> can be applied to each individual line.

### §. V.

### On the Nine-syllable Meter, or verse of nine syllables.

The Iambic Archilochian dimeter hypercatalectic <term>hypercatalectic: A line of poetry that has an extra syllable at the end beyond its standard meter.</term> is nine-syllabled, of which type is every third line in the four-line stanzas of Horace, specifically:
*The woods laboring with the cold* <note>Original Latin: *Sylvæ laborantes geluque*</note>
When, however, it consists of only four iambs <note>A metrical foot consisting of one short syllable followed by one long syllable.</note> along with one extra syllable, it is an Alcaic Iambic dimeter, such as:
*The parricides love poisons.* <note>Original Latin: *Amant Venena parricidæ.*</note>
Both meters are measured with the same musical metrometer notes, as is clear in the accompanying example.

### §. VI.

### On the ten-syllable meter.

The Iambic Alcmanian trimeter catalectic <term>catalectic: A line of verse lacking a syllable at the end or ending with an incomplete foot.</term> is ten-syllabled, of which the following verse is an example:
*You despise the beautiful marriage-beds of the Virgin.* <note>Original Latin: *Spernis decoros Virginis thoros.*</note>
However, since a poem of this sort receives a varied mixture and has a rhythm <note>Original Latin: *pedem*—literally 'foot'</note> that is more mobile than is proper, we reject it as less suited to harmonic poetry. Nevertheless, if anyone wished to use them, they would have to maintain the measure of the verse placed a little before this with a perpetual and unchangeable pace. If that were done, then one could apply the preceding metrometer notes to the syllables of that type of meter with no trouble, if one divided the second-to-last note into two equally valued notes. § VII.
Concerning the hendecasyllabic <note>A line of verse consisting of eleven syllables.</note>, Phaleucian, Sapphic, and Alcaic dactylic meters, commonly called Horatian.

The hendecasyllabic meter is varied; from many types, we have selected three more suited to harmony. The first of these is the Phaleucian. This is especially suited to harmony because of its frequent trochees <note>original: "choręos"; a metrical foot consisting of a long syllable followed by a short one.</note>. Indeed, the Italians use hardly any other type of verse more frequently in their poetry, as none is better suited to harmonic melodies. To establish perfect harmony, they usually join to it an Anacreontic heptasyllabic <note>A seven-syllable line named after the Greek poet Anacreon.</note>, as will be seen in the following.

Whoever, therefore, desires to adapt musical poetry to this type of meter should first take care, as much as possible, that the Phaleucians are "pure"—meaning they consist of frequent trochees—while rejecting dactyls, anapests, and tribrachs <note>Different types of metrical "feet" or rhythmic units.</note>; thus he will easily achieve his goal. The metrical notes <note>Kircher refers to his "Metrometro," a system of mechanical music composition that assigns musical values to poetic rhythms.</note> are placed in the margin, any one of which you may apply from the twelve to any of the Phaleucians. <margin>Metrical Notes of the Phaleucian. [A grid of musical/metrical symbols]</margin>

Sapphic meter.

The other hendecasyllabic is the Sapphic, a very common verse, usually a *tristrophon dicolon* <note>original: "tristrophon dicolon"; a stanza structure where three lines of one meter are followed by a fourth line of a different meter.</note>, meaning it consists of three stanzas <note>Though the text says "strophis" (stanzas), in this context it refers to the three identical long lines.</note> to which an Adonic <note>A short five-syllable line.</note> is attached at the end. It is called *dicolon* because of the two different species of meter that constitute it. This meter is in no way inferior to the preceding one in its suitability for forming excellent harmonies. For this type of meter has a certain hidden harmony within it so effective that beginners in poetry usually scan it in no other way than by singing; this is a clear sign of its great kinship and affinity with Music. It differs from the previous Phaleucian hendecasyllabic because that one consists of pure trochees (alongside iambs), while this also consists of dactyls and anapests. Of this kind are the hymns in the Roman Breviary: 

*He, the Confessor of the Lord, whom the faithful worship...* <note>original: "Iste Confessor Domini colentes"; a famous hymn for the Common of a Confessor.</note> etc. 

Also the hymn usually recited on the feast of St. John the Baptist:
*So that your servants may resonate with relaxed vocal cords*
*The wonders of your deeds,*
*Dissolve the guilt of the polluted lip,*
*Saint John.* 
<note>original: "Ut queant laxis resonare fibris / Mira gestorum famuli tuorum / Solue polluti labij reatum / Sancte Ioannes." This hymn is of immense historical importance; the first syllable of each line—Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La—provided the names for the musical notes in the system of solmization.</note>

This is truly a most famous meter, upon the occasion of which Guido of Arezzo <note>The 11th-century monk credited with inventing modern musical notation.</note> invented figured music <note>Polyphonic music notation.</note>, as was shown extensively in the preceding books. The metrical notes are placed here. <margin>Metrical Notes of the Sapphic Poem. [A grid of musical/metrical symbols]</margin>

Note in this place that the metrical notes of the preceding Phaleucian can be applied to the Sapphics, just as the Sapphics can be accommodated to the Phaleucians without hesitation. For the metrical notes of the Adonic which must be joined to the three-line stanza, you will take them from § 1 of this section.

To the hendecasyllabics explained here, the Hipponactean Iambic <note>A meter named after the Greek poet Hipponax.</note> may rightly be added, such as this one:
*Three measures of old Falernian wine*
*The bold ruler and arbiter of Kings*
*Drained, of the powerful grandsons of Romulus...* <note>original: "Ternos vetusti Congios falerni / Hausit potentum Romuli nepotum / Regnator audax arbiterque Regum"</note> etc.

# THE MIRACULOUS MUSURGIA
## PART III.
### EXHIBITING THE PRACTICE OF MUSICAL NUMBERS FOR COMPOSITION.
### CHAPTER I.
#### On the goal and purpose of the Author.

Since in the preceding sections we promised that we would provide a method by which anyone, even one unskilled in Music, could arrive at a perfect knowledge of composing, we wished in this place to fulfill those promises—after first explaining where our invention lies.

Having become more learned through frequent experience, I observed that "one thing is contained in all, and all things in one" by a certain admirable reasoning. That is, I more keenly perceived that in all sciences and faculties, there is one principal foundation <note>original: "principium"</note> to which all other things are returned according to a certain analogy. Since these matters cannot be handled without a perfect knowledge of combinations, I established the **Combinatoric Art** <note>Kircher refers to his system of using mathematical permutations to organize knowledge or create new ideas.</note> to reveal the thoughts of my mind. <margin>In all sciences, there is one principal foundation.</margin> I represented the principles of all sciences to the eye through various movements <note>original: "orchemata," likely referring to diagrams or mathematical "dances"</note>, so that nothing could seem easier than to reach an exact knowledge of all things in a short time with their help. Since I found such a marvelous power in the combination of things—as in all other things, so most of all in Music—nothing else seemed to be required but that the principles of Music (explained more fully in the previous sections) should be reduced here into methodical tables, which we call **Musarithms** <term>Musarithms: A portmanteau of "Music" and "Algorithm," these were Kircher's mathematical tables used for automatic composition.</term>, or harmonic numbers. This, as it was conceived in the mind, was immediately put into execution.

Lest anything in Music remain hidden even from the *unmusical* <note>original Greek: "amouson," meaning someone without the favor of the Muses or musical training</note>, that is, those unskilled in Music, we have constructed three collections <term>syntagmata: organized sets or treatises</term> of tables. In these, through several musical charts <note>original: "Pinaces melotheticos"</note>, we have arranged whatever is rare and excellent in the entire art of musical composition <note>original: "Musica melothetica"</note>, according to the order and method that follows.

<margin>The order of the tables constructed for the composition of songs.</margin> The First Collection contains ten charts or tables in which we present the whole of poetic or metrical Musurgy <note>the art of setting verse to music</note>, so that given any type of verse, you can compose a melody upon it according to any requested method.

**Chart I** shows us the Musarithms of polysyllabic feet, from two-syllable feet up to seven-syllable feet. We have included in this chart only those polysyllables whose second-to-last syllable is long, as the heading of the table itself demonstrates. At the bottom of the columns are placed the "metrometer" notes <term>metrometer: a system for measuring musical time or meter</term> that measure the given feet.

**Chart II** shows us the Musarithms of polysyllabic feet together with the metrometer notes corresponding to each, where the second-to-last syllable is short.

**Chart III** shows us Musarithms for Adonic and dactylic meters <note>classical poetic meters often used in hymns</note>, the forms of which are: *Gaudia mundi* <note>original: "Joys of the world"</note>, *Tollite lumina* <note>original: "Lift up your eyes"</note>.

**Chart IV** shows Musarithms for Euripidean Iambics and dactyls, the form of which is that most celebrated hymn *Ave maris stella* <note>original: "Hail, star of the sea"</note>. For such a verse, therefore, you will complete the desired melody with no effort with the help of this table; other minor details of the table will be explained in their proper places.

**Chart V** shows Musarithms for Anacreontic meters, the form of which is *O ter quaterque felix* <note>original: "O thrice and four times happy"</note>, together with the metrometer notes corresponding to each, added at the bottom of the columns.

**Chart VI** shows Musarithms for eight-syllable Archilochian Iambics...

<margin>In what this new method of composition consists.</margin>

This new **Musurgia** <note>From the Greek 'mousa' (muse) and 'ergon' (work); Kircher’s term for the art of musical composition.</note> of ours consists primarily in the ingenious arrangement of **melotactic columns** <note>From the Greek 'melos' (song) and 'taxis' (arrangement). These were columns of numbers used in Kircher's mechanical composition box.</note>, from which, however they are used, a new harmony will necessarily and always result. Since these types of compositions are infinite, an infinite diversity of harmonic variations is born. For example, the combinations of the first table are so great that the entire world, from the earth even unto the firmament, could more easily be filled with sand than the diversity of harmonies resulting from it could be exhausted. Indeed, if all the writers of the whole world since the creation of the orb had always applied themselves to the description of such harmonic combinations, they would not yet have exhausted them. But since these things are known only to those imbued with the <term>mysteries of numbers</term> <note>Pythagorean numerology, where numbers were seen as the building blocks of the universe.</note>, I do not wish to pursue them further, especially since we have demonstrated them at length in the first part of this book. I have chosen to add these points here to restrain the slander of certain practical Musicians, who, upon seeing these things, immediately object that the Music produced is "always the same." Truly, we do not dwell on their ignorance; experience itself will teach the truth. Therefore, whoever knows how to skillfully adapt these columns into movable tiles <note>original: 'tessellas'</note> according to the rules to be prescribed in the fourth part of this work, and knows how to rightly transfer the harmonic numbers into the melotactic scale, will find that he can compose any artistic melodies for any given tone and any given words. Just as in **Algebra**, a mathematician <note>original: 'logista'</note> achieves the clarification of paradoxical questions by following the tenor of the rule with such ease that the worker himself does not know what he has done—and thus an unexpected effect is produced with the mathematician hardly thinking—so here, by following the tenor of the rules, even for those who are **unmusical** <note>original: ἀμούσοις (amousois)</note>, the desired harmony will emerge. But lest we keep the eager Reader in suspense any longer, let us now approach more closely the secrets of our Musurgic art.

# CHAPTER II.
## Concerning the Requirements for our Musarithmic Composition.

A **Musarithm** <note>Kircher's term for a numerical code representing a musical phrase.</note>, as was stated in the definitions, we call nothing other than a certain aggregate of harmonic numbers, through which perfect harmony is drawn out by means of rhythmic signs applied to the musarithm. To perform this with excellence, the following things are required.

### Requirement I.
### The Phonotactic Palimpsest.

Since every mathematical science consists more in demonstration for the sake of finding the truth than in a wandering style of disputation subject to many obscurities of opinion, it was necessary to represent these demonstrations with sensible signs so they might be better perceived. Hence, the first Masters of wisdom discovered points, surfaces, solids, numbers, and infinite other characters which, when depicted on paper, would reveal the thoughts of the mind and the meaning of conceived things. In a similar way, **Musurgi** <note>Music-makers or composers.</note>, in order to bring their speculations into action and present their demonstrations to the senses, discovered certain signs by which sounds (otherwise imperceptible) might become known through the positioning of visible marks. Following them, in order to bring our speculations into practice, we first ordain a **Phonotactic Palimpsest** <note>literally a 'sound-arranging' reusable writing surface.</note>. 

<margin>What a Palimpsest is.</margin>

A Palimpsest is nothing other than that leathery membrane made from donkey skin of which notebooks or writing tablets are commonly made, and which modern Musicians are accustomed to use as being, for the most part, more suitable for this business than all others. For as it is easily written upon, so the writing is easily erased.

The staves are marked primarily with three signs, which are called the "principles of the musical scale," and these are **F, C, and G**. The sign **F** (or the starting point of the scale) is placed on the **Bass** staff either on the middle line, the fourth, or the fifth. In transposing songs, it is most often placed on the middle line, and then the bass sounds higher. If it is placed on the fourth line, it indicates a medium pitch that is most natural for the voices, a **minor third** <term>semiditono: a musical interval consisting of a tone and a half</term> lower; finally, if placed on the fifth line—which happens rarely—it denotes the deepest pitch, a minor third lower than the previous one. The markings of the remaining voices follow this bass arrangement, as shown just above. This is the first type of marking, which they call **"hard"** or **"natural."** The other is **"soft,"** which they also call **"feigned"** <note>original: "fictam," referring to *musica ficta* where notes are altered outside the standard scale</note>; it differs in no way from the previous one, except that a **flat symbol (♭)** is placed in the appropriate space for each voice, as seen in the second row.

Note in this place that wherever you find this sign [F-clef symbol] placed on the bass staff, know that the **F-clef** is there; for from this point, by counting up or down, we arrive at the knowledge of the positions of the clefs or the seven principal characters **A, B, C, D, E, F, G**. These are like keys <note>a play on the word "clavis," which means both a musical clef and a physical key</note> that open the door to all melody.

In the **Tenor**, wherever this sign [C-clef symbol] is found, know that the **C-clef** is there; from which, by counting up or down, you will arrive at the knowledge of any other desired clef. These same rules are to be observed in the **Alto** (or Counter-Tenor) and the **Soprano**. In the **Soprano** (the higher voice), you will begin the positions of the remaining clefs from the line on which you see the **G-clef** placed. Let these things be said for those who are unskilled in practical music, for whose sake we have decided to add here the entire system of the **phonotactic palimpsest** <note>Kircher uses "palimpsest" here to describe a musical chart or template used in his composing machine</note>.

### Requirement II.
### The Tonographic Table.

Just as the preceding phonotactic system is a certain "material" principle for organizing melodies, so we may not undeservedly call this the "formal" principle of the same. It is nothing other than a representation of the 12 Tones according to the 7 species of the <term>octave</term> <note>original: "diapason"; the Greek term for an octave</note> in columns appropriate to each tone, according to their harmonic numbers. However, instead of using many words, we place the entire system here before your eyes, so that we are not forced to repeat what we have treated at length in preceding books regarding the tones and their nature and condition.

<margin>Points to be noted concerning the Tonographic Table.</margin>

We have constructed this Tonographic Table with a certain secret artifice so that we might encompass absolutely infinite combinations of harmonic modulations within a very few columns. Indeed, this Tonographic Table can rightly be called the basis and foundation of our entire "Miraculous Music-making" <note>original: "Musurgiae mirificae"</note>. We have set down twelve tones commonly used throughout the Church (which we therefore call "Ecclesiastical Tones"), so that nothing should be lacking for the curious composer <note>original: "melothetae"</note> in achieving an immense variety of melodies.

Although, strictly speaking, there are only six Tones that undergo perfect mutations—for the other Tones either fall into the same intervals or derive their difference from the transposition of "hard" into "soft" <note>Referring to the change from major-like to minor-like qualities</note> (which musicians call transposition), as will be discussed later—we have not preserved the natural order of the tones in this table. This was done so that the numerical order and the difference between intervals might be more clearly visible. 

To ensure you can name each one correctly, we have attached the ancient names to each tone, along with the specific nature of each. Thus, according to the requirements of the theme you wish to bring to life through harmony, you may find the corresponding "affects" <note>In Baroque theory, "affects" are specific emotional states triggered by musical devices.</note> within these tones. We have labeled each tone as either "hard" or "soft"; if a tone is "hard," it is suited to the character of the ancient "hard" song; if "soft," to the "soft" song. Furthermore, so that you may call any tone by its proper name, we have added the ancient designations alongside the nature of each, so that depending on the subject matter you wish to animate with harmonic melodies, you might find the corresponding emotions—namely joy, love, compassion, pain, grief, dissolution, religion, vanity, ferocity, indignation, and similar feelings suited to stirring the souls of men. For just as a melody composed according to the first tone possesses a certain effectiveness upon men...

### Requirement III.
### On the value of notes, and the measure of time.

To prevent someone unskilled in music from finding any delay or obstacle in this musical work of ours, we have decided to set down here the value of the musical notes (which we call "metro-meter" notes <term>metrometras: from the Greek for "measure-meters," referring to how they dictate the rhythm</term> in our tables of *Musarithms* <term>Musarithmi: Kircher's system for mechanical composition using mathematical tables</term>).

Since there is such a great variety of harmonic movements (all of which come together in a single melody of several voices), where some proceed at a fast pace, others at a slow, and some at a moderate pace, it seemed best to musical composers to establish a fixed signal to avoid confusion. By this signal, singers could direct their voices. Because this signal acts as a kind of rule and a standard <term>amussis: a precise tool used by builders to ensure a surface is level</term> for harmonic movements, it was not appropriate for it to be immobile. Therefore, they made it mobile through the raising and lowering of the hand (or any other object held in the hand). They called this motion *arsis* and *thesis* <note>original: ἄρσιν & θέσιν. In music, these refer to the "lift" (upbeat) and the "setting down" (downbeat)</note>. The Italians call it
<margin>
Things to be noted concerning the Beat.
</margin>
*la battuta*, Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose writings on music theory were used for a thousand years</note> calls it the *plausum* <note>original: "the strike" or "applause"</note>, others call it the *tactus* <note>the pulse or beat</note> or measure; we entitle it the *Chronometron* <term>Chronometron: Greek for "time-measurer"</term>. This measure consists of two parts: one the lowering, which the ancients called *thesis*, the other the raising of the hand, which they called *arsis*. These correspond to the movement of the blood in the body, which Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> calls *diastole* and *systole* <note>the expansion and contraction of the heart/pulse</note>. Just as one pulse of the veins is made of one *diastole* and one *systole*, so one full time or measure is completed from an *arsis* and *thesis*. The characters of the *Chronometron* are those musical notes commonly used, whose values we place before your eyes here in a single glance.

->**Table I.**<-
->**Of the Value of the Notes.**<-

| 2 | 1 | 1/2 | 1/4 | 1/8 | 1/16 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [Breve] | [Semibreve] | [Minim] | [Semiminim] | [Fusa] | [Semifusa] |
| **Brevis** | **Semibrevis** | **Minima** | **Semiminima** | **Fusa** | **Semifusa** |

The first note denotes two measures; the second one; the third a half-measure; the fourth a quarter part of a measure; the fifth an eighth; and the last denotes a sixteenth part of a measure. Each decreases from the note immediately preceding it in a double proportion. Thus, a *semibrevis* <note>modern "whole note"</note> taken twice makes a *brevis* <note>modern "double whole note"</note>; a *minima* <note>modern "half note"</note> taken twice makes a *semibrevis*; a *semiminima* <note>modern "quarter note"</note> taken twice makes a *minima*; a *fusa* <note>modern "eighth note"</note> taken twice makes a *semiminima*; and finally, a *semifusa* <note>modern "sixteenth note"</note> taken twice makes a *fusa*. Furthermore, sixteen *semifusae*, 8 *fusae*, 4 *semiminimae*, and two *minimae* are always equivalent to one *semibrevis*. Indeed, these are clear in the following illustration.

**Semi-** [16 semifusa symbols] **fusae**
**Fu-** [8 fusa symbols]
**Semi-** [4 semiminima symbols]

### Book VIII. Wondrous Music-Making. 53

But so that these matters might be better understood, we must first indicate something here regarding **time**. Musical time, therefore, is nothing other than a fixed and determined quantity of smaller notes or figures contained within one *breve* <note>A note value that, in Kircher's time, was a standard unit of measurement, though it is rarely used in modern music.</note> or *semibreve* <note>The ancestor of the modern "whole note."</note>, as is clear in the preceding diagram.

Time is twofold: **perfect** and **imperfect**. 
**Perfect time** is found at the beginning of a melody marked with this character: **O** <note>original: "O"</note>. This indicates that the *breve* measure is "perfect" in all respects—that is, it is equal to **three semibreves**, as shown here to the side:

[Musical staff showing a circle 'O' followed by three semibreve notes] **Perfect Time**

[Musical staff showing a broken circle 'C' followed by two semibreve notes] **Imperfect Time**

But when a "half-circle" <note>original: "medius circulus"</note> like this **[symbol: broken circle with a vertical line through it]** is placed at the beginning, as appears to the side, it indicates by this character that the *breve* is **imperfect**—that is, it is equal to **two semibreves**. However, since these matters were discussed at length in previous sections, we only wished to recall them to memory here.

->**On Rests.**<-

Finally, since all voices are not always in motion, it happens that they must occasionally be silent. For this reason, certain notes were devised to indicate to the singer <term>phonascis: a Greek-derived term for a vocalist or music teacher</term> how much time they ought to rest. The Greeks call these notes *pauseis* <note>original: "παύσεις"</note>, while the Latins, changing the name, call them *pausae* <note>original: "pausas"</note>. To understand these, nothing more seems required than a summary of rests, which I present to you here.

The lines inserted into the five-line staff <note>original: "pentagrammo"</note> in this diagram signify rests; the numbers placed above denote the value of the rests—that is, for how many beats <term>tactus: the basic unit of time or "pulse" in Renaissance and Baroque music, often directed by a hand motion</term> the singer should remain silent. 

For example: the first rest marking shows a silence of eight beats; the second, seven; the third, six; the fourth, five and a half, and so on until the last. For the last shows a silence of 1/8th of a beat; the second to last, 1/4th of a beat; and the third to last, 1/2 of a beat (or a "half-pulse"). But as these things are very easy and well-known even to young beginners <note>original: "Tyronibus"</note>, I did not think they needed further explanation; I have only included them to provide some introduction for those who are completely ignorant of music.

**Requirement IV.**
**Knowledge of Musarithms.**

In this context, we define a **Musarithm** <term>Musarithmus: A word invented by Kircher, combining "Music" and "Arithmetic" (or algorithm), referring to the numerical building blocks of his compositional system</term> as nothing other than a collection of harmonic numbers that correspond to specific metrical feet <note>Rhythmic patterns based on poetic meters, such as iambic or dactylic</note> and are organized into charts or methodical tables. 

By using this new and highly appropriate title, we intended to bring honor to this new art. For a "Musarithm" is the same as a "musical number" <note>original: "μουσικὸς ἀριθμὸς"</note>—that is, a grouping of sounding numbers that is perfectly suited for expressing harmonic periods, as you will see later—

### CHAPTER III.
### Concerning simple counterpoint and how it can be composed from the first Collection of Musical Rhythms even by someone unversed in Music.

The first Collection <note>Kircher uses the term *Syntagma* to describe a set or volume of his musical building blocks.</note> contains, besides ten others, two tables <note>original: "pinaces"</note> of multi-syllable Musical Rhythms. The first table contains multi-syllable words with a long second-to-last syllable; the second contains those with a short second-to-last syllable. With the help of these, anyone—even someone unacquainted with music <note>original: "ἄμουσος"</note>—may easily perform all simple counterpoint through the practice to be explained shortly. We have placed this collection of Musical Rhythms <note>Kircher's "Musarithmi" are mathematical-musical units used for algorithmic composition.</note> before the others as it is simpler, so that by starting with the easier and simpler elements, we might find less difficulty in the remaining sections that follow. Furthermore, so that we do not proceed in this educational business without a method <note>original: "ἀμεθόδως"</note>, we have followed the style of mathematicians and seen fit to demonstrate the artistry of our entire Music-making system through practical propositions or certain "problems." Let us therefore begin the matter with the favor of the good God.

#### Problem I.

*Given any text of words, and any tone, to compose the requested song in simple counterpoint from the first table.*

<margin>A new way of composing.</margin>
If, therefore, anyone desires to take a trial of our art in simple counterpoint, let him first of all have prepared a phonotactic palette <note>original: "Palimpsestum phonotacticum." This was a reusable writing surface, like a slate, used for arranging musical notes.</note> according to the requirements of the second chapter of this part. Second, a Tone-Writing Table. Third, let him keep the Text of words written out separately, and let him choose a tone appropriate to the energy of those words. For example, to implore the grace of the Divine Power, let the text of words be: *Come Creator Spirit* <note>original: "Veni Creator Spiritus," a famous medieval hymn.</note>. Since these words denote hope and trust in divine mercy, the sixth tone (or Hypolydian) will suit them best. For it to be established, it must necessarily have as many notes as there are points marked in the spaces of the musical staffs; and you shall place these notes above the points of the **Bass** [*Basis*] in order; then you shall write these same notes for the points of the **Tenor**, the same for the points of the **Alto**, and finally the same for the points of the **Soprano** [*Cantus*]; and you will have the first period or stanza of your theme, complete in all its parts. 

However, you must carefully observe that the notes are placed precisely in their spaces as indicated by the points. ->Come, Creator Spirit, visit the minds of your people, fill with heavenly grace the hearts which you have created.<-
<note>original: "Veni Creator Spiritus mentes tuorum visita imple superna gratiae qui tu creasti pectora." This is a famous 9th-century Gregorian hymn.</note>

But at this point, practical musicians will object that by this method, the same harmony will always be produced, and consequently, that variety of harmonies which the Author claims will not result. We shall easily shut their mouths once we have demonstrated the wonderful diversity even in this single example. Therefore, the objection is false. For it will then be clear that this theme is capable of infinite variation, once we have first laid down certain principles.

<margin>This new method of composing is capable of infinite variation.</margin>

I say, therefore, that this aforementioned theme can be varied in four ways. First, by the transposition of the <term>Musarithms</term>; Second, by the variety of the tones; Third, by the types of notes to be applied; and Fourth, by the columns, which, through the different poetic feet that even a single stanza possesses, admits infinite combinations; but let us examine each one separately.

First, since this four-stanza theme is composed of four polyphonic Musarithms; it is certain by the power of the number four (as was demonstrated at length in the first part of this *Musurgia*, Problem 1) that it is changeable twenty-four times—that is, it admits 24 combinations—so that a new harmony, different from the previous one, always emerges. For any of the said four Musarithms can occupy the first place six times, with the remaining ones always being variable; since all these things were demonstrated in the cited place, we refer the Reader there. Therefore, this four-stanza theme can first be changed twenty-four times so that the harmony is never the same.

<margin>Variation by way of transposing the musarithm.</margin>

Secondly, it is changeable another twelve times by reason of the Tones. For the movable scale of keys, when applied to the individual columns of the Tones, will always produce essentially different harmonies according to the varied nature of the tones. If, therefore, you multiply 24 by 12, we will already have 288 mutations by which this mentioned four-stanza theme is variable.

Thirdly, it can be changed by reason of different notes and according to the 12 series of notes placed at the bottom of the column: first according to the simple arrangement, 3,456; but according to the combinations of notes made among themselves in any way you like, 16,554,298,160,800 mutations will be born—and in so many possible ways is this single four-stanza theme strictly variable.

# First Diagram.
### *The mutation of a composed theme from the sixth tone to the first tone of the keys.*

<margin>The method for changing a song from one Mode to another Mode.</margin>

If, therefore, anyone should desire to change this subject into the first tone, he should apply the column to the column of the first Tone. In the phonostatic palimpsest <note>original: "palimpsesto phonostatico"; this refers to Kircher's invention, a sliding mathematical table or "composition box" used to generate music</note>, he should first change the character of the "soft" song into the "hard" <note>original: "mollis cantus in durum"; this refers to shifting from a B-flat (soft) to a B-natural (hard) hexachord</note>, which is done by removing the flat (*b*). Then, he should diligently observe which letters in the column of keys correspond to the same four numbers of the <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher’s term for mathematical musical building blocks or short melodic fragments</note> extracted from the three columns. For we wish these same Musarithms to always remain the same, so that a greater variety among them may be revealed. If you press the points of the letters indicated by the numbers into the spaces of the five-line staff <note>original: "pentagrammis"</note>, and apply the rhythmicized notes <note>original: "metrometras"</note> to each one according to the preceding paradigm, as has been said, you will have a harmony composed in the first tone. This will be essentially different from the sixth tone, as appears in the first example of the following universal diagram.

Where you should first note that in the column of the first tone, a flat (*b*) is always attached to the number 6 <note>original: "τῷ 6 id est senario numero"</note>. Since this number corresponds to the letter B in the column of keys, you should know that a <term>flat</term> <note>original: "b molle"</note> must be placed before the note occurring in that place, wherever and in whichever voice's staff it is found. This is seen in the flat note of the Bass in the first column of the first tone in the following diagram, and in the fifth note of the Alto, and in the third note of the Tenor. All of these things must be noted most diligently. For whatever we say in this place must be observed irrevocably hereafter.

Note secondly, that in the aforementioned column of the first tone, the number 7 is marked with the 𝄪 sign of a semitone <note>this refers to a sharp or an accidental that raises the pitch</note>. This denotes that wherever the letter C is found (which the number 7 of the column of the First Tone indicates in the column of keys), the sign 𝄪 must always be prefixed to the note occurring in that place. This applies if the note immediately following ascends, or if it is the final note, or if a rest immediately follows. It should be omitted, however, if the melody descends, except in rare cases which are discussed elsewhere. You should know that this is also to be understood for the columns of other tones in which 7 or any other number is found marked with this sign. You have an example in the Alto voice, where you will find the first and sixth notes marked with this 𝄪 sign, with the following note immediately ascending. In the Soprano voice <note>original: "Cantus"</note>, you will find the last note marked with this sign because it is the final note.

# Second Diagram.
### *The mutation of a composed theme from the sixth tone into the second "soft" tone.*

If, however, anyone should desire to compose this thematic composition in a pleasant, sweet, and flattering style <note>Kircher often assigned emotional or psychological characteristics to specific musical modes</note>, he should choose for himself the second tone. This is done by applying the column of keys to the column of the 11th Tone, the <term>Hypodorian</term>. For if he marks the letters indicated by the four Musarithms in the column of keys with points and rhythmic notes (as has been said) upon the staves of the four voices, a new kind of harmony will emerge. It will be composed in that pleasant, sweet, and flattering style which the second tone contains, as the second column of the following universal system shows. Meanwhile, one must diligently observe that wherever a note occurs on the E key in the staves of the four voices, you must prefix a flat (*b*). This is indicated by the number 6 in the column of the second tone, where you will find a *b* attached, according to the first warning given previously. And wherever the letter indicated by 𝄪 7 occurs, you should always prefix 𝄪 to this note in a similar fashion—provided, as I said, that the following note ascends or is the final note. You have an example of the flat B in the fifth note of the Bass and the third note of the Tenor; and an example of the 𝄪 semitone in the first and sixth notes of the Alto in the example of the Second Tone.

### Third Diagram.
*On the transformation of a composed theme from the sixth mode into the third "hard" mode.*

Furthermore, if anyone should wish to transform a theme first composed in the sixth mode <note>original: "sexto tono." In Kircher's system, the sixth mode is the Hypolydian mode, often associated with a gentle or devout character.</note> into the third mode—which is mournful and suited to sad subjects—he will achieve his goal if he applies the "column of keys" <note>the vertical list of musical clefs used in Kircher's combinatorial system</note> to the column of the third (or Phrygian) mode. For if he marks the positions of the letters on the musical staves using the numbers of the <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for his mathematical musical building blocks, which allowed non-composers to generate music through combinations of numbers.</note> denoted in the column of keys—first with simple points, then, as previously described, with metrical notes—a new kind of song will emerge, shaped according to the desired nature of that mode. This is beautifully demonstrated in the third column of the following system. However, one must observe with all diligence the placement of the sharps (♯), or even the naturals (♮) and flats (♭), according to the rules indicated in the preceding sections.

### Fourth Diagram.
*On the transformation of a theme from the sixth into the fourth mode.*

You will change the chosen theme into the fourth mode <note>The Hypophrygian mode.</note> if you apply the column of keys to the column of the fourth mode. Indeed, if you mark the positions of the letters on the staves as indicated by the <term>Musarithm</term> numbers—initially with points, and then with the appropriate rhythmic notes—the sought-after mode, suitable for weeping and lamentation, will emerge. See the diagram for Mode IV in the following system. Therefore, whoever correctly understands this method of changing the aforementioned song from one mode to any of these four modes will find no difficulty in forming the remaining modes. Consequently, nothing remains but to place before the eyes of the curious reader a general system of the transformation of the chosen theme according to the twelve modes in a single synopsis; from this, the procedure for the remaining modes will be clearly evident.

You have here, Reader, the transformation of a single theme into all the tones demonstrated in one musical system, so that you may see from this the immense variety of even one *Musarithm* <term>Musarithm: Kircher’s term for his mathematical formulas or "musical algorithms" used to generate harmony</term>; to which, if a different value of notes is added, a completely inconceivable variety of these same changes will emerge. I wanted to show all of these here more extensively so that the universality <note>original Greek: καθολικισμὸς (katholikismos)</note> of our art would be more clearly evident. But now let us say something about the value of the notes, or the change of time <note>In this context, "time" refers to what we now call meter or rhythm.</note>.

### Schema V.
### On the mutation of meter-measuring notes.

Whoever has properly considered Chapter 8 of the first part of this book will easily see that there is almost no end to the variations of any theme according to different time. There is, however, a double time—perfect and imperfect—about which enough was said in the third Requirement, so I do not wish to be wordy here. Instead, I will finally explain how that can be applied in various ways to our theme. We have placed the notes of perfect time below the individual columns of the Musarithms, which we also call meter-measuring notes <note>original: *notae metrometrae*</note>, because they perfectly correspond to the numbers of the Musarithms regarding both number and time. Indeed, the first ones written without a proportion number signify imperfect time; but those which have the number of the proportion of time prefixed are called notes of perfect time, and are commonly called "triple" <note>triple meter</note>.

And although, as I said above, a truly infinite variety arises from the mutual combination of the eight notes explained in the third Requirement, we have nevertheless—to facilitate our "Musurgia," so to speak—chosen only twelve from all of them, which will abundantly suffice for the variety of modulations to be established. Therefore, our theme, which was first taken up and replicated twelve times in the preceding system, can be replicated just as many times by applying one series of any of the twelve notes to each of the four voices. 

To understand this, it must be noted that since in this place we are teaching simple counterpoint that is isochronous <note>original Greek: ἰσόχρονον (isochronon); meaning moving in equal time or uniform rhythm</note>—that is, proceeding in equal time—in which the same notes are applied to each of the four voices, it is sufficient to apply any one series of notes to the four voices. For if anyone applied different series to different voices, the whole harmony would be destroyed, as it would have a rhythm that does not fit the Musarithms at all. Having noted this beforehand so that you may see the method of application and let it be more perfectly clear here, we wished to present only the bass of the chosen theme, marked with the different values of the notes. Anyone will then easily be able to mark the remaining corresponding voices with the same series and order of notes. 

Therefore, we place the artifice before your eyes in a single synopsis. This variety of different time will serve to excite various emotions <note>original: *affectus*</note> in the music; for just as slow times require the emotions of sadness, languor, and lamentation, so fast times require the emotions of joy, cheerfulness, abandonment, and indignation.

# Book VIII. Miraculous Music-making. 69

We have placed eight columns here; the first column shows the excess of voices that ascend beyond their natural constitution. The second column shows the change of voices when they are reduced to a **moderate range** <term>moderate range: original Latin "mediocritatem," referring to the standard, singable range of a voice, neither too high nor too low</term>; thus you see that for the **Alto** voice to be brought to a moderate range, it must take the place of the **Soprano** <note>original: "Cantus"</note>, and for the Soprano to have a moderate range, it must yield to the place of the Alto. If the **Tenor**, however, does not have a moderate range, it ought to proceed an octave lower. If you strictly follow this rule, you will find no further difficulty in proportioning the voices; for voices are so prepared by nature that when one exceeds its moderate range, its change into another necessarily reduces that excess to a moderate range. This mutual transformation especially takes place in the Alto; for whether the Soprano has exceeded its range, either voice migrating into the Alto will be considered reduced to a moderate range. Nevertheless, a migration into the Tenor’s octave is more suitable than to the Soprano; if, however, it should descend so deeply that it proceeds below the notes of the **Bass** <note>original: "Basis"</note>, as happens in the Tenor, then the Soprano will be able to swap its seat with the Tenor.

Furthermore, these things must be declared more extensively; if, therefore, the four voices had the constitution shown in the third column—that is, if each descended more than is proper—then they would have to be changed into the voices corresponding to the first ones in the fourth column. Namely, the Soprano <margin>How the transformation of voices is to be performed.</margin> into the Alto; the Alto into the Soprano; and the Tenor and Bass ought to proceed an octave higher, as the fourth column shows. In the same way, if the voices proceed higher than is proper, as the fifth column demonstrates, then they would have to be changed into the voices shown in the sixth column: specifically, the Soprano into the Alto; the Alto into the Soprano; and the Tenor must be changed either into the Alto or, like the Bass, into the octave below. But since these things are clearly evident from the examples, we shall not dwell on them. Only one doubt might occur here to the **Beginner** <note>original: "Tyroni," literally a recruit or novice</note>: by what method can those voices be changed immediately?

I respond that nothing is easier to do. For if you mark the positions of the clefs or letters on the staff of the Soprano, and the same on the staff of the Alto or any other voice, with points and notes, you will have what you seek. For the positions of the clefs are common to each of the four voices, and it is exactly the same whether you place the positions of the Alto clefs in the Soprano, or those of the Soprano or Tenor in the Alto. From this it follows that in any **Musarithm** <term>Musarithm: Kircher’s term for a mathematical-musical table used to generate compositions</term>, the series of three numbers pertaining to the three remaining voices after the Bass are interchangeable. Thus, the first series suits the Alto as much as the Tenor; the second and third suit the Soprano as much as the Alto and Tenor. The "indifference" <note>the lack of fixed assignment</note> consists only in this: that in one voice they may occasionally proceed higher or lower than is proper, and in this case, the voices are to be swapped in the manner described. But to give the Beginner some satisfaction here: let the Soprano voice in the preceding example be reduced from its excess to a moderate range—that is, it is to be changed into the Alto. You will work it thus: since the first two notes of the Soprano consist of F, the third in E, the fourth in C, the fifth in B, the sixth and seventh in C, and the eighth in D; you will see where the locations of the said clef-letters are on the Alto staff. Notes placed in these positions will give the Soprano part reduced to a moderate range in the Alto voice. You will work in this way in all other cases. Where you will also note that the Tenor and Soprano are so similar that one can be taken for the other without any hesitation at all, since on the staves they are only one interval apart. Therefore, the transformation should only be made from either one into the Alto, which is distant from the said voices mostly by a **major third** <note>original: "ditono"</note> or a **perfect fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>.

### CANON IV.
### *On the selection of Tones.*

All <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Musarithms were the "musical building blocks" or pre-calculated mathematical tables Kircher invented to allow non-composers to write music.</note> neither should nor can be adapted to each of the twelve tones at will and indiscriminately, since there are many Musarithms which cannot be applied to certain tones because of the occurrence of "forbidden intervals" (of which we shall treat more fully later). Hence, so that we might consult the convenience and ease of operation in the tones, we have assigned to each column the tones appropriate to the Musarithms of said columns; if these are followed, all errors will undoubtedly be easily avoided. The fourth and fifth tones are rarely in use, and are accommodated to only a few Musarithms, because of the following occurrence of forbidden intervals, as I said. All the rest can easily come into use. Hence I advise that the **Beginner** should first exercise himself especially in six tones, namely 1. 2. 3. 6. 7. 8. For these, since they are the principal ones and agree with almost all the six remaining, will be abundantly sufficient for every harmonic modulation; indeed, hardly any song can be assigned which is not composed according to one of these six tones. If someone, however, wishes to use the remaining six tones as well for greater variety, we do not oppose him, provided he proceeds with the caution that has been mentioned. The Beginner would also do better to practice first in the 2nd and 6th tones.

### CANON V.
### On the avoidance of forbidden intervals.

It happens from time to time that by changing the tone <note>original: "tonum"; in this context, Kircher refers to the musical mode or key</note>, the notes fall into forbidden intervals. The first series of intervals shows the forbidden intervals; the second shows the corrected intervals. In the first and second column, you see *mi* against *fa*, and *fa* against *mi* <note>original: "mi contra fa"; the tritone or augmented fourth, famously called "the devil in music" due to its harsh dissonance</note>, a most absurd interval, corrected by changing the "hard" hexachord into the "soft" one <note>original: "Cantus durus" and "Cantus mollis." You see, therefore, by what method the prohibited intervals ought to be corrected. Whenever, therefore, you fall into one of these, either the cadence <note>original: "clausula"</note> must be changed from hard to soft, or from soft to hard; or—which I would judge more advisable—the <term>Musarithm: A set of numbers representing musical notes and rhythms in Kircher’s mechanical composition system</term> must be changed. This is done if you seek another Musarithm whose last two numbers in the bass are different from the previous ones, and you will have the whole business completed without such a great change. Hence, we form the rule as follows:

**Whenever the numbers of the Musarithms result in prohibited intervals, then the Musarithm must be changed; this is done if you take another one whose two last numbers in the bass are different.** Here is an example:

Let the two last numbers of the bass Musarithm be 5 and 1, which in the column of the 5th tone will result in **F** and **B**. If the song is "hard" <note>using B-natural</note>, the notes will have a cadence like that shown in the second column—that is, a forbidden one. Therefore, seek another Musarithm for the bass whose numbers are not 5 and 1, but for example, 6 and 2. If you apply these to the same column of keys, two letters will be produced...

*On the change of Tones in one and the same song, or on the mixture of Tones.*

Lest any musician should be able to object that we have no variety in our <term>Musarithms</term>, we have chosen to hand down here the method regarding the mixture of Tones <note>In this context, "Tones" refers to the musical modes or keys used in a composition.</note>. However, so that students may understand this mixture of tones, it must be known that Music is so fond of variety that if, in one and the same song of whatever kind, the constant tenor of the assumed tone is maintained and the same intervals are always kept, it can neither please nor provide any delight to the ears; rather, it brings annoyance and boredom. Hence, the more skilled <term>Musurgi</term><note>Kircher's term for composers or makers of music, from the Greek "musurgia."</note> are accustomed to exhibit their melodies with great delight for the listeners by using the cadences of different tones, as if using so many different colors. Therefore, lest the said composers think our "Musurgical" art is deprived of this way of ingeniously interweaving tones, I will show by this canon by what reasoning we can adorn our <term>Melothesias</term><note>A term for the composition or arrangement of a melody.</note> with similar textures, so that we do not seem to have omitted anything in this our Music-making art.

You see, therefore, how easily the mixing of tones is achieved. In songs composed in the **soft song** <note>original: "cantus mollis." This refers to music using a B-flat, often sounding "sweeter" or "sadder" to period ears.</note>, the greatest care must be taken so that the application or movement of the column of numbers does not land on a step that properly belongs to the **hard song** <note>original: "cantus durus." If a song is made in the soft song, the tones belonging to the hard song cannot and should not be mixed in any way, except in certain and very rare cases—namely, when we wish to artistically suggest a massive shift from joy to sadness. To correctly recognize which tones can be mixed, observe these two rules, but let us provide another example.

Whenever you select the **second tone** to complete any composition, know that those same <term>musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's term for musical building blocks represented by numbers.</note> of the second tone can be changed three or four times by using **transpositional rods**. If you apply the said column of numbers so its number 1 matches the letter **C** in the column of keys, and then resolve the musarithm numbers into notes according to this application, the second change of the cadence will come forth as it appears here. # CANON VII.
### *On avoiding prohibited intervals.*

I. Whenever any melody is marked with the character of "soft song" <note>original: "cantus mollis," referring to the musical system or hexachord that uses B-flat</note>, the number 1 or 8 of the mentioned column should by no means be applied above the letters A and E. Since these intervals belong properly to "hard song" <note>original: "cantus duri," the system using B-natural</note>, not only would they be inserted into tones of a different nature, but they would also fall into forbidden intervals. However, for all remaining letters, the said number 1 or 8 can be applied.

II. If the melody is marked with the character of "hard song," then the number 1 or 8 should never be placed above B and above E with the signs ♭ or b applied, except very rarely. If you observe these two rules correctly, you will proceed without any danger in the mixing of tones.

# CANON VIII.
### *On the placement of chromatic signs ♭ b ♯.*

In truth, in both parts of the applicator column <note>referring to a component of Kircher's musical composing machine</note> you will find chromatic signs attached to both letters and numbers. By these, we have indicated that whenever both a number and a letter occur marked with the same signs, then a sign of that kind must be placed before the note. If, however, either cell of the columns is empty of them, it must be omitted. Thus, in the first column, you will find the letter C marked with the ♯ sign. However, the corresponding number 5 lacks it; by this, we intended to indicate that the C is not to be marked with this sign, but rather it should be omitted entirely. Again, in the same column, you will find the seventh number likewise marked with this ♯ sign, to which E responds with a b prefixed. Because the letter lacks the ♯ sign and the number 7 lacks the letter b, it will be a sign to you that in this tone both the letter b and the ♯ are to be omitted. All these things must be noted diligently.

However, when the column of numbers is moved forward by one step—for example, from F to G—you will find the number 6 marked with a b, and the number 7 marked with the ♯ sign. Since the corresponding E and F are marked with these same signs, it will indicate to you that just as E must have a b prefixed, so F must have a ♯ prefixed. Thus, this can be a universal rule: Whenever both the letters and the corresponding numbers appear marked with the same signs, the letters require the application of the signs; if, however, only one or the other—either the letter or the number—is marked with these signs, the letter is by no means to be marked with that sign. Note also that the ♯ sign should not always be placed as we warned in the third Canon, but only when the following note ascends, or a pause follows immediately, or it is the final note. But all these things will be treated more extensively in the following part; therefore, we refer the reader there.

Let the following sequence be assumed as an example of a "base logarithm" <note>used here in a pre-modern sense to mean a foundational numerical sequence</note> for the first theme: <margin>Example.</margin> 5 1 4 5 6 5 5 1. To this correspond the letters in the key column CFBCDCCF; the notes in the Bass, however, correspond as appears on the side.

...binds and constrains the text, not in a wandering or free style, but according to a certain metric rule <note>original: "metrica quadam amussi," literally meaning a mason's level or ruler, implying perfect precision</note> under a fixed number of syllables and feet. Meters, moreover, can be applied to all languages. This certainly provides us with a very great shortcut for reaching our goal; however, putting aside wordy evasions, let us proceed to the matter itself, beginning with Latin verses.

Therefore, just as a body is formed from various limbs, a painting from various images, and harmony from diverse voices; so from various feet arise various verses, meters, or rhythms. Thus, a verse is nothing other than speech bound by a specific type and order of feet. Some authors have identified nine species of these, others twenty-four, while some have suggested more and others fewer. We discuss each of these at length in the second part of this book. For now, leaving behind the disputes of these minor poets <note>original: "poetastrorum," a derogatory term for petty or bad poets</note>, we shall adopt those types of meters which appear to have more energy for stirring the emotions <note>original: "animi affectiones," referring to the "Affections," the Baroque theory that specific musical structures could reliably trigger specific emotional states in the listener</note> and more suitability for musical rhythms.
