### Notes on the completed procedure.

**N**ote first: in musical compositions of this kind, exactly the same cautions and rules must be observed as those we handed down in the preceding 10 canons. To progress more successfully in this business, you must master these perfectly, so that if any difficulty arises, you can deliberate on what should be done. For in those 10 canons, we have solved whatever difficulty can occur in the entire <term>Musurgia: The art or practice of musical composition.</term>. However, in the following proposition, we will assign some particular rules, by which anything omitted here will be abundantly compensated.

Note second: musarithms of this kind can be adapted to any tone <note>Here 'tone' refers to the musical modes or scales used in the 17th century.</note>, except for those which, due to a tritone <note>An interval of three whole steps, often called the 'Devil in music' due to its dissonance.</note> or a diminished fifth <note>original: "semidiapente"</note>, do not permit them.

Note third: the placement of accidental signs <note>Sharps and flats used to alter pitches.</note> must be observed. Without these, an error could easily occur.

Note fourth: the same effect can be produced either by applying a single musarithm to various tones, or by using four different musarithms adapted to different strophes.

Note fifth: to introduce mixtures of tones more skillfully in the 2nd and 3rd strophes, the natural order of the columns must be kept; so that the first column corresponds to the first strophe, the second to the second, the third to the third, and the fourth to the fourth. In this way, every error in the mixing of tones will be avoided, and the melody, established by a natural process, will strike the ears more sweetly. All these things must be observed with the greatest study.

*Given an Euripidean Iambic meter, and given any musical mode, how to compose any harmony upon it.*

**T**he Euripidean Iambic meter is a six-syllable line <note>original: "hectasyllabum"</note>, the Musarithms <term>Musarithms: Kircher’s invented term for mathematical tables that map poetic syllables to musical intervals, allowing non-composers to "calculate" music.</term> of which we have arranged in four columns in Table IV of the second section, organized into four-line stanzas, as the title of the columns demonstrates. *Happy gate of heaven.*

Once the <term>phonotactic system</term> <note>Kircher’s method for automatically mapping the rhythm and syllables of words onto musical notes</note> has been prepared and as many spaces have been marked out for the individual syllables, you shall begin the composition as follows.

First, you will process the <term>musarithm</term> <note>A mathematical sequence of numbers representing musical intervals or pitches, used here as a shortcut for composing</note> of the first stanza, then the rest in order. Look, therefore, to see which letters in the column of keys correspond to the first series of numbers—123423—in the first musarithm; you will find GABCAB. Look for the locations of these letters on the <term>pentagram</term> <note>the five-line musical staff</note> of the *Cantus* <note>the highest vocal part, similar to Soprano</note>, and mark the points there. Then, as you see, look to see which letters in the column of keys correspond to the second series of numbers in the first musarithm—578878—and you will find DFGGFG. Look for the locations of these letters on the pentagram of the *Altus*, and mark the points there. Third, see which letters correspond to the third series of numbers—321155—in the same musarithm, and you will find they correspond to BAGGDD. Look for the locations of these letters on the pentagram of the *Tenor*, and mark the points there. Fourth, see which letters in the column of keys the musarithm for the *Bass*—876458—corresponds to; you will find GFECDG. Carefully note the locations of these letters on the pentagram of the *Bass* and mark the points there. 

Once these points are marked, take any series of <term>metrometric notes</term> <note>symbols indicating the rhythmic duration or "measure" of the notes</note> (which you will find at the bottom of the columns) and apply that one and the same series to each of the four voices—specifically, above the points marked on each pentagram. For these points show the spaces in which the notes corresponding to the number and the points ought to be placed, and you will have the first stanza composed. You will process the remaining stanzas in order by exactly the same method. Thus, given an iambic four-stanza poem by Euripides and given the desired tone, we have composed the given melody, which was the task to be performed.

### VI
### *Notes on Table IV* <note>original: "Pinacem IV"</note>

I. **S**o that the melody of the stanzas may be kept more pure, the musarithms should be selected from the columns of stanzas arranged in their natural order. We advise this so that musarithms plucked from here and there without any selection do not provide a melody that flows less sweetly. For this reason, we have ensured that musarithms taken in their natural order always exhibit a perfect harmony, which consists of the exact mixing of tones. We have advised this above, and it must be observed in all the tables that follow. I would not want this said, however, to mean that no harmony is produced in musarithms taken indiscriminately; for harmony will always emerge in whatever order you take them, but rather that those do not produce an effect equal to those taken from the columns in their natural order. Yet, if someone is more practiced in this business, they will also easily achieve the intended effect by taking the numbers from here and there based on their arrangement.

II. The locations of ♯ and ♭ must be observed with the greatest zeal, according to the rules handed down in the preceding sections.

III. Even a single musarithm will suffice for the perfect harmony of four stanzas if, as was said in the preceding sections, it is applied to different tones—or, what is the same thing, to different letters in the column of keys—by means of <term>transposition rods</term> <note>physical tools, likely part of Kircher's "Organum Mathematicum," used for calculating musical transpositions</note>. In the meantime, observe that the last stanza should always correspond to the first in terms of its tone.

IV. You will be able to apply these aforementioned musarithms for four stanzas to all the tones described at the head of the columns; observing this, however: if in any part a voice is too high or too low, you should swap it with another voice, as was described in the <term>canons</term> <note>the set of rules or instructions for the system</note>.

### Proposition III.

**Given a four-stanza poem of a single meter in the Anacreontic style, to compose any desired harmony upon it.**

Let a double four-stanza poem be given as follows, one in the Anacreontic style <note>A Greek poetic meter named after the poet Anacreon, usually light, airy, and celebratory.</note> properly so-called, and the other in the Boethian style <note>Refers to the meters used by the philosopher Boethius in his "Consolation of Philosophy."</note>.

### Proposition IV.
#### Given a four-line stanza in a single Archilochian Iambic meter, and given a tone, to compose the requested harmony.

<note>The "Archilochian Iambic" refers to a specific poetic meter named after the Greek poet Archilochus; here it refers to the 8-syllable lines of the hymn.</note>

Let the following four-line stanza <term>Tetrastrophon: a poem or stanza consisting of four lines</term> be given, which is a hymn very widely sung in the Church.
*The Royal Banners forward go* <note>original: "Vexilla Regis prodeunt"</note>
*The mystery of the Cross shines forth* <note>original: "Fulget crucis mysterium"</note>
*Where life endured death* <note>original: "Qua vita mortem pertulit"</note>
*And by death brought forth life.* <note>original: "Et morte vitam protulit"</note>

And let the first tone be given, upon which someone desires to compose <margin>1st Tone</margin> a harmony; they shall proceed as follows.

I. Align the column of keys with the column of the first tone. Then, you will mark the four voices on the musical staves upon the composition board <term>palimpsesto phonotactico: Kircher's "phonotactic board," a mechanical invention for composing music by selecting pre-calculated harmonies</term> according to the first tone, which is of the "hard" character <note>original: "characterismi duri" — referring to the use of B-natural (B-durum) rather than B-flat</note>.

II. Take any four <term>Musarithmos: Kircher’s term for numerical sequences that represent specific musical intervals or chords</term> from the following table <term>Pinax: a Greek word for "table" or "chart" used frequently in scientific texts</term>, from which we have selected four equal musarithms corresponding to the four lines of the stanza.

[Table to the right of the text:]
| | |
|---|---|
| F | 3 |
| E | 2 |
| D | 8 |
| C | ♮ 7 |
| B | ♭ 6 |
| A | 5 |
| G | 4 |
| F | 3 |

[Table of musical numbers:]
| I. | II. | III. | IV. |
|---|---|---|---|
| 85766555 | 57755445 | 58765443 | 77766555 |
| 33334223 | 33282222 | 33287777 | 33388778 |
| 55588778 | 55487667 | 55533445 | 55543223 |
| 88564558 | 33785225 | 88563773 | 33348551 |

[Musical notation grid follows, showing four voices set to the text:]

The Royal Banners forward go / The mystery shines, etc.

Then work by marking points on the staff, as was said in the preceding sections; then apply a series of whatever note values you choose to the base of the columns (we have chosen triple time here), and the requested four-line harmony will emerge, as appears here. You must carefully observe that the placement of the chromatic signs—natural ♮ and flat ♭—is done in the appropriate places. Regarding how these types of song compositions can be varied in infinite ways, we have spoken in the "canons" <note>rules or sets of instructions</note>, which you should consult, and in the first proposition of the first table. In the meantime, I would like you to note with the greatest care what we also warned about above in Canon II: if the voices in any tone should descend or rise higher or lower than is proper, they must be swapped among themselves <note>a technique known as voice-crossing to keep the singers within a comfortable range</note>, as we have taught at length in the cited place.

# Proposition V.
### *Given a four-line stanza of nine-syllable meter, to complete a musical composition upon it.*

Let there be a four-line stanza <note>Latin: *tetrastrophon*</note> of a single meter <note>Latin: *monocolon*</note> consisting of nine syllables, as follows:
*Hail, Queen of Angels* <note>original: *Aue Regina Angelorum*</note>

But so that you may better understand our thinking, we shall here provide a specific type of varied transposition. Whether you take any series in the first arrangement of five columns, AB; or any other in the second arrangement, FC; or finally a transverse or any other series in the third arrangement, XY; it is all the same: a <term>Melothesia</term> <note>original: "Melothesia"; the art of composing a musical setting for a text</note> will always be produced that serves your purpose.

### Corollary I.

<margin>The multitude of combinations</margin>
From this arrangement, the infinite multitude of combinations is clear, which can result from the various positioning of these five columns. These are certainly so great that if some Angel had begun to combine them from the beginning of the world, he would not have finished them even to this day; this is made very clear from the demonstrations in the first part of this book. <note>Kircher often uses the metaphor of an angel working since the dawn of time to illustrate the staggering scale of mathematical combinations.</note>

### Corollary II.

From this single paradigm, it is therefore clear how one must proceed in all other chosen themes; for the method of operating is no different in the remaining cases.

## CHAPTER IV.
### On the organization of columns pertaining
### to Poetic Music.

<margin>The use and application of the tables contained within the Musurgical Ark.</margin>
Just as in the preceding example we arranged the columns of many-syllabled words in order to animate any context of words into a harmony, so now we shall teach by what method the metrical columns inscribed in the <term>Musurgia</term> <note>Referring to the "Arca Musurgica" or Musurgical Ark, Kircher's mechanical composing machine</note> ought to be arranged.
It must be noted first that if the chosen "Theme" is a poem of many stanzas but a single meter <note>original: "polystrophon monocolon"</note>, all the columns are to be selected from the same compartment. For example: if someone chose an Anacreontic poem of six stanzas as a theme, he would join six columns taken from the fourth compartment of the twelve-part space according to the order of the six verses, combined in whatever way; and then he should proceed according to the rules handed down in the preceding part, and the desired musical setting for the six-stanza Anacreontic poem will be produced. You will arrange any kind of multi-stanza, single-meter verse in no different a manner. But if the theme of the words is multi-stanza and multi-meter—that is, composed of different types of verse—then the columns must be selected from the cells inscribed with said meters. But the matter will become clearer by an example.

If someone were to compose a multi-meter piece, of which the:
1. First stanza was a Phalaecian Hendecasyllabic; | 1. Hendecasyllabic |

### CHAPTER V.
### On Florid Poetic Musarithms.

### On the Mixture of Poetic Musarithms.

The matter is clearer than to deserve to be declared more extensively.

From which it is clearly evident in how many infinite ways even a single song can be changed. But I leave these things for the ingenious student <note>original: "Tyroni," a novice or learner</note> to weigh further.

**Proposition II.**
*Given a Bass voice, to build any number of voices above it.*

**I**f the phrase <note>original: "clausula"</note> of the bass voice is the same as the preceding one, place it in the musical slate <term>phonotactic pentagram; a five-line musical staff designed for the physical arrangement of sounds</term> of the bass using the same notes and distinct clefs as was done in the previous operation. Once this is finished, since the first note is in F, look for column F at the top of the Chart. In the musical staff for the Cantus <note>the highest voice, or Soprano</note>, select any point along with the number assigned to it, and transfer it to the Cantus staff of the slate <term>palimpsest; a reusable writing surface, here referring to the prepared music paper or slate</term>. Then, from the staff of the Altus <note>Alto voice</note>, simply transfer any point along with its number into the Altus staff of the slate. Similarly, from the Tenor staff, transfer any point along with its corresponding number into the slate’s staff. Once the points are transferred, since the second note of the phrase is B, take column B in the Chart and proceed as before. Then take the column marked G, and so proceed with the remaining notes of the phrase until you have completed the entire section. Always observing, meanwhile, that two octaves (88) or two fifths (55) do not immediately follow one another in different voices. Once these points are so transferred, if you place those same notes of the bass phrase above the points in each individual voice, the desired musical composition <note>original: "Melothesia"</note> will be produced. It should also be noted that the intervals of the voices should be united as much as possible, avoiding all unrefined cadences. 
But these things are so easy that they may be grasped at the first glance; therefore, let us proceed further.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the "Musarithmetic Ark," a mechanical composing machine invented by Athanasius Kircher. ### 196 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

-> **How to outline the Scepters of the Muses.** <-

Nine parallelograms <note>These are the rectangular rods or slats used in Kircher's composing box.</note> should be made from wood or thick paper in the shape of plectra; you will apply these in order over the lines of the previously prepared palimpsest <note>original: "palimpsesti"; here referring to a master template or grid used for alignment.</note>, and you shall draw lines on each one in the same order and distance as was done on the palimpsest. They must correspond to the underlying lines in such a way that, however they are applied to them, they match perfectly. Each scepter should be "serrated"—that is, they should have protruding points at the ends, the tips of which must have precisely the same distance between them as the parallel lines have from each other, and you will have what is required.

We have called the first scepter the **Scepter of Thalia**, and it contains phrases for Adonics or Polysyllables. The second is the **Scepter of Terpsichore**, and it contains phrases for Euripidean Iambics, or six-syllable verses. The third is the **Scepter of Melpomene**, and it contains phrases for Anacreontics or six-syllable verses. The fourth is the **Scepter of Clio**, and it contains phrases for Archilochian Iambics or eight-syllable verses. The fifth is the **Scepter of Euterpe**, and it contains phrases for Alcmanian Iambics or nine-syllable verses. The sixth is the **Scepter of Calliope**, and it contains phrases for Iambic Trimeters or ten-syllable verses. The seventh is the **Scepter of Polyhymnia**, and it contains phrases for Phalaecian or eleven-syllable verses. The eighth is the **Scepter of Erato**, and it contains phrases for Sapphics. The ninth is the **Scepter of Urania**, and it contains phrases for Choriambics of twelve syllables. <note>Kircher names each rod after one of the nine Muses of Greek mythology, assigning each a specific poetic meter that dictates the rhythm of the music to be composed.</note>

<margin>The arrangement and multiplication of the Scepters.</margin>

There are, therefore, nine musical scepters, each of which you will multiply tenfold, so that there are ten scepters of Thalia, ten of Terpsichore, ten of Melpomene, and so on for the rest; in total, there are ninety scepters, with which you will easily master the entire business of music through this industrious method. Let some learned and skilled <term>Musurgus</term> <note>A composer or "music-maker."</note> or <term>Melotheta</term> <note>A composer of melodies.</note> compose twenty highly ingenious musical phrases for the five-syllable Adonic meter, of which we show only one here for the sake of brevity on each of the nine scepters: namely, 10 for <term>simple counterpoint</term> <note>Note-against-note composition where all voices move in the same rhythm.</note> and 10 for <term>florid</term> and ingenious counterpoint. For the simple style is placed on one side of the scepter, and the florid on the opposite side. Again, he shall compose 20 harmonic phrases for the six-syllable Euripidean meter, and so on in order for each polysyllable: 10 for simple counterpoint and 10 for florid counterpoint.

He shall compose all these phrases upon one determined <term>tone</term> <note>A specific musical key or mode.</note> and then write them individually upon their scepters; thus, he will describe the Adonic phrases on one face of the 10 scepters of Thalia, and the florid ones on the other face of the same. In simple counterpoint, the phrases are determined only by their points <note>Kircher uses dots as shorthand for notes in simple rhythm.</note>, as you see done here in the example of the nine rods; but in florid counterpoint, you will write the musical notes themselves on the rods of the phrases, as was done on the 11th scepter of Terpsichore.

The reason why we show simple counterpoint only with points is that in simple counterpoint—being smooth and always moving with an equal progression of voices—the points are suited to take on any shape of note. For from the twelve series of <term>metrometric notes</term> <note>Rhythmic templates found elsewhere in Kircher's book.</note> contained at the end of the tables of the first book, you can apply whichever one you like here; thus, in the column for Adonics in the cited place, 12 series of notes can each be applied to the said points. This, however, does not happen in florid counterpoint, because the voices proceed with unequal timing. Therefore, the entire phrases, along with the individual notes, must be written on the rods. Once the phrases are written on the said 90 rods, you will store them in the chest, constructed according to the model of the **Musarithmetic Ark**, for the use which we shall now explain.

### Section III.
The Use of the Staff-Lore of the Muses.
<note>original: "Vsus Sceptrologiæ Musarum." Kircher uses the word "sceptrologia" to describe his system of using rods—resembling scepters—to mechanically compose music.</note>

**First, it must be noted** that this invention is so designed that however the "teeth" or points of the base of the staff are applied to the space of the keys on the underlying writing-surface, <note>original: "palimpsesto." Here, Kircher refers to a pre-ruled musical grid or a reusable writing tablet used with his system.</note> a new harmony of four voices always emerges. For example: if the last tooth of Thalia's rod is placed on the musical writing-surface above F, all the remaining voices will produce a harmony in the sixth tone. If you apply the said tooth above the key of G on the writing-surface, <margin>The use of the rod</margin> you will have another musical setting, <term>Melothesia<gloss>The art of composing a melody or a complete musical setting.</gloss></term> namely a four-part piece in the second tone. If <margin>in the changing of the Tones.</margin> you apply the same point again above A, you will have another four-part setting in the ninth tone, and so on for the others. For by changing the position of the base, all the remaining voices will change their positions proportionally.

**Second, it must be noted** that one side of the rods holds phrases for simple counterpoint; the other side holds phrases for florid <note>Ornate or decorative music with moving parts.</note> counterpoint. We have shown the phrases of simple counterpoint using only dots for the reason provided a little earlier. But we have marked each phrase of the florid style with its own notes, as appears on Terpsichore's rod, the reason for which we likewise gave in the preceding sections. With these things observed: if anyone intends to create a musical setting over a given theme, he should arrange the columns or rods of the Muses with the exact same diligence as was done in the "Musarithmic" setting, <note>Kircher's term for his method of composing music by following the mathematical patterns of poetic meters.</note> following the order of the syllables. <margin>The practice to be established.</margin> Let the following, for example, be the theme:

*Serve God, all you kings of the earth, for honor befits Him alone; the first phrase "Serve God" corresponds to the five-syllable Adonic meter on Thalia’s rod; the second phrase "all kings of the earth" corresponds to the six-syllable Euripidean on Terpsichore’s second rod; the third phrase "for honor befits Him alone" corresponds to Melpomene's rod, namely the seven-syllable Anacreontics; we have taken three rods in sequence so that we would not be forced to make another separate description.* <note>The Latin text names several Greek poetic meters—Adonic, Euripidean, and Anacreontic—which Kircher used to categorize rhythmic patterns in his composing machine.</note>

With the rods thus placed in order, you will begin the composition in this way: first, choose whichever of the 12 tones you wish; here we will choose the sixth which, since it ends in F, (from what was demonstrated above when we explained the Tone-Table), you will apply the last tooth of the base of Thalia’s rod above the lower F, and the other two rods in this order, and you will have a perfect musical setting.

For if you press dots onto the musical writing-surface in those spaces that correspond and match the dots of the phrases described on the rods, and then over those marked dots you overlay one of the twelve series of time-measuring notes <note>original: "notarum metrometrarum."</note> contained at the bottom of column I of Table III in Section I, the sought-after musical setting will emerge. And if you wish to mix an artistic, florid phrase with simple ones, turn the rod, as was done in Terpsichore's second rod. For if, with the position changed, you write the notes of the individual voices in the corresponding spaces of the writing-surface, you will have the artistically arranged phrase you were seeking. You will proceed no differently in all other musical periods. But because we showed in the previous sections that it would be unpleasant to the ears if phrases always had the same final cadence from C to F, you will easily avoid this if you observe what we have handed down at length regarding the mutation or mixing of tones in the preceding part. For if, for example, you place the second rod of the florid phrase with its last tooth on G on the writing-surface, the phrase will immediately migrate from the 6th tone to the 2nd, and thus the desired variety will be born. For as I said a little while ago, the last tooth of the base, when applied above different notes on the base, will always produce new and different melodies; where, however, you must keep the rule handed down previously: namely, that the first and last phrases of the song are always in the same tone, but you can vary the middle ones as you please. With all these things observed, the following melody will finally appear on the writing-surface.

§. V.
On the comparison between Musarithmic Music-making and this Plectrology.

These two arts of Music-making first invented by us relate to each other as the "exceeding" and the "exceeded." While the Musarithmic invention delivered in the preceding part is the most universal and filled with incredible variety, this current method is much more splendid, ingenious, and perfected. Although this **plectrology** is not as universal as the preceding one, it possesses this convenience: it is concise, easy, and shows the progression of any voice on its musical staves immediately, without any prior application of a tone-column to a key-column. <margin>The difference between Musarithms and Plectrology.</margin> However, it has this disadvantage: on one part of a **plectrum**, only a single musical phrase (which corresponds to one of our four-voice Musarithms) can be described. Therefore, to make the art more universal, a great multitude of phrases and a wealth of material should be supplied to the **composer** <note>original: "Melotheta"</note>. If someone were to multiply the plectra to 300, he could reach the same level as the previous Musarithmic art. Here it should also be noted that if someone were to have as many plectra made as are contained in the tables of the three "Syntagmas" of the Musarithm, and transferred each Musarithm from the tables onto corresponding plectra, he would possess a Plectrology as widely extended as the Musarithmic art. I thought these things should be declared here more fully so that the Reader might see how to bring this kind of plectrology to the highest perfection and render it plainly universal. 

But these things are reserved for those who have greater leisure and who profess this faculty. For us, distracted by an infinite variety of the most disparate occupations, it was no small thing to have invented these, to have calculated the individual Musarithms by our own industry, and to have performed other things which posterity—unless I am mistaken—will wonder at, according to the smallness of my talent. These are seeds which, I do not doubt, will bloom into the most abundant sprouts through the continual watering by others following me. And together with these, with **GOD**, to whose goodness we ascribe all things, we place an end to our **Wondrous Music-making**.

# PREFACE.

**H**AVING set forth all those things which seemed to pertain in any way to theoretical and practical music, I deemed it worthwhile to give here a sample of certain things which, by the help of music, can be performed within the secret science of sounds that are truly marvelous. So that we do not proceed in a disorganized fashion <note>original: "ἀτάκτως"</note> in such an unusual work, it seemed fit to divide this book into six parts; in which:

<margin>Medicine <note>original: "ἰατρική"</note></margin>
<margin>Teratology <note>original: "τερατολογία"</note></margin>
<margin>Anacamptics <note>original: "ἀνακαμπτική"</note></margin>

The **first part**, the **Physiology of the Consonant and Dissonant**, scrutinizes more deeply the secret power lurking within consonance and dissonance.
The **second part**, **Iatrics** <term>Iatrics: the art of healing</term> or the **Medicine of the consonant and dissonant**, investigates the prodigious cures of diseases <note>Kircher is famously known for discussing the use of music to cure the bite of the Tarantula spider in this section.</note>.
The **third part**, the **Teratology** <term>Teratology: here meaning the study of natural wonders or "marvelous" sounds</term> **of sounds**, explains the prodigious sounds occurring throughout nature by means of genuine reasons.
The **fourth**, **Anacamptics** <term>Anacamptics: the science of reflected sound</term> **of the consonant and dissonant**, or **Echology**, treats the miracles of reflected sounds, in which the entire science of forming an Echo is handed down from its first foundations.

The **sixth**, **Musical Cryptology**, teaches how the hidden concepts of the mind can be communicated through sounds to two or more distant friends.

# PART I.
# THE PHYSIOLOGY OF CONSONANCE

## CHAPTER I.
## On the Miraculous Power of Music.

[Decorative initial M] We say that the **magic of consonance and dissonance** is nothing other than that faculty which produces prodigious sounds, which certainly holds a significant place among the other types of <term>Natural Magic (the study of the hidden forces within nature)</term>. For some sounds have such a wonderful power to alter and attract that the human intellect seems scarcely able to reach the true reason for them. No one is ignorant of how much <term>Magnetism (a hidden force of attraction)</term> resides in musical modes, or how much efficacy lies in their attractive power. Thus, it was not without reason that the Ancients portrayed Orpheus—the Musician and Magician—drawing animals, forests, and even the stones themselves with the magic sound of his lyre. The poet Claudian wrote quite elegantly about this in the preface to his second book on the *Rape of Proserpine*, using these words:

*Then the bard, gladdened by his country's festive time,*
*Takes up the sounding strings of his long-neglected Lyre,*
*And sitting there, modulating the strings with a gentle plectrum,*
*He guided the noble ivory with a festive thumb.*
*He had scarcely been heard when the winds subsided and the waves grew calm;*
*The sluggish Hebrus River grew numb with frozen waters.*
*Mount Rhodope came forward, its mountains thirsting for songs,*
*And Mount Ossa, more prone to shake off its icy snows.*
*The towering poplar descended from stripped Mount Haemus,*
*And the friendly Pine tree drew the oak as its companion.*
*Even though the Laurel had looked down upon the arts of the God of Phoebus,*
*It came, drawn by the voices of Orpheus.*
*The gentle hounds saw the hare without harm,*
*And the lamb offered its side to the neighboring wolf.*
*The harmonious does played with the spotted Tigress,*
*And the Stags did not fear the Massylian lion's mane.*
<note>original Latin: "Tum patriae festo laetatus tempore vates... Massylam Cervi non timuere iubam."</note>

<margin>What the attraction of stones by Orpheus signifies.</margin>

This prodigious attraction of animals, forests, and stones must be understood partly <term>tropologically (morally)</term> and partly <term>allegorically (symbolically)</term>. For the Ancients noted that the greatest power of Music is upon the soul; they saw that the soul changes according to various sounds and harmonies and, like wax, follows wherever one might mold it. For this reason, they called music the <note>original Greek: ἀρχὴν πάντων</note> "principle of all things," and as the scholar <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and polymath.</note> Psellus says in his work on Music, <note>original Greek: τὴν μουσικὴν οἱ πάλαιοι συνέχειν ἅπαν τὸ πᾶν</note> "the ancients held that music holds together the whole universe." Furthermore, they saw that this same Music could compose and vary a person's character; for nothing flows so easily into tender and soft minds as the various sounds of singing. It can hardly be said how great its power is in either direction: for it both incites those who are listless and makes the excited feel faint; it now relaxes the mind, now contracts it, as will be explained more fully later. Therefore, Orpheus led stones, forests, and animals—that is, men who were utterly senseless, bestial, and monstrous in their cruelty—toward humanity and a civilized way of life, attracted by the divine sound of his Lyre. Others, however, understand this aforementioned attraction allegorically with...

<margin>In what the power of music consists.</margin>
Once these things are established, I finally conclude that the marvelous power of Music—which it possesses in moving the passions of the mind—does not flow immediately from the soul. Since the soul is immortal and immaterial, it has no direct proportion to voices and sounds, nor can it be changed by them. Rather, it flows from the **spirit**, which is the instrument of the soul, or from the soul’s primary union by which it is joined to the body. <note>Kircher is referring to "animal spirits," which 17th-century thinkers believed were a subtle fluid or vapor that acted as a bridge between the physical body and the non-physical soul.</note> For a spirit of this kind, being a most subtle, bloody vapor, extremely mobile and thin, is easily stirred by harmonically agitated air. The soul, sensing this agitation, induces various effects according to the different movements of the spirit. Thus, when the spirit is stirred by faster and thicker harmonic motions and is, as it were, "rippled," a certain rarefaction arises from that rippling. From the thinning of the spirit, a dilation arises, followed by gladness and joy. All these things will produce greater passions the more the melodies are harmonious, fitting, and more proportional to the natural temperament and constitution of the person. Hence it happens that while we perceive a perfectly composed harmony and a most sweet melody, we seem to feel a certain tickling in the heart and the mind, as if we were attracted and absorbed by this fitting agitation. This variety of passions is greatly promoted by the different musical modes or tones, which were discussed extensively in the preceding sections; furthermore, the shortening of notes, the various rise and fall of pitches, and the various combinations of dissonances artfully mixed with consonances. I demonstrate by this experiment that the spirit is moved in this way, and no other.

**Musical Experiments.**

**T**ake a glass goblet of any size, which you will fill with pure, clear water. Once this is done, if you rub the outer rim of the goblet in a circle with a moistened index finger for a little while, you will eventually perceive a certain wonderful sound like the ringing of metal. By this sound, the water is so vehemently agitated and "rippled" that it seems to be stirred by a wind. If you fill this goblet only to the middle, you will indeed hear a sound, but twice as deep as the other, so that this sound resonates at a perfect harmony of an **octave** <note>original: *διαπασῶν* (diapasōn)</note> compared to the first, and consequently, you will also notice a more relaxed rippling of the water. If you divide this same goblet into five parts and fill three with water, leaving the other two empty, the glass will ring a harmony for you, which a weaker rippling will also accompany. Likewise, if the vessel is divided into seven parts and you fill four, leaving three empty, you will perceive a harmony which a rippling of the water, weaker than the previous ones, will follow. From this, it is clearly evident that our humors—and principally the spirit, which has its seat and dominion in the heart, the workshop of all passions—are moved in exactly the same way. Hence, when we perceive some violent sound like thunder or the explosion of a

<margin>Why we are terrified by violent sound.</margin>
cannon, we are seized by a certain horror, because the spirit suffers too violent a striking and dissipation from a sound that is disproportionate to it; hence come horror and terror. For this reason, we also cannot bear the screeching sound if someone scrapes iron with a knife, since by its harshness it affects the muscles leading to the teeth and brain by painfully twitching them. All these things apply to animals as well; for there are some that both 

<margin>How animals are delighted by Music.</margin>
rejoice in and are soothed by melodies, which could not happen if that power of music flowed immediately from the rational soul. However, man is delighted by Music in infinitely more ways than animals are, because he recognizes the patterns more perfectly and fully.

### CHAPTER III.

#### On the emotional states of the soul which Music inspires.

The soul, therefore, according to the diversity of the harmony, takes on various passions: joy, <term>impetus<note>original: "impetus"; here meaning a sudden surge of energy or drive</term>, relaxation, fear, hope, anger, and compassion. For we are moved most greatly to eight emotional states by musical melodies—as was said in the preceding book—either because they are consonant or dissonant, or because they are rapid or slow, or (what is more significant) because they rise to a high pitch for cheerfulness, or sink into a deep and relaxed sound for compassion and tears. <margin>The passions of the soul that are most moved.</margin> However, Music does not excite one to love or hatred—even though these are the most powerful passions of all—because love and hatred must be directed *toward* someone or something, as has been stated elsewhere. Music only moves the general passions of the soul; nevertheless, love is excited by the general passion of joy, as if by a certain friction. Truly, since Music cannot generate sadness, it cannot generate hatred either. That Music cannot generate sadness is evident from this: sadness leads toward death, while Music leads toward life.

<margin>Why Music does not please those settled in sadness.</margin> Why then is Music, as <note>The author likely refers to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 22:6: "A tale out of season is as music in mourning."</note> Ecclesiastes rightly says, "an untimely story in time of mourning," and why do we—when mourning, or when the heart is suppressed by a certain heavy sadness—reject all Music? This is the reason: because the <term>spirit<note>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle fluids that carried signals between the soul and the body.</note> or humor, frozen and constricted by the imagination of impending evils through fear or sadness, rejects every movement and renders itself, as it were, incapable of it. If there were a musician who could dissolve this condensed spirit with well-ordered Music, he would not move the person to sadness, but would bring a relief of the pain by dilating the spirit somewhat. We have said that we are moved by Music to eight primary passions, which can nevertheless be conveniently reduced to these three: namely joy, relaxation, and mercy, as was also said above. That other passions result from these afterward—such as love, sadness, audacity, fury, temperance, indignation, solemnity, and religion—happens <term>incidentally<note>original: "per accidens"; a philosophical term meaning a secondary or indirect effect rather than a primary one.</note>; for all these follow from those three general passions of the soul, as we have taught in our *Rhetorical Music-making* <note>original: "Musurgia Rhetorica"</note>.

Therefore, the various tightenings and loosenings of tones, the various ascents and descents, the various and differing reverberations of voices, are the cause of a "magnetic attraction" of souls. Four things greatly increase these effects. **First**, the skillful mixing of tones and the various bindings of sounds according to the <term>upbeat and downbeat<note>original: "arsin & thesin"</note> or syncopation, by which consonances are connected to dissonances by such strict laws of friendship that nothing sweeter can be perceived; these are greatly enhanced by various vocal ornamentations <note>original: "diminutiones"</note> and the mutual, friendly intersections of skillfully woven fugues. <margin>What is required to increase the attractive power of Music.</margin> **Second**, a determined meter, as contained in verse. **Third**, the words themselves, or the text of the songs. **Lastly**, the very disposition of the listener; if these things are absent, no movement will follow from the harmony. 

<margin>The agreement of harmony with the vital spirits.</margin> For since the different dispositions of men arise from no other cause than the movements of the <term>spirit<note>the "animal spirits" mentioned previously</note>, the chief power of all the organs and instruments of both the sensing and moving soul; and since this is caused by alteration or even vocal movements—by which movements the spirit (as has been said) is now gathered, now distracted, now loosened, and a little later tightened—it follows that it undergoes various cycles of alterations caused by sonorous harmony. It necessarily follows that the soul inclines toward the state and disposition of the spirit. Hence, the "wanton" enjoy charming, soft, and higher-pitched melodies, because the effect these produce in the arousal of the spirit is proportionate and similar to the passion toward which they incline. Thus, two people—one of whom burns with celestial love and the other with earthly love—may be agitated by different movements or desires by one and the same <term>Dorian or Lydian mode<note>Ancient Greek musical scales used in the Renaissance and Baroque to evoke specific moods.</note>. The former feels a longing for the heavenly Fatherland joined with a contempt for earthly things; the latter feels the heat of carnal companionship joined with a desire for fleeting things. The same must be judged for the rest. Thus, everyone is most delighted by that harmony which is more similar and proportionate to their own nature and <term>complexion<note>The balance of "humors" (fluids) in the body that determined personality.</note>, and more agreeable to their present disposition.

# CHAPTER IV.
## An investigation into the causes of consonant and dissonant numbers.

<margin>Why some numbers are resonant, others not.</margin>
Furthermore, how Music moves the affections of the soul through its melodies is easily understood from what has been said previously. Now it only remains to be explained why some sounds are consonant and others are not, and why only consonant sounds move the emotions while dissonant ones do not. To understand this, it must be known that just as consonance is a proportion of different voices or sounds reduced into one, or a mixture of high and low sound falling sweetly and uniformly upon the ears; so dissonance is a harsh and unpleasant striking of the ear coming from a mixture of high and low sounds.

<margin>What consonance and dissonance are.</margin>
Since pleasure is perceived from the hearing of two different tones, the cause is that the tremors <note>Kircher uses "tremors" to describe what we now call sound waves or vibrations.</note> resulting from the vibration of the string are often united and agree as one. By this union and agreement, the spirit, similarly excited, stimulates the imaginative faculty toward pleasure. Displeasure occurs, however, if the said tremors either do not unite at all, or do so only rarely. So that anyone may be able to know how this union happens, it seemed best to demonstrate the whole business here through several propositions.

### Proposition I.
*Two strings of the same tension <note>original: "Isotonae," referring to strings tuned to the same pitch.</note> plucked at the same time necessarily produce a unison, and they unite themselves perfectly and in equal time with every vibration.*

Although we have demonstrated all these things at length and from first principles in our *Chordosophia* <note>meaning "Wisdom of the Strings," a section of his work.</note>, which is the first part of Book VI titled *Musurgia Organica* <note>"Organic Music-making," likely referring to instrumental music.</note>; nevertheless, because this place rightfully demands the origin of consonances, we thought the same things should be briefly repeated here. I suppose, therefore, from the demonstrations in the cited book, that all the oscillations <note>original: "diadromos," the back-and-forth movement of a vibrating string.</note>—whether equal or unequal—of a single string last for the same amount of time. Let there be two strings, AB and CD, equal in both tension and thickness; I say that from their plucking, a unison is necessarily born.

->[Diagram showing two parallel vibrating strings. String 1 is labeled A at the left and B at the right, with a vibration peak at E and troughs at S and M. String 2 is labeled C at the left and D at the right, with a peak at F and troughs at T and I.]<-

Since, according to the demonstrations in the cited place, strings of equal tension relate to each other as 1 to 1, the time is also equal and of the same duration; the end of the vibrations in each string will necessarily be isochronous <note>original: "ἰσοχρονος," meaning happening in the same amount of time.</note>, that is, it will happen at the same time. For each string—AB indeed pulled to point E, and CD pulled to point F—will strike the air at points M and I at one and the same time during their reflections, causing exactly the same tones. In the return, however, striking the air at points S and T at one and the same moment of time, they will cause the same tones as before. And so they will always produce the same and identical sounds until the trembling strings, having reached their center of gravity, come to rest. Since the striking of the air at the points of reflection unites perfectly at the same moment of time, and this happens with every oscillation (or back-and-forth run), it necessarily follows, as has been said, that the unison tone will result—the source and origin of all consonances. Therefore, two strings of equal tension necessarily produce a unison, which was to be demonstrated, etc.

## Proposition II.
Two strings of equal thickness, one of which is double the length of the other, will necessarily produce the **Octave** <note>original: *Diapason*, from the Greek for "through all [notes]"</note> when plucked, and their vibrations will meet at unequal intervals of time.

Let there be two strings, AB and BC, where the latter is in a double proportion to the former <note>meaning string BC is twice as long as string AB</note>. I maintain that the sounds produced when they are plucked will meet not in equal, but in unequal time. For since the relationship of one string to another is the same as the duration of one movement to the duration of another—specifically, the movements of the plucked strings—it follows necessarily (according to Book VI, Proposition 6) that string AB completes its **swings** <note>original: *diadromos*, a term for the back-and-forth path of a vibration</note> twice as fast as string BC completes its own.

Suppose both strings are plucked at the same moment; string AB at point G, and BC at point F. String AB will necessarily traverse the entire space from G to O once, while in that same time, string BC travels from F to D. At that moment, because the first string is at point O (its limit) and the second is at point D (still in motion), no union of sounds occurs. However, when string BC reaches point V, string AB will have reached point S in that same time. Having both reached their respective limits—BC at V and AB at S—the sounds caused by the striking of the air will perfectly unite for the first time. Since string AB runs twice as fast as string BC, it will necessarily sound an **octave** <note>original: *diapason*</note> against the other at the moment the sounds unite. The octave, therefore, is caused by the union of sounds flowing in unequal time, which was to be demonstrated; but let us demonstrate this in another way.

[Geometric diagram showing two horizontal lines of different lengths, with diagonal lines forming a diamond shape in the center to illustrate the paths of vibration. Points are labeled A, B, C, D, E, F, G, O, S, V.]

### Another demonstration of the same.

<margin>
How the **Octave** <note>original: *Diapason*</note> consists in a 2:1 ratio.
</margin>

Let the larger string be the **lowest note** <note>original: *hypate*, the "highest" string on a lyre but lowest in pitch</note>, and the smaller string (which is half the length of the larger) be the **highest note** <note>original: *Nete*, or the octave G</note>. Let the space of the *hypate* string be BC, through which the vibrated string runs back and forth, and let the space of the *nete* be FG, which is half the size of the first. The ratio of the spaces traveled will be the same as the ratio of the strings themselves. 

Suppose these strings are plucked simultaneously at points B and F. Both strings will travel from B and F: the larger toward S, the smaller toward G. When the smaller string reaches point G, having reached the limit of its motion, it will produce a sound from the percussion of the air. Meanwhile, string BC is still at point S, remaining at a distance from its limit C equal to the distance it just traveled from B to S; thus, it remains silent. Soon, however, it reaches point C, where it resonates from the percussion of the air. But in that same time, the smaller string has returned from G to F. Because it travels that distance in the same time it takes the string BC to go from S to C, it resonates at point F (the other limit of its path) at the exact same moment string BC resonates at its limit C. 

This creates the first union of the sounds of both strings. This union will happen as often as the trembling string BC strikes the air. Furthermore, since the smaller string travels its path twice while the larger string travels its path BC once, the smaller string will strike the air twice as fast as the larger one. Consequently, it sounds higher in pitch. Because of the frequent union of vibrations—which powerfully affects the hearing and sweetly influences the **vital spirits** <note>In 17th-century physiology, "vital spirits" were a subtle fluid that carried sensory information to the soul</note>—it creates that delight in the soul which we call the first degree of harmony. 

Therefore, in strings stretched to equal tension, when the striking of the air occurs in both strings at the same time and space, a **unison** is produced. The unison relates to harmony as **unity** <note>the number 1</note> relates to numbers, or as a **point** relates to a line; for this reason, it cannot strictly be called a "harmony" itself. But the **octave** <note>original: *diapason*</note> is the sweetest of all consonances because the union of the low and high sounds is perfectly and frequently mixed...

...the motion of the larger string will first begin to sound at C; therefore, where the smaller string, coming to D, resonates a second time, the motion of the larger string returning from C will be poised at point X. For since they reach the limits of their motion in equal time and space—namely, the larger at C and the smaller at D—a union occurs there for the first time. Thus, in this consonance, the smaller string always skips three tones which do not unite with the sounds of the larger string, finally uniting the sound resulting from the fourth vibration. The same judgment applies to the other consonances, which will always be more imperfect the further they recede from the simplest **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note>, and the more rarely they unite their sounds, as occurs in the **major third** <note>original: "ditono"</note>, **minor third** <note>original: "semiditono"</note>, the **sixth** <note>original: "hexachordo"</note>, and similar intervals. Thus, the major third, always skipping four sounds that do not mix, unites only the fifth; the minor third, however, skipping five unsociable sounds, joins only the sound resulting from the sixth vibration of the string to the larger string. See what we have treated most extensively regarding these matters in my *Chordosophia* <note>The "Wisdom of Strings," likely referring to a section within Kircher's larger work, the *Musurgia Universalis*</note>.

But if, therefore, slow and fast motions are proportionate to each other and mix easily, a **consonance** arises; if, however, they are disproportionate and admit no mixture or union, a **dissonance** is born. Moreover, they will mix more easily the more similar they are and the closer they are to the source—that is, to unity or the unison. Hence, the consonance of the **octave** is the most perfect of all consonances, <margin>The octave is the most perfect of all consonances.</margin> because it is completed by the first, most perfect proportion and by a simplest unity distant only by a single unit from the "monad" <note>The number one, signifying God or the starting point of all numbers</note>; such is the **double** ratio <note>2:1</note>; and it relates as one to two. Closest to this in perfection is the "superparticular" proportion, or the **fifth** <note>original: "sesquialtera diapente"</note>, which relates as 2 to 3. This is followed immediately by the **fourth** <note>original: "sesquitertia"</note>, relating as 3 to 4, which corresponds to the consonance of the **fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>. This is perfect in the harmonic arrangement of tones, but in the arithmetic arrangement it is judged imperfect and dissonant; hence, it is only perfect and consonant according to certain conditions. It is added that these proportions—the fifth and the fourth—are consonant because the octave is constituted from them when they are joined; moreover, they could not constitute the most consonant of all things if they themselves were not consonant. Indeed, all Music consists of three consonances, <margin>All Music consists of 3 consonances.</margin> and all Music is nothing other than harmony consisting of these three consonances, nor is any symphony possible without these three. Therefore, the perfect ratio of consonances, whether simple or composite, consists in the number four; however, from this up to the number six, the consonances depart from their perfection. These are the **Major Third** <note>original: "Ditonus"</note>, the **Minor Third** <note>original: "Semiditonus"</note>, and the **Major Sixth** <note>original: "Hexachordon maius"</note>. The first of these, consisting in a 5:4 ratio <note>original: "sesquiquarta"</note>, relates as 4 to 5; the second, in a 6:5 ratio <note>original: "sesquiquinta"</note>, relates as 5 to 6. The third, in a ratio of 5 to 3 <note>original: "superbipatiente tertias"</note>, relates as 3 to 5. These are called **imperfect consonances**, by which, together with the perfect ones, the entire circle of consonances is completed. You see, therefore, how the consonances flowing from unity finish the circuit of their total perfection in the number six, so that no other consonances besides those mentioned can be assigned. He who penetrates these things more deeply will clearly see how **GOD**, the Best and Greatest, is the source of all harmony, and how the world flowed forth from Him, which was established by Him as a **six-day work** <note>original: "ἐξάμερον" (hexaemeron), referring to the biblical six days of Creation</note>. But we have delivered these matters more extensively in Books III and IV, pages 100 and 187.

These consonances, therefore, according to their different arrangement in the musical scale, also cause a different constitution of tones, semitones, quarter-tones <note>original: "diesium"</note>, and chromatics. From their various combinations, the human spirit is also affected in various ways according to the various temperaments of men. Whence result various affections and impulses of the mind, as was said a little earlier; for our spirit is moved according to the ratio of the stirred air, not otherwise than how a struck string excites another untouched one. Thus, if our spirits were strings, they—being excited by musical measures—would perfectly express harmony, which I shall make manifest through the following experiments.

**210 *Universal Music-making***

**Experiment I.**

<margin>A string usually moves a distant string.</margin>

Upon a solid, smooth, and hollow board, let nine strings be stretched in the order that appears in the following diagram. First, let there be two strings, A and F, which are equal both in quantity and quality—that is, in tension—so that they sound at a unison pitch; let the remaining strings be arranged tone by tone according to the diagram placed below. Therefore, if you strike the first of these strings, F, with a <term>plectrum (a small tool for plucking strings)</term>, it will cause all the strings that are <term>equal in pitch <note>original: ἰσοτόνους (isotonous)</note></term> or equally tensioned to resonate, even though they are untouched. There is, however, this difference: the string that is closer to the unison will resonate more and will be seen to move more perceptibly. Thus, the motion and sound of the untouched unison string F will be felt most strongly in response to the sound of the first; it will also incite the octave, A, to sound, though a little more weakly than the former, as it recedes somewhat from the unison. It will also incite the fifth, but scarcely perceptibly as it recedes more than is fair from the unison; for if you place a feather upon it, you will feel some trembling of the string, albeit a slight one. I have found this to be noted by hardly anyone else, as most have thought that only the <term>hypate <note>The lowest note/string in the ancient Greek musical system.</note></term> in unison, and the <term>nete <note>The highest note/string in the ancient Greek musical system.</note></term> relative to others, would be moved when untouched; but long experience has taught me the opposite. For all strings consonant with the *hypate* are moved, but as I said, they move more effectively the closer they are to their source sound. Truly, the dissonant strings alone, being unable to be moved by a friendly provocation, persist in their stubbornness.

<margin>Organ pipes also move strings stretched proportionally to them.</margin>

Furthermore, it is not only strings that incite similarly stretched strings, but organ pipes and trumpets also cause strings enjoying a similar tone to sound. So that the truth of this matter may be more fully demonstrated, I will recall in this place an event that happened to me once in Mainz. While I was occupied with certain business during a solemn Mass in a certain <term>odeum <note>A room or building used for musical performances.</note></term> separated from the church, behold, I perceived a <term>large viol <note>original: chelys; a term for a stringed instrument.</note></term> (which a certain singer had left behind before departing, hanging on the wall of the room, exactly tuned to the church organ without any loosening of the strings) resonating untouched and with no one present, by some hidden motion at intervals. Stunned by the novelty of the thing, I drew closer to examine this sort of prodigious sound more deeply. While I did so, I discovered that as soon as the organist activated the pipes that exactly corresponded in every way to the strings of the said viol, the strings themselves were incited by that tone no differently than if they had been struck by a plectrum. I later showed this harmonic sympathy to many others, not without great admiration. I subsequently attempted to show this <term>sound-working <note>original: phonurgiam</note></term> in other places, but it was not possible to find a layout of the place similar to the one mentioned, which was found by chance rather than by art; for in a harmonic wonder of this kind, I noted that a perfect adaptation of the pipes with the strings is required, as well as an exact distance of the pipes from the strings, along with a certain arrangement of the place and the walls that propagate the sound. But regarding the construction of this, since it is not for this place, we shall perhaps speak more fully elsewhere, God willing. Now only the cause of this prodigious effect remains to be investigated.

Book IX. The Magic of Consonance & Dissonance. 211

-> CHAPTER V. <-

-> On the reasoning behind the sympathy and antipathy of sounds. <-

**Note first:** In sound of this kind, three things can be considered. First, the body that moves by sounding, and the body that is moved by another toward sound. Second, a certain proportion or similarity between the sounding bodies. Third, a suitable medium, such as air.
**Note second:** Sound is not propagated through the medium of air alone, but wherever it finds a body in its path suitable for its preservation, it exercises its powers therein. For the air, which is dissipated by the sound, seeks union by its very nature; however, motion or sound maintains its tone better and more faithfully in a body apt and suitable for its propagation, such as stretched strings. From this I infer that a struck string excites another similarly stretched string that remains untouched, either because of the greatest similarity and proportion which the sounding <margin>How one string moves an untouched string.</margin> body and the resonant body have toward each other; since similarity and proportion are a kind of imitation of similarity, serving as the base and foundation of the whole motion. Secondly, it is due to the moving air; for when the air is moved by the motion of the sound, and the proportion of sound to sound is the same as that of excited air to excited air (as shown previously), it happens that air excited by sound—still imbued with the "image" <note>original: "simulachro"; Kircher uses this to mean a formal representation or 'echo' of the sound's frequency carried in the air.</note> of the sound it carries—when it strikes a similar, proportional sounding body capable of receiving the quality it carries, it attacks it in the same way the air was attacked by the first sound. Both the air and the sound seek union and propagation in the body, which is highly resonant and airy, due to their innate nature. Thus, a string moves another string stretched equally, or any other body or harmonic instrument, like a string similar and corresponding to it in sound, because the air, equally excited, strikes a body similar in both quantity and quality to the one by which it was excited. Hence, that body, already disposed by itself and longing for its perfection or "good," is similarly excited by the plucking <note>original: "vellicatione"; literally a twitching or plucking sensation.</note> of the surrounding air. Moreover, a string sounding the Octave, though untouched, is nevertheless excited by a lower one because of the greatest similarity and proportion it has to it. For in everyone's opinion, it differs from the lower one only by its sharp sound; hence it is considered the same, or rather is virtually contained in the lower as the high in the low (as Aristotle <margin>Why do boys and adults singing together stay an octave apart?</margin> testifies), and is nothing other than a certain sharper and more intense repetition of the lower voice. Whence naturally women with men, and boys and eunuchs with men of advanced age, when singing psalms, naturally sing the interval of the *diapason* <note>original: "diapason"; the Greek term for an octave.</note>. Bells also and other sounding instruments resonate the *diapason* as if mixed with the lower tone, which would not happen unless the greatest similarity and proportion intervened between the two. Furthermore, since the external air is related to the internal air of the string as the extension of one string is to another, and the string sounding the *diapason* is in a 1:2 ratio <note>original: "subdupla"; refers to the mathematical ratio of the octave.</note>, it follows that the air, according to this proportion, also moves and excites the air internal and innate to the auditory organ, contained within the membranes. And from what has been said, it is clear by what reasoning Music excites various affections of the soul: for it has the power to move the hearing either with delight or compassion, or in another similar way, according to the variety of the sound and the moved air, which moves the sense of hearing with this or that proportion. For while the air, moved in this or that way and inhaled by a person, moves the spirit in the same way, <margin>Spirits in the heart are moved by sounds.</margin> various affections are excited in living beings according to the variety of sounds, just as the spirit <note>Kircher refers to "animal spirits," which 17th-century science believed were subtle fluids or vapors that carried signals between the heart, brain, and muscles.</note> is moved in various ways when the air is moved. For since the heart is the throne of the spirits, they receive the trembling and leaping air into the chest and sound as one with their kindred [spirit]; the remaining spirits located in other parts of the body follow these, moving or restraining the muscles according to the law of rhythms—either quickening with excitations or resting with a composed tenor, or imitating rest with slowness—not differently than in the strings mentioned a little before: when one string is touched, another equally stretched trembles. For the spirits in the heart are excited by the motion of external sound so much more easily than strings, as there is a greater union [between them]. Hence, with much care, the depressed and withered soul rests when an addition of external, entering air is made...

<summary>Kircher explains the physics of sympathetic vibration, arguing that sound travels through air to trigger motion in similar bodies (like strings tuned to the same pitch or an octave). He then links this mechanical resonance to human emotion, suggesting that sound "plucks" the vital spirits in the heart, causing the body to physically respond to musical rhythms.</summary>

*Experiment.*

Take five glass goblets, all of the same size and capacity, which you will arrange in the order expressed here in the diagram below; let one goblet be filled with "water of life" <term>aqua vitae: a 17th-century term for high-proof distilled spirits or brandy</term>, another goblet with a better wine, another with thin water, another with thick water, such as seawater, or oil; and the middle one with common water. liquids, and indeed more vehemently according to how much thinner one liquid is than another. It must be judged that music excites the affects of our soul in no different a way. rightly said that *music in mourning is an untimely
tale.* <note>A reference to the Biblical Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 22:6.</note>

These effects also exist in strings of equal length but made from different animal intestines or metals; for just as the weight of metal is to metal, so is string to string, and sound to sound, etc.

**Corollary I.**

<margin>How Music heals melancholics and the demon-possessed?</margin>

**Corollary II.**

It is clear from what has been said by what means Music removes the plague, Lycanthropy <note>term: Lycanthropy — the delusion of having turned into a wolf.</note>, madness of the mind, and other movements in all those cases we mentioned previously. This happens by the benefit of the "spirits" <note>term: spirits — in Kircher's time, these were "animal spirits," a subtle fluid believed to flow through the nerves to carry instructions from the soul to the body.</note>, which, being rendered thinner, faster, and hotter, dissipate and thin out or mitigate those humors by which the diseases were created. Furthermore, the mind is turned away for a time from the apprehension of the disease (which afflicts the soul more than is fair) and is so cheered that it directs all the spirits to drive out the infirmity. These spirits, because of the effective command of the mind, run hither and thither and fly together until they have fulfilled their orders—in much the same way that certain Northern winds, once stirred up, perfectly purge the air infected with contagion and ward off the rot of the foul vapors mixed in that same air. Since the vital spirit is airy or ethereal, as soon as it perceives sharp sounds and quickly moving air, it imitates that motion and its Rhythm or cadence. For just as the operation of the intellect follows the actions of the imagination, the will, and the sensory appetite, so too do those corporeal spirits—which are the primary instruments of the soul—easily follow the impressions and movements of the air’s alteration.

**CHAPTER III.**

**On the wonderful history of a certain King of Denmark driven to madness by the power of Music.**

The following example will show that Music not only releases one from fury but can also incite one to it. Albert Krantz <note>original: "Cranzius"</note> relates the case in Book 5 of *Denmark*, Chapter 3, as does Olaus Magnus, in these words:

"While Eric <note>King Eric I of Denmark, known as 'the Good' (r. 1095–1103).</note>, having since returned to his kingdom, was holding a solemn court and delighting in the industry of many soldiers and craftsmen alike, there was among others a Musician. And the more he made these great claims of what he could do, the more he made the King desirous of testing it. Now the craftsman began to repent of his boasting and wished he had not proclaimed such great things about himself, since testing such things on a King was not without danger; furthermore, if he failed to prove what he said with action..."

Although Saul’s hatred conceived against David could also have greatly detracted from the skill of David’s art.

-> ### CHAPTER IV. ### <-

-> **On the miraculous cure of those poisoned by the bite of the Tarantula through Music.** <-

Nothing indeed, in my judgment, can be more admirable than the passions and effects which the Tarantula produces with its poison in those it has infected; so much so that, relying on infallible experience, we believe ourselves able to demonstrate all the effects produced by the miraculous cure of diseases performed through Music by the guidance of this case alone. -> #### Question I. #### <-

-> *Why can those suffering from Tarantism be cured by no other harmonic medium, or by music alone?* <-

How great the power of Music is in stirring the passions of the soul, and what the cause of this harmonic energy may be, has been shown at length in the preceding sections; now it remains for us finally to show how the force of the disease in those suffering from Tarantism can be driven out by the force of music, and the infirm person be restored to full health. Without any wordy circumlocutions, therefore, let us begin the reasoning we have proposed.

<margin>The power of harmonic sound.</margin>
Since strings or chords, as we taught in the preceding parts, have the greatest power to stir the air in the same manner in which they themselves are moved, and by this proportional mixture of sounds they excite a harmony pleasing to the ears and the soul; it happens that by this lute-playing harmony, the air is harmonically stirred by the various and proportioned motion of the strings. The air, indeed, being similarly stirred according to the harmonic motions impressed upon it, penetrates within; and the <term>phantastic faculty</term> <note>The "phantastic faculty" refers to the part of the mind that processes sensory images and imagination.</note> being occupied by the pleasant motion, it similarly moves the <term>spirits</term> <note>In 17th-century medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried life and sensation through the nerves.</note> by thinning them. The spirit, thinned and rarefied by the motion, conveniently affects the muscles, arteries, and the innermost fibers—the receptacles of the spirits. Since the vehicle of the hidden poison is a 
<margin>How the sick person is freed by music.</margin>
sharp, biting, and <term>bilious humor</term> <note>One of the four bodily fluids; an excess of yellow bile was thought to cause irritability and heat.</note> hidden in the innermost marrow of the fibers, it happens that this humor, rarefied and heated together with the stirred-up poison, affects the whole genus of muscles with a certain itching or twitching. The patient, indeed, being sweetly affected by this twitching—which is pleasing to him—is forced to break out into leaps; at the very least, there is a commotion of the whole body and the humors. Heat follows the commotion; the relaxation of the whole body and the opening of the pores follows the heat; and finally, the transpiration of the poisonous vapors necessarily follows the opening of the pores. Since, however, the poison is so deeply rooted that it cannot be exhaled in a single dance, a certain portion evaporates step-by-step through the motion every year until the whole is consumed.

Just as in the case of two <term>polychords</term> <note>a general term for multi-stringed instruments like harps or lutes</note> tuned equally, those strings which are similar in tone and equally tense move while the others remain still <note>This is the principle of sympathetic resonance</note>, so they find that, according to the similarity and condition of the Tarantulas, now these, now those dance. If they use this melody, they assert that they achieve an infallible cure.

## On the various properties of different Tarantulas.

Once the disease had been contracted and the poison had gradually spread through his whole body, he soon felt the most severe paroxysms <note>Sudden attacks or violent fits of emotion or physical pain.</note> and the agonies of death. 

<margin>A remarkable story confirms that Tarantulas are imbued with contrary powers.</margin>

Lute players, flute players, and musicians of every kind were immediately summoned, and various types of harmonies were attempted. Then, as the lute player played more briskly, he even raised himself onto his feet. What more?

# Question II.
### *Why are those affected by Tarantism so greatly delighted*
### *by certain specific colors?*

**I**t has been said that different Tarantulas excite those affected by Tarantism toward different colors; the reason why this happens must now be explained. I suppose, as confirmed by experience, that those bitten incline toward that color which the tarantulas themselves display; thus, those who are wounded by red Tarantulas are drawn toward red and flame-like colors; those by green ones, toward green, and so on for the others. Likewise, those Tarantulas found near water, rivers, or the edges of cisterns incline the victims toward water; while those in hot and dry places usually stir the "Tarantics" <note>victims of the tarantula bite</note> to bilious <note>choler-driven or aggressive</note> actions.

If a man’s temperament <note>original: complexio</note> matches that of the Tarantula, the effect will be all the more powerful. There are certain poisonous animals that transfer the exact same condition they themselves suffer into others through their bite. Thus the Dipsas serpent, since it is always tormented by a burning thirst, produces the same in a man by biting, according to the saying:
      *As this thirst, twisting her, is extinguished by no waters,*
      *So she rouses a rabid thirst with her bite.*
   So the bite of a rabid dog produces that passion in a man which it produces in the dog, namely *hydrophobia* <note>original: υδροφοβίαν</note>, or the fear of water. The Cerastes <note>a horned viper</note> also—as I have learned from the Egyptians—strikes *pyrophobia* <note>original: πυροφοβίαν</note>, or a fear of fire and light, into both the serpent and the man infected by its venom. So the sluggish torpedo fish makes limbs sluggish; and just as a parent suffering from gout, leprosy, or epilepsy communicates the same diseases to a son through his seed, so the venoms of different Tarantulas, by an innate property, seem to incline the mind of the victim—through a hidden Magnetism or some blind similarity of nature—toward that color which they themselves reflect, or by which they are refreshed. Moreover, it is clear that the Tarantula is refreshed by a certain color because, when placed on different colored surfaces, they seek out the surface that is similar to their own color.

...by exactly the same reasoning as was discussed regarding the magnetism of the imagination <note>original: "phantasię magnetismo." In early modern psychology, the "imagination" was thought to exert a physical-like attraction or "magnetism" on the humors of the body.</note>.

At this point, one might reasonably ask: in what way does the color white dissipate, black collect, and red inflame? Why do green, crimson, and gold delight the senses? This is especially puzzling since these colors can only act through "species" <note>term: <term>Species</term> (sensory images). In Aristotelian science, "species" were the invisible forms or "likenesses" that traveled from an object to the eye to facilitate sight.</note>, which of themselves produce no real physical action. This is because they possess only an imperfect and diminished essence, which some call "real" and others "intentional" <note>intentional existence: a philosophical term for something that exists as an object of the mind rather than as a physical substance.</note>, as it stands midway between the nature of real things and things of the mind.

I answer: the sensory species of colors are indeed qualities endowed with the power of acting, though to a lesser degree than the physical qualities from which they are shed. For who would deny that the light spread through the air by the sun, or the heat diffused from a fire, has the power to warm? Light is the image and "species" of the Sun, just as heat is the secondary form of fire; therefore, nothing prevents objects from changing the sense organs through these species, acting as their own natural and proper instruments.
