For the humor <note>The "humors" were the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) thought to govern health and temperament.</note> in the human body is so tempered that it is carried to the imagination, led by the "spirit" <note>term: <term>Spiritus</term> (animal spirits). Since redness, by its peculiar action, ignites the eyes because of its similarity to a fiery nature, it twitches the visual muscles (as is seen in the behavior of Lions and Buffaloes). In the eyes, the greatest force of the spirits is gathered; when these spirits are dilated and ignited by the flame-like color, they twitch the visual muscles as well as other connected muscles in the limbs. From this twitching, a certain immense tingling is felt, which gives rise to movements that Music, with its harmonic air, greatly promotes. 

Whence a person—feeling the greatest pleasure from that object of most pleasing color joined with Music—is driven, whether they wish to or not, into leaping and dancing. This analogy of harmonies possesses the greatest power in stirring the emotions. By the same reasoning, since green is composed of those most pleasing colors of gold and purple, it is perfectly tempered. -> CHAPTER VI. <-
-> How Prophecy and divination can be caused by harmonic melodies. <-

**I**t is known from the Sacred Text that prophecy has occasionally occurred by the power of musical harmony. A primary example is the passage in the first book of Kings <note>modern 1 Samuel 10:5</note> where Samuel sent Saul, who had been anointed King, to a group of Prophets. When he encountered them, and saw before them the psaltery, the drum, the flute, and the zither, and the men themselves prophesying, the Spirit of the Lord flowed into him and he prophesied in their midst. In the first book of Chronicles, chapter 25, the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun <note>original: "Hispia"</note>, set apart for ministry by David, prophesied with zithers, psalteries, and cymbals. And in the third book of Kings <note>modern 2 Kings 3:15</note>, chapter 4, verse 15, while the minstrel played, the hand of the Lord came upon Elisha, etc. The question is therefore asked: what force and efficacy can Music have to produce this so miraculous effect even in men who are not supernaturally gifted with the gift of prophecy? But so that these matters may be discussed more solidly, we shall first declare how we define "prophecy" in this context.

Prophecy, therefore, is nothing other than that foreknowledge of future things, a prediction, or an instinct from God, by which one inspired reveals the secrets of the heart or other mysteries that cannot happen by natural means. So much so, that he who knows those secrets and counsels of God through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit without his own labor is called a Prophet. It can also be called "prophecy" when many things alien to human sense are performed by the help of an evil spirit, as happens in the possessed, and formerly in those who were driven by "poetic fury." We are not dealing here with the miraculous production of Prophecy, but with the natural kind; we ask whether that can truly be produced by Music, concerning which there are various opinions of different men.

Astrologers, along with Magi, assign the cause to the <term>Alcocoden: the "Giver of Life" or "Soul-Steward," an astrological planet that determines the length of life and character</term> Soul, the distributor of forms. For they babble that the virtue of all Magic must be drawn from this, and that this is why Saul became a prophet when the harper played. For they think the soul does marvelous things according to various degrees of "fury," so that the soul, stirred by musical fury, having departed from its prison, transcends the bonds of the limbs with nothing restraining it, and, incited by the divine Spirit, comprehends all things and foresees the future. I remain silent about many unworthy things they devise to stabilize their views; while we have reserved these for other works to be refuted, I did not wish to be more lengthy here—

**On the greatest effect of Music, which it has in stirring bod-**

There should be no doubt that Music possesses the greatest power in stirring bodies; for while large bells are struck, while cannons are fired, and thunders roar, how great is the movement of the air, of buildings, of windows, and of towers! These movements occasionally become so strong that men are not only stunned by the vehement sound, but even fall down lifeless. However, we are not speaking of this kind of sound <note>i.e., we are not discussing the blunt physical force of an explosion.</note>, but of that by which certain things are moved by this sound alone, and not by another even louder one. For why one string should sound in response to another of equal tension, and yet not to the blast of a cannon, is a marvel. There is indeed a hidden power in certain sounds toward certain bodies, so proportioned that it moves those only and no others; it impresses its force on some and not on others. Just as a magnet does not exert its power on wood, lead, or similar things, but on a similar body <note>meaning iron, which shares a "sympathy" with the magnet.</note>, so there are certain sounds which are fit and proportioned for stirring certain bodies. If anyone knew these proportions, he could undoubtedly perform the greatest miracles of nature with their help.

It happens occasionally that while many people are talking together, one particular voice makes a bench tremble, while the voices of the rest leave no impression upon it. I have also noted from time to time that one pipe of an organ moved a specific string of a large lute <term>chelis</term><note>Kircher uses "chelis" to refer to instruments of the lute or viol family.</note> so sharply that the string seemed to have been vibrated by a plectrum. There was also a stone of immense mass that always trembled at the sound of a certain organ pipe, yet when this pipe was silent and the rest were sounding, no movement was perceived. Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and music theorist who corresponded with Kircher.</note> reports that among the Franciscan Fathers in Paris, 
<margin>Wonderful experiments concerning sound</margin> 
there is this wonder: while the organs are played, the pavement near the end of the diameter—which arises from the square of which the organs are the side—is so shaken that you would almost fear the earth might gape open. Yet, you do not feel this at all if you move closer to the organs or further away from them. From this are taken the greatest arguments for <term>Natural Magic</term><note>In the 17th century, "Natural Magic" referred to the scientific study of hidden natural forces (like magnetism or acoustics) to produce amazing effects without resorting to the supernatural.</note>, and the solutions to entirely paradoxical effects, such as when statues are moved by one certain sound and not another; these matters will be treated specifically in the section on the *Wonder-working of Sounds*. In this same way, at the waterfalls of Tivoli <note>original: "catadupas Tybu tinas"</note>, a certain iron ring fastened to a neighboring house is seen to be perpetually moved by the vehement sound of the falling river. In my own Museum <note>The Museum Kircherianum in Rome, a famous collection of curiosities and scientific instruments.</note>, I also have a <term>polychord</term><note>A multi-stringed instrument used for acoustic experiments.</note>, of which one string—none of the others—is animated into sound by a wonderful force at the ringing of a nearby bell. Truly, we shall deal with these things most extensively in the following pages. There is no other reason for this phenomenon than the proportioned harmonic commotion of the air, which, wherever it finds a body proportioned to itself, affects it with a similar kind of motion; all those experiments which we produced in the first part of this work aim toward this point.

From this I conclude that if someone knew the proportion which the sound of any instrument has to the spirits, muscles, and arteries of the human body, nothing would be easier for him than to sweep a person into any emotion; and to stir them into dances proportioned to the nature of the melodies, as we have said concerning those afflicted with <term>Tarantism</term><note>A supposed dancing mania in southern Italy, believed to be caused by a tarantula bite and "cured" by specific fast-paced music (the Tarantella).</note>. ### Digression on the capture of the Xiphias fish (commonly called the Swordfish), which is carried out in the Mamertine Strait <note>The Strait of Messina, between Sicily and Calabria</note> at fixed times of the year, and whether Music holds any power over animals.

It is a marvelous thing, and hardly believable to those who have neither seen this hunt nor taken part in it. This hunt is carried out in no other sea in Europe that I know of, except in Sicily, and especially in the Strait during the month of May. It is organized in this way: skilled fishermen, in the said month and on a chosen day, enter the Sicilian sea—which they call the Faro—very early in the morning with a boat prepared for this specific business. One among the fishermen, more skilled and robust than the others, occupies the prow of the boat, equipped with a spear likewise made for this task. Another fisherman <margin>The marvelous hunting of the Swordfish through certain words.</margin> invites the fish, which may be lurking anywhere, with singular words. As soon as the fish perceives these words, it—marvelous to say—presents itself as if lured by them. The spearman at the prow, seeing the fish opportunely appearing, vibrates his spear with great skill and transfixes it, finally making a rich and sumptuous prey for the tables of the Great Lords. But it is not my purpose here to recount the particular details of this hunt, as it is outside our scope; rather, I will speak of how these fish present themselves at certain specific words and peculiar voices, and not at others. Many have thought those words were made up and known only to the sailors of this kind. Some believed the fish were enticed by these words as if by a sort of incantation. While I was passing through Messina on May 17, 1638, I received the entire method of proceeding from the fishermen themselves while present at the hunt. The words with which they are accustomed to lure the fish are the following:

->*Stay with me, O song,*<- <note>original: "Mamaſſu di paianu"</note>
->*Little ball of the song,*<- <note>original: "Pallettu di paianu"</note>
->*Stay there, stay firm,*<- <note>original: "Maiaſſu ſtignela"</note>
->*Little ball of the song again,*<- <note>original: "Pallettu di paenu palè"</note>
->*The stay,*<- <note>original: "La ſtagnela"</note>
->*The failed stay,*<- <note>original: "Mancata ſtignela"</note>
->*For our guard, near to the sight, and from the land.*<- <note>original: "Pro naſtu vardu, preſſu da viſu, & da terra." These phrases are a corrupt mix of ancient Greek and Sicilian dialect, likely passed down through oral tradition since antiquity.</note>

And these are the words taken from the mouths of the fishermen, at the utterance of which the fish, as if attracted, soon presents itself to the boat. Therefore, since this phenomenon has tormented the wits of many, it remains for us to explain how it happens.

It should be noted, then, that this effect of the fish being attracted by words can happen in two ways: physically (by a natural cause), or paraphysically (beyond nature, either by a secret or explicit pact with a demon). If this effect happens in the latter way, as many think, it can rightly be referred to as an incantation. For we know that many serpents, birds, and wild beasts were accustomed to be gathered into one place, enchanted by certain whisperings of words made by a pact. However, since in operations established by a pact there usually intervene other superstitions—rather than physical operations—and other corrupted circumstances concerning the time, place, position, and number of words, which are entirely contrary to physical operations, a skilled philosopher will easily discern true physical operations from superstitious ones based on such listed circumstances. And certainly, for a long and great time...

# 228 Universal Music-Making <note>original title: "Musurgia Vniuerfalis"</note>

I have discovered this to be the case. From this, I suspected that some kind of hidden physical efficacy lay beneath these phenomena. To explain this: I suppose first (as I have explained in various other places) that every sound produced by a source spreads out spherically into every surrounding area. It immediately acts upon any bodies it encounters. Since some of these bodies are more mobile and others less so, it happens that whenever a sound encounters a proportionate and "consonant" <note>In this context, "consonant" means a physical object whose natural frequency or "spirit" matches the sound wave.</note> subject, it moves that object alone, while countless others remain unmoved because they are disproportionate. I have shown this at length in the "Magic of Consonance and Dissonance" <note>original: "Magia Consoni & Dissoni," a section within this same work</note> and in other parts of this volume.

For this reason, among many musical strings, only those that are tuned to the same note <note>unison</note> or an octave will sound, while the others remain still. For this reason, a specific sound from a pipe might move a certain stone, a seat, a railing, or a statue, which no other pipe is able to move. In the same way, experience teaches us that animals shrink back from certain sounds, while they are delighted by others. Almost all animals recoil from the grunting of a pig because of the violence it inflicts upon the <term>spirit</term> <note>Kircher uses "spiritus" to mean the subtle physiological fluid that was thought to carry sensory information through the nerves.</note>. A bear, on the other hand, is delighted by a pipe, because that kind of sound soothingly affects its spirit. Similarly, the Nightingale affects all things with its musical melodies because of the natural disposition of its vital spirit and an innate leaning toward harmonic patterns.

The same must be said of artificial or articulate sound <note>human speech</note>, which possesses greater power over almost all animals than inarticulate sound; for the former affects and moves the imagination <note>phantasia</note> of animals more powerfully than the latter. This is why names are given to dogs, horses, sheep, and goats by shepherds, so that when called, they stop and follow the shepherd. Certainly, the Dolphin, when called by a boy by the name "Simon," always appeared, as authors write. Peter Martyr, in his book on American matters, also tells of a fish of immense size called a <term>Manati</term> <note>The Manatee</note>, which, when called by the name "Martin," would come out of the water and take food from the hands of anyone he met. Thus, animals are captured by certain words and not others; because these words, and no others, have a power proportionate to their articulate sound to move the spirit and imagination of animals, so that once moved, they follow the sound.

Therefore, the same thing can happen in the capture of the <term>swordfish</term> <note>original: "psyphiæ," a corruption of Xiphias. Kircher is referring to a traditional Mediterranean practice of "charming" swordfish with specific rhythmic chants.</note>; for only these specific recited words have the power to rouse the indwelling spirit and the imagination of this animal and to affect it soothingly, and no others—as is established by certain and indoubtable experience. These words alone have the proportion necessary to excite the animal's spirits. Just as among men, not everyone is delighted by the same music, but rather by that which is more proportionate to their <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of "humors" or temperament of a person.</note>, the same must be said of animals. Truly, these words are not entirely made up, but are real words, though corrupted over time so that they may appear <term>dissonant</term> <note>original Greek: ἀσύμφωνα (asymphona), meaning out of tune or jarring.</note>. ### CHAPTER VIII.
### Whether the natural power of herbs, plants, and animals, joined with musical melodies, possesses any power in the cure of infirmities.

There has been no shortage of ancient philosophers—Pythagoras, Theophrastus, Ismenias the Theban—who have been followed with more superstition than is right by Giambattista della Porta among the moderns. I went to the expense of having two <term>polychords</term> <note>many-stringed instruments</note> prepared, one of which was fitted with wolf strings and the other with sheep strings; and the wolf—

I took care to have a multi-stringed instrument made of wolf-gut <note>original: "lupinum quidem polychordum"</note> played inside a sheepfold; then I arranged for both [wolf and sheep-gut instruments] to be played together outside. However, I was unable by any means to observe either terror in the sheep, nor that famous breaking of the strings arising from a natural antipathy. <note>There was a long-standing myth that if a string made of wolf gut and one of sheep gut were placed on the same instrument, the wolf string would "consume" or break the sheep string even without being touched.</note> Nor did I rest there: I placed a wolf’s head upon the sheep-pen, and I tied a wolf’s heart and genitals around the neck of a sheep; yet I could never perceive those "imaginary terrors" which they say sheep are seized by in such circumstances. Therefore, from that time on, I resolved that I would never believe anything of this sort unless my own experiments first made me certain of the report.

<margin>The Author’s experiments on wolf and sheep strings.</margin>

If the more secret searchers of philosophy would apply such tests, volumes would not be stuffed with so many monsters and portents, nor would the chairs of the Teachers be filled with so many fables and false deceptions. I consider it unworthy of a Philosopher to produce anything of this kind for which he has not first undertaken an experiment. But I return to the matter proposed at the start.

Giambattista della Porta <note>A famous Italian polymath (1535–1615) known for his work *Magia Naturalis* (Natural Magic).</note> (which I find surprising in a man otherwise so wise) thought that any disease could be driven away by the power of music, provided the flutes were made from the wood of plants that regard said diseases with a natural sympathy. For example: if one were to make a flute from the stalks of Hellebore, its sound could cure the "lymphatic" <note>original: "lymphaticos"; here referring to those suffering from madness or delirium.</note> because hellebore, when ingested, is said to heal them. In like manner, he claimed a flute made from the poplar tree would mitigate sciatic pains with its sound, for poplar ointment is extremely useful for pains of the hip. So too, the listener would be incited to Lust <note>original: "Venerem"</note> by using a flute constructed from the stalks of Satyrion; and a musical instrument constructed from cinnamon bark would cure fainting or "lipo-thymia" <note>original: "lypothimiam"; a sudden loss of consciousness or fainting.</note>. In the same way, he claimed a flute constructed from the legs of a kite <note>A type of bird of prey.</note> would render larks and other small birds motionless by the force of antipathy. Time would fail me if I wished to cite every single delusion and "old wives’ tale" <note>original: "aniles fabulas"</note> of the unskillful. For who is so moderately—and, so to speak, only on the very surface—tinted with philosophy that they do not see these things have absolutely no affinity with Music? 

For if these things possess a healing power for certain diseases, they can certainly exercise it without any help from sound, merely through a natural application. Furthermore, I argue as follows: either the harmonious sound produces these effects, or the medicinal power implanted in the flute does, or both together. If the first, then the power joined to the wood will be superfluous. If the second, then the sound will be unnecessary to produce that effect, as it is pointless to do through many means what can be done through few. Finally, if the third, this must happen either because the sound carries that healing power like a vehicle, or through some hidden sympathy resulting anew from the union of both—neither of which can or should be admitted. Not the first, since the virtues of natural things have a faculty sufficient in themselves to change and alter objects placed within their sphere, without the acquisition of any new vehicle to carry them. Add to this that since the "intentional species" <note>A philosophical term referring to the sensory impression or "image" of the sound as it travels.</note> of sound is entirely unfit for carrying anything else—as sound itself requires the vehicle of air to propagate its length and breadth—it certainly cannot give to another what it lacks itself. That is, if a vehicle could be substituted to carry a flow of powers into another thing, no new sympathy could result from this, since the power of sound and the occult power of the natural thing implanted in the flute have very different essences, and "intentional species" are not capable of receiving any such impression. 

Therefore, whatever the wits of idle men devise concerning such things is false. For sound is not "sympathetic" in the proper sense, nor is it the cause of the recited effects; rather, it is the harmonious air that excites the "spirit" <note>The "vital spirits"—the subtle fluids thought to move through the human body to control health and emotion.</note> according to the various laws of numbers. It matters little, therefore, whether the flute with which a Shepherd soothes his sheep is made of Elder wood or from the leg-bones of a wolf; they will be captured by the sound of either flute. By the same reasoning, it was not necessary for Hismenias the Theban to use a poplar instrument to chase away sciatic pains, nor for Xenocrates to use the hollow stalks of Hellebore to heal the mad; for they could have performed this with instruments constructed from any suitable material. For Music cures diseases by no other quality than this: it scatters and loosens "thick spirits," refines those that are loosened, relieves the mind weighed down by the dissolution of sluggish and melancholic vapors, and finally restores health by removing the causes of the diseases. Those who [believe such things] are also to be laughed at...

## CHAPTER I.
### On the definition and division of the wondrous sound.

[Decorative initial S] A wondrous sound <note>Original: *sonus prodigiosus*.</note> is nothing other than a certain unusual noise intended to signify something, which, while it strikes the ears vehemently and the listeners do not know its cause, sweeps them into the greatest admiration. To the miraculous sound belongs that great sound which suddenly arose while Christ was speaking (John 6) <note>Likely referring to the voice from heaven, though commonly associated with John 12:28-29.</note>, filling all listeners with great wonder; such also was the music of the Angels at the Birth of Christ; such a sound occurred on the day of Pentecost according to that passage in the Acts of the Apostles...

From the Acts of the Apostles (**suddenly there came a sound from Heaven, like a rushing mighty Spirit**) <note>original: "factus est repente de Cælo sonus, tanquam aduenientis Spiritus vehementis"; see Acts 2:2</note>; such sounds are mentioned throughout Holy Scripture, like the clangor of trumpets on Mount Sinai, while Moses received the law from GOD.

->### CHAPTER II.<-
->### Regarding the fall of the walls of Jericho following the sound of the trumpets.<-

It is a matter of dispute whether that prodigious sound of trumpets and the shout of the people caused the fall of the walls of Jericho physically or miraculously. Among the Rabbis, Ralbag <note>Rabbi Levi ben Gershon, also known as Gersonides (1288–1344)</note> first thought that they collapsed due to the violence of the sound; the Holy Fathers themselves were of this opinion, namely St. Augustine in his 206th sermon *On Time* <note>original: "de tempore"</note>; "after this," he says, "they came to the city of Jericho, and its walls were cast down to their foundations at the shout of the people and the sound of the trumpets." St. Jerome, in his epistle to Abigaus, says, "the walls of Jericho fell, overturned by the blasts of the priestly <term>sacerdotal|Relating to priests; in this case, the Levites who blew the shofarot</term> trumpets." St. Ambrose asserts the same in Book 30, Chapter 10, as does Origen in his 6th homily. Among more recent authors, Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French mathematician and music theorist who corresponded with Kircher</note> thinks they fell entirely by the violence of the sound; indeed, he even prescribes a proportion between the mobile object and the moving force. Since these ideas are more clever than they are true, we shall not dwell on them, but say briefly that <margin>The walls of Jericho fell by a miracle.</margin> they fell miraculously at the sound, as a sign of the divine will. I prove that they could not have been moved naturally (whatever Mersenne may say) as follows: No sound of men or trumpets, however huge, intense, and multiplied, can by itself naturally cast down or move a wall or any great mass. I demonstrate it thus: Three things must coincide for a sound to occur: first, the collision of two bodies, either solid or quasi-solid; second, the breaking and crushing of the air (or a similar body) trapped between those two; third, the diffusion of this broken and crushed body, and its "flight" or recession, as it were. And it is by this flight that something can be moved and impelled; for while it thus flees and recedes, if it encounters any bodies, it strikes them, and if it can in any way, it propels them. Indeed, it always moves and propels the <margin>How sound moves things.</margin> neighboring and most immediate air, because otherwise there would be a "penetration of bodies" <note>A philosophical impossibility in Aristotelian physics where two objects occupy the same space</note>; and air is, by its own nature, very easy to set in motion. But it does not always move distant air, because the impetus of that fleeing air is gradually weakened, and thus it ceases to progress or impel further on its own. But in this progress of the air and its impulse upon foreign bodies, one must consider that for it to progress and impel far and strongly, it is necessary: first, that it be broken, crushed, and extruded with great force; second, that it not be something meager and thin, but possess a larger quantity. For if the first is lacking, the flight is halted immediately, nor will it move even the nearest air vehemently at the very start. If the second is lacking, the "voice" <note>The sound-wave or impulse</note> will be suppressed by the surrounding air diffused far and wide, and it will be unable to either progress or push anything. To this is added the fact that even the greatest sounds have very little force in a "free medium," such as open fields, and that the force is easily dissolved and dissipated into the vast air that surrounds us; so much so that most Philosophers assert that not the true and real sound, but only its <term>species|In scholastic philosophy, the "sensible species" is the image or likeness of an object that travels to the senses, rather than the physical matter of the object itself</term> or image, reaches ears that are somewhat distant.

For if sound possessed this power, then in the besieging of cities, there would be no need for battering rams and catapults, but only the discordant noise of men, horses, drums, trumpets, and engines of war. As for what we said in the preceding part—that sound obtains great power over certain things by moving them, as when an organ makes a stone or a statue or something similar tremble with its sound—I would not want that to be understood as anything other than a harmonious agitation of the air. For it is possible for even a single smaller pipe to move a huge mass, which nonetheless ten pipes larger than said pipe could not move. We are not, therefore, speaking in that passage precisely about the violent agitation of the air, but about that by which we say sounds move another body proportioned to themselves, just as one string... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; Kircher is likely moving toward an explanation of sympathetic resonance.</note>

...we have said that one string moves another. As for the testimonies of the **Holy Fathers** <note>The early influential theologians of the Christian Church.</note> cited a little earlier, I say that none of the Holy Fathers believed that the walls of Jericho fell solely by the natural power of trumpets and shouting, but rather as a sign, upon which **GOD** Himself, or through the ministry of Angels, destroyed and laid waste to the City. It remains, therefore, that the ruin of the walls of Jericho was not caused by the natural sound of the trumpets, but was entirely miraculous. Thus, leaving these matters behind, let us proceed to describe other sounds.

## CHAPTER VIII.
### On the portentous sounds of the second class, that is, those which occur through a natural agent, but with a force greater than human power.

We speak here of certain portentous sounds which seem to possess a power that is neither entirely supernatural nor entirely natural, but are effected either by Angels, or by good or evil Spirits <note>original: *Genijs*; Kircher refers to "genii" or guiding spirits.</note> for good or for ill.

->**A Remarkable History of a certain Magician, who fascinated children with sound.**<-

In the year of Christ 460 <note>Most historical accounts of the Pied Piper date the event to 1284; Kircher uses an earlier, perhaps traditional or mistaken chronology.</note>, something marvelous beyond description happened in **Hameln**, a town of Lower Saxony situated on the **Weser**; the history is as follows: Since the inhabitants were infested that year by huge armies of mice and rats, and the evil grew to such an extent that almost nothing, whether fruit or grain, could be found that was not subject to the gnawing of the rats, various plans were being discussed to remove such an annoying and destructive plague. In the meantime, there suddenly appeared a certain man, never seen before and of prodigious stature; he promised that he would soon remove whatever mice were in that district, provided they would bargain with him for a certain sum of money. No sooner said than done; the reward having been promised, the said man drew a pipe from the pouch with which he was girded. As soon as he sounded it, behold! Great armies of mice, breaking out from every corner of the houses, the eaves of the roofs, and holes in the floors, followed that strange sound of the Piper right to the river. There, the Piper, with his garment tucked up, entered the river; 

<margin>Mice attracted by the sound of the pipe.</margin>

the rats followed him and were all extinguished there by a voluntary drowning. The man, having performed the incantation, demanded the agreed reward; but when the citizens hesitated over the promised sum, he rebuked them with threatening words, saying that unless they gave the reward, he would exact another much heavier than the one promised. The threats were received with laughter.

But on the following day around noon, the said man appeared again in the habit of a Hunter, with a terrible countenance and a purple hat of unusual design. As soon as he sounded another pipe, far different from the first, behold! All the children of the entire town, from four-year-olds to twelve-year-olds, went out and followed the prodigious sound. Now, there is outside the town on the bank of the Weser a certain cave in a mountain, large enough for the stabling of beasts; into this cave the hunter led all the children along with himself. And from that time, none of the children ever appeared again, nor was it ever known afterward what became of them or where they went. Because of this most wonderful event, the entire town, widowed of its children, is accustomed to calculate its years to this very day from "the departure of our children." I too have been in that same city; I saw the mountain itself, and I contemplated with the greatest wonder the history displayed in a detailed painting in the Church...

### CHAPTER XIV.
### On the prodigious sounds of Bells.

Among the other bells that have stunned the world with their miraculous sound, the first place surely belongs to the Bell of Velilla <note>Velilla de Ebro in Spain</note>, the continuous miracle of Spain. Concerning this, Varius writes in Book 2 of *On Enchantment*, chapter 14: "In the Kingdom of Spain, in a town called Velilla in the Diocese of Zaragoza <note>original: "Cæsaraugustanæ"</note>, there is a certain bell which they call 'The Miraculous One.' For several months before any adversity befalls the Christian Republic, this bell rings of its own accord with no one pushing it. I myself have read the testimony of this fact, documented by public notaries with many witnesses present, which the Viceroys of that Kingdom recorded in their letters." Our fellow Jesuit Juan de Mariana describes it in these words: "Thirty-six miles below the city of Zaragoza, the town of Velilla is situated on the banks of the Ebro, built upon the ancient Roman ruins of the colony of Ilergetis. It is famous for nothing in this age or in human memory more than its Bell. The people are convinced that its unusual and extraordinary ringing, without anyone moving it, signifies major events for better or worse <note>original: "nobilissimos in vtramque partem euentus"</note>. Whether they believe this foolishly or truly, I do not dispute; however, men of no small weight are cited as eyewitnesses to this miracle. They say the Bell rang of its own accord on the day before the Kings were captured <note>This likely refers to the capture of King Francis I of France at the Battle of Pavia in 1525.</note>. It rang again on the third day before the Kalends of November, and on the next Nones of January—ringing a third time when the treaty was settled in Milan and the King of Aragon was restored to liberty. Furthermore, before the death of Philip II, and several times in these most recent years, witnesses beyond all exception <margin>Various examples of the prodigious sound of bells.</margin> have heard it ring, according to the testimony of Nieremberg."

There is a similar Bell among the Japanese which rings spontaneously whenever great seditions and tumults threaten the kingdom. Juan Lupus, the Bishop of Monopoli, reports that a bell in the Dominican Monastery of Zamora <note>original: "Camorensi"</note> used to ring of its own accord three days before the death of any monk, even if no one was confined to their bed at the time. The same author reveals there was a similar small bell in the Monastery of St. Dominic in Córdoba, which portended the fate of either a brother of that monastery or some distinguished man of the same order by its own sound. Angelus Rocha reports similar things regarding the prodigious sound of another bell in the Dominican cloister of Salerno, which announced those about to die. Gibellinus, in his *Life of St. Menulphus*, reports that a bell in the Böddeken <note>original: "Bodkensi"</note> Monastery in Germany signaled the death of a nun in the same way by a spontaneous tolling.

There are also other musical instruments that sound of their own accord when the more serious dangers of a kingdom are imminent; thus, at the Tomb of St. James in Compostela, war instruments and noises declare future seditions. Some prefigure the victories of Catholics against infidels, such as the clashing of the bones of Fernán González <note>A legendary Count of Castile whose remains were said to rattle in their tomb before a Christian victory.</note>, regarding which see Nieremberg. I could bring forward innumerable examples of prodigious sounds in this place, but he who desires more of this kind should read the *Theater of Human Life* regarding prodigies, or Hegesippus and Josephus on the signs preceding the fall of Jerusalem, or Cornelius Gemma in his *Cosmocritics*, and others.

It remains to be investigated how that sound is produced. Certainly, it is not natural; therefore, it must happen beyond the course of nature. I say, therefore, that these prodigious sounds are caused by the help of Guardian Angels through the merits of some Saint—both for certain ends and reasons known to God alone, and as a warning of the imminent evils of a kingdom... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence: "preui-" likely leading to "preuisa" or "preuenienda," meaning "foreseen" or "to be prevented."</note>

### CHAPTER V.

#### On the hidden causes of certain sounds, such as the formidable sound of the Smellen cave in Finland.

Let us now look at that terrible cave in Finland, which Olaus Magnus beautifully describes in Book 11, Chapter 3 of his *History of the Northern Peoples*. This is located near the coastal city of Vyborg, <note>original: "Viburgium." Modern-day Vyborg, now in Russia near the Finnish border.</note> close to the Muscovite lands. It possesses such a secret power that if a living animal is cast into it, the sound excited within is so formidable in its vehemence that it almost suffocates the ears of those standing nearby, so that they can neither hear, nor speak, nor stand. Indeed, it strikes the ears with this power much more severely than a very powerful <term>bombard<gloss>An early type of heavy cannon used for sieges.</gloss></term>, or it weakens them in a moment so that they are hardly masters of themselves. But this work of nature does not seem to be useless; for when a hostile attack is imminent, the governor of the land orders everyone's ears to be plugged with wax, and those who are to survive to be hidden in cellars and caves. Finally, fortifying himself, he plunges some animal, suspended by either a rope or a spear, into the mouth of the cave. From this, such a horrific sound is immediately stirred up that the enemies besieging the area fall down like cattle to be slaughtered, and having fallen, they remain there for a long time to be despoiled. When they return to their senses, they no longer plan to fight, but to provide for the flight of their lives. Thus it happens that those who cannot be restrained by arms or strength from their warlike fury are overcome, wasting away by the mere horror of bellowing nature. He further asserts that this cavern is surrounded by several walls to ward off the dangers of those who might approach it rashly. According to the same witness, the Russians <note>original: "Rutheni."</note> left behind to their posterity miserable examples of having experienced this calamity, having lost many thousands of their men. Pliny tells of a similar cave in Dalmatia with a vast, precipitous opening, into which if any light weight is thrown on a calm day, a storm similar to a whirlwind bursts out. Peter Martyr tells of a similar cave in Hispaniola, an island of America, of such horrendous sound and followed by such an atrocious storm that no one dares to approach within five miles of it with impunity—that is, without danger to life or the risk of deafness.

-><margin>The wonderful power of the sound of a cave in Finland.</margin><-

The cause of such a prodigious sound, if the things Olaus reports are true, is none other than the natural internal constitution of the mountain. This multiplies the sound through an infinite reflection of the voice and stirs the air; and since the agitated air can have no other exit except through the hole and orifice of the cavity, it is no wonder that, being constricted and squeezed there, it excites such a formidable sound along with the vehemence of a storm. I hear that something similar is found in the Swiss mountains, especially on the mountain they call "The Cucumber" <note>original: "Cucumerem." Likely referring to a peak shaped like a gourd or cucumber, possibly the Gurten or a similar formation.</note> because of its shape. At its summit, a deep abyss is seen; if even a single stone is thrown through its orifice into the interior of the mountain, it excites such vehement sounds that it not only strikes fear into those standing by, but also forces them to flee by the vehemence of the exiting wind. For there is a wonderful power in enclosed mountains for multiplying sound, which experience also teaches us in very deep wells. In my own homeland, in Fulda, there is a certain well on the Mountain of the Blessed Virgin <note>The Frauenberg in Fulda, Germany.</note> having a depth of almost 300 <term>palms<gloss>A unit of length based on the width of a human hand; 300 palms is roughly 70-75 meters.</gloss></term>, in which a stone thrown in excites such a sound that it could seem like the explosion of a piece of artillery. I remember observing the same thing on a certain mountain of the Lipari Islands; consequently, I do not think Olaus’s cave is entirely fabulous, since prodigies of sounds of this kind occur everywhere to those traveling the world. However, since we have reserved these miracles of mountains for our *Subterranean World* <note>original: "Subterraneo Mundo." A reference to Kircher's other famous work on geology and the earth's interior.</note>, we refer the curious reader there.

### CHAPTER VI.
### Concerning the prodigious sound of certain shores of the Bothnian Sea.

While Olaus Magnus <note>original: "Olaus magnus"; a 16th-century Swedish archbishop and cartographer famous for his "History of the Northern Peoples."</note> discusses the towering mountains of the Bothnian Sea <note>The Gulf of Bothnia, the northernmost arm of the Baltic Sea, between Sweden and Finland.</note>, he also makes mention of the **prodigious sound** of the coastal caverns. He states that no one can approach the bases of these mountains due to the sheer violence of the noise; indeed, those nearby experience such horror from the deep collision of the waves that, unless they escape by swift rowing or a strong wind, they are rendered nearly lifeless by fear alone. 

The bases of these aforementioned mountains possess certain winding fissures and internal chambers where the waves rush in and out—structures crafted by the **astonishing workmanship of nature**. Within these, through a long, swirling abyss, that formidable sound generates a noise resembling a subterranean roar. Whenever some have attempted to investigate the cause of this phenomenon too imprudently, their vessels were instantly swamped with water, and they lost their lives in the midst of their wonder. # COROLLARY

<margin>Miracles of nature in an acoustic mirror, or auditorium.</margin>

From this, it is clear that a huge rock hollowed out in a parabolic shape <note>A curve that reflects light or sound to a single focal point.</note> can return a whispered voice at a distance of 50 paces, such as Father João Paes describes in his *History of the Abyssinians* <note>Portuguese Jesuit missionary to Ethiopia (Abyssinia).</note> as being found in the mountains of Gojjam. In these mountains, there is a huge rock hollowed out by the industry of nature so that it appears like a mirror to those looking from a distance. To this rock, he says, another rock is opposed, on whose summit nothing can be said so softly, even from a great distance, that it is not heard. Indeed, for those shouting in said place, the sound is so intensified that it seems like the voice of some army. The local priests <note>original: "sacrificuli," literally "petty sacrificers," often used by Kircher to describe non-Christian clergy.</note> know the hidden power of this resonating nature; to prove themselves divine, they warn men placed on the mountain peak of future events with hidden voices of this kind. Those men, thinking themselves inspired by the voice of a Deity, not infrequently fall into the greatest calamities while they hasten too thoughtlessly to execute the commands. If these things are true, I would believe it happens by no other means than through a <term>sound-capturing</term> <note>original Greek: φωνοκαπτικὸν (phonokaptikon)</note> object endowed by nature with a parabolic figure, by which the species of sound flow together into a single point of the rock situated directly opposite. From this, many accounts reported by historians—which were commonly held by most to be fables and superstitions—are explained. Herberstein narrates in his *Russian History* <note>Sigmismund von Herberstein’s "Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentarii" (1549).</note> that in the province of Candora, the northernmost land, there is a river which no one has yet crossed

<margin>Herberstein in the Russian History.</margin>

because of the frequent ghosts that appear there, and the voices of men and animals that are commonly heard on the opposite bank. He also says that hardly a day or a week passes, especially in summer, in which such prodigious voices are not heard. I certainly judge these portents to be nothing other than the real voices of men and animals arising in the nearer fields of the river, reflected from the hollow "mirrors" of the rocks across the water. These strike the simple and inexperienced men standing on the banks with vain dread and a kind of panic fear, since nothing can more easily deceive men than this playful talkativeness of nature.

<margin>An extraordinary case.</margin>

Cardano, in the 18th book of *On Subtlety* <note>Girolamo Cardano, a famous 16th-century polymath.</note>, tells of a similar deception involving a friend of his. A certain friend of ours, he says, when he was traveling near a river and did not know the ford, began to shout, "Oh?" to which a hidden Echo responded, "Oh?" Thinking it was a man, he asked in Italian: "Where must I cross?" <note>original Italian: "Onde deuo passar?"</note> "Cross," <note>original Italian: "passa"</note> it is replied. Then he asks, "Here?" <note>original Italian: "qui?"</note> "Here," <note>original Italian: "qui"</note> is the reply. But in that spot, the waters were rushing with a deep whirlpool; wherefore, being terrified, he asked again, "Must I cross here?" <note>original Latin/Italian: "Deuo passar qui?"</note> Echo responds, "Cross here!" <note>original Italian: "passa qui!"</note> To him asking the same thing many times, it responded the same. Therefore, since the friend was caught between fear and the necessity of swimming, and a dark and unseasonable night was pressing in, he thought some Demon wanted to persuade him to throw himself into that torrent. Returning from there, he told the whole matter to Cardano, who demonstrated by the facts themselves that it was not the snares of a Demon, nor the illusion of a phantom, but a joke of playing nature. You may perceive a similar portent of nature in Syracuse, in the ruins of the Palace of Dionysius <note>The "Ear of Dionysius," a famous limestone cave in Sicily known for its acoustic properties.</note>, where in a certain receptacle, nature reflects sounds so perfectly that I cannot remember hearing anything more wonderful in similar material. Many things would have to be said in this place about the prodigious reflection of voice and sounds, but since we have reserved all these for the following treatise, here putting an end to "Wonder-Gathering," <note>original: "Teratologiae," the study of marvels or monsters.</note> we proceed to "Echo-Wisdom." <note>original: "Echosophiam."</note>

## PART IV.
## PHONOCAMPTIC MAGIC

### PREFACE.

[Ornamental initial E]CHO is a joke of playful nature, called by the Poets the *image of the voice*, following that line from Virgil: *The rocks resound, and the struck image leaps back in various ways.* <note>original Latin: "Saxa sonant, variisque offensa resultat imago." This quote is from Virgil’s *Georgics* (Book 4, line 50), describing the acoustic properties of a landscape.</note> By Philosophers it is called the reflected, repercussed, or reciprocal voice; by the Hebrews it is called the <term>daughter of the voice</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Bat kol." In Jewish tradition, this term usually refers to a divine voice or a heavenly resonance, but Kircher applies it here to the physical phenomenon of an echo being the "offspring" of the original sound.</note>. <margin>What is an echo?</margin> Its nature is so hidden that, up to this day, there has scarcely been anyone who has explained its latent essence.

It is indeed well-known, and almost common knowledge, that it is a reflected voice; but how, from what sources, by what propagation, at what speed, and at what distance it is produced, is as unknown as anything can be. Nor does it seem that the vastness of the difficulties that arise can be exhausted by any reasoning, except by one who, equipped with the greatest experience and singular industry, has finally captured this fugitive Nymph <note>A reference to the mythological nymph Echo, who was cursed to only repeat the words of others and eventually wasted away until only her voice remained.</note>, eluded by wonderful arts. Since no one has accomplished this until now, I, driven by a desire for her...

->DEFINITIONS<-

1 **M**agic, or the <term>Phonocamptic Art</term> <note>From the Greek words *phōnē* (sound) and *kamptos* (bent/curved). Kircher uses "Magic" here in the sense of "Natural Magic"—the study of wonderful natural phenomena through scientific principles.</note> is a more hidden science of sounds, by which—through the power of reflected and multiplied voices—we produce effects that are prodigious and, to those ignorant of the causes, miraculous.
2 <term>Phonokampsis</term> <note>original Greek: Φωνόκαμψις</note> is nothing other than the reflection of the voice, which the Greeks and others thereafter call an Echo.

# Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic. 239

9. A **phonic triangle** is the name given to any triangle formed by a straight-sound line and an oblique-sound line, together with the distance of the center of reflection from the normal point, such as ABC or ABE.
10. The **line of action** is the entire length of the sound line within which it is perceptible.

18. **Acoustic Organs** are instruments which, when applied to the ears, have the power of multiplying a great voice. <note>These are early versions of ear trumpets or hearing aids.</note>

### Axioms and Hypotheses

1. **Every phonoptotic angle is equal to the phonocamptic angle**; or, what is the same thing, every angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
2. Every phonic or sound center radiates in straight lines in a circle.
3. Nature, in the case of sound, only achieves its end through the shortest lines.
4. All that, and only that, can be heard which the sound line can reach.
5. Sound is intensely strengthened by multiple reflections radiating to a single point.
6. Every reflection of sound occurs either back upon itself or in the opposite direction.
7. The voice reaches the ears more slowly as the reflecting object is more remote, and more quickly as it is nearer.
8. Sound is measured by the line of sound activity.

### Postulates and Given Data

1. **Given any point on a reflecting object** where reflection occurs, to determine the reflected line.
2. From any point of the object, a reflection can be established to any other point.

**Book IX. The Magic of Harmony and Discord. 241**

<margin>No quality is sensible by itself.</margin> 
...by employing an opaque reflecting body; or rather, to speak more precisely, I say that no <term>accident: in traditional philosophy, a "quality" or "accident" is a property (like color or sound) that cannot exist on its own but must belong to a physical substance</term> is sensible by itself, except through the bodies by which it is sustained, or through the quantity which gives them extension—without which it would vanish into a point and become nothing. Therefore, just as light is invisible without air, so too is sound; while sound makes the air sensible to us, it reveals many qualities of bodies that we would not know how to recognize without the help of sounds. And if anyone looks a little more deeply into the nature of light, they will find it to be nothing other than a certain movement of the air, as it were, which carries with it the image of the "prime mover"—namely, the luminous body—to present it to the eyes under the name and appearance of color or light. In the same way, sound is nothing other than the movement of that same air, which carries with it the different qualities of its cause, namely the bodies moving it. Thus, it presents us with an image under the name and appearance of sound. For the sensible form—for example, of a certain ringing bell—presents itself to the eyes of a deaf person in much the same way as it reaches the ears of a blind person. Furthermore, just as light cannot be preserved without the actual influence of the body from which it flows, neither can sound exist without the motion of the air.

<margin>Light reaches the eyes in the same way sound reaches the ears.</margin>
Therefore, we must laugh at those who think that sound, once enclosed in a pipe, can be preserved for a long time (as will be discussed more extensively in our *Echotectonica* <note>original: "Magia nostra Echotectonica," referring to Kircher's work on the science of echoes and acoustics</note>). Indeed, experience teaches us that we are better and more pleasurably affected when we read a history or a vivid description of something—or hear it sketched out by a distinguished orator with various figures of words and thoughts, like colors—than if we were to look at the same things with our own eyes.

Moreover, just as the <term>species: the "images" or "likenesses" that objects were thought to emit so that they could be perceived by the senses</term> of visible things affect the eye and the optic nerve in a hidden way to produce a similar image by the help of the spirits; so too the image of a sounding body, carried by the air, affects the "implanted air" in the acoustic or auricular nerve to represent the image of the sounding body. From these things, unless I am mistaken, the immense similarity between optical and acoustic bodies is clearly shown in how they act and produce both sight and hearing in humans.

<margin>Refraction and reflection of sound.</margin>
Finally, just as sight is refracted in a denser medium, so too is sound; as will be shown extensively later. For what else is sound when received in a very porous and soft body, if not a kind of "shadow" of sound, placing an obstacle in the way so that it cannot stretch further?

**Corollary.**

<margin>How much lower a sound is under water than the same sound outside of water.</margin>
**H**ence follows a certain method of determining how much deeper <note>original: "gravior," meaning lower in pitch or "heavier"</note> a sound made inside water is compared to the sound of the same body made outside water, and consequently, how much thinner <note>original: "rarior," referring to density</note> air is than water. For it was discovered not long ago by a distinguished mathematician's experiment that the sound of a certain bell, which was (for example) at two degrees outside the water, was at five degrees inside the water. Consequently, it was deeper by one minor harmonic tenth. The cause of this thing is nothing other than the rarity and density of the different media. For water resists the "image" of the sounding body more inside the water than outside; from this resistance arises a slowness of the medium's motion, and a deeper sound follows this slowness. For just as one medium relates to another medium, so do the vibrations made in one medium relate to the vibrations made in the other; and as vibrations relate to vibrations, so sound relates to sound. If, therefore, as in the proposed example, the ratio is 5 to 2, the motion of the air and the motion of water will hold the same proportion. From this, the rarity of air compared to the density of water will be as 125 to 8.

<margin>A sound-event is similar to a light-event.</margin>
You see, therefore, that <term>phonisms: Kircher’s term for sound phenomena</term> are entirely parallel in their operations to <term>photisms: Kircher’s term for light phenomena</term>, except for the motion, which is instantaneous in the diffusion of light but successive (taking time) in sound. Sound also is not only able to propagate along straight lines, but also along curves, as is evident when it passes through channels and tubes, or through similar sound-conduits. In these, it is not only carried conveniently, but is also greatly increased and strengthened; indeed, it propagates further than in the open air, as will be proven later by various experiments.

# PRELUDE II.
## Concerning the <term>Phonocamptic</term> Object.
<note>Kircher uses "phonocamptic" (from the Greek *phōnē* for sound and *kamptikos* for bending) to describe any object that reflects sound, much like a mirror reflects light.</note>

<margin>The hidden power of the Echo.</margin>
A **phonocamptic object** is not limited to walls, cliffs, ramparts, and similar hard and solid bodies. Even the earth, trees, leaves, wood, simple soil (no matter how porous), and especially water and any suitable liquids will be capable of reflecting voices and sounds. This fact has perplexed me on more than one occasion. Many times, while in the middle of the fields located between Rome and Tusculum <note>The modern area of Frascati.</note>, where there were no walls or trees—only brushwood, inhospitable rocks, and the furrows of the fields—I was able to perceive an Echo, much to my wonder. Indeed, a very small thing can often cause a marvelous effect. I became certain that the brushwood and the furrows of said fields caused the Echo because, passing through the same place at another time after the furrows had been overturned and the brushwood cut down, the Echo could no longer be heard. Many Echoes of great fame in former times have also vanished in our day, either because walls were demolished or because the reflecting objects were changed or altered. Certainly, Boissard reports in his *Topography of Rome* that there was once an Echo of the greatest celebrity at the Tomb of Caecilia Metella (which is today called *Capo di Bove*, situated near the Praetorian camp); however, though I sought it out with singular care, I could not find it. I have included Boissard’s words here so that the reader may judge what to think of his account. In his *Topography of the City*, he speaks as follows:

*The Tomb of the Metelli, he says, is round in shape, constructed of squared white marble like a very large tower, hollow inside and open at the top. Its walls are about 24 feet thick. it lies near the corner of the walls, and around its circumference are carved marble ox-heads stripped of skin and flesh, as was customary in sacrifices. These are held by ribbons and cloth wrappings which join together clusters of fruit, flowers, and leaves—commonly called "festoons"—and in the spaces between are placed sacrificial bowls. There are nearly two hundred ox-heads, which is why it is called "Capo di Bove" (Head of the Ox). Antiquarians claim that a double hecatomb <note>A sacrifice of 100 oxen.</note> was performed at the famous funeral of Caecilia Metella, whose name is read on the front of the tomb on a huge marble tablet facing the gate of the Praetorian citadel: "To Caecilia, daughter of Quintus Metellus Creticus, [wife] of Metellus Crassus." At the base of the hill on which the tower is built, if anyone pronounces a full heroic verse, a wonderful Echo will return the same verse, articulated several times. I myself clearly detected that first line of Virgil’s Aeneid—"I sing of arms and the man"—hearing it eight times in full, and several times more confusedly thereafter. Nowhere else in the world is such an Echo heard. It is said to have been constructed with such great skill so that during the funeral of this Caecilia, the wailing, cries, and funeral laments of the mourners would be multiplied immensely while that double hecatomb was celebrated and funeral games were held in honor of the Matron. Thus says Boissard.*

I was truly kindled with a desire for this curiosity, and I sought this prodigious Echo two or three times with the greatest care, but in vain. I was never able to find it, nor was any other curious person here in Rome. Certainly, anyone who has closely examined our following "phonic exercises" will easily see that the layout of this place is not at all capable of such an Echo. Therefore, I do not know how the Author could have pronounced these things so boldly. Was the condition of the site perhaps changed? Or was a nearby building that stood in the way demolished? Certainly, I found these things to be written with great zeal <note>Kircher is politely suggesting Boissard may have exaggerated.</note>, and so we leave this to be more fully investigated by others who are more curious. For my part, as I said, I explored all the walls round about several times, but I confess I could find nothing such as the aforementioned Boissard describes.

<margin>Why Echo does not occur in straight-built wells. Echo in the Vatican Palace.</margin>
Furthermore, experience teaches that water can be a reflecting object, since almost all wells produce a very distinct Echo. This is evidenced by the well in the courtyard of the Vatican Palace, which returns the voices of men—even the lowest whispers—so distinctly that you would swear people were hiding inside. And indeed, it returns everything more perfectly the more it is exposed to the open air; for if the well is covered with a roof or a cloth, it performs not at all. The cause of this thing is not...

Thirdly, all other rough and soft objects do reflect, but more weakly and out of order, as seen on the grassy slopes of mountains, or in forests enjoying a great crowding of massive trees. But we will pursue all these things more extensively in the following sections.

->**PRELUDE III.**<-
->**On the Phonocamptic medium, or the line of action.**<-

[Marginal note: The double phonocamptic medium: physical and mathematical.] In this place, the medium must be considered in two ways: Physical and Mathematical. The Physical medium is that aerial space through which the voice is propagated, and it is of diverse quality and constitution. The Mathematical medium is the magnitude or smallness of the interval measuring the duration of the propagated voice. We will treat both briefly in this prelude, starting from the Mathematical medium.

->**§. I.**<-
->**On the line of Phonic action.**<-

[Marginal note: What the line of action is and its types.] We call the "line of action" or "phonic line" 그 that which terminates the action of radial or phonic diffusion. It is twofold: simple and mixed. The simple or direct line of action is that which terminates the propagation of the voice and is called the semi-diameter of the sphere of phonic activity. The mixed line is that which is composed of the incident and reflected lines, which we therefore call the "direct-reflected" line. Although Blancanus <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit mathematician and contemporary of Kircher.</note> establishes this as equal to the direct or simple line, [Marginal note: In strict rigor, the direct line is greater than the reflected line.] in strict rigor it must necessarily be smaller. For it is certain that a voice striking a wall—as if broken there and having suffered some loss of vigor—returns more weakly than the direct voice, which is known to be propagated with "uniformly-difform" <note>A Scholastic physics term meaning the rate of change (loss of volume/energy) is constant over distance.</note> vigor when hindered by no obstacle, as we have demonstrated extensively in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>Original: "Arte Lucis & Umbrae," Kircher's 1646 work on optics and perspective.</note>. However, how much smaller this mixed line of action is than the simple one can be determined only with difficulty; certainly, I judge the difference to be so tiny that it can be called a matter of reason rather than sense. Therefore, without scruple, it can be physically established as equal to the direct line; and thus we have accepted it both here and in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*, page 576. Since the voice is somewhat increased by the repercussion in the nearby medium, it easily restores what was lost by the impact.

This line can be considered according to three cases. The first is: [Marginal note: The first case.] either the reflected line is equal to the incident line, and then the phonocamptic obstacle will necessarily occupy the middle of the line of action. For example, if the line of action in the first case is A-C and the reflecting obstacle is at B, the middle point of the line, the radius A-B reflected from B to V will be as great as A-B or B-C, which is half of the whole phonic action line A-C.

Since, therefore, I find the business of determining a certain measure to be difficult, and moreover that the experiments of various authors differ greatly, I did not wish to be idle in this matter. Indeed, bringing the experiences of others back to the anvil <note>A metaphor for refining or re-testing theories</note> for re-examination, I began all kinds of experiments starting with a single-syllable echo. Using my voice, a trumpet, and a handgun, I tested the whole matter and found that a single-syllable echo admits no change at all within a space of 20 feet. I found, therefore, that the distance for a single-syllable echo is about 110 feet, <margin>A single-syllable echo requires a space of 110 Roman feet.</margin> which had, as I said, a breadth of 20 feet, within which space it always repeated the same syllable. A trumpet, however, gave back the first sound distinctly within a space of 90 and 110 feet. But a handgun within this space was somewhat confused with the first sound. Within 400 and 900 feet, it returned a seven-syllable phrase—for example, *I sing of arms and the man* <note>original: "Arma virumque cano," the famous opening of Virgil's Aeneid</note>—perfectly and distinctly within the time in which one could very quickly recite the *Hail Mary* <note>original: "Ave Maria"</note> up to the words *blessed art thou* <note>original: "Benedicta tu"</note> inclusive. I also used the vibrations of a chronometer, but always with little success. <margin>Various experiments undertaken.</margin> Then, at different times—morning, noon, evening, and night—I took care to have experiments performed, either by myself or by others who were first very well and carefully instructed. We always found a different speed of sound and a different quantity of intervals. In the silence of the dead of night, <margin>At night and in the evening sound is returned best of all; in the morning and at noon worst.</margin> the Echo seemed to exercise its dominion best for the reasons said shortly before. We found it weakest in the morning due to the dewy and foggy state of the air; at noon it shaped itself better, since the air was thinner; and better still in the evening due to the perfect "cooking" <note>term: decoctionem; a contemporary belief that the sun's heat "processed" or purified the air throughout the day, making it a better medium for sound</note> of the air.

Furthermore, I observed the weather with the greatest zeal and diligence. <margin>Changing weather changes the echo.</margin> In rainy or snowy weather, the Echo is dulled in a wonderful way, so that it seems to have hardly any power. After heavy rains, as the air has been purified, it acquires a great deal of strength. Here in Rome, it is marvelous to say that when the North wind <note>original: Borea</note> blows, it acquires maximum vigor; with the South wind <note>original: Austro</note> it grows weak; with the East wind <note>original: Euro</note> and the Southeast wind <note>original: subsolano</note> it behaves passably. When a wall is exposed to the North wind while that wind is blowing, it is marvelous to tell: the direct voice is notably slower than the reflected voice. <margin>The Echo Paradox.</margin> But at the same time, when hitting a southern surface, the direct voice is faster than the reflected one. For in the first experiment, the direct voice, being contrary to the wind, is carried through the medium with more difficulty than the reflected voice; the reflected voice, however, carried by a favorable wind, returns more quickly to the ears, so that what it first lost through the resistance of the medium, it now recovers through speed. The same must be said of the other quarters of the sky, so that from this it appears that there is a great diversity in the speed of sound carried through a medium.

### **Corollary I.**

From this infinite diversity and variation of media, it is clearly evident that every <margin>The difficult determination of echo distance.</margin> determination of the distance of an echo is doubtful, fallacious, and entirely uncertain. Nor is it ever consistent with itself—whatever Biancani <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician</note> and Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a polymath often called the "father of acoustics"</note> may say—unless it is constrained by "catoptric" <note>term: Catoptrica; the study of reflection, usually of light, here applied to sound</note> industry and subjected to geometric laws through acoustic instruments (which will be treated later). Therefore, whatever is said hereafter must be taken only hypothetically.

## CHAPTER I.

### THE CANONS AND RULES OF THE <term>PHONOCAMPTIC<gloss>From the Greek words for "sound" and "bent"; this refers to the science of reflected sound or echoes.</gloss></term> ART OR <term>ECHOMETRY<gloss>The measurement of echoes.</gloss></term>

-> Echocamptic Lemma <-
<note>A "lemma" is a preliminary geometric proposition used to prove a later theorem. This one establishes why sound and light reflect at specific angles.</note>

**S** If two points are placed away from a straight line (which serves as the intersection where two planes meet), and two lines are drawn from those points to a single point on that line such that they make two equal angles with it: then these two lines together will be shorter than any other pair of lines drawn from those same two points to any other spot on that same straight line.

From two points **A** and **B**, let two straight lines **AC** and **BC** be drawn to point **C** on the straight line **CD**, such that the plane passing through **CD** also passes through **A** and **B**. Let these lines form equal angles, **ACF** and **BCD**. Now, from those same points **A** and **B**, let us first draw two other lines, **AD** and **BD**, to another point **D** located to the right of **C**. I maintain that **AC** and **BC** together are shorter than **AD** and **BD**. If we extend line **AC** past point **C** to a point **E**, making **CE** equal to **CB**, and then join **D** and **E** with a line: because angle **ACF** is assumed to be equal to angle **BCD**, and because angle **ACF** is equal to the opposite vertical angle **ECD**, then angle **BCD** must also be equal to angle **ECD**. Since the two sides **BC** and **CD** are equal to the two sides **EC** and **CD**, the base **DB** will be equal to the base **DE**. Consequently, **AD** and **DB** together are equal to **AD** and **DE** together. However, **AD** and **DE** (two sides of a triangle) are greater than the straight line **AE**—which is to say, they are greater than **AC** and **CB** combined (since **CB** and **CE** were made equal). Therefore, **AD** and **BD** must be greater than **AC** and **BC**, which is what we intended to prove.

Next, let two other lines **AF** and **BF** be drawn from points **A** and **B** to another point **F** to the left of **C**. I maintain again that **AC** and **BC** are shorter than **AF** and **BF**. By extending **AC** again and setting **CE** equal to **CB**, we join **E** and **F**. Since the angles **ACF** and **BCD** are set as equal, and **ACF** is equal to the opposite vertical angle **ECD**, then **BCD** and **ECD** are also equal. From this, the remaining angles from the straight line, **BCF** and **ECF**, will also be equal. Since the two sides **BC** and **CF** are equal to the two sides **EC** and **CF**, the base **BF** will be equal to the base **EF**. Consequently, **AF** and **FE** together will be equal to **AF** and **BF**. But **AF** and **FE** are greater than the straight line **AE**—that is, greater than **AC** and **BC**, because **BC** and **CE** were set as equal. Therefore, **AF** and **BF** are greater than **AC** and **CB**, which is what we intended to prove.

<note>The diagram shows points A and B above a horizontal line. Point C sits on the line where lines from A and B meet at equal angles. Points F (left) and D (right) show longer paths. Point E is a mirror-projection below the line used to prove the distances geometrically.</note>

Because Nature, when unimpeded, acts through the shortest paths <note>original: "Quia ergò Natura non impedita agit per lineas breuiſſimas"</note>, it follows that a ray of the Sun or a line of sight falling from **A** onto a surface toward **DF**, so that it is reflected to point **B**, must necessarily fall on point **C**. At this point, the angle **ACF** (which scholars of perspective call the **angle of incidence**) is made equal to the angle **BCD** (which they call the **angle of reflection**). For if the ray fell on **D** or **F** and reflected to **B**, Nature would not be acting through the shortest lines, since both **AD/BD** and **AF/BF** are longer than **AC/BC**, as we have demonstrated. Such a thing would be absurd. And so it is proven, as the experts in perspective assume, that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

->Proposition I.<-

**Every <term>phonoptotic angle<note>From the Greek *phone* (sound) and *ptosis* (falling); this refers to the "angle of incidence," or the angle at which sound hits a surface.</note></term> is equal to the <term>phonocamptic angle<note>From the Greek *phone* (sound) and *kamptos* (bent); this refers to the "angle of reflection," or the angle at which sound bounces off a surface.</note></term>, or what is the same, the angle of a sound’s incidence is equal to the angle of its reflection.**

Whatever we have shown regarding the reflection of light in the *Art of Reflective Light and Shadow* <note>Kircher is referring to his 1646 book, *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*, where he established the rules of optics.</note> can be recalled here. ## Proposition II.

**Whenever the voice strikes an orthophonic object—that is, one that is perpendicular—it will be reflected back upon itself.**
<note>An "orthophonic" object is a surface positioned exactly upright relative to the sound source.</note>

Let the phonic center, or the origin of the voice, be at **A** (see the preceding figure). Let the **orthophonic** <note>original: *orthophonon*; straight-sounding</note> object be **CD**. Let the voice flow from **A** to **B** **orthogonally** <note>original: *orthogōnōs*; at a right angle</note>, or at right angles. I say that it will be reverberated from **B** back to **A**. 

I demonstrate the matter thus: if, by way of impossibility, it were not reflected from **B** back to **A**, let it then be reflected toward **V**. Therefore, by the fourth hypothesis, the angle of incidence **DBA** would be equal to the angle of reflection **CBV**—specifically, an acute angle would equal an obtuse angle, which is absurd. However, we have supposed that the voice is carried from **A** into the wall normally <note>at a 90-degree "normal" angle</note>, and consequently establishes a right angle of incidence, **ABD**. Therefore, the angle of reflection must also necessarily be a right angle, according to the cited fourth hypothesis. Thus, it reflects back upon itself along the line **BA**, through which it moved from **A** to **B**, which was to be demonstrated. Both the nature of light itself striking normally, and a ball when it is dashed normally against a wall and bounced back toward itself, and countless other examples—concerning which see our *Anacamptic Art of Light* <note>A reference to the author's work on optics and the reflection of light</note>—teach the truth of this proposition.

## Proposition III.

**Whenever the voice strikes a loxophonic object—that is, obliquely—the voice will not be reflected back upon itself, but toward the opposite side.**
<note>A "loxophonic" object is a surface hit by sound at a slanted or "oblique" angle.</note>

There can be four cases for this proposition. Either the voice strikes a vertically erected wall obliquely, in which case it reflects either to the right or the left depending on the position of the sound source; or the voice, emitted from below, strikes a higher phonocamptic object obliquely and thus reflects upward; or if the voice is emitted from above and strikes a lower wall obliquely, it will then be reflected downward. We shall demonstrate each case separately.

Therefore, let there be a wall at **DE** (see the figure for Proposition I). Let the phonic center be at **C**, or the voice striking **loxophonically** <note>original: *loxophōnōs*; obliquely or at a slant</note> at **B**. I say that the voice will be reflected from **B** to the opposite side, namely to **A**, under an equality of angles. For if it is not reflected to **A**, it must reflect either back to itself (that is, to **C**), or to **I**, or to any other place outside of **AB**. But it does not reflect back to itself, since according to the preceding proposition, only a perpendicular line reflects back to itself; and the line **CB**, by our supposition, is **loxophonic**, which is to say it strikes the wall obliquely. It does not reflect to **I**, because the angle **IBD** would then be equal to the angle **CBE**—the part would be equal to the whole, which is absurd. Therefore, it will reflect to no other part but **A**, for in this way the angle of incidence **EBC** and the angle of reflection **ABD** are made equal, and nature reaches its end via the shortest possible lines.

Whenever, therefore, a sound line strikes a wall **obliquely**, it will necessarily fall on the opposite side under an equality of angles, which was to be demonstrated. From this it is clear that a sound source placed at **A** will reflect the sound to the left at **C**, and a source at **C** will reflect to the right at **A**.

Furthermore, if the voice is located at **A**, and the phonocamptic object is a tower **BC** positioned on a mountain: I say the voice will be reverberated from **A** to **B**, and from there to **V**. The reasoning is exactly the same as in the preceding cases; for since it strikes **B** obliquely, the voice will necessarily be reverberated toward **V** under an equality of angles. The same would happen if the voice of the tones were located—

# RULES OF SOUND REFLECTION
