### RULE I.

[Decorative initial C] Since the <term>phonocamptic art</term> <note>The study of reflected sound, from the Greek "phone" (sound) and "kamptos" (bent/reflected).</note> follows the laws of <term>photocamptics</term> <note>The study of reflected light; optics.</note> (or the reflection of light) in all things, it preserves not only the principal differences of position—which are upward, downward, to the left, and to the right—but also any intermediate parts according to the position of the reflecting object. If the "echo-surface" or "sound-surface" is perpendicular to the reflecting object and simultaneously parallel to the horizon, the Echo will be produced either <term>orthophonically</term> <note>Directly or "straight-sounding."</note> or <term>loxophonically</term> <note>Obliquely or "slant-sounding."</note>, depending on the different position of the speaker to the right or left.
   But if the sounding surface falls obliquely upward or downward upon some <term>azimuthal surface</term> <note>A vertical surface oriented toward a specific compass direction.</note> of the reflecting object, reflections will be produced that are <term>anophonic</term> <note>Upward-sounding.</note> or <term>catophonic</term> <note>Downward-sounding.</note>; that is, Echoes reverberating upward and downward.
   Finally, if the sounding surface falls upon some sound-reflecting plane that is parallel neither to the vertical nor the horizontal circle, but is inclined obliquely and laterally, then the reflections produced will be lateral and oblique, intermediate between the horizon and the zenith; just as we have demonstrated in the <term>anacamptic art</term> <note>The general science of reflections (catoptrics).</note> of light.

### RULE II.

[Decorative initial Q] Whenever, therefore, the reflecting object is simultaneously parallel and perpendicular to the sound source, then the surface of reflection will be straight to the horizon. But if it is "parallel-oblique"—that is, the reflecting object is equidistant from the sound source but not perpendicular, such as walls that are slanted yet straight, or towers on mountains viewed from a sound source positioned in a valley—then the surface of reflection will be equidistant to one of the azimuthal planes, or, what is the same thing, it will align with one of the vertical planes. But if the reflecting object is neither parallel nor perpendicular to the sound source, then the sound-reflecting surface (or surface of reflection) will be equidistant to one of the inclining or inclined planes.

### RULE III.

[Decorative initial Q] Whenever the sound source A is in a horizontal plane, and the reflecting object C is in the same horizontal plane, a reflection upward to V will necessarily follow. If the object is simultaneously inclining and inclined, it will reflect not upward, but by a middle path according to the ratio of the inclination and declination. Thus, the entire doctrine of <term>sciateric planes</term> <note>The geometry used in sundial making to track shadows.</note>, which we have handed down in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*, <note>Refers to Kircher's 1646 work "Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae".</note> can be beautifully applied to this Echo-measurement.

### Proposition IV.

**Whenever two walls are joined at right angles, a very clear Echo is perceived from a sound-source at such a distance that the axis of the phonic cone bisects the right angle.** For the cone, being reflected there in various ways, wonderfully strengthens the reflected voice, as is evident in the figure.

Let there be two walls **AB** and **DB** joined perpendicularly at **B**, and let the <term>phonic cone</term><note>A conceptual cone representing the path and spread of sound waves from a source.</note> be **EFBO**, with its axis **EB** bisecting the right angle. Because the sound reflecting from **E** at point **F** is then reflected at equal angles to **O**, and from there back again to **E**; conversely, a ray from **E** falling on **O** is reflected from here to **F**, and from there again by a contrary motion reflects back to **E**, it wonderfully strengthens the sound. 

[Geometric diagram showing two perpendicular lines AB and DB meeting at point B. A cone-shaped area EFBO is drawn with its axis EB bisecting the right angle. Rays are shown reflecting between points E, F, and O.]

It is no wonder that an Echo is produced much more resonantly than against a simple wall, as the air is agitated by various reflections. Furthermore, all the lines included between **EO** and **EF** reflect near **E**, and consequently return a more intense Echo for this reason. If, however, the axis of the phonic cone is positioned on the outer side of the walls so that it makes <term>obtuse angles</term><note>Angles greater than 90 degrees.</note> with said walls, then the Echo produced is most ineffective and of no value—as would occur on the opposite side of walls **AB** and **BD**. When the axis of the phonic cone runs into **B**, the sides of the cone fall on **F** and **O**; since these points reflect toward other areas, they return nothing to the sound-source.

### Proposition VI

***The closer the vocal or sounding source is to the <term>phonocamptic</term> object, the further away the reflected voice will be perceived; and the further the vocal source is from the <term>phonocamptic</term> object, the closer the reflected voice will be perceived.***

**S**ince it was shown in the third preliminary exercise that the line of "direct-reflected" activity is always as great as the line of action—that is, the radius of the sphere of activity—it necessarily follows that the reflected line is longer by the same amount that the direct line is shorter, and shorter by the same amount that the direct line is longer. Let the <term>phonocamptic</term> object be HBI. And let the direct-reflected line SBF be equal to VR, the direct line of action; I say that the reflected voice will be perceived further from the object the closer the direct source is to it. For CB and BE taken together equal the line of action VR. Therefore, the closer the vocal source is to the <term>phonocamptic</term> object, the further the reflected voice occurs from the object, and vice versa; which was to be demonstrated.

the third time it will be repeated; for since, by hypothesis, the objects EFG are perpendicular to the voice and "orthophonic" <note>original: "orthophona"; referring to surfaces that reflect sound directly back to its source</note>, the lines DE, DF, and DG from the points EFG will necessarily reflect back upon themselves to point D. Since the line DE is shorter, it will be reflected back to D more quickly. Because DF is longer than DE, it takes more time to return to D, and consequently, the reflected voice F will be perceived after the reflected voice E. Since DG is even longer than DF, it will reach the ears at D even more slowly. Therefore, a "triple-sounding" echo <note>original: "Echo triphona"</note> DE, DF, and DG will be born from these different, unequal times caused by the varying lengths of the lines. If, therefore, the phonocamptic <note>A term derived from Greek meaning "sound-reflecting."</note> objects are arranged in this order, etc.—which was the point to be demonstrated.

-> [A diagram showing a point D with three lines radiating to a surface ABC at points E, F, G. The lines are labeled DE, DF, DG.] <-

In this context, it should be noted that a double duration of the voice can be considered. First, there is the sound of the voice itself, which lasts as long as it is being uttered, and is vigorous and strong in its first production. Second, there is the propagation of the voice along the "line of action." <margin>How an Echo is generated.</margin> This propagation is of such a nature that while the first voice continues, the propagation also continues; but having traveled further, even when the first voice has fallen silent, the propagation continues until, struck and reflected by some obstacle, an echo is generated along the direct-reflected line. Hence, experience teaches us that we finally hear the reflected voice a long time after the first voice. Therefore, the entire duration of a voice from its first production to its end is measured by the space through which the voice goes and returns. If the distance is smaller, the reflected voice will return more quickly; if greater, more slowly. Consequently, at a shorter distance, it can repeat fewer syllables; at a greater distance, more. And although all syllables of the first voice are reflected, not all are heard; this is because the stronger primary voice drowns out the weaker reflected ones so that they cannot be heard while the primary voice lasts. Once the primary voice finally ceases, the reflected syllables are heard sooner or later according to the length of the distance.

**Corollary.**

From this it is clear why, occasionally, only the last syllables of a word are heard and never the first; this is because the reflected voice returns while the primary voice is still sounding, and only when the primary voice ceases are the remaining syllables finally perceived. Let wall AB be at a distance CD, from which someone proclaims the word *PARATIS* <note>Latin for "You have prepared" or "Ready."</note> with a strong voice. It is certain that the first syllable *PA* strikes the wall first, then the second *RA*, and third *TIS* in a forward order; but they are reflected in the opposite order, so that *PA* presents itself to the ears first, followed in order by the two subsequent syllables *RA* and *TIS*. If the distance is suited for uttering a single syllable <note>original: "monoſyllabico"</note>, then in proclaiming the said word *PARATIS*, only the syllable *TIS* will be perceived. For the first syllable *PA*, reaching the point of reflection D and being reflected there, will arrive at C,

-> [A diagram showing a horizontal line CD with points e and f. Above the line are the syllables pa, ra, tis. Below the line are the syllables tis, ra, pa. A vertical line AB is at the right end.] <-

and *RA* will be at point *e*, and *TIS* at point *f*. Thus, the syllables being confused there will return nothing. Meanwhile, as the reflected voice *PA* arrives at C, *RA* moves from D to *f* and from *f* to *e*, while the direct final syllable *TIS* reaches D. Thus, confusion occurs there again, so that the Echo cannot be heard until, the two syllables *PA* and *RA* having ceased, the final syllable *TIS* is finally perceived alone at C without confusion. Having seen the nature of sound according to simple lines, nothing remains but to speak of composite lines as well.

On Phonisms:

A **Phonism** <term>Phonism: Kircher’s technical term for the physical shape or "volume" of sound as it travels through space, rather than just a single line.</term>, as is clear from the definition, is the cylindrical or conical diffusion of the voice; that is, the radiation of the voice in the manner of a cone or a cylinder. It must be noted, however, that sound does not occur through a simple projection of lines, or *ray-casting* <note>Original Latin: *actinobolia*, a term borrowed from optics to describe how light rays spread.</note>; otherwise, nothing could be heard at all, and in this, sound differs from light. Instead, in its projection and reflection, it acts by way of a **sonic cylinder** or cone. Sound, therefore, does not have a purely mathematical width, but a completely sensible and physical one, such that in reflection, it is not a single line but a continuous multitude of lines that produces the sound. 

For example, let the sound-source be **A**, and the target of the reflection be **B**. Let the object or reflecting wall be **CD**. Let the motion of the sound begin at **A**; I say that it is not merely a single line **AO** that will produce the sound at **B** after reflecting at **O**, but rather the whole cylindrical cone **AFE** will be reflected toward **B** through the cylinder **EFB**. But let us demonstrate the matter a bit more precisely.

Thus, the proposition is clear.

### §. II.
### *On Polyphonisms, or the miraculous augmentation of sounds.*

<margin>What polyphonism and polyphotism are.</margin>

Just as light acquires its greatest increase when confined within concave bodies, so also does sound. That which burning mirrors <note>Original: *caustica specula*</note> perform in the gathering of light-patterns <note>Original: *Photismorum*</note>, Hearing or Acoustic organs perform in the gathering of sound-patterns <note>Original: *phonismorum*</note>, so that a polyphonism is nothing other than the flowing together of many phonisms or vocal cones into a single point. Just as a polyphotism is nothing other than the meeting of many light-rays in one point. Because this polyphonism is properly suited to concave bodies—some polygonal, others circular—I considered it my duty to explain such a subtle and illustrious subject at some greater length (especially since there is no one, as far as I know, who has touched upon it).

I assume first, therefore, that a voice in an open field is subject to no reflection, but radiates spherically into every part of the area; yet as soon as it encounters some obstacle perpendicular to it, it then establishes its first phonism. If, however, the voice is placed between two obstacles or walls, in this position it establishes two phonisms, and so on for the rest. This being assumed, nothing remains except for us to see how many and what kind of phonisms a voice produces in various bodies. Let it be, therefore:

### Proposition XII.

*With the phonic center established on the axis of a concave equilateral triangular prism, the emitted voice, increased by a triple phonism, will return to its own center.*

Let there be a concave three-sided prism ABC. Let the phonic center be established at D on the axis of the prism. I say that the emitted voice, increased by a triple phonism, returns to its center. For since the rays or axes of the phonisms DE, DF, and DG are perpendicular <note>Original: *normales*</note> to the sides of the prism (according to Proposition 2), they will necessarily return back upon themselves, increased threefold. Since also all neighboring rays are received in the manner of perpendiculars, and these same (according to Hypothesis 3) meet around the same center D, the voice will be wonderfully intensified there by the various encounters of the reflected lines. Therefore, those rays near the perpendiculars will return to D; the rest, according to Proposition 4, will return a ringing or a confused humming <note>Original: *tinnitum sive confusum bombum*</note> through various secondary reflections off the sides. Thus, with the phonic center established on the axis of a concave three-sided prism, the emitted voice, increased by a triple phonism, will return to its own center, which was to be demonstrated.

# Proposition XVII.

### In pyramids of any number of sides, as well as in concave cones, if the ear is placed on the axis, the voice emitted will never return to itself, except at points L and M, and not at any other points.

[Diagram: A triangle representing a pyramid or cone (ABC), with a central axis. Points E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, N, O are marked. Lines show sound reflections moving upwards away from the center.]

For the voice of sounds does not return outside points M and L within concave conical bodies; therefore, bodies of this kind are unsuitable for multiplying sound. For since the voice strikes each side <term>loxophonically</term> <note>original: λοξοφώνως (loxophonos), meaning at an oblique angle or "slant-wise."</note>, it reflects upward. Let the pyramid be ABC, and the phonic center K, from which the voice, having fallen on G, reflects to E; and from H to F; from N to O, and from here again to L. From this it is clear that the reflection always strives upward and does not return to itself, except in the two points L and M, as was stated.

Book IX. Magic of Reflective Sound. 261

**Proposition 18.**

**If the <term>phonic center</term> <note>The precise point where a sound originates or is focused.</note> is placed at the center of the five regular concave bodies, the reflected voice will return to its source increased by as many <term>phonisms</term> <note>From the Greek 'phone' (sound); Kircher uses this to mean individual instances of reflected sound or echoes.</note> as the body has sides.**

There are five regular bodies: the tetrahedron, the cube, the octahedron, the dodecahedron, and the icosahedron <note>These are the five "Platonic Solids," which are the only three-dimensional shapes where every face is an identical regular polygon.</note>. They are called "regular" because they have equal sides and are the only shapes that can be perfectly inscribed within a sphere; for each of their faces is equidistant from the center. Therefore, it is clear from the very definition of each shape how a voice may be propagated within them. If the phonic center is established in the center of a tetrahedron, the voice will return to itself increased by 4 echoes; in an octahedron by 8; in a dodecahedron by 12; and finally, in an icosahedron, it will return to itself increased by 20 echoes. The proof for all of these depends on the preceding principles and is so simple that it requires no further explanation.

**Proposition 19.**

**A concave sphere is the most suitable of all shapes for propagating sound.**

Since all lines drawn from every point of a circular surface to the center are equal to one another, and all are perpendicular to the spherical surface, it follows that all "species" of sound <note>In 17th-century science, "species" referred to the form or image of a physical sensation—in this case, the sound waves themselves.</note> will necessarily be reflected back on themselves and unite at the center. Therefore, the sound will become most powerful at that point. Thus, just as the concave sphere is the most spacious of all bodies for containing sound, it is also the most fit for multiplying sound, which was the point to be proven.

# Problem II.

*Given two points or stations, to determine both the position of the object and the angles under which an oblique sound* <note>original: "vox loxophona"</note> *goes and returns.*

Let there be two given points, A and B; let B be the center of sound production, and let the other, A, be the destination of the reflected voice. It is asked how the <term>anacamptic<gloss>reflective</gloss></term> object should be positioned so that A can perceive the voice reflected from B. Let two lines be drawn from B and A in any manner, provided they meet somewhere, for example at C. Let a triangle ABC be formed; after this is done, let the triangle ACB be divided in two. For at the end of this dividing line at point C, a perpendicular line drawn there will designate the position of the wall, or of whatever reflecting body it may be. For the voice from B, hitting this wall, will necessarily be reflected to A. I demonstrate the matter thus: since, according to the first proposition, an Echo occurs under the equality of the angles of incidence and reflection, and here the <term>cathetus<gloss>perpendicular line</gloss></term> CS divides

->[A geometric diagram showing a triangle with vertices A, B, and C. A vertical line (the cathetus) labeled S drops from point C. A horizontal line labeled LCM intersects point C, representing the reflecting surface.]<-

the <term>phonocamptic<gloss>sound-reflecting</gloss></term> triangle in two, and the line LCM represents the reflecting object, perpendicular to the cathetus CS, then the angles of incidence and reflection, LCA and MCB, will necessarily be equal. But the angles next to the cathetus are also equal; therefore, the voice from B, hitting the now-determined object LCM, will be reflected to A under equal angles. Thus, given any two points or chosen stations, we have determined both the position of the object and the angles under which the oblique voice travels and returns, which was what was to be done.

## Problem III.

*Given any number of points or stations arranged in any manner, provided they are at a sufficient distance for an Echo to be produced, to arrange the <term>reflective objects<gloss>In this context, these are usually walls or surfaces designed to bounce sound.</gloss></term> in such a way that the reflected voice is heard only by those who occupy the said stations or the lines of direct reflection.*

Let the given stations be **A, B, C, D, E, F, G**. Let the first voice be at **A**. The goal is to arrange the reflective objects according to these points so that the reflected voice is heard by no one else except those occupying the specified stations. Connect these points with straight lines. Once this is done, <note>The author is describing a geometric method to ensure sound travels in a specific "zigzag" path.</note> bisect each angle into two equal parts using the method previously described. I maintain that if you erect <term>perpendiculars<gloss>Lines at a 90-degree angle to the bisecting line.</gloss></term> at the ends of these bisecting lines, these will determine the required positions of the objects. The reflected voice will then be perceived only by those occupying the given stations or the lines of direct reflection.

Because the lines that bisect the angles are nothing other than the <term>normals<gloss>referred to here as 'catheti'; the imaginary line perpendicular to the reflecting surface.</gloss></term> of the reflecting surface, they will create equal <term>angles of reflection<gloss>original: "angulos catheticos"</gloss></term> everywhere, according to Supposition 6.

->[A geometric diagram showing points A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H connected by lines. Perpendicular lines are drawn at each vertex (B, C, D, etc.) to represent the placement of walls, ensuring the sound bounces from one point to the next in a sequence.]<-

If, therefore, perpendiculars are erected at the extreme points, they will form two right angles with the normal at each point. If you subtract the previous normal angles from these, the remaining angles will be <term>direct-reflected angles<gloss>The paths the sound takes as it hits and leaves the wall.</gloss></term>—that is, the angle of incidence will be equal to the angle of reflection, according to Euclid’s 6th definition. <note>original: "angulus incidentiæ, reflexionis angulo æqualis"</note> Therefore, the voice striking wall **B** from **A** will travel reflected from there to **C**, and from there to **D**, and from **D** to **E**, from **E** to **F**, and from **F** to **G**, and finally from **G** into **H**. Thus, the voice striking each object will reflect toward the given points with equal angles. This is what was to be done.

### Corollary.

It is therefore clear that an Ear placed at any of the given points will perceive the Echo. Furthermore, seven different men standing at the seven points will each hear the Echo sent forth from **A**. Indeed, the Echo will be heard not only at the specific points, but along any part of the lines connecting the points, which we call the lines of direct reflection.

### Problem V.

*To construct a polyphonic echo, or one which, after the first voice is uttered, repeats the same and other phrases several times.*

<margin>How a polyphonic echo is to be constructed.</margin> **W**e must recall in this place those things which we handed down in the third Prelude concerning the interval of an Echo. For since a certain and mathematical distance cannot be given in this slippery business, he will do best of all who investigates the said distance by the senses or mechanically. He shall do it thus: Let him select for himself a solid, polished wall, most fit for the reflection of the voice; then let him approach and recede from it perpendicularly until it has perfectly returned one syllable, and let him diligently investigate the space with some known measure. Then let him move backward in a straight path until it has perfectly returned a two-syllable word, and let him diligently measure the space. Afterward, let him move back so far until the Echo has returned three syllables, and so always receding more and more from the wall until it has perfectly returned ten syllables or some verse, perfectly observing the distance in all the multi-syllable counts. And experience will find that the spaces by which the Echo is increased by one syllable are not equal, but always smaller and smaller. In like manner, so that an Echo may be polyphonic <note>Repeating the sound multiple times.</note> and repeat a syllable several times, the spaces by which the distinct seven-syllable echoes grow are not equal, but always smaller and smaller.

<margin>Why the spaces in a multi-syllable Echo are not equal.</margin>

| For example: | |
| :--- | :--- |

| Two syllables | 190 |
| Three syllables | 270 |
| Four syllables | 350 |
| Five syllables | 430 |
| Six syllables | 515 |
| Seven syllables | 600 |
| | **feet** |

The reason for this thing is nothing other than the "fainting" of the voice, which always becomes more and more slack the further the space it traverses, until it is completely exhausted. Since, therefore, the voice is always weakened more and more, it is certain that the spaces can by no means be equal, but the further ones must always be closer together (as happens in the perspective of columns). By what proportion they decrease, however, is difficult to know, since the velocity of motion can hardly admit an exact and certain proportion to the space. He will act more securely, therefore, if he investigates the spaces of a polyphonic Echo by sense, just as he did the multi-syllable spaces. Thus the matter can be tracked mechanically with the help of several people. Let there be a wall AB, from which the "echo-measurer" recedes so far until that phrase: *I sing of arms and the man* <note>original: "arma virumque cano," the famous opening of Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note> is perfectly returned, which happens at point C. ### Given any points arranged in a circle, to construct a circular and multi-voiced echo. See Figure III in Plate XV.

Therefore, a voice from A hitting an acoustic object situated upon line B will reflect the voice back to A. And since lines C, D, E, F, H, I, K, and L are perpendicular to the sound lines described from A, the acoustic objects built upon them will likewise reflect the voice back to A. Since, moreover, the lines produced from A are always longer and longer, it follows also that the voice will be reflected back to A later and later; thus a multi-voiced echo will be born, repeating the voices successively as many times as there were points arranged in the circle. If these points have an equal distance from A in both semicircles, they will reverberate the echo at the same time and render it twice as strong.

### Problem VII.

### To construct a choir for a church with such artifice that only three singers perform as much as a hundred.

Because of the longer sonorous lines <note>The paths along which sound travels</note>, part B is repeated twice; the ending C is repeated a third time because the sonorous lines are carried even further. Thus, the ending D is repeated four times due to the length of the sonorous lines, and so on for the others. <margin>Method for establishing harmonic echoes</margin>

It is therefore clear from what has been said how an Echo can be constructed to represent different choirs. If, however, the space were so long that the voice would vanish over the greater distances, I would recommend assigning trumpets, drums, and other instruments of powerful sound. Since these are carried further than voices, their reflected sounds will also reach the ears more pleasantly than when heard from nearby.

### Inquiry

**Whether a different-sounding <term>heterophona: an echo that returns different words than the ones spoken</term> Echo can be constructed, which returns different words from the original ones.**

At first glance, this business seems to involve a certain impossibility <note>original: "ἀδυναμίαν" (adynamia)</note>. For how, you might ask, can a voice differ from itself? I do not see how, since an Echo is nothing other than a certain continued and reflected flow of the original voice. By no means can it produce anything else through reflection except what was first uttered; it therefore seems to imply a contradiction that an Echo could represent something else. 

I respond that an Echo may be considered in many ways: either as **direct** <note>original: "orthophona"</note> or as **oblique** <note>original: "loxophona"</note>; <margin>Multiple types of different-sounding echoes.</margin> and again, either as **single-syllabled** <note>original: "monophonon"</note> or **multi-syllabled** <note>original: "polyphonon"</note>. I say, therefore, it is true that a direct, single-syllabled Echo cannot represent anything other than what was uttered. However, I claim there are certain oblique echoes which we say can be suited to represent something other than what was uttered. Yet, some believe even a direct Echo can be so arranged that the direct voice carries one thing and the reflected voice another. Thus, some people, while uttering Greek words, make the Echo respond in Latin, as is clear in the following words:

*   The gods accomplish all things through labors. <note>original Greek: "οἵ θεοὶ πάντα πολῦσι πόνοις"</note> — **through good things.** <note>original Latin: "bonis" - which sounds like the Greek "ponois"</note>
*   They accomplish all things. <note>original Greek: "πάντα πολῦσι"</note> — **I have played.** <note>original Latin: "lusi" - which sounds like the Greek "polusi"</note>
*   The gods are here. <note>original Greek: "οἵ θεοὶ ἐνθάδε"</note> — **by age.** <note>original Latin: "ætate" - which sounds like the Greek "enthade"</note>

In this or a similar way, words with similar endings could be selected from any language, provided they have different meanings in the different languages. But such things are as forced and of little wit as they are difficult to put into practice; they are only brought about with long study and little fruit. Perhaps these things could be better achieved in one and the same language, of which we shall provide some examples. See Figure II of Illustration XV.

Suppose, for example, a four-syllable Echo is to be established. Let the objects B, C, D, E, and F be so arranged that each reflects one syllable later than the last. Let the following word be **CLAMORE** <note>Latin for "with a shout"</note>, which is trisyllabic in sound, but in power, four-syllabled. Let the sound source or the speaker be at point A. Since the objects are assumed to be arranged so that each reflects a syllable later, it is certain that each object will reflect different meaningful words. Thus:

*   Object B returns: **CLAMORE** <note>With a shout</note>
*   Object C returns: **AMORE** <note>With love</note>
*   Object D returns: **MORE** <note>By custom</note>
*   Object E returns: **ORE** <note>By mouth</note>
*   Object F returns: **RE** <note>By deed</note>

Therefore, a multi-syllabled Echo will always repeat different and varying words. For example, if someone shouts: "To you indeed I shall give thanks, with what **SHOUT**?" <note>original: "CLAMORE"</note> the Echo will respond: "I shall give thanks **WITH A SHOUT, WITH LOVE, BY CUSTOM, BY MOUTH, BY DEED.**"

Likewise, the word **CONSTABIS** <note>You will stand firm</note> will always reflect different words from different objects, as is clear here. Innumerable examples of this kind can be found, reflecting one word after another successively from the first voice, so that the Echo no longer returns the first word, but always other and different words. In these two ways, therefore—and no other—a direct Echo, and indeed one using various objects, can return different words from the original. 

The question then arises: whether an **oblique** <note>loxophona</note> Echo can be constructed so that it can respond to questions in any other language.

### Problem VIII.
*To construct a heterophonous echo, whose reflected voice always responds with something different and in any language.* <note>The term "heterophonous" comes from the Greek words *heteros* (different) and *phone* (voice/sound).</note>

<margin>What a heterophonous echo is</margin>
This Echo requires the labor of two people, and should be set up in this way: first, let a space be determined that is suitable for perfectly pronouncing four or five syllables—that is, a space that can perfectly express a word of 4 or 5 syllables. Once this is done, let the reflecting object be arranged with this strategy: the voice of someone standing at a first station, upon hitting the object, is reflected to the ears of someone standing at a second station; however, the first person should not be able to see the second, but only hear them. For this reason, the reflecting object must be placed at the meeting point of two walls, or some promontory. As is clear in the diagram: in which **EF** are walls joined at **D**. The rock or obstacle doing the reflecting may be either artificial or natural; it makes no difference. Let the reciprocal phonic center <note>The "reciprocal phonic center" refers to the two points where sound can be sent and received interchangeably.</note> be at points **A** and **B**, separated from the object **DC** by such a distance that it perfectly carries back 4 or 5 syllables, as I said. By this arrangement, as soon as the first person at **A** begins to cry out a word, that sound—falling obliquely <note>original: "loxophonè," a term Kircher uses to describe sound traveling at an angle rather than a straight line</note> onto **C**—will not be reflected back to **A**, but to **B**. As soon as the person standing at **B** hears this, he responds with other words uttered in any language, which then immediately present themselves to the ears of the person standing at **A**. Therefore, the first person will perceive something different than what was first spoken. For example, if the first person asks by shouting, "*What is your name?*" <note>original: "quod nomen tibi"</note> and the other person positioned at **B** responds, "*Constantine*", <note>original: "Constantinus"</note> the person standing at **A** will perceive, immediately following the words of the question, not his own words, but the reflected words of the other. Certainly, this device—especially if set up with care—is so mysterious that when I tested it here in Rome at our estate, there was hardly anyone who understood the logic of it. Everyone was amazed and, as if struck dumb with astonishment, they heard the Echo respond to every question with different words. To hide the trick, however, there ought to be two people who are endowed with voices as similar as possible; in this way, the illusion will remain better hidden. Thus, we have constructed a **heterophonous** echo, etc., which was the goal.

<margin>Corollary I.</margin>
From what has been said, it is clear that two people at points **A** and **B** can signal anything to each other by this method; indeed, two choirs could perform together in an alternating fashion by some wonderful method, and other things could be carried out which are left to the judgment of the ingenious craftsman.

<margin>Corollary II.</margin>
It is also clear that just as there are optical illusions for the sight, so too there are acoustic ones. For the person positioned at **A** will clearly think the voice comes from **D**, and thus that it is the voice emitted by himself. This trick will be all the more secret the more similar the voices are, and the less one person knows about the other. But there will be more abundant material for discussing these things in what follows.

### On the measurement of sound lines.
### Problem I.
*Given the perpendicular distance from a wall, along with the angle of reflection or incidence, to find the distance of all oblique-sound points from the perpendicular point B.*

Let FDB be the wall, and the perpendicular distance <note>The shortest, straight-line distance to the wall</note> be the known measure of 25 paces; let the <term>loxophonic</term> <note>From the Greek 'loxos' (oblique) and 'phone' (sound); these are the diagonal paths sound takes when it hits a surface at an angle.</note> lines be AD and DE. I say that if either angle CAG or GAI—or, what is the same thing, the angle of reflection DAB or the angle of incidence EDF—and the sound angle of the <term>cathetus</term> <note>The perpendicular line or 'leg' of the triangle, in this case, line CD.</note> CDA are known, then the lines BD, AD, AC, CD, and ED also become known. Let the angle CAD (which is equal to the angle of incidence ADB) be known as 76 degrees by means of a sighting instrument <note original: "instrumentum dioptricum">. These, subtracted from 90, leave 14 degrees for GI, the sound angle of the perpendicular CD. Therefore, to find the line BD (or to locate the oblique-sound point D), proceed as follows: as the sine of the <term>phonoptotic angle</term> <note original: "anguli phonoptoti"; the angle at which the sound 'falls' upon the surface</note> of 76 degrees is to the sine of the sound-angle of the perpendicular (14 degrees), so is the distance of 25 paces to the result. Once the calculation is performed, the line BD (the distance of the point of reflection from point B) will be produced. If, however, you desire the length of the <term>loxoptotic</term> line AD <note>The path of the sound falling toward the wall</note>, let it be: as the sine of the angle of incidence ADB is to the <term>total sine</term> <note>In early modern trigonometry, the 'total sine' refers to the radius of the calculating circle, used as a standard denominator.</note>, so is the known measure of 25 paces to the result; the sought-after oblique-falling line AD will be produced. Since the reflected line ED is equal to this, its length is known automatically.

### Problem II.
Given the distance from the phonic center to the terminal point of reflection, to determine the **orthophone line**.
<note>The "phonic center" is the source of the sound. The "orthophone line" (from the Greek *orthos* meaning straight) refers to the path of sound that strikes a reflecting surface at a right angle.</note>

Let the distance AC or CE be known, and let the center of reflection be E or A; the **orthophone line** AB or CD will be determined if we calculate as follows: as the sine of the angle GAI of the phonic cathetus is to the sine of the angle of incidence ADB (noted in the arc CG), so is the known measure DB to the other. Once the operation is completed, AB or CD is produced.

If, however, you wish to know the **loxophone lines** AD and DE, let it be: as the sine of the phonic cathetus angle is to the **total sine**, so is DB to the other. Once the operation is completed, the sought-loxophone lines AD and DE will be produced.
<note>Loxophone lines (from *loxos* meaning oblique) are the diagonal paths sound takes when it bounces off a surface at an angle.</note>
The reasoning is evident from the 15th proposition on the resolution of triangles in **Clavius**, whom you should consult; specifically, problems 1, 2, and 3 of his geometry.
<note>Christopher Clavius was a prominent Jesuit mathematician and astronomer, a contemporary of Kircher, best known for his work on the Gregorian calendar.</note>

### Problem III.
Given the loxophone line, to find the orthophone line and the distance of the phonic center from the normal point (or center of reflection).

Let the loxophone line AD be known. First, you will investigate the orthophone CD in this manner: as the **total sine** is to the sine of the angle ADB of the sound's fall, so is the known measure AD to the other; once the operation is completed, the sought AB or CD will be produced.
<note>original: "sinus totus." In the trigonometry of Kircher’s era, the "total sine" was the radius of the circle used for calculation, often set to a large number like 100,000 to avoid decimals.</note>

Again, to find the quantity of the line DB, let it be: as the total sine is to the sine of the phonic cathetus angle GAI, so is the known measure AD to the other. Once the operation is performed, the sought BD will be produced.

### Problem IV.
Given the orthophone line, to find the loxophone lines and the distance of the phonic center from the center of reflection using tangents and secants.

Let AB be the known orthophone line; and should you desire to know the loxophone line AD, let it be: as the total sine AI is to the secant AG of the phonic cathetus angle of 14 degrees, so is the known AB (25 paces) to the other; the sought quantity of the loxophone AD will be produced.

Again, to investigate BD, let it be: as the total sine AI is to the tangent IG of the 14-degree angle, so is the known measure of 25 paces to the other; the sought quantity BD will be produced. 

If, however, BD were known, AB and AD would be determined in this way: as the tangent GI is to the total sine, so is the known measure BD to the other, and the orthophone line AB will be obtained. Again, for the loxophone line AD, let it be: as the tangent GI of the 14-degree angle is to the secant AG, so is the known BD to the other; the sought quantity AD will be produced.

### III. Given the loxophone quantity, you shall seek the orthophone CD and BD in this manner.

Let it be: as the secant AG is to AI, so is the known AD to the other, and the sought orthophone CD or AB will be obtained. Again, as the secant AG is to the tangent GI, so is AD to the other, and the sought quantity BD will be produced. Once this is completed, all lines pertaining to the business of sound will be investigated.

## Problem V.

### Given two sides in a phonic triangle, to find the third by extracting the square root.

In the phonic triangle ADB, let the first given side be the **orthophonic** <note>original: *orthophonum*; referring to a straight or direct sound path</note> line **AB**, measuring 25 paces, and let line **AC**—the distance of the phonic center from the phonic **cathetus** <term>cathetus: a line falling perpendicularly on another line or surface</term>—be 8 paces. You will find the third side **AD** in this way: multiply the given sides by themselves (square them), and from the sum of the two sides joined together, extract the square root. According to the 4th proposition of the 1st book of Euclid's *Elements* <note>While the author cites Proposition 4, the calculation described for finding the hypotenuse of a right triangle is the Pythagorean theorem, famously found in Proposition 47 of the same book.</note>, you will have the desired line **AD**.

Secondly, if sides **BD** and **AD** are known, you will find the third side **AB** if you subtract the square of line **DB** from the square of the whole **AD**. The root of the remaining square will give the desired line **AB**. Thirdly, if the two sides **AB** and **AD** are given, you will find the third **BD** in this way: subtract the square of **AB** from the square of **AD**, and the root of the remaining square will give the desired line **BD**.

### Corollary.

From these brief remarks, it is clear how phonic lines are usually measured in all other **echometric** <term>echometric: the mathematical measurement of echoes and their distances</term> cases. Since in every phonocamptic <note>Reflected sound</note> instance the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, if any side is known along with an angle in the phonic triangle, the remaining parts will be investigated by the exact same method we have prescribed. Therefore, whether the reflection occurs on regular or irregular bodies, the same ratio of dimension must always be observed. I wished to indicate this briefly here so that nothing might seem lacking from our phonocamptic art.

### Acoustic Experiments I.

#### Channels or pipes propagate sound in a wonderful manner.

<margin>Roman aqueducts propagate **audible forms** over a great distance.</margin> Just as light, when enclosed in polished containers, reaches its maximum increase in intensity, so too is sound propagated through channels. I believe that if a cylinder one mile long were constructed with a volume equal to a sphere of sound, a sound which in the open air has a range of only 24 paces would be propagated in that cylindrical channel for a distance of more than a thousand paces. Experience itself supports my opinion; for the Overseers of the Roman Aqueducts say that within the aqueducts, over a very long distance, the voices of people speaking can be perceived even at five hundred feet as if they were present, especially if the channel is remarkably polished. Experience also teaches that a channel of two hundred feet will deliver even whispered voices at either end. Nor should this seem strange to anyone; since the voice, when enclosed in channels and unable to escape, strives to recover through longitudinal propagation what it would have lost by being diffused and scattered in the open air. In these narrow spaces, being repeatedly reflected and multiplied, it acquires a huge increase in strength as well as reaching the most remote limits of its propagation. However, I cannot omit a notable question here, which as far as I know has not yet been decided by anyone, and it is as follows:

#### A curious question.

#### Whether a voice tightly enclosed in channels remains there for some period of time.

<margin>The deception of Porta and Cornelius Agrippa.</margin> There have been some, among them Giambattista della Porta and Cornelius Agrippa <note>Both were famous Renaissance polymaths known for their works on "natural magic" and the occult.</note>, who not only held this opinion but also tried to persuade others of it as an infallible truth: that a voice whispered into a very long, clean, and polished channel—if the other end is closed very tightly before the **audible forms** <note>original: "species sonoræ"</note> can escape—remains inside said channel. They claimed that several days later, when either end is opened, the voices, as if released from a kind of captivity, immediately present themselves to the ears of the listener. This fiction was so plausible that it gained not only many patrons but also very fierce defenders. Wecker, Alessio, and others have tried to defend this thing as most certain, true, and beyond all doubt, even adding invented stories to demonstrate the great utility of such a remarkable experiment. This is what happens when "Experience, the Mistress of Things" <note>A common Latin proverb: *Magistra rerum experientia*.</note> is not consulted, and we rashly and precipitately subscribe to the fantastic agitations of anyone's mind; in this way, intolerable errors are propagated by substitute teachers in the lecture halls. If they had first conducted an experiment on this matter, or had a proper understanding of the nature of sound, they would never have fallen into such a shameful opinion. I say, therefore, that water would sooner be drawn up with a sieve than a voice be enclosed in channels; and I conclude the <term>impossibility</term> <note>original: "ἀδυναμίαν" (adynamian)</note> of the matter with this argument:

For the voice is carried through the channel either by "real forms" or "intentional forms," and neither can be claimed. Not the former, because the real forms of sound are nothing other than the continuous and successive agitation of the air carrying the voice; when this air, being enclosed, finds the exit blocked at both ends and cannot be reflected because the air left behind is unable to yield, then all agitation of the air must necessarily cease in an instant, and with that cessation, the sounding motion also stops. Thus, anyone who tried to enclose sound within a channel would be doing the same as one who believed he could draw water with a sieve. Let there be, for example, a channel AB of 400 feet—of such a length, evidently, as is sufficient for forming a three-syllable echo. Thus, while the one occupying station A whispers a word, for example, "**sing**" <note>original: "cantate"</note>, the other at station B, at the sign given of the finished word, [closes] the end B...

These impostors do not see the manifest contradiction in their own opinion; for it would clearly follow from this that a voice both exists and does not exist. For a voice exists and remains only as long as the motion of the air remains; when that motion ceases, the voice itself ceases. Therefore, at the very moment both ends are closed, the entire body of air comes to rest, and with it, the propagation of the voice.

But they will say that the motionless "sonorous species" remain there. As has been stated, sound essentially depends on motion; when motion ceases, the sound is destroyed. Nor is it a valid comparison to say that a voice remains in an open space without dependence on the speaker; for in an open space, the air does not rest at all, but the sonorous air is in continuous motion, as the nature of the Echo sufficiently demonstrates. Daily experience teaches us that sound can even pass through the thickest walls. It is therefore ridiculous, if not outright stupid, to want to restrain sound with shutters; for when it is enclosed in a channel, it passes through a shutter as easily as it passes through a window or a wall. You see, therefore, from this discussion of ours, how contrary to reason and how discordant are the arguments of these impostors. Let this mythical nonsense about enclosing sound in channels, which has occupied academic chairs until now, be abolished. **Experiment II.**

Book IX. The Magic of Reflected Sound <note>original: "Magia Phonocamptica"; from the Greek 'phone' (sound) and 'kamptos' (bent/reflected).</note>. 275

Suppose a tube **AV** is bent into an arc; I maintain that the sound is intensified more within it than in a straight tube. Because, in addition to the collection of sound, a manifold reflection of that same sound occurs, a vehement intensification is born from this. Thus, you see the sound-ray reflected from **A** to **B**, from **B** to **C**, and from there to **D**; from **D** to **E**, and so on to other and further points, being intensified through many reflections. Likewise, the opposing ray **X** to **Y**, and from there to **Z**; and from **Z** to **α** and then to **β**, having followed another series of reflections. Since, in truth, infinite lines of sound enter the mouth of the tube **AX**, each will observe its own laws in reflecting; hence, as there is an infinite piling up of sound-lines, a <term>polyphonism</term> <note>original: "polyphonismus"; a term used here to describe the layering and reinforcement of multiple sound waves.</note> must necessarily be born from their reflection, becoming more intense as the sound is more compressed toward **V**. This happens very little in a straight tube, for in that case, as has been said, the propagation of the sound occurs only by being collected and narrowed without such great reflection.

->**Corollary.**<-

From this it is clear that a conical tube intensifies the voice more than a cylindrical tube, <margin>A conical channel intensifies the voice more than a cylindrical one.</margin> for the former is better suited for reflecting sound-forms <note>original: "speciebus sonoris"; in the science of the time, "species" were the invisible forms or "images" of sound or light traveling through a medium.</note>. Therefore, if you twist both a conical and a cylindrical tube into a circle, the conical one twisted into a circle will be more powerful than the cylindrical one similarly twisted; for in the circular conical tube, as it moves from wide to narrow, the narrowed and compressed sound-forms will be vehemently intensified—not unlike how wind constrained in narrow places gains greater force. In a circular cylindrical tube, however, the compression of sound is equal everywhere. For this reason, **Alexander the Great's Horn** was so constructed that it widened from narrow to broad; but concerning this, see the *History of Prodigious Sounds* and *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>Two other works by Athanasius Kircher.</note>.

### Experiment IV.

### Sound propagated along circular surfaces acquires immense force.

Experience has taught me many times in various buildings that sound propagated along circular surfaces is extremely intense. There is in **Heidelberg**, Germany, a certain very large round tower, constructed with such artifice that two people diametrically opposite each other can speak of anything, even in the lowest whispers. I hear there is a similar hall in the Palace of the **Duke of Mantua**. I have experienced the same thing in the arches of great bridges. I also took an experiment of this matter with remarkable success in the **Dome of St. Peter’s** here in **Rome**; there is a cornice <note>A decorative ledge or walkway.</note> in the interior of the dome of such great width that a carriage could easily travel there without danger. At opposite locations on the diameter of this encircling cornice, at a distance of nearly a hundred geometric feet, two people opposite each other talk in even the lowest whispers, despite the noisy tumult of people and musicians below. <margin>Sound carried along circular surfaces is most easily perceived.</margin> Truly, in the remaining points of the wall, nothing is perceived. There is no doubt that the same thing happens in all circular structures. To reveal the cause of this, it must be known that sound has this particular quality over light: it is propagated according to the movement of the air. If, therefore, the movement of the air is in a straight line, the sound will also be propagated in a straight line; if in a circle, the sound will also be propagated according to the circle; and so it must be said of other surfaces. Furthermore, since sound diffused spherically on a circular surface seeks a way out but finds no place to escape because the walls block it, it is constrained along the circular surface. Finally, meeting the vocal air coming from the other side of the wall at the same moment in diametrical opposition, it is vehemently intensified. From this kind of union and the flowing together of the "species" <note>sound-images</note>, that great intensification of the carried voice is born; and hence it happens that this "phonism" <note>sound phenomenon</note> occurs nowhere else but in those opposite locations. However, we have decided that this matter must be demonstrated more deeply.

**Experiment V.**
**The voice in "cochleas" <note>original: *cochleis*; referring to spiral shells or screw-like shapes</note>, or a conical tube twisted according to a helical or spiral line; as it is the most suitable of all shapes, it also attains the greatest power.**

This experiment is truly most worthy of observation: that sound within a spirally twisted conical tube—the kind found in spiral shells—is increased in a wonderful way beyond all other shapes mentioned so far. I would never have believed it, had experience not informed me of this very often. I have seen nothing more wonderful in this genre than the **Ear of Dionysius the Tyrant**, which was constructed in the shape of an inner ear and still survives in Syracuse, Sicily; see the description of it in the history of prodigious sounds. <note>The "Ear of Dionysius" is a famous limestone cave in Syracuse, carved in an approximate "S" shape, famous for its incredible acoustics where a whisper can be heard high above.</note> Certainly, we showed in Book 1, in the chapter on the anatomy of ears of all kinds of animals, that most wise Nature chose this spiral tube above all other shapes for designing the ear. The more perfect the hearing of certain animals, the more perfect and open a "cochlea" <note>The spiral cavity of the inner ear.</note> she granted them, as is especially evident in the ears of pigs, hares, mice, dogs, and most of all, donkeys. In the construction of their ears, Nature established perfectly helical tubes; for which reason we thought it worthwhile to explain the purpose of Nature's design. Why then the spiral tube intensifies sound more than all others, I assign this reason: that whatever has been said about conical and cylindrical tubes—whether straight or twisted—applies most perfectly to this spiral cone. For it not only perfectly collects "sound species" <note>The author uses "species" to mean the perceptible form or image of a sound traveling through the air.</note> and reflects them manifoldly, but also reflects them in every direction—backward and forward—mostly with a <term>direct-sounding reflection</term> <note>original: *reflexione orthophona*; a reflection where the sound returns clearly and undistorted.</note>. Furthermore, since the passage of the helix is divided only by a thin membrane, when sound strikes the sides, it does not only increase by reflection, but by penetrating into the other passages, it wonderfully intensifies the <term>sound-images</term> <note>original: *phonismos*; a technical term for the vocal sounds or reflections themselves.</note>. But so that these things may be better understood:

->**The power of the spiral tube in multiplying sound.**<- <margin>The power of the spiral tube in multiplying sound.</margin>

Let there be a conical tube twisted into a spiral helix, labeled **AMQC**. I say that in it, voices are intensified more than in all other hollow bodies. Let the sound source be at **A**, from which the voice is propagated within the cavity of the tube. Since the inner parts of the tube are arranged with an irregular curvature, it happens that a perpetual "star-like" reflection is born. The more it penetrates inside, the more sharply it will always reflect, until at last, in a direct-sounding reflection, it produces the most intense sound. Thus you see the voice from **A** striking **E**, then reflected to **F**, and from here to **G, H, I, K,** and **L**. This line, since it is direct-sounding and reflected back into itself, will vehemently intensify the sound. In the same way, the sound line from **A** striking **M** will then be reflected into **N, O, P, Q,** and the remaining points in a star-like pattern, until at **RS** it again produces a most intense direct-sounding reflection. Since indeed infinite lines can be drawn from point **A**, each striking different points of the interior surface—

## PRACTICAL STUDY I.

Certain surfaces result from the sections of certain bodies, whose powers and properties are so wonderful and secret that nature alone seems to have reserved them for herself to perform wonders; and while I remain silent about countless others, who does not know the paradoxes of the **conic section**? There are three main types of these, filled with truly admirable powers: the **Ellipse**, **parabola**, and **Hyperbola**. The especially admirable property of these is that if concave bodies are shaped by applying these figures to material, certain points are born in the imaginary middle, to which all lines falling within the concave are reflected. In a single point of reflection, they produce wonderful effects both in illuminating and in burning; from which also **burning mirrors** <note>original Latin: "caustica specula"</note> found their origin. 

But since we have treated these professionally in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original Latin: "Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae," Kircher's 1646 work on optics</note>, we refer the reader there. For here we will only repeat those things which seem most conducive to our purpose. Just as, therefore, the united rays of light within the said bodies produce wonderful effects of vision, so also I think no one can doubt that sound rays can do the same within the said concaves, if they have rightly understood the preceding. How, then, acoustic conic sections are to be described in structures to provide wonderful effects of hearing, will be discussed then, after we have first taught how to describe the said sections in physical material. Let it be, therefore.

**Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic: 279**

**Problem I.**
*To describe an ellipse with a single pull of a string.*

Since we have already provided various methods for describing ellipses and other sections in Books 3 and 10 of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Artis Magnæ Lucis & Vmbræ"; this refers to Kircher's 1646 work on optics and geometry</note>, we did not wish to repeat them here. Instead, we will only teach the method that seems more suitable for mechanical <term>Echotectonics</term> <note>The art of designing buildings specifically for their acoustic or echo-producing properties.</note>. Thus, you shall describe an ellipse with a single pull of a string in this manner:

Every ellipse consists of two diameters, the major and the minor. If they were equal, it would not be an ellipse but a circle. The more the minor diameter decreases, the sharper the ellipse will be; the more it increases, the more obtuse the ellipse will be and more similar to a circle, until the diameters become equal in size and the ellipse turns into a perfect circle.

[Diagram of major axis A-E-B and minor axis C-D]

<margin>The wonderful power of the ellipse.</margin> Note, moreover, that in every ellipse except a circular one, two points are found which Geometers commonly call "foci" <note>literally "fireplaces" or "hearths"</note> from the comparison made, because in them the ignition occurs in <term>burning mirrors</term> <note>concave mirrors designed to concentrate sunlight to a single point to start a fire.</note>. These two points are located on the major semi-diameter, and they will always be further from each other the sharper the ellipse is (that is, the more it differs from a circle). Conversely, the closer the ellipse is to a circular one, the closer they will be, until they meet at a single point, which is the center of the circle.

With these things observed: Let the given diameters of the ellipse to be formed be AB (the major) and CD (the minor). Place the minor diameter CD at the midpoint E of the major diameter at right angles, so that the ends of the minor diameter are equidistant from the midpoint E. This being done, you will find the foci or "points of comparison" in this way: take the major semi-diameter AE or BE with a compass. From either end of the minor semi-diameter, C or D, transfer this distance with the compass onto the major diameter AB. 

[Diagram of an ellipse being drawn with a string and pins at foci I and L, with a stylus at point R]

Where the compass cuts the line AB on both sides, there the two foci will be: namely, at I and L. Having found these points of comparison I and L, fix two pins into them. Around these pins, place a string double the length of LA or IB. Within this string, a certain stylus <note>original: "graphium"</note> being drawn around will describe the desired ellipse. The string is represented for us by the two lines LR and RI; it is tied at the two points I and L and is applied precisely to the stylus R at point A. Then, from A, the stylus R drawn within that string will describe the sought-after ellipse. From this, it is clearly evident that the two parts of the string extended from R toward either focus (for example, LR and RI) are always equal to the major diameter of the ellipse. For the demonstration of all these things, see *The Art of Light and Shadow*, Book 4, in the treatise on conic sections.

**Problem II.**
*To fashion an ellipse-shaper in solid material.*

We call an <term>Ellipsioplasten</term> <note>from the Greek for "ellipse-molder."</note> that form or mold which we use to press an ellipse into soft material such as plaster, cement, or clay by moving it around. Just as a potter or sculptor uses various instruments to describe various figures, so for describing ellipses in plaster, a plastic form is needed by whose rotation the shape is produced. We call this form or rule an "Ellipsioplasten," as if it were a potter’s mold for an ellipse.

# CHAPTER IV.
# ECHOTECTONIC MAGIC
### OR
### On Acoustic Structures.

# PREFACE.

Whatever wonders we have shown in our *Catoptric Magic* <note>The study of mirrors and reflected light</note>—how we placed the images of distant things before us as if they were present with the help of telescopes; or how we provided a view of the marvelous composition of tiny things, both living and inanimate, to be inspected through microscopes—we trust we shall achieve the same in this present treatise regarding the representation of distant sounds. <margin>Whatever has been said in Catoptric Magic can be applied to Phonocamptics <note>Sound reflection</note>.</margin> By confining voices (which are otherwise imperceptible) within instruments, we present them to the ears of the astonished listeners so vividly and sonorously that they might not undeservedly seem to be recalled from death to life. We undertake this task all the more gladly because the matter is quite obscure and highly anticipated. Let no one persuade themselves that we will hand down things here that have their only certainty in theory, but meet with no success when brought into practice. Indeed, let the reader be certain that we will show no technical devices here whose infallible certainty has not first been made safe and secure for us by undeniable experiments observed in various places around the world. But having said these things, let us now get to the matter.

### Prelude I.
### *On the Vitruvian Theater and the Sounding Vessels <term>Echæa</term> <note>Ancient bronze or clay vessels placed under theater seats to resonate with the actors' voices</note> arranged within it.*
### *See Illustration XVI. fig. 1.*

It can hardly be explained how great a variety of opinions and how much disagreement there is among authors regarding the structure of these Sounding Vessels in the Theater. Almost none of those who have commented on Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect and engineer whose "De Architectura" is a foundational text</note> show that they have correctly understood the matter. But as usually happens in difficulties of this kind, when they are unable to penetrate an obscure business, most have substituted a view copied from others as their own, so as not to seem to have said nothing at all. They do this lest, by passing over such a memorable thing in silence, they demonstrate that they have "drawn water with a sieve" <note>A Latin idiom, *aquam cribro hausisse*, meaning to waste one's labor on a useless task</note>, as the saying goes.

As I frequently considered this confusion—which arises from nothing other than an ignorance of music—I judged that I would perform a worthwhile service if I opportunely inserted my own opinion regarding the structure of the said theater here in this treatise on "Echotectonics" <note>Building for echoes/acoustics</note>, and explained what those famous Sounding Vessels finally were. This will be done after I have first cited the text of Vitruvius.

Vitruvius, therefore, in Book 5, Chapter 5, describes the **Acoustic Theater** <note>original: "Theatrum Echæum"</note> in this manner:

Therefore, from these investigations, bronze vessels are produced according to mathematical principles in proportion to the size of the Theater. They should be so constructed that, when they are struck, they can produce sounds in harmony with one another, specifically the <term>fourth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>, the <term>fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente"</note>, and so on in sequence up to the <term>double octave</term> <note>original: "disdiapason"</note>. You see, therefore, in these two preceding diagrams, two series of vessels: the first is according to the mind of Vitruvius, the other is according to the arrangement of the Moderns <note>original: *Neotericorum*; referring to contemporary music theorists of the 16th and 17th centuries</note>. For since the vessels arranged according to the fourth and the octave-plus-fourth in the third or sixth place are dissonant to the first vessel and are rejected by the Moderns, we have therefore changed the fourth into a minor third <note>original: *semiditonum*</note> or a major third <note>original: *ditonum*</note>, so that there would be a greater harmony among the bronze vessels, as is clear in the second diagram.

But having described these things in passing, let us now demonstrate the form of the theater described by Vitruvius a little more fully, so that the location and arrangement of the vessels may be more clearly illuminated.

Let the Orchestra <note>The central semi-circular space of an ancient theater</note> of the Theater be **AB**, as is clear in **Illustration XVI, Figure I**; there are three orders or levels in the largest Theater, **M, L,** and **K**, of which the first corresponds to harmonic <note>The Enharmonic genus</note>; the second to Chromatic; and the third to Diatonic symphony. There are thirteen cells in each, according to the description of Vitruvius; **MOP** is the Colonnade <note>original: *Xyxtus*; a covered walkway or portico</note> or walkway of the theater. The sounding-vessels <term>Echæa; bronze jars used in ancient theaters to reinforce the actors' voices through resonance</term>, however, are placed on their wedges, separated by half a foot from the floor, but otherwise completely free in the middle of the cells (as in the highest...

286 *Universal Music-Making* <note>original: "Musurgia Universalis"</note>

In the highest tier, the small room (labeled KL) shows that the vessels are arranged in this order. Two vessels in cells CD are in unison, and they sound a double octave <note>original: "decimam quintam," literally the fifteenth note</note> relative to the bronze vessel in cell MP. They stand in a ratio of 4 to 1; that is, they have a quadruple proportion between them, meaning they resonate with vessel MP at a double octave <note>original: "disdiapason"</note>. The vessels in the following cells, marked with the numbers 1 and 12, are in unison and of equal size; they stand in a ratio of three to one relative to the acoustic vessel MP, meaning they have a triple proportion and resonate a twelfth <note>an octave plus a fifth</note> with vessel MP. The vessels marked with numbers 3 and 11 are in unison and of equal size; they stand in a ratio of eight to two <note>Mathematically this is 4:1, though Kircher identifies it here with the eleventh</note> relative to the acoustic vessel PM, and they resonate an eleventh with said vessel PM. The vessels in the cells marked 4 and 10 have a ratio of two to one relative to vessel MP, which is a double proportion, and they sound an octave <note>original: "octauam"</note> relative to MP. In this same way, vessels 5 and 9, being in a <term>sesquialteran proportion|a 3:2 ratio</term> to PM, sound a fifth. Vessels 6 and 8, in <term>sesquitertian proportion|a 4:3 ratio</term> to PM, sound a fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>. Finally, there follows the fundamental acoustic vessel MP, to which all the others are proportioned, as has been demonstrated. It should be noted that in small theaters, according to the description by Vitruvius, the lowest row or tier should be moved to the middle, omitting the chromatic and diatonic tiers. In larger theaters, however, such as this one, the theater must be divided according to its height into four parts by four arches into three tiers; then the lowest is assigned to the enharmonic <note>original: "harmonię"</note>, the second to the chromatic, and the third to the diatonic. How the vessels of the remaining chromatic and diatonic tiers are to be arranged, Vitruvius shows with these words:

*But if the size of the Theater is larger, then the height should be divided into 4 parts, so that three regions of cells are created, designated crosswise: one for the enharmonic, another for the chromatic, and the third for the diatonic. And starting from the bottom, let the first tier be placed according to the enharmonic scale, just as was described for the smaller theater. In the middle section, first, in the furthest corners, let vessels be placed having the sound of the <term>chromatic hyperbolaion|the highest tetrachord in the Greek system</term>; in the second cells from these, a fourth away, the <term>chromatic diezeugmenon|the "disjunct" tetrachord</term>; in the third, a fourth away, the <term>chromatic synnemenon|the "conjunct" tetrachord</term>; in the fourth, a fourth away, the <term>chromatic meson|the middle tetrachord</term>; in the fifth, a fourth away, the <term>chromatic hypaton|the lowest tetrachord</term>; in the sixth, at the <term>paramese|the note B</term>, because it shares a harmony of a fifth with the chromatic hyperbolaion and a fourth with the chromatic meson. In the middle, nothing is to be placed, because no other quality of sounds in the chromatic genre of symphony can have a harmonious resonance. In the highest division and region of cells, in the first corners, let vessels be constructed and placed with the sound of the <term>diatonic hyperbolaion</term>; in the second, a fourth away, the <term>diatonic diezeugmenon</term>; in the third, a fourth away, the <term>diatonic synnemenon</term>; in the fourth, a fourth away, the <term>diatonic meson</term>; in the fifth, a fourth away, the <term>diatonic hypaton</term>; in the sixth, a fourth away, the <term>proslambanomenos|the lowest note of the scale</term>; in the middle, at the <term>mese|the central note</term>, because it has harmonic commonalities of an octave with the proslambanomenos and a fifth with the diatonic hypaton.*

Now that this most accurate description of the theater has been set before the eyes of the curious reader—a task attempted by no one else until now, as far as I know—let us now discuss the individual parts a little more precisely. Note that in Figure I of the illustration, we have left only 9 cells open; in the highest tier, in the three open cells, we have represented the size, position, and shape of the acoustic vessels <note>original: "Vasorum Echæorum"</note>. In the second open tier, we have shown the cavity and the interior construction of the cells, along with the wedges upon which the acoustic vessels were to be placed. In the third open tier, we have shown only the interior construction of the cells; the remaining closed cells show the exterior construction facing the theater. These must be dealt with one by one in order.

§. I.
## On the Cells

Within the interior tier, thirteen cells were arranged in order, separated from one another in such a way that each had certain passages or channels in their sides, through which the voice, propagated into the neighboring cells, would always receive greater and greater increase...
