*Book IX. Reflected Sound.* 287

...then it would take it up. The shape of the interior surface of the cells could be no other than circular <note>original: *Cyclica*</note>, as it is most suitable for propagating and amplifying the voice, as we have described here. The size of the cells corresponded to the size of the theater; and indeed the cells were not visible, as they were hidden within the flooring. However, they had an opening on the outside, either rectangular or oval, two feet long and half a foot high, of the sort we have delineated in the spaces CM and DP at compartments 1, 2, 3, and the rest of the cells in certain order. Through these, the voice of the actors, working its way inside, was multiplied by various reflections. Once multiplied and driven through various circuits, it was finally communicated through the side passages (which we have depicted on the side in the open cells MLR) to the neighboring cells, and from each individual cell to the next in order. Therefore, it was no wonder that such a great resonance was created in the theater. I say "through the side passages," because without these the voice could by no means achieve its vigor, being instead absorbed and smothered within the cells without an exit.

->### §. II.<-
->### Concerning the Echea or bronze vessels.<-

**Echea** <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἠχεῖν* (apo tou ēchein)</note>, so named from "to sound," or bronze vessels, were placed individually into each cell in this manner: in the middle of the floor of the cell, a wedge or fulcrum was erected, as the cell ML indicates. This was inserted into the bottom of the vessel with great industry so that it might rest upon it most freely, not unlike what is often done with our bells. For vessels placed on sharp points resound better, since there is no obstacle that can hinder the vibration of the bell. The shape of the vessels could be none other than that which our bells have, from which they differed in no way. For they could not be angular, because the corners would have hindered the sound; nor spherical, as some wish, since this is against the intention of Vitruvius <margin>The shape and figure of the Echea.</margin> <note>Vitruvius was a Roman architect whose work *De Architectura* is the primary source for ancient theater acoustics.</note>, who expressly says the vessels were open at the bottom and rested on wedges. Others think they were like mortars, which I do not contradict, for a mortar is entirely similar to a bell and does not differ from it, except that a bell is somewhat more contracted than a mortar. They had, therefore, something of a conical shape, like our bells and mortars. Experience has taught for many centuries that these produce the best resonance of all; and we have shown this extensively in our treatise on bells.

->### §. III.<-
->### How they sounded and by what means the Echea vessels were stimulated.<-

There is a great controversy in this place concerning the stimulation of the vessels, as many cannot grasp how these harmonic vessels produced a sound. Some think the vessels had little hammers attached to iron wires or cords which, when pulled, struck the bells and made them sound, not unlike what is done in modern bell-tower organs; so says Cesare Cesariano <note>An Italian architect and the first to publish a translated commentary on Vitruvius in 1521.</note> in his commentaries on Vitruvius. Others think the vessels sounded solely by the impact and force of the air stirred by the voice of the actors. However, this cannot hold up, since no voice is so great that it suffices to stimulate a bell; and this is evident in our own bells, which, if they could sound by the mere agitation of the air, I would certainly say they would produce a perpetual sound, since they are perpetually exposed to the air, and usually in a high place where the wind dominates. Yet no experience has ever shown that even the most impetuous wind ever caused a sound of this kind. <margin>An experiment on the sound of the Echea.</margin> Indeed, so that I might gain some experience of this matter, I arranged for glass bells to be cast, and I carefully arranged them in concave places situated according to the Vitruvian method. I applied voices according to all degrees of intensity, yet no sound was perceived, but only a ringing <note>original: *tinnitus*</note> such as is usually felt in wells and concave places. Most people maintain, however, that those concave cells and vessels were only used to provide a great resonance to the theater; which I do not deny;

<summary>Kircher describes the architectural design of "Echea" (bronze acoustic vessels) used in ancient theaters to amplify sound, arguing that their bell-like shape was essential for resonance. He remains skeptical that the human voice alone could make these vessels ring, citing his own failed experiments with glass models.</summary>
<keywords>Echea, Vitruvius, theater acoustics, resonance, bronze vessels, Cesare Cesariano, bell-making, architectural magic, sound amplification</keywords>

288 *The Art of Universal Music*

I deny it; for I do not see what such ingenious industry in proportioning the vessels according to harmonic consonances <note>Harmonic consonances refer to intervals like the octave or fifth that sound pleasing to the ear.</note> could have contributed without the vessels being immediately touched. To what end such a studious and subtle distribution of vessels—ordered according to the triple musical genus: <term>diatonic</term>, <term>chromatic</term>, and <term>enharmonic</term> <note>These are the three "genera" or systems of tuning used in ancient Greek music theory.</note>—would have been arranged, I am least able to discern, since without an actual symphony <note>In this context, "symphony" refers to the sounding together of instruments or voices.</note> all these things would have been useless and of no use. 

Either it must be said that they were established only to increase the voices of the Actors, or that they had some other use. However, it is not likely that the <term>Echea</term> <note>Resonating bronze jars placed under theater seats, as described by the Roman architect Vitruvius.</note> were constructed with such great harmonic artifice for the sake of a greater resonance of the voice alone; nor can it be said (as was proved a little earlier) that they were stirred into harmonic symphony by the voice alone, or by the striking of the air within them. 

For this reason, Bonaventura Cavalieri, in his short work on the *Burning Mirror*, thinks that these Vitruvian cells—as well as the <term>Echea</term>—were partly of a parabolic and partly of a hyperbolic shape. He suggests that the voice, having entered and been struck, was increased by a certain infinite multiplication of rays. To prove this, he brings forward a construction of this theater much different from the one we read described by Vitruvius; for he imagines parabolic arches from the place of the voice all the way to the cells, in which—as if from a center—

<margin>
How the 
*Echea* vessels 
were stirred 
into harmony.
</margin>

the voice of the parabolic arches was diffused and multiplied infinitely, producing a marvelous effect both in the intensity of the voice and in the stirring of the <term>Echea</term>. But as I have said, because he imagines a new theater in this way—of which nothing similar is read in Vitruvius—he does not seem to have satisfied Architects to such a degree, since by drawing away from the text of Vitruvius, anyone could easily devise new <term>Echea</term> structures. 

The question is asked, therefore: how did these theaters have such great resonance, and how were the vessels arranged for such a brilliant effect as historians report? It should be noted, then, that a double harmonic sound can be considered in this kind of <term>Echea</term>. The first was made through a certain ringing or harmonic hum, while external voices entering the small cells and being struck by various agitations, finally—with the sound multiplied and a certain force applied to the <term>Echea</term> vessels—produced that ringing which the tremor of the vessels exhibited. The second could be through small hammers pulled by cords and arranged to strike the <term>Echea</term>. 

The use of the first seems to have been so that the voice of the actors, received into those hollows and multiplied there, would acquire a greater resonance, as has been said; and all the Commentators on Vitruvius agree with me. This was indeed nothing other than a certain symphonic ringing caused by the tremor of the <term>Echea</term> distributed in various harmonic proportions. 

The other use could have been in the preludes or interludes. For, in order to excite the listeners and sharpen their expectation of the things to follow, the <term>Echea</term> were sounded before the characters entered the theater. But they could not sound unless iron wires, equipped with their own hammers, were led through all the cells. Indeed, with this wire skillfully drawn through all the cells, someone specifically assigned to this task stirred all the vessels into a most perfect harmony. These vessels excited a vehement sound in the cells, perceptible far and wide, and it was a source of all the more admiration because the music-making machinery was hidden. 

Vitruvius himself hints that this was the chief use in these words: "It stirred up an increased clarity and a harmony appropriate to the singing." <note>original: "Excitauit auctam claritatem & concentu conuenientem sibi consonantiam."</note> The harmony, therefore, was of vessels arranged according to musical consonances; but it was said above that a similar vehement harmony could not be made by the striking of the voice alone. Therefore, having been stirred into harmony by the stated method of hidden cords, they sounded—a thing which Cesare Cesariano, cited above, also suspected. And unless it happened by this method, I do not see what other way there could have been by which they were stirred into consonance. For by this same artifice, according to Pliny, they exhibited thunder and other rumblings. 

As for the fact that Vitruvius says nothing openly about the said cords and hammers, this happened because he himself never saw such a theater, but only received the account from the Greeks. Thus he frequently alleges Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist.</note>—who likely stood as the Author of this kind of theater—and follows his musical precepts, though he himself is doubtful. Nor was there any other theater of this kind in Greece or Rome besides the Corinthian one; we read (as Vitruvius himself testifies) that after the defeat of Corinth, the <term>Echea</term> were taken away and hung in the temple of Fortune in Rome by Mummius <note>Kircher's text says Pericles, but historically it was Lucius Mummius who brought the spoils from Corinth; Vitruvius mentions the vessels being brought to the temple of Honor and Virtue.</note>. And certainly, Vitruvius himself seems to have had some objection regarding the construction of this theater from the more skilled Architects of his time, which he contends to propose and solve at once in these words:

                                                                                                                                  He will say

# Book IX. Sound-Reflecting Magic 289

*Perhaps someone will say that many theaters are built in Rome every year, and yet no account of these matters <note>The author is referring to the placement of acoustic resonance vessels (echeia) used to amplify the voice.</note> was taken in them; but they are mistaken in this, because all public wooden theaters have many levels of planking <term>tabulationes|wooden tiers or floorboards</term>, which must necessarily resonate. This indeed can be observed even with lyre-players <term>citharoedi|performers who sang while playing the lyre</term>, who, when they wish to sing in a higher pitch, turn themselves toward the stage doors <note>original: "scenæ valuas"</note>, and thus receive a harmony for their voice from their assistance. However, when theaters are constructed from solid materials—that is, from masonry, stone, or marble, which cannot resonate—then these vessels must be deployed according to this method. If, however, it is asked in which theater these were used in Rome, we cannot show one, but they are found in the regions of Italy and in many cities of the Greeks. We also have as an authority Lucius Mummius <note>A Roman general who destroyed Corinth in 146 BCE.</note>, who, after destroying the theater of the Corinthians, brought its bronze vessels to Rome and dedicated them from the spoils of war at the Temple of the Moon. Many skillful architects also, due to a lack of means, chose earthenware jars <term>dolia|large ceramic storage vessels</term> that resonated in this way, and by arranging them according to this logic, they achieved very useful effects.*

Indeed, I have received testimony from many that a voice sent out from there is returned twenty-four times—indeed, thirty times and more, depending on the greater or lesser exertion of the voice. I even believe that there is no certain and determined number for the reflection of the voice, but that it can be multiplied unto infinity; and that the same thing happens as occurs in the vibrations of a string, whose strikes appear clearly enough at the beginning, yet at the end disappear due to extreme speed, and the sound gradually dies away. The same thing appears in the reflection of mirrors. The cause of this Echo is therefore asked. I respond that the cause is the position of two parallel buildings situated at a proportionate distance. Furthermore, since the said walls possess the highest degree of equality and flatness, being free of all roughness, the voice is reflected with the greatest ease. I demonstrate the matter thus:

-> [Diagram Description: A geometric representation of sound reflecting between two walls. Two vertical lines represent walls AC and BD. A central horizontal line labeled IE connects them. From point E (the window), sound travels to point I on the opposite wall. Let the walls **AC** and **BD** placed here in the figure be parallel and very flat, having a distance proportioned for returning a two-syllable voice. For the <term>phonismus</term> <note>Kircher's term for a "sound-ray" or the path of a sound wave</note>, according to the first proposition of <term>Echometry</term> <note>The mathematical science of measuring echoes</note>, is propagated from **E** to **I**, and is returned from that same place along the same path to **E**; from **E** again to **I**, and from **I** once more to **E**, and thus by infinite alternating repercussions until the voice, weakened by too much rebounding, finally fails. This is no different than a ball which, struck violently back and forth between two narrow walls, finally fails after five or six rebounds as its impetus ceases. And it is certain that there is no other cause for this thing than what we have said; because, since according to the first proposition of Echometry the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, an Echo can be made by no other means except through that normal, cylindrical <term>phonismus</term> **IE**, established between two parallel walls. For if other parts of the wall (for example, **A** and **C**) reflected the voice, the angles **A** and **C** would necessarily have to be right angles; but according to Book 1, Proposition 15 [of Euclid], they are acute, and propagate the voice to other parts (for example, through **K** and **N**). Therefore, from point **I**, and from no other place, does such a manifold reflection of the voice occur; even though concave—

**Corollary I.**
From this, it is established that if someone were to construct a similar building—that is, two walls separated by a distance of about 63 paces—they would obtain a similar Echo, since nothing else is required to return the voice distinctly except a proportionate distance, which 63 paces provides <note>Kircher calculated that sound requires a specific distance to be perceived as a distinct echo rather than just a blurring of sound.</note>. ### Prelude III.
### Regarding the surviving Ear of Dionysius in Syracuse.

A most famous structure is still on display today in Syracuse, Sicily, which some call the Prison of the Tyrant Dionysius, others the "Little Ear," and others by different names. It was architected with such ingenuity that someone standing in the region of the doorway can perfectly hear whatever is spoken, returned with a multiplied sound. Having heard much about this, partly from authors and partly from the reports of others, I undertook an investigation of it in the year 1638 while I was passing through Syracuse, and I finally discovered its causes. Mirabella describes this with singular care in his *Ichnography of Syracuse* <term>Ichnography: a ground plan or map showing the relative positions of parts of a building.</term>.

It was constructed by the Tyrant in the shape of an ear, following the model of nature, with singular ingenuity and industry.

...the castle or Ducal Palace, commonly called the *Salone*, or known as the Arsenal, once served for public games; now it is a storehouse for military equipment. A Roman *braccio* or "arm" was a unit of measurement roughly equal to 64 centimeters or 25 inches.</note> up to the ceiling; its length is 124 Roman cubits; its width is 24. We have briefly set forth the description of the entire building insofar as it pertains to our purpose; therefore, nothing remains but to explain the reason for such a manifold Echo.

<margin>The reason for the Pavia Echo explained.</margin> When the northern and southern doors are open—the latter of which is situated nearly 30 paces from the city walls—the Echo responds eleven times to one standing in the middle; with the southern door closed, it responds eight times; and with both closed, only six times. There can indeed be no other reason for this than the obstacles of the walls outside the doors, which reflect the <term>audible species</term> <note>original: *species sonoræ*. In Kircher’s physics, "species" refers to the physical emanations or forms of sound traveling through the medium of air.</note> eleven times in proportion to the distance when the doors are open; however, with the doors closed, since it has a shorter distance to travel, it must necessarily have fewer reflections. It has been observed, however, that this Echo has its greatest power in reflecting two-syllable words, just as was said regarding the Echo of Milan. The natural voice is most fit for forming an Echo in this place; however, an artificial sound made through a trumpet or drum confuses the echo by the violence of the sound (the reason for which we have shown extensively in the preceding pages). It is written, however, that if a trumpet or the flute commonly called a *cornetto* <note>A Renaissance wind instrument made of wood covered in leather with a trumpet-style mouthpiece.</note> sounds these intervals: *do, mi, sol* <note>original: *ut, mi, sol*. These are the first, third, and fifth notes of the scale, forming a major chord.</note>; through these single syllables, the Echo forms a certain harmony in the manner of an eleven-voice fugue—a wonderful thing to hear.

Furthermore, this Echo has different properties according to the different positions of those shouting. For it appears one way to those standing in the middle when people shout from the front or side, and another way to those standing at the doors when someone shouts from the middle. The reason for this is nothing other than the position of the opposite walls, in which, either through intentional or accidental distance, the reflected sound species, being struck back multiple times, present various deceptions to the ears. The cause of all these things can only be unknown to someone who has either not read our preceding arguments regarding <term>polyphonisms</term> <note>Kircher’s term for the phenomenon of multiple-repeating echoes.</note> or, if they have read them, has not understood them. As for the fact that today it does not provide those miracles of reflected voice as it did in the time of Cardano and Blancanus <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician.</note>, the reason is that the place is now filled with various military apparatuses, which hinder the manifold reflection of the voice. A manifest proof of this is that on the western side, where such obstacles are seen to be placed, the Echo is not perceived by those standing there, as the species are dissipated and absorbed. And these are the things I thought should be said concerning this famous Echo of the city of Pavia.

# About the Mantuan Hall, and another in the famous Palace of Caprarola of the Farnese Duke, which wonderfully intensifies the voice.

The trick is easy and can be easily introduced by architects into any vaulted building.

### <term>PRACTICAL APPLICATION I.<note>original: "PRAGMATIA I"; a technical or practical instruction.</note></term>

->To arrange the Halls of Princes in such a way that nothing can be said so softly that it is not heard either in the same or in another room.<-

<margin>Channels have a wonderful power for gathering voices.</margin>
Some have thought this could be done by a hidden system of pipes, such as [Giambattista della] Porta describes; namely, when channels are led from various rooms into a single location, a Prince, by applying his ears to the opening where all the channels meet, will perceive the voices from the different rooms. If this is understood to mean that any soft word spoken in the bedrooms will fly through the pipes and present itself to the Prince's ears, it is false. Voices produced in a room are not gathered at the opening of a pipe; rather, they are scattered and absorbed in the open air of the room, and they expire, already weak, before they ever reach the channel. If, however, the mouth is applied directly to the pipe and the voices are murmured inside, there is no doubt that the Prince will distinctly perceive those murmured words from the individual rooms. For I have heard a voice over 500 feet away, not only in a lead tube of great length, but also (along with others) in an earthen one. 
<margin>A channel of 500 feet conveys voices.</margin>
The tube, however, ought not to be too wide, nor too narrow; the proper width or diameter for tubes intended to transmit voices should be three inches. For drums and trumpets, somewhat larger channels may be used. 
<margin>Why tubes embedded in a wall convey the voice better than those exposed to the open air.</margin>
When these tubes are built into a wall, they convey the voice better than when they are exposed to the open air. The reason for this is simply that, when walled in, they do not admit as much noticeable vibration as they do when they are free. Vibration greatly hinders the forward movement of voices, easily confusing them with its own shaking. The exact opposite is found in solid beams and other long, solid bodies, 
<margin>The opposite happens in a solid beam.</margin>
which lose all the power of a murmured voice when walled in. They acquire a much greater power of conveying sound the more they are exposed to a free medium, as was demonstrated above. Since the vibration of the whole object carries the noise excited at one end to the other end, a beam buried in the earth or walled in loses its freedom to vibrate, and must therefore lose its freedom to propagate the voice.

And although this matter of pipes is very simple, it cannot be denied that many truly paradoxical things can be achieved by the aid of such hidden channels, if the craftsman and <term>Echotect<note>original: "Echorectus/Echotectus"; an architect or engineer specializing in the science of echoes and acoustics.</note></term> uses sufficient wisdom and skill. The subterranean workshop of a certain chemist taught me the truth of this matter; it had no hole or window, using only a single pipe to draw away smoke, and was equipped with a very small door. When the door was closed, any voices spoken inside were perfectly—and to my great admiration—heard at the far opening of the pipe. Having been taught by this experiment, I am thoroughly persuaded that something similar can undoubtedly be put into effect in the palaces of Princes. The Echotect should set the matter up as follows:

Let a receptacle be made, capable of holding a few people, 8 palms long (as shown in the following figure), 8 palms wide, and 8 palms high. In the figure, the width is marked RX (8 palms) and the height DV (8 palms). It should have a very small, low door, A, which can be closed very tightly. A window of very thick crystal should also be set into the side and embedded in the wall so that when voices resonate inside, the sound can escape neither through the window nor the door, but only through the channel DE. 
<margin>How the acoustic channel ought to be directed.</margin>
This channel, led through a hidden passage of the house into Room F, you will connect to the vaulted ceiling (D) of the chamber (which, according to the proposed model, must be highly polished and shaped like a twisted cone) in such a way that they appear as one continuous surface. At the other end, the pipe should have a flared opening at E, so that the exiting sound can spread itself freely, and you will have a completed structure. For if anyone enters Chamber AD with the door and window closed and makes any sound, the sound of those voices, since it cannot escape elsewhere, will pass through—

# Practical Application III.

*How to arrange halls designed with parabolic surfaces so that an ear placed at a certain point can perceive anything spoken in a low whisper.*

Although the nature and properties of the parabola have been discussed sufficiently above, lest you commit some error in practice, I have thought it best to put forward some difficulties here. It should be known, then, that a parabolic surface can be considered in two ways: obtuse and acute. The more obtuse the concave surface is, the closer it will have its focus, or <term>acoustic point</term> <note>The "focus" of the parabola where sound waves converge.</note>, to the vertex of the parabola; however, the more acute that same surface is, the farther the acoustic point will be from the vertex of the parabola. Moreover, the point or meeting-place of the rays is always on the axis of the parabola.

<margin>It is necessary that the lines within the parabola be parallel to converge at a single point.</margin>

Secondly, it must be known that for all sound-lines to flow together into the acoustic point, it is necessary that the sound-lines falling within the concave parabolic surface be parallel to the axis. Hence, if the parabola is sufficiently wide, even all the smallest "images" of the voice <note>original: "vocis species" — a term from medieval and early modern optics/acoustics referring to the form or energy of the sound traveling through the air</note> will flow together into one point. But let us demonstrate the matter a little more clearly: let the parabola be ABC, the focus D; I say that the images of the voice will not radiate into point D unless they are all carried parallel to the axis BDE. For if the voice radiates from E into O and I (for we showed above that voice is propagated through conic <term>phonisms</term> <note>Kircher uses "phonismus" to describe the geometric shape of a sound wave as it travels.</note>), it is certain, according to the rules of reflection handed down above, that the lines falling from E into O and I will reflect not into D, but into X; for in this case, the angle of incidence will equal the angle of reflection. Again, if the voice is positioned outside the axis and radiates into the concave surface, it is indeed true that only one single ray will be reflected into D; however, the other radiations will establish different centers of reflection outside the axis—as is evident in the sound-line falling from G into V and reflected from there into D—while the lines radiating from G into R and Z will converge neither in D nor in X, but in P.

[A geometric diagram showing a parabola with various lines of reflection labeled with letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, N, O, P, R, V, X, Z.]

<margin>Conic sound propagation <note>original: "Phonismus conicus"</note> in a parabola acquires different centers or reflections on the axis.</margin>

You see, therefore, that a voice radiating conically within a parabola provides nothing singular unless it is positioned on the axis; for then, the lines of only one conic phonism will radiate together into a single point. Let there be a phonism ABC in the following figure of the parabola BDC; let the source of sound be on the axis of the parabola AD. I say that the lines of the conic phonism ABC falling on the concave surface of the parabola will reflect into D. Since all the lines on the concave surface of the parabola establish a circle which is the same as the base of the cone, it is certain that all will reflect, under an equality of angles, into a certain and determined point of the axis. But since this cone is not of one single type...

->Another method.<-

<margin>Another method for increasing parabolic sound reflection.</margin>

**Mersenne** <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath often called the "father of acoustics."</note>, in his *Universal Harmony* <note>original: *Harmonia Universali*, Mersenne's most famous work on music and acoustics published in 1636.</note>, provides another method, which I will add here so that one may judge what should be thought of it. Since he saw that **cylindrical phonism** <term>cylindrical phonism: a term describing sound waves traveling in a straight, parallel beam rather than spreading out</term> was difficult to achieve, and that the conical shape was not sufficient, he hoped to achieve something better with a **double parabola**. He turned a smaller parabola toward a larger concave one, arranged so they shared a common **focus** <note>The mathematical point where all reflected waves meet.</note>. In this arrangement, the sound falling on the larger concave surface would be reflected through the focus into the smaller concave surface. From there, it would finally be sent out in parallel lines through a hole cut in the larger parabola (sized to match the smaller one) to the ears of a person standing behind it.

[Diagram 1: A geometric diagram showing two parabolas sharing a common focus G, with lines representing sound waves reflecting between them and exiting as parallel lines towards points H, I, L, M. Labels include A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, L, M, N, O, P, Q, R, S, T, V, X, Y, Z.]

Let the larger parabola be **ABC** and the smaller **DEF**, applied to each other in such a way that the focus **G** is common to both. Let the larger parabola be cut away from **V** to **P**. Once this is done, let there be sounds at **X** and **Y**, and sound-lines **XT**, **XV**, **YP**, and **YQ**. Falling upon the concave surface of the larger parabola, they are reflected through **G** into **S** and **R**; meanwhile, **XT** and **XV**, falling on **N** and **O**, will be reflected again into **LM** and **HI**, until they finally present themselves as a **cylindrical phonism** to ears positioned at **HILM**. 

Certainly, these ideas have a beautiful theoretical appearance at first glance, but they achieve absolutely no success in practice. For besides the very few sound-lines the larger parabola can catch, the smaller one will transmit even fewer, and those will be significantly weakened by that parallel projection. I would even dare to say that the method we described on the previous page is a hundred times better than this one. Indeed, Mersenne himself, foreseeing the difficulty of the matter, gave up on it as if it were a lost cause and fled to another method, though it is not much better. 

It is clearly evident that there can be no success for this device, both for the reasons stated and because of the focus; since it is common to both parabolas, it would require skill greater than that of **Archimedes** <note>The ancient Greek mathematician renowned for his precision in geometry and mechanics.</note> to align both precisely. 

<margin>Many things which theory proves are difficult to put into practice.</margin>

In this second attempt, let the larger parabola be **ABC**, and let the smaller one **D** be placed opposite it as shown in the figure. Let it have a **convex** parabolic surface, and let both share a common focus at **E**. With the device arranged this way, the sound-lines from **G** and **F** falling on the concave surface of the larger parabola reflect from points **o**, **n**, **x**, and **h**—not into the focus **E**, but onto the convex surface of the smaller parabola **D**. Finally, they will reverberate the captured sound in a cylindrical projection into the ears of the listener at **I** and **R**. But who does not see that this too contains nothing in itself besides mere theory?

For a smaller parabolic curve, besides the fact that it matches the focus of a larger one only with great difficulty, also casts back such few and weak reflections into the convex side of the smaller one that I think someone placed at <note>original: "IR"</note> point IR could hardly gain any notable increase in the volume of the voice. Therefore, whoever intends to build an acoustic structure using parabolic curves should proceed by no other method than the one we have described, and he will achieve an infallible result. For it is not necessary for parabolic surfaces in this business of <term>echotectonics</term> <note>the art of designing buildings for specific acoustic or echo effects</note> to be as mathematically exact as is required for <term>burning mirrors</term> <note>curved mirrors used to focus sunlight into a point of intense heat</note>. For since sound lines have their own width—and indeed a quite notable one—only a person who has failed to understand what came before could be ignorant of the fact that the acoustic center of a parabola is not a mathematical point, but a physical one, endowed with its own breadth.

### Practical Exercise IV
### To construct a hyperbolic structure that gathers sounds.

<margin>The principle of the hyperbolic structure.</margin>

Whatever we have said regarding the parabola must also be applied to hyperbolic surfaces, so that nothing further remains to be said about forming surfaces of this kind. If anyone possesses a <term>hyperbola-shaper</term> <note>original: "hyperboloplasten"</note> suitable for the capacity of a place, he may mark out two hyperbolic surfaces in any gallery along with their acoustic centers. If an ear is placed at these centers, it will perceive voices, however softly they are uttered, just as in parabolic structures. Let us therefore hasten to other matters.

### Practical Exercise V
### To construct elliptical structures that wonderfully intensify sounds.

Compared to the other <term>conic sections</term> <note>the shapes made by slicing through a cone: circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas</note>, the ellipse is the most suitable of all for our business of echotectonics; for this reason, we have decided to treat elliptical structures more extensively here. What an ellipse is and how it may be drawn has been stated above; let us therefore proceed to the task. Elliptical domes in buildings have this unique property: they always produce two points, or centers, in the open space within. First, let there be an <term>ellipse-shaper</term> <note>original: "Ellipticoplastes"</note> of a length equal to the required length of the oval dome.

### Practical Exercise VII. <note>original: "Pragmatia VII"</note>
*Another way to build the same structure much more skillfully, and to extend it over a greater distance.*

**B**ut if anyone should wish to architect a similar work of art over a very remote distance, he shall begin the matter thus: within two walls determining the chosen space, let 4, 5, 6, or 7 elliptical "eggs" <note>The author uses the term "eggs" to describe the three-dimensional ovoid or elliptical shape of the ceiling vaults</note> be formed in exactly the same way as you see done in the preceding figure. <margin>A remarkable elliptical architecture for multiplying voices.</margin>

[Diagram showing a series of four ellipses connected end-to-end between two walls labeled F-H and G-I. Two human heads are depicted at the ends, one at point A and one at point E. Lines representing sound waves reflect off the elliptical surfaces, passing through focal points labeled A, B, C, D, and E. Vertical lines labeled V-X pass through the focal points B, C, and D.]

In this figure, within the walls FG and HI, let 4 elliptical "eggs" be arranged so that the acoustic centers <note>The focal points of the ellipses</note> or foci are shared between each pair of ellipses. Thus, the acoustic center B of ellipse AB is shared with ellipse BC, and the acoustic center C of ellipse BC is shared with ellipse CD, and the acoustic center D of ellipse CD is shared with ellipse DE. Therefore, the ellipses must be cut off along the lines VX passing through the centers, so that the individual ellipses might look like open-ended jars. You will then have a magnificent secret ready. For if someone positioned at A whispers even the lowest voice, another person positioned at E—even five hundred feet away—will perceive it as clearly as if it were whispered directly into their ears. For all the sound lines reflected in the elliptical vault AB will converge at B as if at a center; there, multiplied and intensified without confusion, each one continues further and will form another reflection in the second elliptical vault at C. Joined and multiplied again in this center, they will enter the elliptical vault CD, and being reflected there, they will join at D. Finally, reflected again from here in the fourth vault, they will at last arrive, intensified and multiplied, at the ears of the person positioned at E, who will perceive the "sound-images" <note>original: "sonoras species" — a term from early physics referring to the form or essence of the sound traveling through space</note> as clearly as if the speaker were present at A. The demonstration of the matter is so clear that nothing besides a consideration of the figure seems to be required to understand it.

But let these things suffice for the ingenious reader to discover innumerable other applications.

**Book IX. Magic of Sound Reflection. 303**

**Practical Project VIII.**

*To arrange a spiral twisted cone, or screw-like tube, within a certain building in such a way that it renders any articulate sounds from a public area—no matter how remote—into an inner chamber so surely and distinctly as if they were right at the listener's ears, without anyone suspecting where the sound might be coming from. See Illustration XVI.*

We have deservedly reserved for the end this most perfect and most admirable echo-building machine <note>original: "Echotectonicum machinamentum"</note>; I know not what could be more wonderful in the realm of natural magic. But lest I keep the curious reader in suspense any longer, I shall explain the matter in few words. <margin>Amazing acoustic construction via a spiral tube.</margin> Let a screw-like <term>cochleate</term> <note>From the Latin "cochlea," meaning snail shell; refers to a spiral or screw-shaped structure.</note> tube or a spirally twisted cone be carved into stone or a natural cliff face. If the location does not allow for that, let it be shaped from plaster, clay, or <term>tufa</term> <note>A porous volcanic rock easy to carve.</note>. It should be designed with this ingenuity: that at a distance, it has a very wide opening facing toward some public place frequented by a crowd of people; the other end of the tube, however, should terminate in a small hole within a private inner chamber, far removed from the public crowd. 

The interior spiral surface should be polished as exactly as possible (as far as is achievable in stone); or if the stone is too rough, the interior surface should be coated with plaster for a smoother finish. Once this machine is finished, I say that nothing can be said so secretly in the opposite forum, square, or public place facing the opening of the spiral tube that is not transferred through the spiral into that hidden room. In this room, therefore, you will perceive the various voices of animals, the secret whispers of men, singing, weeping, and wailing as distinctly and clearly as if they were happening in the room itself. No one will even suspect the source of such a prodigious sound effect. 

Observe the construction in the following Illustration XVI, where the palace is represented by the letters ABCD. The spiral tube inserted in the wall or cut into the rock is G, its opening is H, and its end is E. The forum <note>The public square or marketplace.</note> is L; in this space, nothing can be uttered so secretly that it is not perceived within the room, however distant it may be. This is the machine which far surpasses not only <term>parabolic</term> <note>Curves that focus sound to a single point.</note> but also elliptical and all other acoustic structures proposed thus far. This is because it is constructed according to the model of nature observed in the structure of the human ear, and it abounds with infinite reflections of voices (as we showed in problem 8, which is why the voice is so miraculously intensified). 

Furthermore, such a tube can be set in two positions: either horizontal (or sloping) as marked G, or vertical as marked PO. Both produce remarkable effects, though the vertical is more powerful because sound is carried upwards more easily than downwards or laterally. We have represented both tube paths here in the illustration. We discovered this admirable machine by studying the "Ear of Dionysius" <note>A famous limestone cave in Syracuse, Sicily, shaped like a human ear, known for its incredible acoustics where a whisper can be heard high above.</note> which still survives in Syracuse, the description of which can be found in the history of echoes provided a little earlier.

**Digression on the Spiral Cone.**

Why there should be such a great power of sound multiplication in a twisted helical cone should rightly seem a wonder to anyone. Certainly, when I thought long and hard about this business, I finally discovered that a helical cone twisted in a certain ratio imitates the properties of a parabola. Within this shape, while infinite clusters of sounds are formed, it is no wonder that it obtains such great power in multiplying sound.

It is also known that a helical line can be created that is equal to a parabolic curve, which the curious reader may understand as follows: Let there be a helical line within the circle marked with the letters *a b c d e f n*. Then, through the vertex *G* of the axis, the parabola *GT* is described which passes through the end of the semi-ordinate *ST*. I say, *GT*...

III. Instruments modeled after the ears of animals that possess great acoustic power also have a great capacity for strengthening the sense of hearing. Indeed, some animals are endowed with exceedingly sharp hearing, such as the deer, the dog, the hare, and all other animals with large ears. Among these, the structure of the hare’s ear is especially marvelous. Since it is a very timid and entirely defenseless animal, Nature seems to have fortified it with both extremely acute hearing—serving as a scout for sensing approaching dangers—and with feet like weapons, well-suited for running. If anyone, therefore, possessed a hearing tube fashioned after the model of a hare’s ear, he would find a wonderful secret for strengthening the hearing. An organ of this kind has, first, a very long external ear and a sort of elliptical cartilaginous envelope, which can be turned in every direction to better collect the "sound rays" <note>Kircher conceptualizes sound traveling in rays, similar to light.</note> within it. Then, it narrows from a long, cavernous space and finally ends in a spiral <term>cochlea; the spiral-shaped part of the inner ear</term>. Stretched across this spiral is that membrane which in anatomy we call the **tympanum** <note>the eardrum</note>, along with the **malleus, incus, and stapes** <note>the hammer, anvil, and stirrup bones of the middle ear</note>. The voice is thus collected by that oblong and versatile ear within the cavernous passage of the inner ear, where, increased by a single reflection, it glides with great force into the spiral meander. Striking the eardrum there, it moves the internal air, from which finally arises that very sharp sensation we admire in hares. If you compare a hearing tube to this industry of Nature, you will find, as I said, a certain admirable secret for easily strengthening the hearing.

In order to proceed more securely in this imitation of Nature, we have seen to it that the ears of certain animals possessing superior hearing were prepared by the most skilled anatomists. We have displayed these to be viewed alongside the tube in **Illustration II**, so that you might shape your artistic work according to the hidden structure of the hearing organ brought out into the open, and manufacture hearing tubes with diligent industry.

# PREPARATORY 
## EXERCISE I.
### *On the construction of Aeolian Chambers for the use of hydraulic organs.*
### Practical Procedure I.
### *To construct Aeolian Chambers.*

We call those "Aeolian Chambers" <note>Named after Aeolus, the Greek god of the winds.</note> which, being "pregnant" with wind generated from the fall of water, produce the most vehement blasts, exceeding all the force of bellows. Furthermore, chambers of this kind have the greatest utility in all mechanical work; for here in Italy, they supply a perpetual wind to iron smithies everywhere for the forging of tools. For an organ—

...they also provide an abundant supply of wind for the hydraulic <term>organ</term>—<note>Kircher is describing a water-powered pipe organ.</note>—and they turn the **phonotactic drum**. Through these means, artificial animals of all kinds are brought to life with voices, along with many other things which will be mentioned extensively in the following pages. These **Aeolian Chambers** can, however, be constructed in various ways.

### First Method: See Figure 2 in Illustration 18

<margin>First method for the construction of an Aeolian Chamber.</margin>

Let a hollow receptacle be constructed of bricks in the shape you see here. At the bottom, a marble stone **I** should be erected, brought to a highly polished surface. From **A**, let a spiral channel **A-L** be led, which should be open at the top at **A** and below at **L**; however, it must be joined to parts **A-E** in such a way that the air enclosed within finds no other exit except at **F**. Furthermore, the Chamber should have a drain-cock at **C** suitable for drawing off the water. Finally, let a channel be led out at **F** to carry the air—commonly called a **wind-trunk** <note>original: "porto vento"</note>—and you will have a completed machine. For the water, diverted from either a spring or a river through the channel **A-K**, will discharge itself with great force into the spiral channel (which ought to have very steep coils). Through this channel, accompanied by a great quantity of compressed air, it will fall onto the polished surface of stone **I** with great force and a very loud noise. From the violent impact of the rushing waters and the agitation of the splashing drops, the air enclosed within will be powerfully stirred. Constricted by these narrow spaces, as it seeks an exit and finds none except through the channel **F**, it will fly out through it with great force into the chests designated for receiving the wind. And thus, at last, a perpetual wind will be supplied to the pneumatic instruments.

<margin>Why more air is generated by a winding tube than by a cylindrical one.</margin>

I will explain in a few words why we have employed a spiral siphon and why a polished stone surface. It must be understood, therefore, that rushing water is full of air and carries a vast quantity of it down in all <term>cataracts</term> <note>original: "catadupis" — a term often used for the waterfalls of the Nile.</note>. The reason for this is sufficiently demonstrated by the abundant foam, like snow, which is nothing other than infinite little bubbles, all filled with air; from their infinite multitude and crowding, the water takes on a white and snowy color. This being the case, as soon as the water drawn through channel **A-K** has wound its way down the steep fall within the spiral curves of channel **A-L**, it will generate a great deal of air by being struck repeatedly within those curves. This would not happen in a cylindrical tube, for in such a tube it finds no impediment and, rushing in a simple fall, it would not carry as much air with it onto stone **I** as it does through the aforementioned winding channel. Therefore, the water, accompanied by copious air through said channel, will rush onto the surface of stone **I** with the greatest force. From this crash and the shattering of the water particles, new air will constantly be generated. This air, constricted within the cavity of the receptacle and finding no other exit but through **F**, will escape through it with great force and noise. So that this wind may be perpetual, and to prevent the receptacle from filling with water over time, we have provided the drain-cock **C**, through which as much water is always discharged as was let in through the winding channel; and thus, finally, the wind will be made perpetual.

### Practice II
#### To build an Aeolian Chamber in another way.

Since at the same time I was writing these things, the care of constructing a hydraulic organ in the **Quirinal Garden** <note>The gardens of the Quirinal Palace in Rome, then a papal residence.</note> was entrusted to me by the command of the Supreme Pontiff **INNOCENT X**, we constructed an Aeolian Chamber with truly remarkable success in the following manner.

The length or height of the Chamber **A-H** was 5 feet (as Figure 1 in Illustration 17 shows), and the width nearly 3 feet. Constructed of brick, it held two diaphragms in the middle, **C-D** and **E-I**, pierced with many holes in the manner of a sieve. A little below, the channel **G** bringing the water in was inserted; at **H**, a drain-cock provided an exit for the same. Thus, the water through channel **G**...

310 *Universal Music-making, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance* <note>Original title: *Musurgiæ Universalis sive Artis Consoni & Dissoni*. This is the monumental 1650 work by Athanasius Kircher on music theory and acoustics.</note>

...rushing with the greatest force, it soon excited a most powerful wind within. Because this wind was saturated with excessive moisture, these diaphragms <note>Partitions or internal walls</note> were arranged with perforations in the middle, like a sieve, so that the air might emerge purer and drier. Within these, the violent agitation of the water was broken and fractured, emitting a purer and more refined air through the A-channel. However, since it was later discovered that air which is more humid than it ought to be causes the greatest damage to the internal passages of the organ, we have, in order for the watery air to acquire the driest consistency, arranged a lead pipe **QR** twisted into a spiral <note>original: *helicem*</note> and inserted into a somewhat larger vessel **S**, shaped like an urn. Within this lead urn and its winding pipe, the humid air was so purified of all wateriness that it could be said to have been derived from an oven into the organ. And I have found this method to be the most suitable of all for hydraulic organs. Others pass down other methods, but they agree with us in almost every respect.

The Chamber ought to be situated in a place as dry as possible, so that the water is derived into it through a long channel, lest the place affect the organ with its humidity. For this reason, some people even derive air into the Chambers using bellows driven by water, instead of using the Chambers themselves. But having touched upon these matters first, let us now proceed to others.

# Practical Study III.
### *Another construction of the Aeolian Chamber.*

There are some who construct the Aeolian Chamber by this artifice. They build a Chamber of a certain size out of stone, of whatever shape is needed for the size of the organ, such as may be seen in *Figure III of Illustration XVIII.* In the bottom of this, they erect another tube **FG**, either square or cylindrical in shape—it makes no difference. Inside this, they lead another tube from **E** on the outside into the tube **FG**, leaving a space of one foot until it reaches **H**. The structure will then be complete. For the perennial water, having glided through tube **E**, will exert itself within tube **FG** until it overflows. From the spreading and force of the overflowing water falling onto the bottom of the vessel **CD**, a powerful wind will be excited. Since this wind has no other exit except through **B**, it will discharge itself through this tube into the wind-chests <note>original: *Anemonthecas*, the storage boxes for pressurized air in an organ</note> or the wind-boxes and channels. Truly, I would advise no one to use this artifice, for at the beginning it will have air that is too great and violent, and at the end, air that is too meager and weak. For the water will continuously rise within the Chamber until it is completely filled, and once full, it must be emptied again through the tap **I**. Therefore, the constructions we taught in the two preceding studies are better and much more efficient than this one, unless this were adapted so that the water collected inside the vessel, rising to a certain point (as at **MH**), neither increased nor decreased. In this way, it would always supply equal air to the wind-chests.

Having thus handed down the methods by which we force air into the wind-chests caused by the force of rushing water alone, we must now also hand down the method by which we can continue the same air, forced into the channels by artificial industry with the help of bellows.

Let it be planted near the stream in the place where the hydraulic organ is to be built...

...a suitable post **CD**, into which a transverse beam is inserted at **R** in such a way that it can move up and down at **R** as if on a pivot. Next, let a wheel **NO** be made, equipped with its own buckets, whose axle is extended and bent in the exact manner seen in the figure, inserted into the support **M** so that it can rotate there as if on a pivot. Above this, in a convenient place, two bellows equipped with weights should be fixed at **G** and **F**. Two rods are to be tied to their handles, which are inserted into the transverse beam **AB** at points **A** and **B** so that they can move freely within rings. At the end **E** of the transverse beam, another rod **LK** is let down, inserted into the curved handle at the end-ring **K** so that it can run freely within the axle **K**. Once these things are prepared, while the falling water **K** turns the wheel **NO** with its force, the wheel will rotate both the axle and the curved handle **MK** together. Since the rod is attached at **K**, as it descends toward the lower part, the handle **KE** to which it is attached will pull the transverse beam **AB** down with it. As this beam descends, one bellows (namely **G**) will necessarily be raised, while the other **F**, by descending, will promote the ascent of bellows **G** by its own weight **M**. However, as the handle **K** ascends, the rod will lift the bellows **F**, while the other bellows—pressed both by weight **G** and the rod—necessarily descends; and thus they will continue in alternating turns. From the pressure of the bellows, air is violently forced into the **Aeolian Chamber** <note>The "Aeolian Chamber" (Camera Aeolia) was Kircher's term for a wind reservoir used to provide a steady supply of air to organ pipes.</note>, from where it will finally be diverted through channels wherever one pleases. Anyone who wishes to multiply the number of bellows can easily put this into effect by using many curved handles arranged in different ways, as appears in figure **V** of the said illustration <note>original: "Iconismi"</note>. In that figure, four bellows **A, B, C, D**, one after the other in order, lift the axle **EF** equipped with four handles **K, I, H, G**, and will stir up a great wind. For the moving water, gliding onto the wheel, moves the axle **EF**. <margin>Another method using bellows</margin> The curved handles, corresponding to the rods of each individual bellows, now lift and now depress the bellows according to the position of the handles; but the figure places the matter before the eyes better than I can explain with many words.

The use of these bellows is varied and manifold; for by these, organs are brought to life, the songs of birds are staged, rooms are cooled, and various motions are established, about which we shall speak partly here and partly in other places, God willing. <margin>Uses of bellows.</margin>

### Practical Application V.
### How to arrange the prime mover to drive stringed or bowed instruments.

Since instruments equipped with strings find moisture most hostile, and cannot remain in damp places for long without notable damage, craftsmen have found another way of driving said instruments. They prepare certain steel springs <note>original: "pinnas chalybeas"</note> with singular industry, <margin>Use of steel springs.</margin> having a length determined by the size of the instruments. These are usually enclosed in cylinders and drums, coiled within the cylinder using tensioners; from their forced state and continuous effort, the cylinder must necessarily turn, and thus provide the same effect as the cylinders driven by water described previously. This is a craft known everywhere; for the makers of wheeled clocks <note>Kircher refers here to clockmakers who use spring-driven gears.</note> apply almost every kind of motion to said machines through these steel springs. These springs, enclosed in cylinders, have such force that they can equal the power of huge weights. However, since we deal with these and their construction in our *Universal Statics*, in the treatise on wheeled clocks, I did not wish to be more verbose here. Anyone who desires to have a greater knowledge of these springs should in the meantime consult the clockmakers. If, therefore, in place of the wheel **NO** described in Practical Application 4, you place a cylinder animated by said steel plates or springs, it will lift the bellows **G** and **F** through the curved handle **K** just as easily as the wheel **NO**, though not with a motion of equal duration. For the motion through water is perpetual, while through the springs it will last only as long as the duration of the organ's sound requires. These springs have a dual function, for they both lift the bellows and rotate the phonotactic cylinder <term>phonotactic cylinder: a revolving drum with pins (like a music box) used to trigger specific notes in a sequence</term> to produce the harmony, as will be made clear in the following figures.

312 Universal Music-Making <note>original: *Musurgia Universalis*</note>

# Preliminary Exercise I.
## To construct a phonotactic cylinder.

In order for organs to play by themselves, it is necessary that the keys <note>original: *palmulæ abaci harmonici*, literally the "little palms of the harmonic board"</note> be pressed in a harmonic fashion. However, they cannot be pressed harmonically except by hands, or by something pressing the keys in place of hands, such as a toothed cylinder. From the rotation of this cylinder, the teeth pull the small levers <note>original: *brachiola*, little arms</note> of the keys, thereby producing a harmonic sound. We must now describe how a cylinder of this kind is made, how it is divided, and how it is equipped with its teeth. For in the preparation, division, and application of this cylinder lies whatever is rare, hidden, and subtle in the business of automata; without this, nothing can be constructed correctly or with ingenuity. We call it a **phonotactic cylinder** <note>from the Greek *phone* (sound) and *tassein* (to arrange), meaning "sound-arranging"</note> because, in its harmonic division, songs are arranged with the greatest skill, as will become clear in the progress of the work.

<margin>What is a phonotactic cylinder?</margin>

# Example I.
## To design a phonotactic cylinder harmonically.

The phonotactic cylinder can be considered in two ways: either in the manner of an oblong column, or in the manner of a military drum. Either can serve our purpose. The columnar cylinder (A) serves for shorter songs of 15, 20, or 30 measures <note>original: *tactuum*. A "tactus" was the basic unit of time or "beat" in Renaissance and Baroque music, roughly equivalent to a modern measure.</note>, for it makes shorter rotations, as appears in cylinder A.

[An illustration showing two types of cylinders connected to a crank mechanism. Cylinder A is a long, horizontal cylinder with vertical lines. Cylinder B is a large, drum-like vertical cylinder with horizontal lines.]

The drum-like cylinder (B) serves for longer songs, for it has circles much larger than the columnar one, as is clear from the figure. You may choose whichever one suits your purpose. Let us suppose, therefore, a cylinder prepared in the stated manner, of a size sufficient for a song of 14 measures or beats. It should be arranged beneath the keyboard <note>original: *Abacum palmularum* or *Tastaturam*</note> so that the length of the cylinder corresponds to the length of the keyboard. It is divided into as many equal parts or circles as the keyboard contains keys <note>original: *palmulas*. Kircher notes these are also called *tastis*, though he calls that a "barbarous" or non-classical term.</note>, so that each individual key corresponds to a circular division on the cylinder.

Once the cylinder is placed and prepared in the stated manner, you will choose for yourself a beautiful and ingenious song, not exceeding 14 measures of time. You will resolve this song into its separate voices, distinguishing each beat with lines and adding the number of the measures at the top or bottom, as is clear in the following example. In this example, it seemed best to first show a simple song expressed in larger notes, so that we might move from simpler things to more perfect ones. We have, however, somewhat "diminished" <term>diminution: a technique of breaking a long note into many fast, shorter notes</term> the melody of the soprano voice <note>original: *Cantus*</note>, so that you might have an example of how to represent note diminutions placed upon the cylinder.

->[A musical score is displayed here on four staves using diamond-shaped notes, a style common in the Renaissance and Baroque periods. Below the measures, the numbers 2 through 13 are printed to mark the rhythmic divisions or measures.]<-

You may transfer this melody either directly onto the Cylinder; or, you may first outline it separately on paper. As the latter is easier, it allows the entire composition to be placed before your eyes, displayed as if on the flat surface of the cylinder.

Therefore, you shall proceed in this way: First, prepare a piece of fine paper of such a size that the paper exactly matches the convex surface of the entire cylinder; this will be achieved if, by precisely wrapping it over the cylinder, you have first perfectly measured its breadth. In this task, you may also employ geometric techniques—specifically, those concerning the unfolding of the surfaces of curved bodies into a flat plane. We have described these at great length in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*, Kircher's 1646 treatise on optics and perspective</note> on page 328, to which we refer the Reader.

Let there be, therefore, the following square <term>ABCD</term> <note>a diagrammatic square used for mapping the cylinder’s surface</note>, exactly proportioned to the given music-making cylinder <note>original: *cylindro phonotactico*</note>. Onto this, you will transfer the preceding melody using this ingenious method: Divide side **AD** into 36 equal parts—which is to say, as many parts as the keyboard of the organ has keys <note>original: *palmulas*, literally "little palms" or keys</note>. From each point of division on side **AD**, let parallel lines be drawn to side **BC** (which is the base of the square). These lines will represent the spaces within which the cylinder's pins <note>original: *dentes*, literally "teeth"</note> must be placed, corresponding to the notes of the individual voices in the chosen melody. Then, let side **AB** be divided again into 15 equal parts, and let transverse lines, all parallel, be drawn from each point of division on side **AB** to side **DC**. Each of these spaces will represent one beat <note>original: *tempus*</note>, or

# 314 Universal Music-Making <note>original: *Musurgia Universalis*, Athanasius Kircher’s 1650 masterpiece on music theory and acoustics.</note>

...the measure or beat <term>tactus: the steady pulse or beat in Renaissance and Baroque music, often represented by the motion of the hand</term>, just as the numbers written next to side A B indicate. Furthermore, you will divide these individual spaces of the beats or measures, or times, again into 8 equal parts if you wish to show *fusas* <note>eighth notes or quavers</note> in the song; if *semifusas* <note>sixteenth notes or semiquavers</note>, you will divide the said spaces into 16 equal parts; if you wish to show the three-tailed notes of very fast motion <note>thirty-second notes or demisemiquavers</note>, 32 of which constitute one measure, you will divide each space of the beat into 32 equal parts, and so on to infinity. To avoid confusion, we have here divided one space of the beat into only 4 equal parts; each of these you will mentally divide again into two parts. Thus, with the cylindrical square marked out in a grid in the said manner, you will determine the spaces corresponding to the notes, beginning the work from the base.

->Drawing or translation of a song onto a phonotactic cylinder.<-

Since the first note in the bass voice is a *semibreve* <note>a whole note</note> on G, look at the front of the square between the keys for the letter G or g. Then, within the parallels encompassing one beat, draw a complete line, yet in such a way that it does not fill the entire space g to a; since the line of the second space marks the beginning of the second beat, the end of the first beat must not be placed exactly upon it, but a little before, as you see. Again, since the notes of the second beat in the bass of the song are two *minims* <note>half notes</note> equivalent to a whole time and occupying the same key, namely G; you will mark a small line within the same space g of the phonotactic square, starting from the line of the second beat up to the 2nd and 1/2 line, which represents a *minim* on g; and then from the 3rd line within the space up to the 4th and 1/2, you will mark another line equal to the first, which represents another *minim*; and thus the two encompass the beats. Furthermore, since the notes of the third beat are again *minims* placed on 'a' in the bass of the song, you will look for that 'a' at the front of the phonotactic square, and within the spaces of the 3rd beat, you will mark two small lines representing *minims*, as before. Again, since the notes of the fourth beat in the bass of the song are a dotted *minim* and a *semiminim* <note>a quarter note</note> placed on g, you will arrange them exactly within the space of the 4th beat corresponding to g, just as you did with the notes of the second beat. Since the note of the fifth beat occupies the G key and is a *minim*, you will arrange it within the fifth beat space of the phonotactic square corresponding to g, as you see. But since the following note of the same beat in the bass of the song is a *minim* and occupies the f key, you will look for the f key at the front of the square and arrange the said *minim* within the space of the fifth beat from the third line to the 4th and 1/2. Again, since the note of the 6th beat is a *semibreve* placed on E, you will mark a small line within column E of the square in the 6th beat space from the first line of the beat to the 4th and 1/2; in the same way you will mark the note of the seventh beat placed on D in the 7th beat space of the column from the first D line of the 7th beat to the 4th and 1/2, and you will have half the song completed. Furthermore, since the note of the 8th beat is preceded by a *minim* rest, you will omit the line in the 8th beat space corresponding to a *minim*; but since the note of this space is a *minim* and placed on d, you will arrange the *minim* within the middle of the 8th beat space from line 3 to 4 and 1/2. Moreover, since the ninth beat contains 4 *semiminims* on D, you will mark them upon the individual lines in the said space of column D, which will represent 4 *semiminims*; for a *semiminim* always occupies 1/2 of the beat space without completing it, as you see. Again, since the space of the 10th beat contains a dotted *minim* on D and a *semiminim* on b, you will transfer those into the appropriate spaces of the cylinder; the notes of the eleventh beat are two *minims* on C; of the twelfth, one *semibreve* on D; and finally, the note of the thirteenth beat is the final note, of any duration, on G; all of which you will transfer into the appropriate spaces of the cylinder, and you will have what was sought, as the figure of the cylinder extended onto a flat surface clearly shows.

**Example.**

One should proceed in no different a manner with the other voices of the Alto and Tenor; for there is a single method of operation for all of them. However, since the highest voice <note>The Soprano.</note> has been deliberately <term>diminished</term> <note>In 17th-century music, "diminution" refers to the practice of breaking down long notes into many fast, decorative notes to create an ornament.</note> and set with somewhat fast <term>cadences</term> <note>original: *clausulis*.</note>, it seemed appropriate to show briefly here how these are transferred into the phonotactic square, so that nothing remains that could cause any doubt.

Note, therefore, that individual **semibreve** <note>A whole note.</note> notes occupy nearly the entire space of one beat in the phonotactic square. I said "nearly," because the note must not fill the entire space, so that a clear beginning may be given to the note of the second beat. A **minim** <note>A half note.</note> indeed occupies almost half the space of one beat; a **semiminim** <note>A quarter note.</note> almost a fourth part; a **fusa** <note>An eighth note.</note> an eighth; and finally a **semifusa** <note>A sixteenth note.</note> a sixteenth part of the said space, and so on for the rest. Since, therefore, the highest voice of the chosen song is...

expressed in very fast musical phrases, so you shall insert them into the square. Since the first note of the song is a <term>semibreve<note>A "semibreve" is the equivalent of a modern whole note.</note></term> placed on the pitch **b**, you will look for the last key **b** occurring at the top of the square; in the first space of this column, you will mark the semibreve with a small line. However, since the notes of the second <term>tactus<note>The "tactus" refers to the basic unit of time or "beat" in Renaissance and Baroque music theory.</note></term> are partly <term>semiminims<note>A quarter note.</note></term> and partly <term>fusae<note>An eighth note.</note></term>, you will mark a line for the semiminim on pitch **b** in the second beat-space, corresponding to the semiminim, or—what is the same thing—occupying nearly 1/4 of the beat-space. When the first of the eighth notes is placed on **g**, look for column **g**, and there in the second beat-space on the second line, make a small line nearly equal to 1/8 of a single beat-space. You will record the following eighth note on **a** with a small line arranged in column **a** of the second beat-space, in the middle of that space; and thus you will proceed in order according to the ascent of the notes, until you have aptly inserted all the notes in their individual corresponding places in the square. The resulting "phonotactic square" will appear as shown previously, in which everything said up to this point is precisely displayed. For this reason, I urge you to compare that square diligently with the preceding song; for from this single paradigm, you will grasp all other matters without difficulty.

Once the phonotactic square has been divided and prepared in the stated manner, you shall wrap it around the cylinder, or even glue the whole thing to it. Once this is finished, you will drive iron "teeth" <note>These "teeth" are the pins or pegs used in a mechanical music box or barrel organ.</note> into the cylinder according to the notes expressed by the lines in the square. The <term>semibreve</term> notes must have a tooth filed and polished to a length as great as the line representing it. Truly, for a better understanding of these things, we have wished to place the "teeth" here: **a** refers to the semibreve, **b** to the <term>minim<note>A half note.</note></term>, **c** to the semiminim, **d** to the eighth note, and **e** to the <term>semifusa<note>A sixteenth note.</note></term>; all of them, however, must project from the cylinder to the same height with perfect equality.

For the perfection of the entire harmony consists in this business. Therefore, since the lengths and locations of the individual teeth are now perfectly expressed by the lines on the cylinder, nothing else remains to be done except that the teeth, previously prepared and skillfully made, be properly fixed into their individual places. We shall then have a cylinder complete in every part. You see, therefore, how when the handle of the cylinder is turned, the entire cylinder moves and changes at once, while the iron tongues of the <term>palms<note>Kircher uses "palmulae" (little palms) to describe the keys or levers that are tripped by the cylinder pins to produce sound.</note></term> remain always unmoved.

But if anyone should wish to transfer ingenious preludes, which they call *Toccatas* or *Ricercatas*, onto the phonotactic cylinder, he should construct a larger cylinder, capable of holding perhaps 100 beats. I have thought it best to include one of this kind here, composed by **Johann Caspar Kerll**, the exceptional musician and organist to the Most Serene Archduke Leopold, our most munificent patron. In this piece, the method of this most perfect style shines forth as if in a clear vision—a method most worthy for an ingenious craftsman to exhibit, both in the artistic construction of automatons and in the industrious manual playing of organs.

320 *Musurgia Universalis, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance* <note>Original: "Musurgiæ Vniuersalis siue Artis Consoni & Dissoni." This is the title of Athanasius Kircher's 1650 encyclopedic work on music theory and organology.</note>

### *How several melodies can be transferred onto the same cylinder.*

**N**ote that multiple melodies can be transferred onto one and the same cylinder. For the wider the columns or the spaces for the keys are, the more melodies can be placed upon them. For example: if the spaces were of the width AB, eight different melodies could be placed on the cylinder. Since each individual space is equal and divided into eight parts, the iron <term>tongues</term><note>The "tongues" or "teeth" are the metal tips of the levers that are lifted by the pins on the rotating barrel to trigger a note.</note> at the ends of the levers in the organ's keyboard, which catch the teeth of the cylinder, will correspond to one space AB—that is, they can be applied to any one of the aforementioned eight parts. Thus, it is certain that eight melodies can be placed there. For this reason, the axis of the cylinder must protrude outward, divided into as many notches as there are divisions in the space. However, you will understand my meaning more easily from the following figure.

->[An illustration of a mechanical cylinder mechanism. A large barrel is marked with various letters (A, B, Y, Z). Levers (marked X) rest above it. A handle (T) on the side allows the entire cylinder to be shifted laterally into different notches (L, m, n, o, p, q, r, s) to align the pins with the levers for different songs.]<-

Let the spaces AB, BY, and YZ be the cylinder spaces divided into eight parts, marked with the letters c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, continued through the entire circuit of the cylinder, and corresponding to three keys <note>Original: "b quad. CD," referring to B-natural, C, and D.</note>. We have chosen an eight-part division here instead of thirty-six so that the figure would not be more extended than necessary. Since each eight-part space corresponds to one of the thirty-six keys—that is, to one lever in the keyboard, which we have marked here with the letter X—it is certain that when the handle TS is placed over the last notch L in the support TL, the levers X in all the eight-part spaces of the cylinder will be moved immediately above key C, as is apparent to anyone considering it. Again, by moving the handle T over the notch M in the said handle, I say that the iron tongues at the ends of the levers X will no longer correspond to the spaces C, but to the spaces d, and consequently, a place will be given for a second melody. Furthermore, if you place the handle T over the support TL at point n, the iron tongues of the levers X will no longer correspond to d, but to e, and consequently, a place will be given for a third melody. In this way, by moving the handle over the remaining points n, o, p, q, r, s, the levers X will necessarily change their position, and new spaces will always open up on the cylinder, up to eight, for the melodies to be applied.
