### Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic. 321

Regarding the following phonotactic <term>cantilena</term> <note>A simple song or melody</note>; you will operate in exactly the same way as was done in the preceding example. To take your starting point from the soprano part, proceed as follows: since the soprano has a <term>suspirium</term> <note>A "sigh" or short musical rest</note> in the first position, do not make any division on the phonotactic cylinder for the first half-part of the <term>tactus</term> <note>The "tactus" was the standard unit of time or beat in Renaissance and Baroque music</note>. 

However, since the first note is a <term>minima</term> <note>A half-note</note> and is set on the pitch D; you will arrange a line in column D corresponding to half a beat after the first half-space of the cylinder, for this will syncopate the note. Then, you will determine the second note, placed on C, in column C, so that you leave half of the first beat in the first space, and place the other half of the minim in the space of the second beat. You will proceed in this order through the remaining appropriate keys for the syncopated notes. You will also insert the second and third voices onto the cylinder with equal diligence. 

All of these instructions are presented so precisely in the following phonotactic square <note>Kircher refers to the musical notation below as a "square" because it serves as a grid for the mechanical programmer</note> that you can learn how to proceed simply by comparing the notes with the "teeth" (pins) of the said cylinder. For he who has deeply understood the previous instructions will encounter no difficulty here. 

Note, however, that here in the keyboard of the phonotactic cylinder, the key **b** always corresponds to the "soft" signature <note>original: "b molli"; this refers to B-flat</note>; and on the keyboard it occupies the third position of the black keys. But **b-quadratum** <note>B-natural</note> corresponds to the "hard" signature and occupies the fifth white key. Furthermore, whenever you find the sign **#** added to any key—for example, **c#**, **d#**, **f#**, etc.—these will indicate the positions of the semitones on the black keys marked with those letters. Keys that are written simply [without signs] will indicate the white keys on the manual.

### Paradigm I.
### How notes of the smallest value can be placed on the cylinder.

This geometric division is so incredibly useful that no manual dexterity of the hands <note>literally "skillful play of the hands"</note> can match it. It is capable of representing every imaginable subdivision of time so perfectly that not even the smallest note—even those with four tails <note>original: "quadricaudata," referring to hemidemisemiquavers or sixty-fourth notes</note>—will escape the listener's ear. However, so that the Musical Reader <note>original: "Lector Musurgus," a reference to Kircher's famous work *Musurgia Universalis*</note> has material to practice with, we will set down some "diminutions" <note>the Renaissance and Baroque practice of breaking a long note into many short, decorative notes</note> here, and at the same time, we will demonstrate the method by which they may be transferred onto the cylinder <term>cylinder: the rotating drum of an automatic musical instrument, such as a barrel organ or a programmed carillon, where pins or pegs trigger specific notes</term>.

324 *Universal Music-making, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

*An example of the division of notes into sixteenth notes and sixty-fourth notes.*

[Musical notation on two staves]
1. Sixteenth notes. 2. Three-tailed or sixty-fourth notes. 3. Sixty-fourth notes.

To transfer these rapid trills <note>original: "teretismos" — a Greek term Kircher uses to describe fast, bird-like musical ornamentations or divisions.</note> onto a cylinder, you must divide the space of one beat <term>tactus (the standard unit of time or pulse in music)</term> into 32 parts, for that many sixty-fourth notes <note>original: "tricaudatæ," literally "three-tailed notes"</note> constitute one unit of time or beat. Then you shall proceed as you see has been done in the following example, in which you will find the arrangement of only two beats. If, however, 16 notes should correspond to one unit of time, as happens in thirty-second notes <note>original: "bicaudatis seu semifusis"</note>, then the space of one beat would have to be divided into 16 parts. But if 64 notes should correspond to one unit of time, as happens in certain three-tailed notes, then the individual spaces of the beats would have to be divided into 64 parts, and then one should proceed according to the rules handed down, and so on into infinity.

**Corollary.**

From these things, it follows that no motion of notes can be devised so swift that it cannot be performed with the help of this practical art. And therefore, our automatic art will be able to reach that point where no skill of human hands can attain; nor will any organist <term>Organœdus (organ-player)</term> be found in the world who is able to achieve anything similar with his hands.

**Paradigm IV.**

*How Triple, Sesquialtera, and similar proportions of time can be introduced onto a phonotactic cylinder.*

Since motions of "perfect time" <note>In the music of this period, "perfect time" refers to triple meter, symbolized by a circle.</note> occur quite often in harmonies, and some of them are so difficult that there are scarcely any—even among the most excellent musicians—who (I will not say) can sing them, but cannot even play them on instruments; we shall show here by what method the cylinder is to be divided so that their motion may be exhibited most perfectly. Indeed, nothing in the entire treasury of music is so hidden that our phonotactic <term>phonotactica (Kircher’s term for the art of mechanical music recording/playback)</term> division cannot make it manifest. Let the following song, therefore, be used as an example to be transferred to the cylinder. Note, however, Reader, that we here take "triple" in a broad sense for any proportion of perfect time in which three quarter notes <note>original: "minimæ"</note> are equivalent to one unit of imperfect time <note>imperfect time refers to duple meter.</note>. We did not wish to use more obscure terms in this place, lest we confuse the craftsman with misunderstood terminology. However, all those songs which have the numbers 3, 3/2, or 6/4 prefixed to them are commonly called "triples." You may draw the genuine reasoning and true knowledge of these from Book 7, to which we refer the studious Reader, where he will find treated whatever can be desired concerning this business. The following song is by Simplicio Todeschi of Verona <note>Simplicio Todeschi was a minor Italian composer of the early 17th century.</note>, printed in Venice in the year 1627; although the Author committed many errors against the precepts of music in it, because it nevertheless served our purpose, we have seen fit to place it here, corrected as much as was possible.

326 *Universal Music-making, or the Art of Consonance and Dissonance*

[Musical notation on five-line staves, featuring various notes, rests, and clefs arranged in three systems.]

When you are about to transfer this melody-setting <note>original: "Melothesiam"</note> onto a cylinder, you must first divide the individual beat-spaces into three, six, or twelve equal parts, if you wish to play with diminutions <term>diminution: the breaking up of long notes into shorter, faster ones</term>. One-third of a part will serve for minims <term>minim: a half note</term>; two-thirds for semiminims <term>semiminim: a quarter note</term>; and finally one-twelfth for the triple fuses <term>fusa: a quaver or eighth note</term>, as is clear in the preceding example.

Indeed, triple rhythms <term>tripla: a musical meter where three notes are played in the time of two</term> sometimes occur that are so ingeniously syncopated that a singer must be exceedingly skilled to be able to either sing or play them. You can arrange these triple rhythms on the cylinder with the same ease as the preceding ones. Thus, it will happen that nothing in music is so intricate or complex that it cannot be displayed by this automatic phonotactic cylinder <note>Kircher's term for a programmed musical drum, like those found in a music box or barrel organ</note>. Not long ago, for the sake of an example, I composed a triple-meter piece of this kind, so roughened with sheer syncopations that even the most expert Roman musicians were only just able to sing it after great practice. The French, however, being more practiced in this kind of rhythm, performed it exactly, though not without the confusion of others; we present this in the seventh book.

Therefore, if you desire to transfer the preceding song in perfect time <term>tempus perfectum: a rhythmic system in early music where the basic pulse is divided into three parts rather than two</term> onto the cylinder, proceed as follows: since the first two notes of the voice—a breve <term>breve: a long note value, usually double a whole note</term> and a semibreve <term>semibreve: a whole note</term>—set on the note *a* correspond to one beat; you will first seek the key *a* at the top of the square on the cylinder. Then, for the breve, you will apply a small line within column *a* in the first tripartite space, occupying nearly two-thirds of the first space. Then, in the same column, you will apply another small line for the semibreve, filling nearly the third division. 

But in the second space, you will apply small lines corresponding to the notes of the second beat: namely, one for the semiminim in column *d* in the second space, determining 1/3 of the space; then nearly 1/3 of the second space for the dot; then for the minim, set on *e*, in the space of the second beat, from the middle of the second line of the said space up to the third line; and finally for the semibreve set on *f*, in the column of the key *f* in the space of the second beat from the third nearly to the fourth line, you will determine the small line for the beginning of the third beat. By doing this, you will have the locations for the teeth <note>the pins or pegs on the cylinder that strike the instrument's mechanism</note> of the cylinder determined in the second space.

### Example V.

### To transfer chromatic and enharmonic musical phrases onto a cylinder.

**The Chromatic** and **Enharmonic** genera <note>In ancient Greek music theory, revived during the Renaissance, 'genera' refers to different ways of tuning the four-note scale (tetrachord).</note> are so difficult and arduous that I will not say many musicians cannot sing or play them, but they do not even perceive what their names mean; they think them a musical paradox and impossible <note>original: *ἀδύνατον* (adynaton)</note> to sing. I myself admit the difficulty of the matter; since these genera possess the most subtle intervals, it seems hardly possible for the human voice to perform such minute intervals exactly and distinctly. With instruments, the matter will meet with somewhat better success; yet, because there are hardly any craftsmen who can play such subtle intervals exactly, the matter still suffers from the greatest difficulty.

But with our **phonotactic cylinder** <note>A mechanical device, like a music box barrel, designed by the author Athanasius Kircher to record and play back music automatically.</note>, the matter is entirely easy. Indeed, I believe there is no other way to perfectly, exactly, and distinctly present these types of genera than in such automata. In these machines, all intervals—no matter how small—can be arranged with such exact division that they achieve an infallible effect. Therefore, so that you may see a specimen of this thing, here is a chromatic-enharmonic monody <term>monody: a style of solo vocal music characterized by a single melodic line and instrumental accompaniment</term> in...

Who, I ask, possesses a voice so skilled and flexible that they could perfectly pronounce the intervals set down here? Surely all musicians would seem to despair at the very first sight of them. Yet, in our **phonotactic cylinder** <note>A "phonotactic cylinder" is a revolving drum with pins or "teeth" that trigger organ pipes or strings, much like the mechanism in a modern music box.</note>, all these things are arranged and composed with the same ease and exactness as the other examples we have proposed thus far. 

However, it must be noted that the **keyboard** <note>original: *Abacum clauiarium* or *tastatura*</note> must be arranged quite differently for this genre of music. In an ordinary keyboard, one mostly finds **diatonic** steps rather than **Chromatic-Enharmonic** ones; thus, a single octave of a common keyboard has only 12 keys <note>original: *palmulas*, literally "little palms"</note>, as we demonstrated in the chapter on keyboards in the section on *Organic Music*. But a Chromatic-Enharmonic keyboard has a total of 32 keys; we have placed such a design, among others, in the fourth section of the aforementioned place. 

Therefore, since a keyboard consists of at least 4 octaves, and one octave consists of 32 steps or keys, the entire quadrupled keyboard will consist of 128 keys. With the organ tuned in this manner, if you determine the placement of the "teeth" <note>The pins on the mechanical cylinder.</note> according to the value of the notes within the spaces corresponding to the chromatic-enharmonic signs, you will obtain the sought-after **chromatic-enharmonic music**, which has been unheard until now. In the preceding example, we have shown only one voice for the sake of avoiding confusion, so that no doubt might remain for you.

### Corollary

From these things it is clear that if someone were to divide a whole tone into 5, 6, 7, or 8 intervals or steps, and were to arrange the keyboard and the pipes of the organ to correspond to the individual differences of those intervals—and finally, if they were to transfer a song composed according to said steps onto a cylinder—the result would be that this automatic organ would exactly reproduce every subtle difference of the steps. This is truly a marvelous machine, reaching a level that no human voice or industry would seem able to attain.

# Paradigm VII.
## Concerning toothed wheels moving the cylinder in a circle, and concerning the speed of time <note>rhythm or tempo</note>.

A cylinder can be driven in a circle in two ways: either by the aid of water, or by springs <note>original: "pinnarum," referring here to the mechanical tension of a spring-driven clockwork</note>. In hydraulic organs, the water does not only move the cylinder, but also provides the necessary wind by its fall within the <term>Aeolian Chamber</term> <note>A specialized vessel in a water organ where falling water traps and compresses air to blow the pipes</note>; other instruments, however, such as <term>Harpsichords</term> <note>original: "Clavecymbala"</note>, which are enemies of humidity, are brought to life into harmony by springs violently twisted and coiled within cylinders. The difference between the two types of instrument is this: that instruments driven by water promise a perpetual motion, whereas those driven by springs provide a motion lasting only for a certain time. *Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic* <note>The term "Phonocamptic" refers to the science of reflected sound or echoes.</note> 331

I thought I would do well if I first placed the text of Vitruvius in this place; so that the curious reader, comparing each detail with the text, might be able to discern what we have achieved in the elucidation of this most intricate matter. Vitruvius, Book 10, Chapter 13.

*Concerning hydraulics <note>original: "De hydraulicis"; referring to the water organ or hydraulis</note>, I shall not omit to describe as briefly and accurately as I can in writing the principles upon which they are based. On a base of compacted material, a chest made of bronze is placed. Above the base, uprights are erected on the right and left, joined in a ladder-like form; these enclose bronze cylinders <term>modioli</term> with movable bottoms <note>pistons</note> carefully fashioned on a lathe, having iron rods <term>ancones</term> fixed in their centers and joined by pins to levers, and wrapped in woolly skins. Likewise, on the top surface, there are openings about three fingers wide, near which bronze dolphins are placed on pins, holding bronze cymbals hanging by chains below the openings of the cylinders within the chest where the water is held. Inside is a device like an inverted funnel, beneath which small blocks about three fingers high are placed to level the space between the lower lips of the pressure-chamber <term>phigeos</term> and the bottom of the chest. Above its neck, a small joined chest supports the head of the machine, which is called in Greek the* musical canon <note>original: κανὼν μουσικὸς</note>; *in its length, if it is a four-rank <note>original: "tetrachordos"</note> instrument, four channels are made; if six-rank, six; if eight-rank, eight. Within each channel, individual valves are enclosed, fitted with iron handles; when these handles are turned, they open the vents from the chest into the channels. From the channels, the "canon" <note>the action-frame</note> has holes arranged transversely, corresponding to the vents in the top board, which is called a* pinax <note>original: πίναξ; a tablet or board</note> *by the Greeks. Between the board and the canon, sliders are interposed, drilled in the same manner and rubbed with oil so that they may be moved easily, the back-and-forth motion of which closes some holes and opens others. These sliders have iron linkages <term>choragia</term> fixed and joined with keys <term>pinnis</term>, the touch of which keys effects the movement of the sliders. Above the board are the openings which allow the breath to exit from the channels. Rings are fastened to the sliders, into which the individual pipes of all the registers are fitted. From the cylinders, pipes are continuously joined by wooden necks reaching to the vents in the small chest, in which lathe-turned valves are placed; when the small chest receives the air, these valves prevent the breath from escaping back by blocking the openings. Thus, when the levers are raised, the rods draw the bottoms of the cylinders to the lowest point; and the dolphins, which are enclosed on pins, let the cymbals down into the openings, filling the space of the cylinders; then the rods, raising the bottoms within the cylinders with great speed and force, and closing the upper openings with the cymbals, force the air trapped there by pressure into the pipes, through which it rushes into the wooden necks, and through the necks into the chest. By the more forceful motion of the levers, the frequent gathering of breath flows through the openings of the valves and fills the channels with air. Therefore, when the keys, touched by the hands, continually push and pull the sliders, alternately blocking and opening the holes, they produce sounding voices in the multiple varieties of musical scales according to the musical arts. I have striven as much as I could to ensure that this obscure matter might be clearly expressed in writing. But this is not an easy system, nor readily understood by everyone except those who have experience in these kinds of crafts. If any should understand little from these writings, when they come to know the thing itself, they will find everything perfectly, carefully, and subtly arranged. Thus far, Vitruvius.*

<margin>Explanation of the hydraulic organ.</margin>

This machine has four principal parts which must be considered according to the mind of Vitruvius. The first part is the **Bronze Chest**, with the inverted funnel, which he also calls the *phigeum* <note>the air-pressure chamber submerged in water</note>. The second is the construction of the **Cylinders** along with the channels, levers, and "dolphins"; for this is the primary part that animates the machine by supplying the wind. The third is the **Small Chest** with the sliders, keys, linkages, vents, and the *pinax*, which are the ways and paths of the winds, with covers to either open or close them. The "small chest" <term>arcula</term> is the same as what modern organ-builders call the **wind-chest** <term>secretum</term>; the "sliders" <term>regulae</term> are the same as what are commonly called **pallets** <term>battiuenti</term>; the "linkages" <term>choragia</term> are the same as the **keys** <term>tasti</term>; the "keys" <term>pinnæ</term> are the same as the **trackers** <term>trufillis</term> or iron wires which, when the keys to which they are attached are pressed, they in turn press the pallets to which they are likewise connected, opening the holes through which the wind trapped inside the pressure chamber is given passage into the organ pipes. The fourth part is the **Organ Pipes**, which, if there were 4, the organ was called a *tetrachordon*; if 6, a *hexachordon*; if 8, an *octochordon*; if 12, a *dodecachordon*; and they were arranged according to the intervals of the octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>. And with these four parts, the entire hydraulic organ of Vitruvius is completed; but let us teach its structure a little more deeply.

### Book IX. Phonocamptic Magic. 333

...nothing other than a certain type of atmospheric <term>siphon</term><note>original: "anthlea," a Greek-derived term for a pump or water-raising engine</note> or a device designed to compress air into the air chamber. From the small cylinders **YY**, through the channels **T**, air was forced into the receptacle which Vitruvius calls an "inverted funnel." This was done in such a way that these two cylinders—along with the pistons or rammers **VY** and the valves **δ**—resembled nothing so much as that machine which we call an <term>Aeolian gun</term><note>An air-powered gun or pneumatic blower, which Kircher previously described in his work *The Magnetic Art* (*Aris Magneticæ*)</note>; these components functioned like two bellows supplying wind to the air chamber. Within the Chest **ABCD**, there was a kind of inverted funnel **EFGH**, situated 3 fingers' width from the bottom and resting on certain small blocks marked **λ** and **ξ** as supports, so that the water inside the chest could enter into the funnel (which lacked a bottom). However, the Chest **ABCD** was not entirely filled with water, but only to a certain point, so that the air occupied the space between the water and the top part of the funnel, as appears in the figure. From this arrangement, it happened that—just as a shepherd’s squeezed bagpipe supplies a great deal of air—this air, pressed by the incoming air supplied in turns by the pump, was thrust through internal channels into the <term>wind-chest</term><note>original: "anemotheca," the box where pressurized air is held before being released into the pipes</note> **X**, where it was condensed for the purpose of making sound. Inside the air chamber, there were certain paddles or handles, which Vitruvius calls <term>choragia</term><note>Historically, the *choragium* refers to the organ's key-action or the space for the mechanisms</note>; these corresponded to the "tongues" or paddles of our own organs. When opened by means of iron wires, they provided the wind with an entrance into the pipes. We have marked these paddles in the figure with the letter **I**; they rested upon the openings, driven by certain pins, in exactly the same way that modern organ-builders are accustomed to arrange the valves which they call <term>wind-slaps</term><note>original: "Battiventos"</note>. Above these corresponded the keys **S**, which were joined by brass wires to the paddles **I**. It thus happened that when the keys were pressed by the hand of the organist, they pushed the corresponding paddles inside the wind-chest via the iron wires **I** and **S**. When these were pressed in this manner, the wind—enclosed and compressed within the wind-chest—entered through the openings into the corresponding pipe channel, causing the desired sound. We have expressed this entire operation in the figure through the key **V**, the paddle **y**, and the opening **X** placed beneath it. From this, it is clearly evident that, except for the method of supplying the wind, almost everything was common to our own organs. For the man operating the pump pushed the air hidden in the cylinders through the channels **T** into the funnel using alternating valves; there, the compressed air departed into the wind-chest or "wind chest," where, once collected, the air entered the open pipes at the pressure of the pins or keys moved through the mechanism, producing the desired sound according to the pressure of the pins. One thing has seemed necessary to explain here which neither Vitruvius nor any other commentator has noted.

<margin>
The nature of Vitruvius's hydraulic organ is explained part by part.
</margin>

Namely, why organs of this type are called "hydraulic," since no mention is made of any use of water for power, and for what purpose Vitruvius kept water in the Chest. I respond, therefore, briefly: the water was placed there so that, being agitated by the movement of the air compressed in the air chamber or funnel, it might impart a certain singular <term>tremolo</term><note>Kircher argues that the water adds a vibrating, "shimmering" quality to the sound, similar to a modern vox humana or tremulant stop</note> to the sound. It was from this trembling sound alone that the organ was called "hydraulic," for there appeared in such a trembling sound something strangely foreign and especially pleasant to the ear. We say the water was placed in the chest for this use, even if Vitruvius hints nothing of it. Let these remarks suffice for the Hydraulic Organ of Vitruvius.

From this description, it is most clearly evident that if these types of organs are compared with our modern organs, they were entirely childish, and the work was very meager, thin, and crude. For I do not see what kind of harmony a layout of 4, 5, 6, or 8 pipes could excite—so much so that I greatly marvel that <term>Nero</term><note>The Roman Emperor Nero was famously obsessed with the *hydraulis* (water organ), even as his empire faced collapse</note> could be so deeply moved by such a cheap and tiny hydraulic organ that (as Vitruvius testifies) amidst the dangers to his life and empire, and during the sedition of his soldiers and leaders, he did not abandon his care and study of it in the face of imminent total ruin. But if he had possessed the abundance of modern organs—not with 4, 5, 6, or 8 pipes, but like the larger organs of Germany with **1,152** pipes brought to life by the help of **24** different registers—and if he had heard such <term>automata</term><note>Self-playing musical machines, a favorite topic of Kircher</note> playing without any labor of human hands, with what great pleasure would we judge him to have been captivated? Truly, these most enlightened ages have discovered many things to which the inventions of the Ancients can in no way be compared, as has been shown elsewhere. But with these things having been prefaced, let us now approach the Mechanics itself.

# Mechanism II.
## To build an automatic hydraulic organ.

For a hydraulic organ <note>A "hydraulic" organ in this context refers to an organ powered by water pressure rather than manual bellows.</note>, three things are required: Water, air, and a phonotactic wheel <term>phonotactic wheel: a rotating cylinder or drum fitted with pins that trigger specific notes, similar to a modern music box barrel</term>. Water is the "prime mover" or source of energy; air is the soul of the organ; and the phonotactic wheel is the instrument of self-sounding <note>original: "αὐτοφωνίας" (autophonias)—the ability of the instrument to play itself without a human performer</note>. You shall proceed as follows: once the organ has been constructed in a suitable place according to the rules handed down in the section on Instrumental Music, before all else, you shall construct an Aeolian chamber <term>Aeolian chamber: a vessel (Camera Aeolia) where falling water and air are mixed to create a steady stream of pressurized air for the pipes</term> as was described just before in Practice II.

[A large technical illustration showing the internal mechanisms of an automatic hydraulic organ. It includes several sub-figures:

- **Fig. IV**: A vertical chamber on the right (the Aeolian Chamber) showing water falling through perforated diaphragms to create air pressure, which then travels through a pipe (O) to the organ. At the bottom, a water wheel (R) is turned by the escaping water to drive the cylinder's rotation.

Therefore, let the Aeolian Chamber **VXYR** be 5 palms in height and 3 1/2 palms in width, equipped with diaphragms <note>Internal plates or partitions</note> pierced in the manner of a sieve, and provided with two channels. The larger of these, **TS**, provides the "living water" <note>Running water from a natural or constant source</note>; it should, however, have a stopcock <note>A valve or faucet</note> at **T**, to...

<note>original: "Magia Phonocamptica." This branch of science, as defined by Kircher, deals with the "reflection" of sound, including echoes and the mechanical reproduction of music.</note>

to stop the water whenever desired. This mentioned pipe should be diverted into the lower part of the vessel; let there be another pipe above, V, Z, which may transfer the air stirred up within the **aeolian chamber** <note>A "camera aeolia" is a vessel where falling water compresses air to create a constant wind source for an organ.</note> into the <term>wind-chest</term> <note>original: "anemothecam," the pressurized box that holds air for the organ pipes.</note> or the wind-box of the organ. For the water, rushing with great force through the pipe TS into the inner part of the vessel R, will agitate both the air already existing there and the new air being generated; this air, seeking a larger space and finding none, will fly out through VZ into the wind-chest, having been "combed" through the <term>sieve-like diaphragms</term> <note>internal filters or screens</note> and stripped of excessive moisture. Furthermore, the water escaping with most violent force through the orifice R will turn the wheel MR, which is adorned with a complex circuit of buckets; this wheel, by means of a gear L attached to its axle and revolving with it, will rotate the **phonotactic cylinder** <note>original: "cylindrum sive rotam phonotacticam." This is the "pinned barrel" or "music roll" that determines the melody.</note> or wheel HK. This cylinder, by means of its teeth arranged harmonically on the wheel according to the preceding patterns, will catch each of the spatulas inserted in order by the iron wire AB. Finally, the spatulas caught by the teeth of the wheel will depress the keys of the keyboard or the <term>trackers</term> <note>original: "palmulas abaci Clauiarij siue tastos," the levers that trigger the notes.</note> EF to which they are attached by iron wires 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc. Once depressed, these will open the <term>pallets</term> <note>original: "paltismatia" or "Battiuentos," the valves that let air into the pipes.</note> (or as the Italians call them, *battiventos*), and thus the wind, now violently forced into the wind-chest, will enter the pipes through the open valves; and at last, the desired harmony will be perceived. We do not teach the internal structure of the organ and its individual parts here, as we have already delivered that in our work on *Organic Music*.

Note at this point that the phonotactic cylinder can have **mobile** or **fixed** teeth. They are fixed when they are fastened into the cylinder in such a way that they cannot be removed further. <margin>Mobile and fixed cylinder teeth.</margin> They are mobile when they can be removed at will and others put in their place, so that any composition or **musical arrangement** <note>original: "melothesia"</note> whatsoever can be adapted to it at any time. To achieve this, divide the cylinder VG into 24 beats, and each of those again into 8, for the display of the notes which they call <term>fusas</term> <note>equivalent to modern eighth or sixteenth notes</note>; you shall make holes at each point of the division, so that different teeth—already prepared in great quantity for the various note values and contained in a certain small box connected to the organ—can be inserted at the musician's discretion. This can, however, be properly done only in larger and more spacious cylinders; in very small ones, this method will not meet with such good success.

Note secondly: This mechanical device can be applied not only to organs but also to any kind of **stringed instrument**.

->Mechanism III.<-
->To construct an automatic lute by another method.<-

Some people, among whom is **Robert Fludd**, <note>original: "Robertus de Fluctibus," the English physician and mystic (1574–1637).</note> construct an automaton of this kind by another method, for which three things are required. One of these sounds by strings stretched for harmony. The second, inserted distinctly between the strings, strikes them. The third regulates the striking of the strings themselves by certain balances of weights. First, a triangular figure (as shown in Mechanism II, figure II) or a square—it makes no difference—is constructed from three fir planks BB. <margin>Construction of the automatic lute according to all its parts.</margin> On two equal sides of this, about 40 brass wires are stretched, attached by their pins, so that they can be tightened and loosened according to musical laws. The middle of its base at BB must be slightly slotted, so that the sounding machine can be moved steadily through the openings BB. Furthermore, a square CDEF should be formed from more solid wood, distinguished by parallel bars; this is nothing other than a **phonotactic wheel** flattened out. This must be inserted within the sides of the lute through the openings BB so that it may be moved lightly up and down. Upon this, you will distribute your musical arrangement by its teeth and pins according to the practical rules delivered shortly before, so that they can be removed from there if desired. Let the width of this phonotactic square have as many parallel pieces of wood as the keyboard has keys; the length, however, should be divided into beats suitable for the music. In the center of each division, let holes be made into which small <term>jacks</term> <note>original: "pinnae," similar to the quills or jacks in a harpsichord.</note> are inserted, which can easily be bent to strike the string and return to a straight position once the string is plucked, as is customary in harpsichords. Finally, lest the strings, once struck, produce a longer sound than is proper, other <term>plectra</term> padded with thin cloth should be fixed above the jacks—

# Book IX. Phonotactic Magic. 337

They turn a spindle—commonly called a *rocchetto* <note>original: "rocchetto," an Italian term for a bobbin or spool</note>—into the phonotactic cylinder **A**; this, rotated by its teeth <note>original: "dentibus," referring to the pins or pegs on the cylinder</note> which are harmonically arranged, will press the teeth of the levers **BC**. These, when pressed through their axles, will strike the hammers against the corresponding small bells, and in this way the harmony will be completed. However, so that the cylinder may proceed more evenly, a chronometer **X** is arranged, as Figure I of Illustration XIX shows, in exactly the same way as is usually done in clocks. Furthermore, two cylinders are most often placed, the larger of which serves to turn wheel **A**, while the other serves to show the hours on the index $\eta$ <note>the Greek letter eta</note>. The bells or chimes must be cast harmonically; the method by which this should be done we have shown in *Organic Music* in the treatise on Bells, and the preceding figure beautifully demonstrates it. In that figure:

*   The diameter **AB** of the largest bell refers to the diameter in **C** (sol, fa, ut);
*   **CB** refers to the diameter of the second bell in **D** (la, sol, re);
*   **DE** shows the diameter of the third bell in **E** (la, mi, re);
*   **EB** shows the diameter of the fourth bell in **F** (fa, ut);
*   **FB** shows the diameter of the fifth bell in **G** (sol, re, ut);
*   **GB** shows the diameter of the sixth bell in **A** (la, mi, re);
*   **HB** gives the diameter of the seventh bell in **B** (fa, b mi);
*   Finally, **IB** gives the diameter of the eighth bell in **C** (sol, fa, ut).

This is as the attached figure beautifully shows. However, as to how these diameters are found, we have taught at length in Book 6, Chapter II, to which we refer the Reader. The site or position of the bells can also be varied; I preferred the one which is in the manner of a little tower, as can be seen in the present Illustration XIX. In this, the phonotactic cylinder **A**—rotated from within by the twisting and forceful winding of a steel plate <note>a mainspring</note>—moves the levers <note>original: "spatellas," literally small paddles</note> **BC** placed in order; these, by means of the iron wires to which they are attached, lift the hammers of the bells corresponding to them in the little tower. These hammers, returning to their natural state, strike the little bells harmonically; from this, the desired effect of harmony is finally achieved, as we said. Each hammer must be restrained by certain pins, which we have expressed in Figure II by the letters $\rho$ <note>the Greek letter rho</note>, so that when they fall upon the bells they do not remain resting on them, but are pushed back slightly to avoid confusion and the dulling of the sounds. But let us explain the matter better in Figure II of Illustration XIX.

Let there be a phonotactic wheel **A** equipped with teeth harmonically arranged. Let the board or keyboard <note>original: "Clauiarium"</note> be **BC**, whose levers <note>original: "palmulæ," literally 'little palms' or keys</note> are one and a half feet in length, inserted into an iron wire **DE** acting as an axle; let the outermost part **IS** represent the keyboard. Each lever should have rings inside the line **DE** connected to iron wires; let the iron wires then be connected to the hammers of the bells, as can be seen in the iron wire **HK**, the hammer **KL**, and the small bell **M**. Thus it will happen that as soon as the cylinder **A** is rotated by the mechanism <note>original: "automato"</note>, having struck the ends of the levers at **BC** with its harmonically arranged teeth and pressed them by lifting each one, the levers **IS**—inserted into the iron wire **DE** as a fulcrum <term>hypomochlio: from the Greek 'hypomochlion,' the pivot point of a lever</term>—are depressed. From this depression, the iron wire **HK** will depress the hammer **KL**, which, having been depressed and striking against the small bell **M** with force, finally completes the desired sound; you shall judge the other wires in no different way.

Since the bells are always larger and larger, the iron wires cannot be led straight to their hammers; therefore, lest the wires become entangled by various slants, the Masters have arranged certain oblong iron tools, which they commonly call *cadentiae* <note>linkages or bell-cranks</note>, but we call "axes" [axles]. Each has two little arms, as it were, to which two wires are attached: one which lifts the hammer, the other which, connected to the lever, moves the two-armed iron part. These axles or linkages in Figure II are marked with the letters **NO**, **PQ**, **SS**, each of which has two arms, whence we also call them *dybrachia* <term>dybrachia: Greek-derived term for 'two-armed' levers</term>, as if you were to say "bibrachia." These are marked with the letters **TV**, **XY**, **Z$\beta$**, to which are attached iron wires: the first ones, **TXZ**, are attached to the levers $\alpha, \eta, \chi$ <note>alpha, eta, chi</note>, and the remaining three **VY$\beta$** are attached to the hammers $\delta, \phi, \lambda$ <note>delta, phi, lambda</note>. # Mechanism V.
## Concerning the Hanging Cymbal-Wheels. See Illustration XX.

<margin>The origin of the Cymbal-Star of the Church of Fulda.</margin>
It so happened that this mechanism was seen nowhere else but in the greater Church of the Monastery of Fulda, and I judged it most worthy of a somewhat more detailed description. After the building of the Church in the said place was completed, and when St. Boniface <note>The "Apostle of the Germans" (c. 675–754 AD) who founded the Abbey of Fulda.</note> had given himself entirely to the conversion of souls, it happened that among other most illustrious women, he also converted an Englishwoman. Since she had previously worshipped a golden star as a deity, once converted to Christ, she wished to place a golden star—chiming with countless little bells—in the Church founded by St. Boniface as a monument to her perceived deliverance. This remained the greatest ornament of the Church for several hundred years, until finally, amidst the turmoils of war, the Abbot, being in need of money, was forced to take down the golden star and spend it on military expenses. So that such a famous monument should not perish, he ordered a bronze star of the same shape and size, equal to the first, to be put back in its place. To this day, it is viewed in the said Church with the greatest admiration by all, and it is perceived by the ears to resonate with a sweet sound no less pleasant than the original. Both ends of its axis rest upon silken ropes, twisted with singular skill, which hang down from the highest vault of the temple, so that the star is suspended in the air as you see in Fig. IV. The said ropes are moved around an axis in a wheel (<term>peritrochio</term> <note>A "wheel and axle" or treadmill mechanism</note>) above the vault, inside of which a man walks, turning the star, which is bright with 14 rays. Each ray has a length of 12 feet from the center to the tip. These rays are equipped with countless small bells, and when the wheel is turned, it produces a sound that—though very loud and powerful—is nonetheless sweet and most pleasing to the ears, full of majesty (especially if it sounds in harmony with the vast organ on the opposite side during major festivals and times of public joy in the city). Truly, I thought that I should not omit a very minute description of the said star, which the most Illustrious and Reverend Abbot of the Monastery of Fulda, Joachim <note>Joachim von Gravenegg, Prince-Abbot of Fulda from 1644–1671.</note>, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire and Arch-Chancellor to the Empress, took care to have most exactly drawn and sent to me by his most learned Secretary, Mr. Christopher Emerus—a man most ready not only of hand, but also of wit; the description is as follows. See Illustration XX.

### Description of the Cymbal-Machine or hanging star in the Cathedral of the Monastery of Fulda, which they commonly call the Golden Wheel, most worthy of being seen and heard.

<margin>I. Figure.</margin>
It is still unverified what metal this hanging star is manufactured from; however, it seems to be partly cast and partly forged. Its form and figure are as follows: its interior and front part, where the inscription can be read and which faces the eastern choir, is seen drawn in the first figure; the back part, turned toward the western choir, can be seen by holding the paper up to the light. The diameter of the entire machine, from the point of the highest tip of one ray to the point of the summit of the opposite one (excluding, however, the little bells hanging there), contains twenty-four feet, which our German craftsmen call a <term>Werckschuh</term> <note>German: "work-shoe," a standard unit of measurement roughly equivalent to a foot.</note>, one of which consists of twelve inches; the length of half a foot is designated in the third figure after the drawing of the axis. The specific division of the principal parts and the proportions of this wheel, both of the circles and spaces as well as the rays, can easily be found from the drawing with the help of a compass. This star consists of fourteen rays, which, as far as the interior decoration is concerned, are of transparent and most skillful workmanship, so varied that no one ray corresponds to another in this regard, but is clearly different, while a similar and equal exterior decoration and proportion is maintained. In each of these rays there were at least nineteen—and some still are—little bells or cymbals; and although some have fallen off, many still hang there, which by the treading of a certain machine like a pulley, to the length...

Let an instrument be made about 6 feet long, marked **ABCD**, with a curved outer surface similar to the larger viols, which are colloquially <note>original: "barbarè," literally "barbarously." Kircher often uses this to refer to non-Latin or common vernacular terms.</note> called *violones*. Next, let a wheel be made with a diameter of 4 palms, and a thickness of only 2 or 3 fingers. You will house this wheel, rotating on its axis, within the interior body of the instrument in such a clever way that only a sixth part of the wheel's circumference emerges through the curved exterior surface of the instrument; we have marked this protruding sixth part of the wheel with the letters **NG**. Let the edges of the instrument, **AC** and **BD**, be parallel to this wheel, and equally high and curved. Once this is done, the instrument should be fitted with strings made of animal gut (for brass strings have no place here) in the quantity and thickness usually used for Harps. These should be arranged so that the largest string always corresponds to the lowest key or <term>palmulæ<note>A "palmulæ" or "tastus" refers to the individual keys of a keyboard.</note></term>, which is *C sol, fa, ut* <note>The traditional Guidonian hexachord name for the note C.</note>; the remaining strings should be smaller and smaller in proportional decrease, corresponding in order to the sequence of the keys, just as is done in Harps. This continues until the whole task is completed with 49 strings (which is the number of keys a standard keyboard <note>original: "Abacus Clauicymbalorum," referring to the keyboard of a harpsichord or similar instrument.</note> usually has) stretched across the curved surface. The keyboard of 49 keys is represented here by **XZ**.

To ensure each string obtains its proportional length, you will glue a curved bridge or <term>fulcrum<note>A "fulcrum" here acts as a bridge that supports and divides the vibrating length of the strings.</note></term> **OP** to the curved surface of the instrument. This bridge, by gripping the strings obliquely between iron pegs, will determine their length from **P** to **O**. At the **BD** end, the strings are fastened with other iron or wooden pegs; at the **AC** end, tuning pins <note>original: "verticelli," the small pegs or wrest pins turned to tune the instrument.</note> are fitted, by which the wound strings can be tightened or loosened according to the desired tuning. The strings, however, should not touch the Wheel **GN**, but should remain about half a finger’s width away from its outer circumference. 

The levers, which we also call <term>choragia<note>Kircher's technical term for the mechanical linkages between the keys and the strings.</note></term>, are applied within the space **HL**, so that each individual string has its own lever. These are attached with such industry to the stems of the keyboard keys (which turn inward) that as soon as the keys of the keyboard are pressed, the levers attached to the key-stems are pulled downward, pressing the strings they correspond to against the wheel. When the wheel is turned—having been previously well-rubbed with <term>colophony resin<note>Pine resin used to create friction on bows; in this case, applied to the wheel to "bow" the strings.</note></term>—it finally produces the sound of stringed instruments. However, so that these things may be better understood, it seemed best to show the hidden mechanism separately.

Therefore, let there be made within the space **HL** a curved arch or support made of wood, carved with as many notches as the instrument has levers or strings. An iron or brass wire is passed through these notches and simultaneously through the "tails" of the levers, so that the levers can be raised or lowered around the iron wire as if around an axis. 

Let us explain the matter more deeply using one or two levers and keys: let **N** be the key of the keyboard, and **NML** its stem, which is secured by a pin inside the wood **KL**. Let the levers be represented by **SVT**, which are secured through the notches *rm* of the support **QR** by the iron wire passed through them. Let the levers also have rings at **V**, where a wire is inserted to connect them with the rings of the key-stem **NL** at **M**. The end of the levers at **T** is made slightly curved, so that with this curvature it can more easily grip the strings at **T**. Let the string *ab* be placed immediately beneath the lever, yet in such a way that it does not touch the end of the lever at all, but sits slightly away from it, as string *ab* shows. 

The result is that as soon as key **N** on the keyboard **XZ** is pressed, the wire **MV** (affixed to the key at **M** and the lever at **V**) pulls the lever **SVT**. Its end **T** then presses the string against the wheel (which has been previously roughened with resin). The wheel's rotation vibrates the string *ab*, finally producing the desired sound of a bowed instrument. What we have said regarding one key and lever is intended to be done for all the others in a similar fashion.

# DEVICE IX.
### *To present automated Pythagorean Music arranged according to the proportioned hammers of three Cyclopes. See Illustration XXII.*

Among other harmonic devices, the following deservedly holds first place. It is Pythagorean Music <note>Music based on the mathematical ratios discovered by the ancient philosopher Pythagoras</note> set for hammers, which we have often presented in various places before various Princes with such applause and admiration that they seemed hardly able to be satisfied by its repetition. This music is especially suited for cleverly presented Comedies. The melody is for eight voices distributed into two choirs. The tempo perpetually follows triple proportion <note>triple time, or a 3/4 feel</note>; the hammers provide the measure in such a proportion that the largest to the medium hammer has a sesquialtera <term>Sesquialtera: a ratio of 3:2, which creates the interval of a perfect fifth</term>, and to the smallest hammer a double proportion <term>Double proportion: a ratio of 2:1, which creates the interval of an octave</term>. Words are attributed to Vulcan <note>the Roman god of fire and the forge</note>, encouraging his Cyclopes to forge weapons for some notable expedition; these, having been called, strike the anvil, and with the triple sound of the hammers while they hit the anvil, the Singers follow the triple measure precisely with both voice and dance and gesture, presenting a wonderful spectacle for the eyes and ears. Therefore, let us see how we can present this performance—which has until now been shown in Comedies with living voice, dance, and movement—using an inanimate automated machine.
We assume here the existence of the Organ with all its related parts—the wheels, the wind chest <term>Aeolian chamber: the pressurized box that holds the air for an organ</term>, and the wheels driving the machine—based on what we have described in preceding sections. The Pythagorean musical composition actually composed by us, together with the text and the proportion of the hammers, is as follows.

positioned and situated so that, like twisted wires, they push back the limbs in alternating turns as the motion of the wheel strikes against them. Thus, when the curved wire **bh** strikes against the tooth **l**, it pushes back the limb **f**; after one-third part of the time has passed, the other limb is pushed back by the curved wire **ig** striking against tooth **q**; and after another third part of the time, the limb **fc** is pushed back again by wire **bh** striking against tooth **hm**. In this way, the limbs will mimic a triple motion in their gait, corresponding to the sound of the hammers and the organ. To make the heads and arms appear to toss about, the heads of these statues should be fixed to thin wood and balanced with a lead weight—which we have marked with the letter **a** in the figure—connected to the arms on the axis **pq**. The result will be that as the statue moves, both the head and the arms will appear to be in a state of perpetual tossing. You may elegantly clothe these statues, animated by this ingenuity, in either wood or cloth so that nothing of the internal machinery is visible, and you will have achieved your goal.

If, however, you wish to represent a <term>choragus</term><note>The leader or conductor of a musical ensemble.</note> of the entire music, providing the measure by the movement of a hand, this is done by a particular handle **MS** which corresponds to the space **GH**. Within this space, you will arrange the teeth that complete a full <term>tactus</term><note>A historical term for a musical beat or measure, often indicated by a down-and-up motion of the hand.</note>, yet they should be separated slightly from one another to distinguish the beats, as the figure shows. Then, in the middle of the fashioned statue, let there be an arm **cb** movable around a small axis **d**. From point **b** of this arm, a wire is connected through a hidden passage to the arm **Y** of the <term>taxillus</term><note>A mechanical toggle or "rocker" component.</note> or cadence-marker **RS**. From the other arm **x** of that same toggle, another wire is connected to the handle **mn**, and you will have the matter completed.

For while the cylinder is rotated by the water-wheel **CB**, its teeth strike the <term>phonotactic</term><note>Kircher's term for the arrangement of pins on a musical cylinder that "program" the melody.</note> handles and open the pipes of the organ, providing first a Pythagorean melody. Meanwhile, the teeth set in a triple order in the space **A HCG** strike the handles **ZYX**, producing "Cyclopean" music—that is, the triple sound of hammers—at a rate that is <note>original: "ἰσόχρονον"</note> isochronous or equal in time to the notes. The statues, through the twisted wires falling upon the hidden teeth of the fixed wheel, will cause a rhythmic movement consistent in every way with both the Cyclopean and Pythagorean music. Finally, the handle **mn**, depressed by the teeth in space **HG**, moves the toggle **RS** to which it is joined by the wire at arm **X**; this in turn depresses arm **Y**, and this depression necessarily causes the rising and falling of the arm in the conductor **N**. Thus, the statue **N** will be seen to give the beat or applause according to the measure of the time, perfectly expressing the <note>original: "ἄρσιν & θέσιν"</note> <term>arsis and thesis</term><note>The "lifting" and "setting down" of the hand in conducting, representing the upbeat and downbeat.</note>. We have therefore exhibited a Pythagorean and Cyclopean musical automaton, which was the task at hand.

->*To construct another automatic harmonic machine which is driven by no service of wheels, bellows, or phonotactic cylinders, but by the wind and air alone, exciting a certain perpetual and harmonious sound.*<-

### Book IX. Phonotactic Magic. 353

...[you should] provide it with strings made of animal intestines, or even more, as is evident in the preceding figure. 
The instrument is marked ABCD, with tuning pegs at CA, bridges at IK and SD; the strings are wound around the tuning pegs, led over the bridges IK and SD, and fixed at the pegs BD. The "roses" <note>These are decorative soundholes, similar to those found on a lute or guitar.</note> are marked FFF. S is a handle by which it can be hung. There remains the matter of tuning which, unlike other instruments, should not be performed through thirds, fourths, fifths, or octaves <note>Kircher means the standard intervals used to tune a harp or lute.</note>. Instead, all strings must be tuned to a <term>unison</term> <note>the exact same pitch</note> or in octaves, so that a harmonious sound may follow. It is truly wonderful and almost <note>original: παραδοξον (paradoxon)</note> paradoxical how strings stretched to a unison or in octaves can constitute such diverse harmony. However, so that this musical phenomenon—which I do not know has been more deeply observed by anyone until now—may be further explained, and the causes of said sound assigned, we shall begin our experiment "from the egg," <note>original: "ab ouo" — a Latin idiom meaning "from the very beginning."</note> after we have first declared the conditions of the instrument and where it ought to be placed.

The location of the instrument should not be in the open air, but in a closed place, yet in such a way that the air has free passage in and out on both sides. The wind can be channeled in various ways: first, through conical and spiral tubes <note>Kircher previously described these "cochleate" tubes for amplifying voices</note> by which we collected sound inside a house earlier; second, by means of valves. Let there be two wooden valves EF and BVCD, joined at F and VD, yet in such a way that they provide an entrance for the wind into the space contained between the parallel boards FV, K, and FE.

->[Illustration of a rectangular stringed instrument with various components labeled with letters A, B, C, D, E, F, K, R, S, V, and N. Three circular soundholes are labeled FFF.]<-

The valves should be placed outside, and the boards inside the room; the instrument is attached behind them at the slit SN. It should be turned at an oblique angle to the slit SN so that the wind, collected through the valves and compressed within the narrow space of the boards BV and EF, escapes through the slit and strikes all the strings SONR of the instrument. For if the instruments are placed parallel to the boards, it will not be as successful; but if, as we have said, it is tilted so that all the strings are exposed to the wind, it will achieve the best results. For according to the softness or the violence of the wind, you will perceive a wonderful harmony within the room; at times all the strings will express a certain trembling sound, sometimes the songs of birds, or a <term>hydraulic organ</term> <note>A water-powered pipe organ popular in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</note>, and occasionally a concert of flutes and other foreign sounds. No one will even suspect what kind of instrument it is, or by what hand, by what bellows, or by what craftsmanship it produces the harmony. This instrument will be all the more hidden and worthy of admiration the more it is concealed and covered. Furthermore, if you close all the windows of the room, the sound, likewise enclosed, will fall silent; but as soon as even one is opened, it will bathe those present in its customary sound with wonderful pleasure.

# Experiment.

If someone exposes a string made from animal intestines, stretched tight, to the wind in the place prepared a little earlier, he will observe that the string soon sounds—not with the note expected of a stretched string, but with one entirely different. At one moment it maintains a third, then a fifth, now a fifteenth, or a twenty-second; and occasionally a third, fourth, or sixth. Since there has been no one who could explain the cause of this, we considered it our duty to reveal the genuine cause of this matter here.

I propose, therefore, first: that the wind does not always strike the string with a uniform force, but hits now this part of the string, now that part, with "rays" as it were—sometimes with a slower and sometimes with a swifter impulse. I shall demonstrate that this unequal impulse of the wind is the cause of such diverse sounds.

But if the "ray" (stream of air) **C** alone touches it, that [Diagram of a string AF with points B, C, D and a wind source G blowing on it] is, if it divides the string in two, it will happen that the remaining parts **CA** and **CF** will sound an <term>octave</term><note>original: "diapason"</note> relative to the whole, just as we demonstrated in the division of the <term>monochord</term><note>A single-stringed instrument used to study mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note>.

Thus, the stream of wind produces different sounds in the string according to its various points of contact. 

From this, the more of the string the wind-stream leaves untouched, the deeper the sound it will produce; the smaller the part, the higher the sound. <note>The Latin text repeats the word "grauiorem" (deeper) twice here, but physics and context dictate the second should be "acutiorem" (higher).</note> Therefore, what the wind does in one string, it will do in countless other identical strings, and this is the genuine cause of such great diversity of sounds perceived in this instrument. Frequently, a certain tremulous sound is born, affecting the ears wonderfully, which certainly has no other origin than the undulation of the wind, which does not always glide onto the string with a straight force, but in the manner of waves, and thus consequently incites the string with the same motion with which it strikes.

From these things it is also clear that one and the same string can produce infinite different sounds; for even if the wind presses the string more strongly in one place, by pressing more weakly in various other places, it will give birth to new and different distinctions of sound. For if, for example, it presses strongly at **C** and weakly at **B**, it is certain that **CA** will not quite achieve an octave, but will aim for something in between. But let these explanations suffice regarding the cause of the diversity of sounds in a single string.

## Machine XI.
## Presenting all kinds of sympathetic harmonic experiments.

We call "sympathetic experiments" those which resonate without being touched when other sounds are made, through a certain wonderful proportion and similarity of sounding bodies. By this, it happens that at the sound of one, another is also moved though untouched. This proportion takes place not only in <term>homogeneous</term> (uniform) bodies, but also in <term>heterogeneous</term> (diverse) ones. From this arise many miracles of nature; however, no one will easily give a reason for them unless they possess an outstanding knowledge of musical secrets. It is almost common knowledge that one string can move another untouched, not only when tuned to the same note, but also when tuned to the <term>octave</term> and <term>fifth</term>, although the untouched string always vibrates more vehemently the closer it is to a <term>unison</term> (the same note). We shall not assign the reason for this effect here, since we have discussed it most extensively in previous sections, but we shall only open up the way in which many admirable things can happen in <term>natural magic</term>.

### Experiment I.

*To demonstrate Sympathetic Music; that is, to prepare an instrument which, by no other agent than Sympathy, produces a harmonious sound.*

<margin>A stringed instrument can be set in motion by the sound of an Organ.</margin>

We shall not establish harmony here in homogeneous bodies <note>Kircher means instruments of the same type, like two identical lutes.</note> such as stringed instruments can be, but in heterogeneous ones—that is, in an organ and a stringed instrument, and others—for in this way the harmony will be perceived more distinctly. Take an instrument distinguished by its strings and constructed of the most resonant wood, such as we proposed in Machine X; you shall tune its strings most perfectly to some organ, so that each individual string is in perfect unison with the individual pipes of the organ. Once this is done, you shall move back from the sound of the organ with the instrument until you see the strings move and find them giving back a perfect sound; and this will be its proportionate distance. But if any strings do not move, it will be a sign that the pipe does not respond perfectly to the string, or is an octave higher. Or, you will work more advisedly in this way: apply the instrument to the interior walls of neighboring rooms, or best of all, upon a beam continuous with the organ, moving it here and there until you detect the movement and sound of the strings, and you will have what was sought. For the stringed instrument will perfectly exhibit all the harmony of the organ within a separate place. 

And do not think I am merely handing down speculation; read what we reported above concerning the Mainz Organ, which by chance set a Lute <note>original: "Chelyn," a term derived from the Greek word for tortoise shell, referring here to a lute or lyre-style instrument.</note> hanging in a nearby choir into motion, and no doubt will remain regarding the truth of the matter. In this alone is the only difficulty: that one finds the perfect similarity and proportion of bodies with the proportionate distance; whoever finds this can undoubtedly boast that he has found something marvelous in nature. For there is such a similarity between certain resonant bodies that as soon as one sounds, the other is found to sound also, as we have shown curiously in parts 1 and 2 of this book. All of which teaches us another experiment: if someone were to lightly suspend harps, theorbos, citterns, harpsichords, and similar stringed instruments in a very resonant room (after first removing all carpets that dull the sound), he will perceive—not without wonder—a certain exotic harmony caused by the mere movement of the air from the voices of speakers, or from the voices of those playing the organ.

## Experiment I.
*Concerning sympathetic harmony through conic bodies.*

If anyone knows how to fashion a parabolic or hyperbolic cylinder, he should know that he has penetrated the greatest secret in <term>musurgia</term> <note>Kircher's term for the art and science of musical composition and sound production.</note>. Let us reveal the secret. With the help of a <term>paraboloplastic</term> <note>original: "paraboloplastæ"; a tool or mold designed to carve or shape a perfect parabola.</note> mold, let a concave parabolic semi-cylinder be formed. This is done if you move the parabolic mold with a steady and straight motion through suitable material along its length; for by 그 motion in the yielding and soft material, the aforementioned parabolic semi-cylinder will be formed—a device of wondrous power in exhibiting <term>sympathetic harmony</term> <note>The phenomenon where an object vibrates automatically when it encounters a sound wave that matches its natural frequency.</note>. Let the work be set up in this way: The two foci of the bounding parabolas must be observed with the greatest diligence. If a string is drawn from one of these to the other opposite focus of the parabola and stretched tight, the instrument will be ready for sympathetic sound. 

But let us explain the matter with letters and a figure. Let ABCDEF be the parabolic cylinder; let the two parabolas bounding the cylinder be ABC (the upper) and DEF (the lower); let HG be the foci of the equal parabolas. I say that the string or gut-cord HG, stretched through both foci, will be set in motion by any movement [of air], even the smallest. For since any section of the semi-cylinder made normally to the axis is a parabola, and infinite parabolas can be conceived in that semi-cylindrical surface, it happens that any voice or sound and motion of the air falling upon this parabolic semi-cylindrical surface—provided it falls upon the cylinder at right angles—produces as many <term>actinobolisms</term> <note>original: "actinobolismos"; a term derived from Greek meaning the radiation or projection of rays. Kircher treats sound waves like rays of light that can be focused to a single point.</note> as there are equal parabolas that can be conceived in the said semi-cylinder. Furthermore, since the string is stretched through the foci HG, it will consequently pass through the foci of all the other parabolas conceivable in the said semi-cylinder. Now, since the union and confluence of rays occurs in the centers of the foci, an intensification of sound also occurs in those same spots. Therefore, the entire string, agitated by the multiple confluence of rays and the multiplication of the impulse, will tremble and sound.

->[Illustration: A tall, semi-cylindrical trough. A vertical string (HG) is stretched down the center. To the right, a small mechanical figure holding a cross is attached to the vibrating mechanism.]<-

<margin>A string producing a nearly perpetual sound.</margin>

**Corollary I.**

Hence it is clear that if someone were to stretch three or four strings near each other around the foci, tuned in <term>consonance</term> <note>In musical intervals of a third, fifth, and octave.</note> at the 3rd, 5th, and 8th, the machine would perpetually exhibit a harmonious murmur when placed in a suitable location or exposed to the wind. For this sounding line HG has a certain physical width and some space within which the intensification of the rays and the <term>caustic</term> <note>The "caustic" refers to the concentrated area of intensity where reflected waves (light or sound) meet.</note> or sounding effects occur.

### Experiment III.

*To excite untouched strings with the sound of glass.*

If anyone rubs the rim of a glass cup with fingers previously moistened, they will soon perceive a certain ringing sound. If, furthermore, they stretch a string over the cup tuned to that same pitch <term>equisonant: having the exact same pitch or frequency</term>, they will perfectly perceive not only the vibration of the string but also its sound. If, therefore, someone stretches corresponding strings over several glass cups, they will have music composed of a wonderful ringing and the sound of strings; regarding this experiment, see our more detailed discussion in the first part of this book.

### Experiment IV.

*So that one thinks they hear the great ringing of bells.*

This is also a remarkable experiment that carries the listeners away into great admiration. Take one of the strings of a larger viol <note>original: *chelis*; specifically the *Violone*, a large ancestor of the double bass</note>; to this, hang a brass plate or any other ringing and sonorous body. Then, with both ends of the string wrapped around your fingers, insert them into your ears. When the hanging plate is struck against another nearby body, you will perceive a sound that you would never have first believed—namely, a sound far exceeding the ringing of all bells. If, however, instead of a plate, you use a brass rod (the longer it is, the more suited to the task), you will perceive a formidable sound indeed, ranging from deep to sharp; and the longer the string, the more intense the sound it will produce. The cause of this is nothing other than the vibration of the ringing metal which, while it communicates the ringing to the string, the string conducts the vibration communicated to it to the hearing. There, the enclosed internal air is violently shaken through its acoustic muscles <note>Kircher's term for the delicate structures of the inner ear</note>, and thus it exhibits an extremely powerful sound. It is truly wonderful that no other bodies, but only those that delight in ringing—such as all metallic plates and rods—produce this effect.

### Corollary.

If you lower an instrument of this kind into some loudly echoing cistern by the string, and insert both ends of the string into your ears, and then strike the plate against the wall, you will hear a violent roar composed of various voices beyond what can be described.

### Experiment VI.
### On various ways to alter the sound of strings.

A string produces its sound according to the nature of the objects placed beneath it at the bridge. For instance, if you place a wind-filled bladder (into which small pebbles have been previously tossed) under a large, stretched string and then scrape the string with a horsehair bow, you will hear a certain ridiculous sound, well-suited for <term>theatrical interludes</term> <note>original: "scenicis intermedijs"; these were musical or comedic performances held between the acts of a play</note>. If you place a glass object under that same string, the string will imitate a strange, tinkling ring; and so it goes with other materials. All of these methods provide a vast amount of material for creating exotic instruments.

### The Steganographic Art, by which the hidden thoughts of the mind

Just as we taught in *The Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Arte Magna"; referring to Kircher's 1646 work *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*, which discussed mirrors, lenses, and optical signaling</note> how the hidden thoughts of the mind can be communicated to those who are absent through light and shadow, so too can they be shared through sound. The silent is that in which the same thoughts of the mind are communicated through musical letters or characters, woven together in an impenetrable style of writing.

When secret communication <note>original: "Cryptologia"</note> must be established over a distance that is not too far, it can easily be set up using the instruments described in the art of acoustic engineering <term>Echotectonica: the science of sound reflection and architectural acoustics</term>. These primarily consist of various types of pipes—straight, conical, elliptical, or spiral—led from one place to another through hidden passages. With the help of these, two Princes can reveal anything to each other as if they were present together, even when they are apart. However, since I have already described the construction and use of all these acoustic instruments very precisely in the aforementioned work on acoustic engineering, I have judged it unnecessary to deal with them more extensively here with tedious repetition. Indeed, the reader will be able to deduce countless other things pertaining to this subject from the instruments already cited. Furthermore, all the musical instruments discussed in the preceding pages can serve this secret communication. In fact, as many differences as there are in sounds, so many ways can there be to reveal one's thoughts to another. For the sounds of pipes, cymbals, bells, strings, and the simple or singing human voice can all serve as signs. To provide an introduction to this matter, let the alphabet be divided into six rows, assigning four letters to each row, and you will assign a specific type of sound to each row, as is clear in the following table.

<note>This table shows a grid for a musical cipher. Each instrument represents a row, and the number of strikes or notes represents the column.</note>

The use of this alphabet is as follows: Suppose these words are to be signaled to a friend: "Come quickly" <note>original: "Veni cito"</note>. Since the first letter of the word "Veni" is V, and V holds the fourth position in the fifth row of letters <margin>Method of revealing secrets.</margin> and corresponds to row five, four strikes of the rattle will represent V. Then E, the second letter of the word, is contained in the second row assigned to cymbals and corresponds to the first position; this will signify that one strike of the cymbal is to be given. N, meanwhile, occupies the first place in the fourth row of letters [assigned to strings]. Finally, I, corresponding to number 1 in the third series of letters, will instruct you to give one strike on the bell to signify I. Thus you see that the letter C signifies three sounds of the pipe; I signifies one strike of the bell; T signifies three sounds of the rattle; and finally, the letter O signifies two strikes of the string. In this way, you can signal anything you wish. The white circles denote a tablet provided with holes, so that as soon as you hear a specific sound, you can mark the place with a pin <note>original: "taxillo" — literally a small die or peg</note>, arranging the individual tablets in order.

362 *Universal Music-making, or the Art of Harmony and Dissonance* <note>original: "Musurgia Vniuersalis siue artis Consoni & Dissoni"</note>

However, you can combine all the instruments listed in the previous table into a single, very simple instrument consisting of four handles. For you can produce the sound of the pipes with your mouth, so you are not forced to add bellows to the instrument. The first handle serves for striking the cymbal, the second the bell, the third the string, and the fourth the rattle.

From these things, it is clear that an alphabet can be constructed whose 24 individual letters correspond to different types of sound, so that for whatever type of sound, the letter immediately becomes known. However, since all these matters are too minor to be explained more extensively, we leave them to be refined by others.

# §. II.
# *Musical Steganography.*

The other type of <term>Steganography</term> <note>The art of writing secret messages so that no one otherwise suspects the existence of the message; here, Kircher applies it to music.</note> consists of an impenetrable method of writing through musical characters, and it is manifold. First, all the keyboards or key-frames of the aforementioned instruments can serve this purpose, so that the individual letters written on the keys <note>original: "palmulis"; literally "little palms," referring to the keys of an organ or harpsichord.</note> correspond to the individual letters of the alphabet. Or it can be done through musical notes, and this again through the rise and fall of the notes, yet in such a way that <term>breves</term> <note>original: "breues"; a musical note of long duration.</note> denote a rising pitch and <term>semibreves</term> <note>original: "semibreues"; a note half the length of a breve.</note> denote a falling pitch, as in the following example.

# THE TEN-STRINGED LYRE OF NATURE
