# P R E F A C E.

[V] WHEN THE ANCIENTS more carefully contemplated that admirable order in the universe of things and the great majesty of nature, they convinced themselves it was impossible not to believe in that Divinity whose machine <note>Kircher uses the word "machinam" to describe the universe as a complex, engineered system designed by God.</note> they saw constructed with such an admirable series of things and with such signal wisdom and providence. But while they were deprived of the light of faith, having fallen into various errors, they gave birth to various and altogether dissonant monstrosities of the imagination. For some, considering the world itself to be some great God and Spirit, worshipped it in place of the true Divinity. Others believed in a **Spirit** or **Soul of the World** permeating and constituting all things by its power. Some even devised the <term>Calchodea</term> <note>original: "Calchodeam." This is a term used in Hermetic and Platonic philosophy to describe a presiding spirit or "governess" of the world of Ideas that helps manifest forms into the physical world.</note>, that is, the Presiding Power of worldly Ideas, bestowing their forms upon all things. <margin><unclear>Illegible notes in margin</unclear></margin>

He reflects on how ancient philosophers recognized the divine order of the world but, lacking Christian faith, often mistook the universe itself—or a "World Soul"—for the Creator.</summary>

Book X. The Ten-Stringed Lute of Nature. 365

...they have said; But we, searching a little more deeply into the nature of things and her innermost secrets, have found that this is not a "world soul"—or what the Arabs call the <term>Calchodea</term> <note>original: "Calchodeam"; a term from Arabic philosophy often referring to the "Giver of Forms" or a celestial intelligence governing the sublunary world</note>—but rather nothing other than Nature herself: the true and unique **art of God** <note>original: "τέχνην τᾶ θεᾶ"</note> (that is, of God, who establishes all things through her). We assert that her power, which permeates all things, is nothing other than a **fitting power** <note>original: "δύναμιν ἁρμόζουσαν"</note>, the adapter and arranger of all—namely, **harmonic proportion**. By this proportion, all things are disposed and preserved; it is the unique cause and origin of all the admirable effects and operations lying hidden in the bosom of nature. And so that the goal of our intention may become more and more clear, we have progressed through every grade of natural beings. We show that those hidden agreements and disagreements of things—the laws of "hate" and "friendship" by which individual things are joined in a friendly gathering or separated in enmity—consist of the "consonant-dissonant" and possess their own harmonic ratios. If you were to separate these ratios from Nature, it would be necessary for all things to fall into a confused chaos and an abyss of nothingness. Here the curious reader will find the causes of the powers of stones, herbs, animals, and their various states detected and revealed. He will find open a gateway to a certain new workshop of **natural magic**, in which, by applying consonants to dissonants, one may produce stupendous effects in all things. Indeed, he will find almost nothing so hidden or abstruse in the whole bosom of nature that it remains hidden from him by the help of this book, or through which he cannot perform wonders. We have called this the **Decachordon** <note>From the Greek "deka" (ten) and "chorde" (string); a ten-stringed lute or harp</note>, so that we might more perfectly contemplate the harmony of natural things displayed in a ten-fold order. This is like the ten strings of a perfectly tuned lute, or like ten registers in an organ representing ten different systems of nature. Thus, finally, having been carried higher through the contemplation of worldly harmony, we might at last rest most sweetly in the "unison" of such an admirable and incomprehensible **Organ Player**—in God, I say, the center of all harmony.

# PART I.
# THE TEN-PIPED ORGAN.
## CHAPTER I.
### God, the Best and Greatest, is compared to an Organ Player; the World to an Organ.

**M**AGNIFICENT and incomprehensible GOD, from eternity and before any condition of created nature, was most sufficient unto Himself. He was compelled by no necessity or indigence, but solely from the abundance of His infinite goodness, to show forth the riches of His glory and bounty, He was pleased to found the world in time. He arranged it not with a confused order of things, nor by some rash efficiency of beings, but with a certain supreme and ineffable providence. He fashioned it so that man—the son of the world, contemplating the **cosmos** <note>original: "κόσμον"; Kircher notes this means "ornament" or the "order of all things connected by an inviolable law"</note> of this Great Machine—might recognize the Author of inexhaustible power. By recognizing Him, man might admire Him; by admiring, desire Him; by desiring, love Him; and by loving and worshipping Him, finally possess Him eternally. Therefore, the order and beauty of the world is a certain "Idea" of the divinity. It exhibits that "Idea of Ideas" which enfolds all things most perfectly—that **Monad** <note>The mathematical and philosophical concept of "The One" or absolute unity</note> which rolls together the proportion of all numbers in the ineffable breadth of its center. And since He wished to show that the number of perfection is infinite, He disposed all things in **number**; as for **weight**, He drew the multitude and variety of scattered things into one, as if to a center of gravity; and finally, as for **measure**, He willed to exhibit each thing adorned with a certain infinite symmetry and harmonic proportion. He did this so that there might be a perpetual love, agreement, and "concert" of created things, both with their Author and among themselves—a symphony most absolute in all its numbers. Since, therefore, Music or harmony is nothing other than number...

Kircher establishes the metaphor of God as an Organ Player who created the world's orderly "cosmos" to lead humanity toward divine love.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion of how the universe is structured according to musical proportions, moving from abstract theory into a grand metaphor of God as a divine organist creating the world.</meta>

->366 *The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance*<-

...number, measure, and weight, as has been shown extensively in the preceding pages; for the World, according to the testimony of Plato, is a **harmony holding all things together** <note>original: "ἁρμονία πάντα κατέχουσα"</note>. Since Nature is truly the art of God—a **harmonizing force** <note>original: "vis ἁρμόζουσα"</note> that adapts all things—and the World is a perfect likeness of God, it necessarily follows that the **Cosmos** (that is, the harmonic world) was founded upon the likeness and analogy of that archetypal harmony. It follows that Nature, the art of God, looked toward musical proportions in all worldly operations. But, lest the assertion of our contemplation be seen as vain or idle, let us now show how, in that primeval origin of things, God—the Creator of all and the **Divine Organist**—played.

<margin>God as the Organist.</margin>
Just as a craftsman about to build an Organ first lays down various foundations, like the first rough elements of the work; then constructs pipes of every kind; arranges the channels that conduct air and wind; and, to demonstrate a greater variety of harmony, adapts various "rules" which the common people call **Registers** <term>Registers: Also known as 'stops' on an organ, these are the mechanisms that allow a player to control which sets of pipes are active, changing the tone and color of the music.</term>; and afterwards arranges the bellows as certain receptacles of the winds, by whose perpetual motion the air is constricted, forced into the wind-channels, and supplied. Finally, he arranges the **Keyboard** <note>original: "Clauiarium"</note> as the ultimate director of his art, and at last, with the help of his fingers and the various combinations of registers, striking the keys or "palms" (which they call **tasti**), he produces that variety of harmony which we perceive with admiration in organs. In a way not unlike this, God—the Best and Greatest—being about to build this worldly organ with an inexhaustible variety of dissonance and consonance;

<margin>The production of Matter <note>original: "Hyles"</note>.</margin>
By the Word of His power, He first founded that formless **Matter** <term>Matter: Here the text uses "hyle," a Greek term for the primordial, unshaped substance of the universe before creation.</term> and undigested chaos, like the foundations and preludes of the future organ. Then, He outlined the "pipes" as the first sketches of forms lying hidden in that formless chaos. Third, with the Spirit of His divinity brooding over the formless waters, He gave birth to the air and winds necessary for the future organ (so to speak) by breathing them forth. Fourth, He arranged that formless mass of matter—now imbued by His Spirit with various differences of sound—into diverse classes of things, like registers. Fifth, He produced the **Keyboard** of the entire organ as its soul and His own art (that is, the Nature implanted in individual things). Finally, the work being perfected, that Supreme **Master Musician** <note>original: "Archimusicus"</note>, inciting His art through the keyboard by the breath of His Spirit animating the organ, produced that wonderful harmony of things which we admire even to this day. But let us see *how* He produced it.

<margin>The Register or Prelude of the first day.</margin>
Therefore, as soon as the first Register of this organ—like the **lowest note** <note>original: "proslambanomenō," the lowest note in the ancient Greek musical system.</note>—was unlocked and sounded by the Word of His power; behold! the Empyrean heaven was filled with an innumerable variety of blessed minds distributed into nine orders of choirs. What did this present but a certain **ten-stringed instrument** <note>original: "decachordon"</note> or a harmonic scale? In this scale, the nine strings denote the distinct Choirs of Angels, while the tenth denotes the **Leader of the Dance** <note>original: "Choragum"</note> himself: God, the Best and Greatest, the celestial Apollo, the ultimate completion of all harmony in the number ten. What does the Earth, together with that Light created on the first day, signify, if not a first prelude of the variety of forms soon to be introduced into matter? Yet, since the lower part of this Register resonated with I know not what unpleasantness due to a confused melody, it had not yet acquired the perfection due to it.

<margin>The Register or prelude of the second day.</margin>
Behold! the Register of the second day was unlocked, and as soon as it sounded by the Word of His power and the breath of the Holy Spirit, the Waters were immediately segregated from the waters and enclosed in the channels of the earth; the Dry Land was uncovered and detected; and the Air, stretched out far and wide in that expanse, displayed a beautiful **stage** <note>original: "proscęnium"</note>. In a word, the primordial nature of the Elements and their neat connection brought forth a new harmony. But the intended perfection of the harmony was not yet established.

<margin>The Register or prelude of the third day.</margin>
Behold! the third Register was unlocked as soon as it sounded, with the Word of His power and the breath of the Holy Spirit cooperating. When, behold! the Earth—struck by the art of the Organist—germinated an innumerable variety of herbs, plants, trees, seeds, flowers, and fruits. What else did this exhibit but as many different musical measures of divine art, which, though dissonant in such great diversity of natures, were nonetheless consonant in their beautiful mixture?

<margin>The Register or prelude of the fourth day.</margin>
Furthermore, the fourth Register was unlocked as soon as it sounded by the Word of His power and the breath of the Holy Spirit: behold the Heaven, the Sun, the Moon, and the Planets proceeding as if from a bridal chamber—

Each day of the Genesis creation story is likened to the opening of a new musical "register" or stop on the instrument, moving from primordial chaos to the complex harmony of the natural and celestial worlds.</summary>

If anyone, therefore, wished to weave a multi-stanza harmony upon this kind of **poly-strophic** <note>A poem consisting of many stanzas</note> verse, let him first choose **Musical Numbers** <term>Musarithms: Kircher’s term for the sets of numbers used to represent musical pitches in his tables</term> based on the logic of his theme. # Rules for Poetic Musurgy.

<note>original: "Musurgiam Poëticam." Kircher uses this term to describe his method of setting poetry to music using mathematical tables and "musarithms."</note>

**L**est we be forced to repeat the same things forever, we shall here set down certain rules by which we may be guided in our <term>Melothetic<note>The art of composing melodies.</note></term> operations, so that we may more easily avoid the reefs of difficulties that arise.

*First Rule.* Since Poetic Musurgy proceeds through multi-faceted periods, it must first be noted that these harmonic numbers of the bass, 5. 1. or 5. 8., whenever they occur applied to the same tone, always produce the same thing: for example, in the sixth tone, they always signify a cadence from C to F; in the second tone, a cadence from D to G, and so on for the rest. Therefore, so that the same sound and tone are not always perceived, the <term>Novice Composer<note>original: "Melotheta Tyro"</note></term> should look for other harmonic numbers among the <term>Musarithms<note>Kircher's term for the numerical sequences used in his compositional tables to represent musical intervals.</note></term> of the bass besides those mentioned—such as 2. 5., or 7. 3., or 6. 5., or whatever others occur—and he can always use these for the second or third stanza. For the first and last stanzas must always keep the tone assumed at the beginning, so that a greater variety may be perceived in the harmonic modulations. We gave an example in the preceding composition, where you see in the 2nd and 3rd Musarithms of the bass that the last notes are different from the notes of the first and last Musarithm. From this, consequently, a harmony of another tone is born, as has been said. For the first stanza has the form of the second tone, the second stanza has the form of the ninth tone, the third stanza the form of the fifth tone, and the fourth stanza finally turns back to the second tone assumed at the beginning. Therefore, this rule must be observed most diligently. 
<margin>A quick method of changing tones.</margin>
For if one always took the same harmonic numbers for the second tone, he would always produce the same tone; which, although permissible, does not happen to be as pleasing to the ears as when a mixture of various tones intervenes, as we also taught above in the sixth canon. If, however, someone cannot find different numbers, he may use the easiest practice of all, indicated in the sixth canon: namely, by moving the column of the assumed tone next to the column of keys applied one step, or two, or four, or five steps higher; and the Musarithms will immediately pass into another form of Tones. And this is the most efficient method of all for mixing tones. It is so fit and convenient for establishing any variety that even a single immobile Musarithm, through the fourfold application of the column of numbers to different steps of the moved column of keys, may always emerge as four different harmonic stanzas. Suppose, for example, the Musarithm of the bass recently cited is 8 7 6 4 5 1; let this same one be shown in four stanzas through a varied mixture of tones. Proceed thus: apply the last number of the Musarithm, 1 or 8, above the assumed tone, namely the second tone (or what is the same thing, above G), and the first stanza of the second tone will come forth in harmonic composition. Again, apply the first or eighth (the last number of the first Musarithm of the bass) above D in the column of keys, and the second stanza composed in the ninth tone will come forth. Then let the same number be applied above B from the composition of numbers made; the third stanza composed in the fifth tone will come forth. Finally, let the first or eighth number be applied in the column of numbers above G as in the beginning, and the last stanza of the second tone will come forth again; meanwhile observing these two rules most diligently.

*Second Rule.* Whenever the song is <term>hard<note>original: "durus." Refers to the "cantus durus" or hexachord using B-natural, often associated with major-sounding modes.</note></term>, the first or eighth number must never be placed above B or above F, and only rarely above E, and even then only with great skill. You may, however, move them above all other letters.

*Third Rule.* Whenever the song is <term>soft<note>original: "mollis." Refers to the "cantus mollis" or hexachord using B-flat, often associated with minor-sounding modes.</note></term>, the first or eighth number in the column of numbers must never be applied to the letters A or E; they may be applied to all others with impunity.

*Fourth Rule.* Regarding the placement of the chromatic signs (flat and natural <note>original: "b b quad." [Kircher uses the square 'b' for a natural sign]</note>), see what we have said at length in the ninth Canon of the rule of the preceding chapter, and above in section IV regarding the placement of those same figures. But lest you always be forced to consult the said rules, we shall place others here much shorter.

Whenever the numbers 5. 1. (or what is the same, 5. 8.) correspond in the column of keys...

<summary>Kircher explains four rules for varying musical modes when using his mathematical composition system, allowing a single set of numbers to produce different melodies by shifting their starting pitch.</summary>
<keywords>Musurgia Universalis, Musarithms, Melothesia, musical modes, Baroque composition, cantus durus, cantus mollis, harmonic variety</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for using Kircher’s "Musarithms," a combinatorial system for composing music. It follows the previous discussion on how to map numbers to musical pitches and rhythms based on poetic meters.</meta>

### Book VIII. Wonderful Music-making. 99

...with the letters C, F, or G, C, or F, B, whether the song be "hard" <note>original: *durus*; refers to the use of B-natural and the hexachord starting on G</note> or "soft" <note>original: *mollis*; refers to the use of B-flat and the hexachord starting on F</note>, then the key or letter that corresponds to the seventh number in the column of numbers should never be marked with a sharp (♯).

Whenever the numbers 5.1. or 5.8. of the Musarithm base <term>Musarithm: A set of numbers representing musical intervals used in Kircher’s automated composition system.</term> correspond to the column of keys for the letters DG, EA, or AD, then the letter that corresponds to the seventh number rightly demands a sharp (♯). However, if the note following the one marked with this sign rises immediately, or if it is the final note; but if the following note descends immediately, the sign must be omitted. We have demonstrated the reason for all these things at length in the preceding book.

Furthermore, whenever in a "soft" song <note>A piece using the B-flat signature</note> the numbers 5.1. fall on DG, then the letter that corresponds to 6 will almost always be B-flat <note>original: *b molle*</note>; that is, a flat must be prefixed to the notes on the B-string. If, however, it is a "hard" song <note>Using B-natural</note> and the numbers 5.1. fall on the letters AD, then similarly the letter that corresponds to 6 will ordinarily be B-flat <note>Kircher is discussing the rules of *musica ficta*, where performers add accidentals not written in the score to avoid harsh intervals</note>, or rather, the notes to be placed on the B-string must be marked with a flat sign—specifically in the 1st and 2nd tones <note>The Dorian and Hypodorian church modes</note>. If you observe these rules, you will produce a harmony subject to no defects at all.

From these things it follows first: that individual four-voice Musarithms, varied four times through a mixture of tones according to the rules produced, generate a harmony for four stanzas <margin>Corollary I.</margin> that is perfect in every measure. For even if the intervals of the notes are the same in each stanza, they are essentially changed by the diversity of the tones, presenting a most pleasing harmony to the ears—which would not happen if Musarithms of different intervals were applied to only one tone. Such is the power in the diversity of tones.

**Fifth Rule, concerning the change from one meter to another.** It also follows by what method an "Iambic Euripidean Catalectic" <note>A poetic meter that is "cut short" by one syllable in the final foot</note> becomes "Hypercatalectic" <note>A meter with an extra syllable added at the end</note>.

An "Iambic Euripidean Hypercatalectic" is that which has one redundant syllable at the end, as appears in this following four-line stanza:

*Hail, Virgin of Virgins* <note>original: *Ave Virgo Virginum*</note>
*Hail, life of the heavenly ones* <note>original: *Ave vita caelitum*</note>
*Hail, light of the celestial ones* <note>original: *Ave lux caelestium*</note>
*Sole hope of the earthly ones* <note>original: *Una spes terrestrium*</note>

Whoever, therefore, desires to transfer the Musarithms of this meter into a particular table, shall perform nothing else except to double the penultimate number in all the Musarithms of Table IV <note>original: *Pinacis IV*</note> adapted for Euripidean Iambics. That is, place the given number twice, and he will have a particular table of Musarithms adapted for the Hypercatalectic Iambic. For example, let the Musarithm of the first stanza of Table IV be as follows:

| Catalectic | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | | From the catalectic becomes the hypercatalectic by doubling the penultimate number in each Musarithm, as follows: | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *Hail, star of the sea* <note>original: *Ave maris stella*</note> | 8 | 8 | 8 | 7 | 7 | 8 | | | 8 | 8 | 8 | 7 | 7 | 7 | 8 |
| **Musarithm** | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 3 | | | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 |
| Hypercatalectic | 8 | 8 | 8 | 5 | 5 | 1 | | | 8 | 8 | 8 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 1 |
| *Hail, Virgin of Virgins* <note>original: *Ave Virgo Virginū*</note> | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |

In the same way, you will either double the penultimate rhythm-marking note <note>original: *notarum metrometrarum*</note> in each series, or you will bisect the penultimate note into two equivalents. You will then also have rhythm-marking notes adapted to the Hypercatalectic Iambic, as can be seen in the preceding musical example.

From this it is also clear that a recently composed Catalectic Iambic composition <margin>Corollary II.</margin> can be changed entirely into a Hypercatalectic one with very little effort, if the penultimate note of each stanza is divided into two notes which, when taken together, are equivalent to said penultimate note.

Finally, from this it is clear how one and the same Musarithm can be adapted to different meters <margin>Corollary III.</margin> with the easiest effort, solely by the division of the initial or final note into two similar equivalent divisions. And I have thought it necessary to note these things especially before I proceed further, so that the novice composer <note>original: *Melotheta Tyro*</note>, being instructed in all things, might more readily prepare himself for practice. Many things should have been said in this place concerning the multiplication of Musarithms and the nearly infinite variety of combinations; but because we have handed all these things down at length in the ten canons of the preceding chapter, we therefore refer the reader to them. For whatever we said there can also be applied to this "Poetic Music-making." Therefore, let us move on to other things.

# APPENDIX.

### *On Poetic or Rhythmic Music-making.*

**W**e have treated thus far the method of poetic music-making in a single limb <note>original: "monocola," referring to a poem consisting of only one type of verse</note>—that is, by what diligent effort we can animate any homogeneous kind of meter with musical melodies. Now, however, we must show by what method and industry heterogeneous meters of different kinds joined together (which those who write on meter <note>original: "Prosodiographi"</note> are accustomed to call "two-limbed" <note>original: "dycola"</note> from a mixture of two verses of different kinds; "three-limbed" <note>original: "tricola"</note> from three meters; or "four-limbed" <note>original: "tetracolon"</note> from a mixture of four verses of different kinds) are to be converted, in order to establish a greater variety of musical operations. We shall settle the whole business with a few combinations <note>original: "syntheses"</note>.

*Combination I.* If, therefore, you apply the musical-rhythms <note>original: "Musarithmos," Kircher's technical term for the mathematical-musical values assigned to poetic syllables</note> from column I of Table <note>original: "Pinacis"</note> I to the musical-rhythms of column I of Table III, you will have musical-rhythms for Pherecratean meter, of which kind is the following:
*Pyrrha, beneath a pleasing cave* <note>original: "Grato Pyrrha sub antro"</note>
*The seas with black winds* <note>original: "Nigris æquora ventis"</note>
*He hopes, ignorant of the breeze.* <note>original: "Sperat nescius auræ." These lines are from Horace, Odes 1.5.</note>

*Combination II.* If you place the first Adonic column of Table III twice, you will have musical-rhythms for Anapestic meters, as follows:
*Gird the temples of the poets with laurel.* <note>original: "Cingite vates tempora lauro."</note>

*Combination III.* If you double the second Dactylic column of Table III—that is, if you place it twice—you will have musical-rhythms for Choriambic Asclepiadean meter, as follows:
*But if you insert me among the lyric bards,* <note>original: "Quod si me Lyricis vatibus inseris"</note>
*I shall strike the stars with my sublime head.* <note>original: "Sublimi feriam sydera vertice." From Horace, Odes 1.1.</note>

*Combination IV.* If you join the first column of the first Table to the second Dactylic column of the third Table, you will have musical-rhythms for Glyconic meter, as follows:
*Breathing through the heavens with voices* <note>original: "Spirans Æthera vocibus"</note>
*Pegasus puts on his wings.* <note>original: "Alas pegasus induit."</note>

*Combination V.* If you join the first and second columns of the third Table together, you will have Dactylic Alcmanic or Horatian meter, as follows:
*You see how Soracte stands white with deep snow,* <note>original: "Vides vt alta stet niue candidum / Soracte"</note>
*And the woods no longer sustain the burden.* <note>original: "nec iam sustineant onus." From Horace, Odes 1.9.</note>

*Combination VI.* If you prefix the first column of Table I to one of the columns of Table V, you will have musical-rhythms for that Iambic meter, namely for the third verse of a Horatian Ode:
*The woods laboring with the cold.* <note>original: "Syluæ laborantes geluque." From Horace, Odes 1.9.</note>

*Combination VII.* If you prefix the first column of the first Table to one of the columns of Table VI, musical-rhythms for Alcmanic Iambic meter will be produced, as follows:
*You despise the honorable marriage beds of the Maiden.* <note>original: "Spernis decoros Virginis thoros."</note>

*Combination VIII.* If you place a column from Table V after one of the three-syllable columns of Table I, you will have musical-rhythms for Sapphic and Phalaecian eleven-syllable meters <note>original: "hendecasyllabis"</note>, as follows:
*More sluggish than old age and resin.* <note>original: "Veterno resinaque pigriores."</note>

*Combination IX.* If you prefix the fourth column of five-syllable words from Table I to the column of Dactyls in Table III, you will have musical-rhythms for Horatian meters of the kind that follow:
*I hate the uninitiated crowd and keep them away.* <note>original: "Odi profanum vulgus & arceo." From Horace, Odes 3.1.</note>

*Combination X.* If you place two columns of Table V or two columns of seven-syllable words from Table II together, you will have musical-rhythms for dactylic pentameter:
*Dreadful in mouth, gushing Avernus seethes with waters.* <note>original: "Horridus ore scatens feruet Auernus aquis."</note>

**Book VIII. Wondrous Music-Making. 101**

And by this practice of joining columns to columns, more and more diverse types of meters will always be born. For example, from the first and second <term>tables<note>original: "pinaces." Kircher uses the Greek word 'pinax' to refer to the large data tables or charts in his book.</note></term>, in which we described polysyllabic <term>musical numbers<note>original: "Musarithmos." These are Kircher’s mathematical codes for musical intervals and rhythms.</note></term>, all kinds of meters will be born through various combinations. Just as this said combination extends almost to infinity, so too does it look toward an infinite variety of meters. Indeed, the columns of the first and second tables, when combined with the columns of poetic metrics, will again give birth to an innumerable offspring of harmonic variation. From this, the reader may understand the immense vastness of our creative system.

Indeed, you will obtain <term>multi-membered<note>original: "Polycola." This refers to stanzas made up of different types of poetic lines.</note></term> meters or heterogeneous Odes if you join different columns from different tables. For example, if someone wished to compose a harmony upon that specific Ode of Horace:
*See how Soracte stands white with deep snow,*
*nor can the laboring woods now sustain the burden;*
*and the rivers have halted*
*with sharp ice.*
<note>This is a famous excerpt from Horace’s Odes (1.9), describing Mount Soracte north of Rome.</note>

He will work in this way: join the first and second columns of Table III twice; to these, apply one of the columns from Table VI; then one second column from Table II; finally, one from the columns of Table V, and you will have the musical numbers arranged for the given Ode.

In no other way will you complete other compositions. Furthermore, multi-membered odes can be assigned as "pure" or "impure." Odes are called "purely" multi-membered when they have every single verse as a different type. For example, if someone were to attach an Archilochian Iambic to an Anacreontic Iambic-Euripidean, and finally an Adonic to this, he would have a four-line stanza of four different types. Odes are called "impure" when meters of one kind are placed twice, three times, or four times, and then another meter of a different kind is added. This happens in the Horatian Odes, where the first two meters are of the same kind, but the following two are of a different kind; hence it is called a four-line stanza of three types, as is clear in the Ode cited just above. Likewise, in Sapphic stanzas, an Adonic of a different kind is connected to three verses of the same kind, which is why it is called a four-line stanza of two types.

The same corresponds in all things of our Musical Poetics; for if someone were to take one of the four-line columns of Table IV, which contains Euripidean musical numbers, and to this again another from Table V, and to this another from Table VI, and finally subjoin to this the first column of Table III, he would have musical numbers for a four-line stanza of four types arranged in order. In this case, the individual meters would be of different kinds: the first would be Iambic Euripidean, the second Anacreontic, the third Archilochian, and the fourth, finally, Adonic.

From all of this, unless I am mistaken, it is most clearly evident that a certain infinite power and potential shines forth in the mutual combination of different columns. But all these things will be demonstrated more fully both in what follows and in our *Combinatoric Art*—if God grants us life.

->**On Hexameter and Pentameter Verses.**<-

The Hexameter or Heroic meter consists of six "feet." The fifth of these is always a <term>dactyl<note>A metrical foot consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones (— u u).</note></term>; all the others are either Dactyls or <term>spondees<note>A metrical foot consisting of two long syllables (— —).</note></term>. The Pentameter, however, consists of five feet, all of which are either dactyls, spondees, <term>chorales<note>original: "Choræi," referring to a trochee (— u).</note></term>, or <term>pyrrhics<note>A metrical foot of two short syllables (u u).</note></term>. But since this type of meter is inconsistent because of the maximum variety it allows, and does not hold its feet fixed in a certain place, we therefore reject it as less suitable for music. However, if anyone should wish to construct a symphony upon similar kinds of meters, he will easily obtain his intent if he arranges the musical numbers of the first and second Tables according to the feet of the meter. For example, if someone were laboring upon this <term>couplet<note>original: "dystichon."</note></term>:
*All human affairs hang by a slender thread,*
*And those things which were strong fall by a sudden crash.*
<note>This is a variation of a line from Ovid’s 'Epistulae ex Ponto'.</note>

If, I say, he wished to compose a four-voice piece upon these verses, he will select musical numbers from the columns of Tables I and II according to the feet of each verse. For the foot [omnia—all], take column II of Table II; for this has polysyllables with a short second-to-last syllable; for the other foot [sunt—are]...

For the words [are of men] <note>original Latin: *sunt hominum*</note> take column III of the same Table <term>Pinax: a table or chart used in Kircher’s system</term>. For [slender] <note>original: *tenui*</note> take again column II of Table II. For [hanging] <note>original: *pendentia*</note> column III of Table II. By arranging the columns with this diligence, you will be able to select any transverse series of Music-arithms <note>Kircher's term for the mathematical-musical combinations in his charts</note> for the desired musical setting <term>Melothesia: the art of composing a melody or musical setting</term>; and then operate exactly as we prescribed in the preceding sections, and a hexameter adorned with musical measures will come forth, just as you requested. In exactly the same way, you will complete a Pentameter, for the method of operation is the same in all cases.

->**Corollary.**<-

From these things it is clear that the columns of the first and second Tables can serve for both free prose and bound verse. Indeed, given any theme of words, whether bound or free, the poetic feet of the given theme will always be assigned within the many-syllabled columns.

### CHAPTER VI.

### Explanation of the Second Arrangement, or Florid and Artful Metric Music-making.

What florid counterpoint is has been sufficiently demonstrated at the beginning of the preceding sixth book. Since we have so far handed down the system of simple counterpoint in our metric Music-making <term>Musurgia: the art of musical composition</term>, in this chapter we will show the method by which anyone—even someone unskilled in Music—can complete a musical setting imposed upon them, not only in simple counterpoint, but also by what means they can adorn their songs with an artful and florid style. This is so that professional musicians cannot object that we have only handed down the lowest principles of the art of melody-making. We call it "florid and artful" Music-making because in it the flow of voices does not proceed by "point against point" and "note against note" in equal steps—as has been shown until now—but rather, the same harmony is depicted with various diminutions <note>diminution: the breaking of a long note into many shorter, decorative notes</note> of different voices and a certain concord of consonant and dissonant notes, like various colors, so that it can soothe the ears of listeners with singular grace and pleasure. We have placed six Music-arithmetic Tables for this effect.

The **First Table** contains florid and artful Music-arithms for Adonic and six-syllable dactylic meters.
The **Second Table** contains Music-arithms for Euripidean Iambics.
The **Third Table** contains florid and artful Music-arithms for seven-syllable Anacreontic meters.
The **Fourth Table** contains florid and artful Music-arithms for Archilochian Iambic meters.
The **Fifth Table** contains florid and artful Music-arithms for nine-syllable and ten-syllable meters.
The **Sixth Table** contains florid and artful Music-arithms for Sapphics and any eleven-syllable meters <note>hendecasyllables</note>.

Behold, in these six Tables we present to you unique Music-arithms containing harmonious, "succulent" <note>Kircher uses *succulentas* to mean rich or full-bodied</note>, and most appropriate symphonies for the Church.
The rhythmic-measure notes <term>Metrometrae: signs or notes used to measure the meter of the verse</term> are unique to each vocal Music-arithm, which differs from the rhythmic notes handed down in the first Arrangement. There, one common series of rhythmic notes out of twelve was sufficient for each of the four voices; here, however, the voice of each individual Music-arithm claims its own unique series of notes, which must not be changed. For they are so connected with the numbers that they neither can nor should be separated from one another. Hence, however many numbers there are in any one Music-arithm, it is necessary to find just as many notes in the corresponding series of notes. Otherwise, the method of working and of expressing the Music-arithmetic numbers in harmonic measures differs in no way at all from the method handed down in the preceding Arrangement. Indeed, I am confident that students of melody-making will find the operation much easier in these than in the former ones. However, having briefly declared these things, let us finally explain the whole business with some examples.

### Proposition I.

**Given a Euripidean Iambic meter in the first tone, to compose a melody <term>Melothesiam|The art of setting words to music or composing a melody</term> upon it in the florid style.**

You will carry out this proposition through double, simple, and mixed operations, just as was done in the preceding section. You may establish the simple operation either with a single Musarithm <note>In Kircher's system, a Musarithm is a set of mathematical tables or "musical algorithms" that represent specific melodic intervals and rhythms</note> corresponding to one stanza of the meter—which, when repeated through a change of tones <note>shifting the musical mode or key</note>, yields the assigned melody, as we demonstrated in the first operation above; or you may use several Musarithms. If using several, the base Musarithm must have its last two numbers different from the numbers 5, 1 or 5, 8, as previously stated; however, ensure the tone for the first and fourth stanzas remains the same, and you will achieve what is sought. But let us provide a varied example <note>original: "paradigma promiscuum"</note>, so that we are not always forced to show the double operation.

Let us therefore complete a composition in the florid style over a Euripidean meter, such as the hymn *Ave Maris Stella* <note>Latin: "Hail, Star of the Sea," a famous medieval plainchant hymn</note>, etc. Let Musarithms of various tones be selected—the kind we said have base numbers different from 5, 1 or 5, 8—or if these are not found, let one Musarithm be repeated through different tones.

### Proposition III.

**Given an Iambic Archilochian meter and any chosen tone, to produce a desired musical setting <term>Melothesia: the art of composing a melody or musical setting</term> arranged in the Florid style.**

The following Table <note>original: *Pinax*</note> corresponds to Iambic Archilochian meters and contains <term>Musarithms: Kircher’s technical term for musical-mathematical patterns or algorithms used for composition</term> adapted to the florid style. Therefore, for anyone whose intention is to adorn songs based on this type of meter, let him bring the selected Musarithms to life in harmony according to the number of stanzas, whether by a simple or mixed operation through the application of the rules and canons prescribed in the preceding sections.

This type of meter is most suitable for harmonic melodies and is encountered everywhere in the Roman Breviary <note>The liturgical book containing the daily prayers, hymns, and psalms of the Catholic Church</note>, since almost all hymns consist of this type of meter. For example: *Now that the sun has risen* <note>original: "Iam Lucis orto sidere"</note>; *O Christ, Redeemer of all* <note>original: "Christe Redemptor omnium"</note>; *O Bounteous Creator of the stars* <note>original: "Creator alme siderum"</note>; *The banners of the King advance* <note>original: "Vexilla Regis prodeunt"</note>; and others of this kind. 

It differs from the preceding Anacreontic meter by only one syllable. Wherefore, if someone wishes to adapt the preceding Musarithms to these, he shall do nothing else but double the penultimate <note>the second to last</note> number of each voice of the Musarithm. As for the musical note corresponding to that number—that is, the penultimate note—he should divide it into two notes that are together equivalent to the original single note.

**Proposition 4.**

*Given a nine-syllable meter and any musical mode, to compose the desired <term>musical setting<note>original: melothesiam; the art of arranging a melody for a text.</note></term> in the <term>Florid style<note>A decorative style of music featuring more complex rhythms and melodic ornaments, rather than simple one-note-per-syllable settings.</note></term>.*

# 122 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

-> NOTE. <-

The rules regarding the mixing of different kinds of meters, which were provided in the appendix of the fourth chapter, can also be applied to these tables. For instance, the Phalaecian <note>A classical meter consisting of eleven syllables, often used in ancient lyric poetry</note> combined with the Anacreontic <note>A light, rhythmic meter named after the Greek poet Anacreon, usually associated with themes of love and wine</note> is very well suited to musical melodies. However, see those matters which we have treated at length in the said appendix regarding the business of this combination.

Thus, having finished the treatise on metric music and its adaptation to various verses, nothing remains but to show now by what means the listed Musarithms <note>Kircher’s term for "musical algorithms"—pre-calculated sets of numbers that allow a user to compose music by following a mathematical grid</note> can be common to all languages. Indeed, there is no language, no idiom in the whole universe so "barbaric" that it cannot use these Musarithms of ours to animate every kind of meter with harmonic melodies.

-> Proposition VI. <-
-> Given Adonic or Dactylic meters, to complete the desired musical composition. <-

A twofold operation can be established by means of Musarithms of this kind: Simple or mixed—or what is the same thing, homogeneous or heterogeneous. It is "Simple" or homogeneous when we use the Musarithms of only one table; it is "Mixed" or heterogeneous when we mix the "florid" <note>An ornate, decorative style of melody with many notes per syllable</note> Musarithms with the Musarithms of simple counterpoint <note>The basic technique of setting one note against another</note> excerpted from the tables of the previous section. Let us explain both methods.

-> The first simple operation. <-

We have said that the simple method of operating is when we use the Musarithms of only one table. However, since the Musarithms in the tables almost all have the same termination—that is, they always provide the same cadences <note>The concluding sequence of notes that brings a musical phrase to a rest</note> of the sixth, second, or another tone <note>A "tone" refers to a musical mode, similar to a scale</note>—which you will recognize from the last two numbers of the base Musarithm, which will always be 151, or 58, or 48. We have shown in the preceding sections that this is unpleasant to the ears. Hence, to obtain the variety required in music, you must diligently observe the sixth Canon <note>A rule or instruction</note> regarding the mixture of tones; but for the sake of the student, let us repeat it in this place.

-> Paradigm I. <-

Suppose, therefore, that some Adonic <note>A short poetic meter consisting of a dactyl followed by a spondee (— ◡ ◡ | — —)</note> musical composition is to be completed in a certain florid style. And let the words be the following:
*Gaudia mundi, blanda remittit, sollicitudo, relligiosa.* <note>original: "Gaudia mundi, blanda remittit, sollicitudo, relligiosa." Translated: "The joys of the world, gentle it returns, religious care."</note>
To animate these words into a florid harmony, a single Musarithm can suffice in this manner. Let the following florid Musarithm (and the given tone VI) be excerpted from the following table.

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

Then you see which letters the Musarithm of the first voice, 54321, corresponds to, and you will find they correspond to C B A G A. Therefore, you will mark as many points on the staff of the first voice or "cantus"; to each of which, if you apply the notes placed in the region of the now-resolved Musarithm... | 54323 <br> 327517671 <br> 54321 <br> 87651 | [musical notation] <br> [musical notation] <br> [musical notation] <br> [musical notation] |

# Book VIII. Wondrous Music-making. 125

**Rule IX.** Wherever these last numbers in the base of the Musarithm <term>Musarithm: A set of numbers used in Kircher's system to represent specific musical intervals or chords, allowing non-composers to "calculate" music.</term> 4.1 or 4.8 occur, you shall never take the cadences <note>original: "clausulas"</note> of these numbers for the beginning, nor for the middle, but always for the end.

**Rule X.** You will diligently observe Canon IV so that when the voices, through some change of tones, ascend or descend more than is proper, you exchange the Soprano <note>original: "Cantum"</note> or Tenor for the Alto, and the Alto for either of the others, as we have prescribed in the said Canon.

**Rule XI.** If, furthermore, it should happen that the melody descends more than is proper, do not interrupt its flow in the notes, but begin the entire phrase an octave higher; these things are also to be observed if the melody should ascend more than is proper: do not interrupt its flow in the notes, but begin the whole phrase an octave lower.

And these rules are abundantly sufficient for the perfection of the art; therefore, let us return to our purpose. After we have shown what simple (or homogeneous) operation is, we shall now also show how we ought to establish a mixed (or heterogeneous) operation.

## Paradigm II. Of mixed operation.

Let the words of the chosen theme be the same, to be performed by mixed or heterogeneous operation. Proceed as follows: for the beginning of the phrase, select from Table III of the preceding section on simple counterpoint any Adonian Musarithm <term>Adonian Musarithm: A rhythmic pattern based on the Adonic verse, a classical poetic meter consisting of a dactyl followed by a spondee.</term> contained in the first column. For the second phrase, however, you shall select a florid Adonian Musarithm from the first table of Florid Counterpoint in the second section. Then, for the third phrase, again select a Musarithm of simple Counterpoint, and finally, for the fourth phrase, again a florid Musarithm. The Musarithms will stand as you see here:

<note>The Latin lyrics in the table are: "Gaudia mundi blanda remittit sollicitudo religiosa."</note>

You see, then, in this single example how simple Musarithms ought to be mixed with florid ones. But who could sufficiently describe the immense multitude and variety of combinations from this mixing of Musarithms? Certainly, their combinations in even one table are so many that the entire Ocean could not have more drops than the individual combinations of mixtures will have different variations. For the number of these combinations far exceeds the number of grains of sand that the entire globe of the earth is capable of holding. These things might deservedly be considered impossible <note>original Greek: "ἀδύνατα"</note>, had we not already confirmed them by the irrefragable truth of Mathematical scrutiny.

Therefore, once the Musarithms have been selected in a mixed fashion from the appropriate tables, and the columns applied according to the given tone, transfer the numbers together with the notes (according to the rules handed down in the preceding sections) onto the musical staff <note>original: "pentagramma vocum"</note>, and the following Composition <term>Melothesia: Kircher's term for the systematic composition of a melody or musical setting.</term> will result.

# CHAPTER VII.

## Musical Panglossia <term>From the Greek 'pan' (all) and 'glossa' (tongue/language); a system for applying music to all known languages.</term> or the Application of Musarithms <term>Kircher’s term for his mathematical-musical algorithms or formulas used for automated composition.</term> to all other languages of the entire universe.

### §. I.

### Regarding the verses and rhythms of the Hebrew language, addressed to the Professors of the Sacred Language of the Society of Jesus. <note>The Society of Jesus refers to the Jesuits, the Catholic religious order of which Kircher was a member.</note>

#### On the feet of Hebrew Verses.

As the Hebrew language is the fountain and origin of all other languages, it seemed fitting to take the first principles of the Musurgical Art from it. In order that we may treat this Hebrew "Musurgia" <note>The art of musical composition.</note> more skillfully, we shall first set forth a few things briefly regarding the properties of Hebrew meters. The poetry of the Hebrews is most ancient, as we have demonstrated elsewhere; its meters consist of their own feet and syllables, just as in Latin. In their verses, they use only two feet: the first they call **Movement** <note>original Hebrew: תנועה (Tnuah), which Kircher transliterates as 'Thema' and translates as 'mutatio' (change/movement).</note>, and it consists of one long syllable. The other is called **The Peg** <note>original Hebrew: יתד (Yated), meaning a nail or tent peg.</note>, and it consists of two syllables, one short and the other long; it corresponds to our Iamb, such as *lecha* (to you) or *mesor* (hand over). From various mixtures of these, three others are formed, namely the Spondee, the Bacchius, and the Creticus, as follows:

| Creticus | Bacchius | Spondee |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **כורמים** | **דברים** | **דבר** |
| *Coremim* | *Deuarim* | *Debar* |
| (Vinedressers) | (Words) | (Word/Speak) |

By all of these, the Hebrews measure their songs.

He explains the basic building blocks of Hebrew verse—the Tnuah (long syllable) and Yated (short-long)—and compares them to classical Greek and Latin poetic structures.</summary>

### Book VIII. The Miraculous Making of Music. 127

The Hebrews call a poem a <term>baith<note>original: "בית"; literally "house," referring here to a stanza or verse unit</note></term>, and they generally join verses in pairs until the end of the poem, as is customary in our elegies and <term>distichs<note>A pair of poetic lines</note></term>. They call the first verse a <term>daleth<note>original: "דלת"; literally "door" or "gate"</note></term>, and the second verse a <term>sagor<note>Kircher writes "legor," but the Hebrew provided is "סגור" (sagor), meaning enclosure or closure</note></term>, because it closes the poem; this is shown in the following verse:

->Mary, you who brought forth grace for us,<-
->Our song shall sing of you.<-

Furthermore, if a poem does not exceed ten verses, it is called a <term>pasuc<note>original: "פסוק"; a verse or sentence</note></term>. If, however, it exceeds ten, it is called a <term>schir<note>original: "שיר"</note></term> or a song.

## On Hebrew Rhythms.

The Hebrews apply rhythm to the composition of their poems like salt <note>A metaphor suggesting rhythm provides the essential "flavor" or "seasoning" to the verse</note>. This rhythm is achieved in roughly three ways. First, when only simple letters—whether one or many—match, without taking the vowel points into account, such as *dabar badar* <note>original: "דבר בדר"</note>; this is called a <term>passing rhythm<note>original: "עבר" (aber)</note></term> or common rhythm, because it passes by the ears so quickly it is hardly perceived.

When the rhythm is conspicuous or elegant, it is called <term>raui<note>original: "ראוי"; meaning "fit" or "worthy"</note></term>, occurring when the ending members of both parts of the rhythm are similar, such as *darech berech* <note>original: "דרך ברך"; meaning "way" and "knee"</note>.

Third, it is called a <term>laudable rhythm<note>original: "משובח" (meschubach)</note></term> when two syllables end similarly, as in: *otnaim schamaim* <note>original: "שמים אזנים"; meaning "ears" and "heavens"</note>.

->I will lift up my heart, and also my hands<-
<gloss>Asse libbi gam caphaim</gloss>
->To the one who sits in the heavens<-
<gloss>El haiofcheu beschamaim</gloss>

But whoever desires to know more concerning the various forms of Hebrew verses should read Elias Levita, Rabbi Kimchi, and others. Lest we seem to overstep the bounds of our Art <note>Referring to the Art of Music</note>, let us return to our intended purpose.

## Section II.

### On Syriac or Chaldaic Poetry, or on the verses and rhythms of the Syrians and Chaldaeans.

->To the Fathers of the Society of Jesus in Syria, and especially the Maronite inhabitants of Mount Lebanon, for whom the Syriac language is their own.<-

->Given any Syriac meter and tone, to compose a desired musical setting over it.<-

Although many and various types of poems are found among the Syrians, especially in the books containing the divine offices <note>The "divine offices" refer to the official set of prayers and psalms recited by clergy and monastics at fixed hours.</note>, we shall not waste time enumerating them without necessity. Since they can be easily understood from what we will say, we have chosen only two as the most noble, frequent, and necessary of all, and the most worthy of study and effort. One of these was established by Saint James, and the other by Saint Ephrem <note>St. Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373) is one of the most celebrated hymnographers in Eastern Christianity.</note>, most eloquent Doctors and the greatest lights of the entire Orient. These forms have taken their names from them: the first is called <term>Mschuchtho iaakuboitho</term> <note>original Syriac: ܡܫܘܚܬܐ ܝܥܩܘܒܝܬܐ</note>, that is, the Jacobite song; the other is called <term>Ephreimoitho</term> <note>original Syriac: ܐܦܪܝܡܝܬܐ</note>, that is, the Ephremitic song.

The song of Saint James consists of three "pauses," as the Syrians call them, each of which must be four syllables long, as is clear in the following rhythm of Saint James:

<note>The original contains two lines of Syriac script here.</note>
On their behalf / Look upon the sacrifices / Look upon the sins
<gloss>Which [means]: In their stead / Look upon the sacrifices / Look upon the sins</gloss>

However, for a meter to be called perfect and complete, and for the sense and song of the poetic speech to be properly finished, two songs—composed of six pauses—are usually constructed and written, as is clear from the passage cited. They will appear more elegant and charming if they end <term>homophonously</term> <note>original Greek: ὁμοφώνως, meaning "with the same sound" or rhyming</note>, that is, in words with similar endings. This occurs in various ways: First, if the first pause of one song corresponds to the first pause of the second; the second to the second; and the third to the third.

<note>The original contains two lines of Syriac script here.</note>
How appropriate are / these breaks / of theft
How light are / these runs / of goodness.

You see how the individual pauses, or members of the verses, end <term>homophonously</term> <note>rhyming</note>. Sometimes only the third pause of one song rhymes with the third of the other, or indeed all the pauses of both songs rhyme; or finally, none of the pauses rhyme, so that one simply follows the other in a similar fashion. But as I said, the greater and more frequent the similarity of the endings of the pauses, the more elegant and charming the songs are considered. There is hardly any language that exhibits its rhythms with greater grace than the Syriac language, due to the multitude of similarly ending terms. But let these remarks on the poetry of the Syrians, made in passing, suffice.

### §. III.
### On Arabic Poetry.

->To the Fathers of the Society of Jesus residing in Egypt, Syria, and all of Asia.<-

Arabic poetry seems to yield to no other in the wit and elegance of its verses, nor is it particularly difficult; indeed, I have found no nation to have greater license in forging verses than this people. I could declare all these things at length, were it not for the fear of overstepping my bounds, which restrains me from handing them down; receive, therefore, its method briefly and in summary.

Just as among the Latins and Greeks, feet are born from syllables and meters from feet, so also among the Arabs, feet are born from syllables and verses from feet. And there are indeed two [basic] feet among the Arabs, the first of which is called <gloss>original: *sabab*</gloss> **sabab**, that is, a cord; the other <gloss>original: *vatad*</gloss> **vatad**, that is, a stake or peg. This comparison is taken from the structure of a house or tent; thus they call the structure of a poem <gloss>original: *beith alschaar*</gloss> **beith alschaar** <note>Literally "house of hair," referring to the traditional Bedouin tent made of goat hair.</note>. For the Arabs fashion their tents from the hair and skins of animals. Just as a house or tent is stretched out by the help of <margin>Of what Arabic verses consist.</margin> cords and pegs, so the structure of meters is perfected by the help of feet, which they themselves call cords and pegs. 

A "cord" consists of two consonant letters, the first of which always has a vowel, as is evident in these: <gloss>original: *men*</gloss> **men** (who), and <gloss>original: *lam*</gloss> **lam** (not). The second [letter] either has a vowel or it does not. If it does not, it is called <gloss>original: *elsabab elchafif*</gloss> **the light cord**, as was evident in the aforementioned words; if, however, both have a vowel, then it is called <gloss>original: *elsabab eltakil*</gloss> **the heavy cord**, as is evident in these: <gloss>original: *labe*</gloss> **labe** (father), <gloss>original: *Abo*</gloss> **Abo** (to him), <gloss>original: *hade*</gloss> **hade** (this).

A "peg," however, consists of three consonants, two of which have a vowel and one is deprived of a vowel. If the ones having a vowel are immediate [neighbors], then they call it a "joined peg," such as *hade* (this); if, however, a silent letter is in the middle between both vowels, as in <gloss>original: *raglo*</gloss> **raglo** (a man), then it is called a "distinct peg." And so there are four feet among the Arabs, neither more nor fewer, for constructing every kind of poem; and from these cords and pegs succeeding each other alternately, the patterns are composed.

#### On Particular Rhythms or Meters.

Even though there are many forms of verse types for the Arabs, they nevertheless seem to agree more with vernacular verses <note>Kircher is comparing Arabic poetry to rhyming European languages like Italian rather than the unrhymed, quantitative meter of Classical Latin.</note> than with Latin ones. Furthermore, they have greater license in composing verses than any other nations; and lest they neglect any notable or sharp allusion in the verses, they do not always observe the integrity of the meter. 

Among the Italians, the measure is always the same, and they mostly use eleven-syllable lines, or twelve, such as those verses they call **sdruccioli** <note>Italian 'sdruccioli' refers to verses ending in a word stressed on the antepenultimate syllable (e.g., 'armonica').</note>. As the Italians do, so also the Arabs join verses in pairs so that the ends of both terminate in <gloss>original: *ὁμοφωνίαν*</gloss> **homophony**, or similar-sounding feet; which the Latins call **Rhythm** [rhyme], and the Arabs call <gloss>original: *kaphieh*</gloss> **kaphieh**. The end of the first verse is called <gloss>original: *alaaruth*</gloss> **alaaruth**, that is, the proposition; but the end of the second verse, finishing similarly, is called <gloss>original: *altarab*</gloss> **altarab**, that is, the pulsation; and each [half] is called <gloss>original: *mesraa*</gloss> **mesraa** — that is, a door.

### 122 The Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

However, he who desires more regarding these matters should read the poets of the most learned Arabs: Al-Khazraji, Al-Medini, Luqman, the *Qamus* dictionary, Khalil ibn Ahmad, and many others. They distinguish their verses into certain "circles," such that one circle is a **varied circle** <note>original: "mochtalfet al daiereth" / مختلفة الدائرة</note>; then there is the composite circle, and the similar circle, of which there are again three types:

| **Al-Hazaj** <note>original: الهزج</note> | **Al-Rajaz** <note>original: الرجز</note> | **Al-Ramal** <note>original: الرمل</note> |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A song or a Madrigal. | A satire or improvised melody. | A brief poem, called "sand" because of its clipped syllables. |

As for the remaining various forms of meter, as I have said, let the curious reader consult the cited Arabic poets.

#### Proposition III.
**Given an Arabic meter and Tone I, to compose a perpetual musical setting over it.**

Let the following Arabic rhythm be in the form of a seven-syllable Euripidean meter:

-> God is merciful <note>original: "Alla elrahmáno" / الله الرحمان</note> <-
-> He created man <note>original: "Chalakallinschána" / خلق الانسان</note> <-

## § IV.
## On Samaritan Poetry.

The Samaritans <note>An ethno-religious group closely related to the Jews, following the Samaritan Pentateuch</note> emulate Hebrew in all things, although poetic books are scarcely found among them, unless you except a few hymns which the people of Gaza <note>original: "Gazęi" — this may refer to the inhabitants of Gaza or a specific group of Samaritan liturgical poets</note> are accustomed to sing in their sacred rites. # §. VII.
## On Greek Music-making.

### *How to adapt a requested musical composition over a given Greek meter.*

**I** have no reason to speak on the poetry of the Greeks, since both Latin and all other poetry flowed from it; but I will add only an example, lest we seem to have contemptuously passed over this most excellent language, from which, as I have said, all sciences and faculties—and most especially Music—flowed as if from a fountain.

#### Anacreon’s Ode I: To the Lyre <note>original: εἰς λύραν. Anacreon was a Greek lyric poet known for his themes of love and wine.</note>

| | | | |

When you are about to compose a melody above the following Anacreontic meter in the <term>Florid Style</term> <note>Stylo Florido: an ornate, polyphonic musical style</note>; first select the tone, which will be, for example, the second; then, from Table III of the *Florid Musurgia*, extract the four following <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Musarithms: Kircher’s term for the numerical sequences used in his tables to represent musical intervals or pitches for different voice parts.</note>.

# §. VIII.
### *On the remaining Western languages.*

The Western languages are properly those, and are called such, which Europe uses. These are mainly Spanish, French, Italian, and German, along with its "daughters" (such as Belgian <note>original: "Belgica," referring here to Dutch or Flemish</note>, English, and Scottish). Also included is Illyrian <note>A common 17th-century term for the Slavic language family</note>, from which come Polish, Ruthenian <note>A historical term for East Slavic languages, including modern Ukrainian and Belarusian</note>, and Bohemian <note>Czech</note>. All these languages observe their own metric laws in the composition of verses; however, it is usually the case that the given meters are similar to Iambics, whether they are seven-syllable <note>heptasyllabic</note> or eleven-syllable <note>hendecasyllabic</note> lines. Indeed, they neglect the Hexameter, Pentameter, Sapphic, and all those meters consisting of dactyls and anapests <note>Kircher is noting that modern European poetry relies on syllable counts and stress rather than the "long and short" vowel patterns of Classical Latin and Greek</note>. Furthermore, all these nations have this in common: they make their rhythms "homophonous," that is, ending with similar sounds <note>original: "homophonos," here meaning they use rhyme</note>, either immediately following one another or in alternating meters. Rhythmic poetry is so innate to men, or rather, comes from nature itself. Now, let us see which meters best fit our <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher’s "Musarithms" are mathematical sets of numbers used in his tables to automatically generate musical melodies and harmonies</note>. The Italians especially love the combination of the Anacreontic with the Phaleucian meter—that is, a seven-syllable line joined with an eleven-syllable meter.

### *An Italian six-line stanza in Anacreontic-Phaleucian meter.*

<margin>Italian Rhythm.</margin>

->*Such sweet harmony,*<-
->*Such well-alternated melody,*<-
->*Are true images*<-
->*Of the turning of the celestial spheres*<-
->*Which, revolving up there with their delights,*<-
->*Make human minds down here rejoice.*<-
<note>original: "Così dolce harmonia / Così bene alternata melodia / Imagini son vere / Del raggirar delle celeste sfere / Che girando la sù co' suoi contenti / Fan che godan qua giù l'humane menti."</note>

To compose a <term>Melothesia Florida</term> <note>An ornate or "flowery" style of musical composition, often involving counterpoint</note> for the aforementioned meter, take three columns from Table II of the *Musurgia Florida* and from Section VI of the second Treatise, according to the number and the progression of the meters which are applied alternately to each other. Thus, the first column should be for the Anacreontics, the second for the eleven-syllable lines, the third for Anacreontics, the fourth for eleven-syllable lines, the fifth for Anacreontics, and the last for eleven-syllable lines. Once these are properly arranged, the Musarithms may be selected in any order—just as we have selected these in no particular order, as they first occurred to us. Once the operation is performed according to the prescribed rules, the following musical composition <note>original: "Melothesia"</note> is produced. Meanwhile, it must be observed with the greatest care that you place the <term>chronometric signs</term> <note>Musical notation indicating the duration/rhythm of the notes</note> corresponding to each point and number above them, with pauses placed beforehand if they occur anywhere. The notes corresponding to each Musarithm are as many as the numbers in the Musarithm to which they correspond; from this, if an error had been made anywhere, a correction is easily given. And these things must be carried out with such diligence that unless everything is followed to the letter <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," meaning perfectly</note>, the desired goal of the composition cannot be obtained.

### §. XI.
### Concerning German meter.

The German language is most suited to verses and rhythms, which is why almost innumerable volumes of this kind, composed in German rhythms, are found on every subject. What we say regarding German should also be understood as applying to Belgian and English, which are the daughters of this language. But see the following example.

#### A German Four-Line Rhythmic Stanza.

<margin>German Rhythm</margin>

*Nothing earthly fills the human heart,*
*No joy, no pleasure stills it;*
*Pleasure and joy are pure pain,*
*For God alone fills it.*

<note>original German: "Nichts irdisch fült des menschen hertz, / Kein freWd, Kein lust eß stillet; / Der lust, die freWd ist lauter schmertz, / Dan Gott allein eß füllet."</note>

These verses are <term>eight-syllable Archilochian Iambics</term><note>A specific type of classical meter consisting of iambs (short-long patterns), named after the Greek poet Archilochus.</note>. To compose a harmony for these, take from the fifth table for simple counterpoint, or the third table for florid counterpoint, the Musarithms corresponding to the given verses; work as you have been taught, and the sought-after composition will be produced. The student will easily be able to derive an example for himself.

§. XII.
On the Illyrian Meter.

The <term>Illyrian language</term> <note>A term used by Kircher to refer to the South Slavic languages, or Slavic languages in general.</note> enjoys a vast number of descendants (for both the Polish and Bohemian <note>Czech</note> languages, and many others, recognize it as their mother). It constructs its verses in a not dissimilar way, rhythmically or through meters ending in a similar fashion. Therefore, nothing else is needed here except for a paradigm <note>An example or model.</note>, which, once set down, allows anyone desiring <term>Melothesia</term> <note>The art of setting melody to text.</note> to work according to the rules provided and achieve their goal. These are the principal languages of all Europe to which our <term>Musurgical</term> <note>The systematic method of musical composition described in this book.</note> art can be applied. If there are indeed any other languages, know that they are almost certainly dialects of one of the languages reviewed; thus, you will have no difficulty in accommodating the <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher's unique mathematical codes used for automated or rule-based composition.</note> to the said dialects. I do not include American languages since I have no knowledge of them; for this reason, I have chosen to include here only the principal and Oriental languages of Asia, Africa, and Europe, an understanding of which the Divine Goodness has deigned to grant me. This I have done for the sake of our Fathers <note>His fellow Jesuit priests.</note> and other religious men laboring for the honor of God in various parts of the world. I earnestly vow that all these things may yield solely to the honor of God, the Virgin Mother, and the salvation of our neighbor.

->**CHAPTER VIII.**<-
->**Rhetorical Music-making.**<-
->PREFACE.<-

Although Rhetoric possesses great power in bending and stirring the minds of men in any direction, only someone who has not read the monuments of the ancient writers could be ignorant of the fact that Music obtains a greater impression in moving those same minds. For we read that through the power of certain harmonic modulations established in various ways, the fierce were made gentle, the lustful were made chaste, those with the most serious infirmities were restored to complete health, and finally, those possessed by a demon were liberated. We have rarely perceived such things regarding Rhetoric. Therefore, a greater force lies hidden within Music, a greater energy and efficacy in affecting the minds of mortals in various ways than in Rhetoric. Since the explanation for this does not belong in this section, we shall treat it more extensively in *Physiological Musurgy*. Since, therefore, we have up to this point treated *Poetic Musurgy* in various ways and through a previously unseen method, it seemed that order required us to follow up with *Rhetorical Musurgy* using a similar method, delivering it by a new means desired by many until now. I trust that, with the assistance of the Divine Power, I shall achieve this in this part; and so as not to be overly long, we proceed to the matter itself.

§. I.
On the constituent parts of Rhetorical Music-making.

Just as a distinguished building of poetic composition rises from syllables into feet, from feet into meters, from meters into odes, and finally from all these; so too, from words and nouns appropriately arranged, various utterances are born. From these come periods, and from the periods—skillfully woven together through <term>tropes</term> <note>Metaphorical uses of words.</note> or figures—there finally arises a speech suited for persuasion. This can be established in three ways: through the judicial, deliberative, and <term>encomiastic</term> <note>A speech given in praise of someone or something.</note> genres. Our Musurgy, proceeding by a certain parallel logic, produces various reasons for the meaning of words while it adapts the Musarithms to them, just as...

But we have treated these matters more extensively elsewhere.

## §. II.
## *Concerning the various affections of the soul to which music inclines.*

Just as Rhetoric—through various arguments and reasons, as if through a varied weaving of figures and tropes—now delights the soul, now saddens it, now provokes it to anger, then to compassion, now to indignation, revenge, vehement impulses, and other affections, and finally, once the mental commotion is complete, inclines the listener to agree with what the Orator intends; so also does Music agitate the soul in various ways through the varied weaving of periods and the diverse arrangement of tones. It moves our soul, however, through three most powerful affections, from which others later sprout as if from a single root. These three general affections are as follows:

The first is **Joy**, which contains within itself the affections of love, magnanimity, impulse, and desire, which find their origin in the blood <note>Kircher is referencing the four humors; the sanguine temperament (blood) was associated with a cheerful, active disposition.</note>. If, however, this joy becomes dissolved and intemperate, it generates properly "choleric" affections: anger, hatred, indignation, revenge, and fury.

The second is the general affection of **Relaxation**. Since it delights in slow movement, it generates affections of piety, love for God, as well as constancy, modesty, severity, chastity, religion, and contempt for human affairs; finally, it moves one toward the love of heavenly things.

The third is the affection of **Pity**, under which remain all those affections that flow from phlegm and "black bile" <note>Associated with the Melancholic temperament.</note>, such as sadness, lamentation, compassion, languor, and similar states that can be recalled to this class.

How these kinds of affections are excited in the soul by the power of Music will be discussed in "Harmonic Physiology"; for now, we must finally show which tones and which tropical clauses <note>Specific musical endings or formulas that define a musical trope.</note> and which figures are proper for stirring the said affections. First, we shall speak of the twelve tones; then of the same number of tropes or harmonic figures, insofar as they possess an aptitude in themselves to stir the soul now to these, now to those affections.

## §. III.
## *Concerning the twelve tones, their nature and property.*

The tones and their arrangement have been treated extensively in the preceding books, so there is no need for anything else here except to declare the nature of each in a few words. Since there is a great controversy among authors concerning the nature of the tones, we—swearing by the words of no particular man—determine the tones here according to our own opinion, yet in such a way that we leave everyone to their own judgment in this matter.

**The First Tone**, if it is more intense and loose, is suited by nature to dances, leaps, and festive processions. If it is relaxed, it can also be suitable for piety, divine love, and the desire for heavenly things. Over this tone is composed the Antiphon: *Sweet Mother of the Redeemer* <note>original: "Alma Redemptoris mater"</note>.

**The Second Tone** is suited to tenderness and pertains to expressing the affections of pity; if it is more intense, it can also serve the affections of joy.

**The Third Tone** inclines toward affections of the third order: suited to sorrow, tears, and compassion. Over this tone is composed the hymn: *Hail Holy Queen* <note>original: "Salve Regina"</note>.

**The Fourth**
