The fourth tone is similar in almost every way to the preceding one; it belongs to the same class of emotional effects <note>Kircher categorizes "affects" or emotions into specific classes earlier in the book.</note> and evokes themes of lamentation, anxiety, and calamity—all kinds of patterns <term>pathemata: a term referring to the emotional movements or "sufferings" of the soul expressed in music</term> suited to expressing miseries.

The fifth is the Ecclesiastical tone; it shines with the greatest decorum, for it possesses a certain indescribable gravity and heroic majesty, by which it seems to summon cheerful minds toward serious and arduous matters.

The sixth prompts those emotions contained in the first class: military ferocity if it is more unrestrained, but if it is more relaxed, it can serve to stir all types of emotions.

The seventh breathes modesty, cheerfulness, and victory.

The eighth serves to excite the emotions of the second class in the minds of men; it affects a sense of gravity and majesty.

The ninth claims for itself lascivious, voluptuous, and threatening words; if it is played more intensely, it also stirs up fury and perturbation.

The tenth breathes modesty, gentleness, a meditation on heavenly things, and divine love; it is most fit for expressing divine matters.

The eleventh requires words that are sweet, soft, pleasant, and material that provides delight.

The twelfth is allotted the same properties as the sixth.

And such is the property of the twelve tones according to my opinion; the reasons for all of these shall, God willing, be assigned in my "Physiology of Music-Making" <note>original: "physiologia Musurgica"</note>.

**§. IV.**
**On the Parts of Musurgical Rhetoric.**

Just as Rhetoric consists of three parts—invention, disposition, and elocution—so too does our Musurgical Rhetoric. Invention in Musurgical Rhetoric is nothing other than the fitting adaptation of Musarithms <term>Kircher's term for mathematical-musical formulas used to generate compositions</term> to congruent words. Disposition, however, is a certain beautiful expression of those same elements through the fit application of notes. Finally, Elocution is the performance through song of the composition <term>Melothesia: the art of composing a melody</term> itself, perfected in all its measures and adorned with tropes and figures. From these parts, the entire form of our Musarithmic art is made clear.

**§. V.**
**On the Opening of a Melody.**

The Exordium <note>The formal opening or introduction of a piece, designed to capture the listener's attention.</note> of a melody is a movement that renders the listener’s mind fit for the remainder. It will be upright if it rouses the listener and makes them eager for what follows. This will be achieved if the opening is serious, sweet, resonant, and full of harmonic gravity, beginning its phrases with words congruent to the chosen tone. For it would be a defect if someone were to begin the start of a composition <margin>VI.</margin> based on the sixth tone from any other tone; likewise, one would create a defective opening if they began a song with immoderate diminutions <note>Rapid, decorative notes that "divide" a longer note into smaller parts.</note> of the voices, unless perhaps the theme of the words persuaded otherwise—as in that song by Monteverdi, *Flee, flee, my beloved* <note>original: "Fuge fuge dilecte mi." Claudio Monteverdi (1567–1643) was a revolutionary composer known for using musical "word-painting."</note>, in which, while he expresses flight, he adorns the flight of the voices with the smallest notes. It would also be a defect if someone were to place a cadence due at the end in the very beginning of the song.

## Section 6. 
## Concerning Ornamentation.

<margin>In what musical ornamentation consists.</margin>

The **ornamentation** of our musical composition <note>original: "Musurgiæ nostræ," referring to the author’s specific system or "work of the Muses."</note> consists in this: that the weaving together of notes and intervals corresponds to the meaning of the words. For instance, if the words signify a rapid movement of the soul, the music should aptly express this with fast notes; if a slow movement, then with slow notes. 

Furthermore, the melodic structure should be harmonious, with musical phrases <term>periods|In both rhetoric and music, a 'period' is a complete thought or a well-rounded sentence that carries a sense of finished meaning.</term> cohering well with one another, and the repetition of the same intervals in close proximity should be avoided. Attention should be paid to the words themselves; since some are found to be more resonant than others, they will also produce a more resonant harmony. Thus, words such as *immense*, *to celebrate together*, *anxiety*, and *they shall be troubled* will achieve a better effect in melodic arrangement than words like *large*, *to sing together*, *care*, and similar terms. <note>The author is arguing that longer, more phonetic, or emotionally "heavy" words provide better material for musical setting than simple or short words.</note>

III. It is called **Climax** <note>original: κλῖμαξ, meaning "ladder"</note> or **Gradation**, and it is a musical phrase that ascends step by step. It is commonly used to express the emotions of divine love and the longing for the heavenly homeland, such as that work by **Orlando** <note>Referring to Orlando di Lasso (c. 1532–1594), a famous Franco-Flemish composer.</note>: (*As the deer longs for the springs of water*) <note>original: "Quemadmodum desiderat ceruus ad fontes aquarum"</note>. To this can also be referred **stenasmus** <note>original: στεναγμός</note>, which means **sighing**; this naturally expresses the emotions of a sighing soul through various musical gasps and pauses.

IV. **Symploche** <note>original: Συμπλοκὴ, meaning "interweaving"</note> <margin>interweaving</margin> or **Complexus** is a musical phrase in which the voices seem to conspire together as if into one; it is usually employed for the emotions of plots or machinations, such as that work by **Clemens non Papa** <note>Jacob Clemens non Papa (c. 1510–1555), a prolific Renaissance composer.</note>: *The Kings of the earth stood up against the Lord, and against his Christ.* <note>original: "Astiterunt Reges terræ aduersus Dominum, & aduersus Christum eius."</note>

V. **Homoioptoton** <note>original: Ὁμοιόπτωτον, meaning "similar case endings"</note> <margin>similar endings</margin> or the **Similarly Ending figure** is a musical phrase that ends in a similar way through frequent repetition; it is typically used in a serious affirmation, negation, or a rebuke of something, such as that work by **Palestrina** <note>original: "Pręnestini," referring to Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina.</note>: (*We, the foolish ones*) <note>original: "Nos insensati."</note>

VI. **Antitheton** <note>original: Ἀντίθετον</note> <margin>Opposition</margin> or **The Contraposed** is a musical phrase by which we express opposite emotions; such as that work by **Giacomo Carissimi**, which he titled *The Laughter of Heraclitus and the Weeping of Democritus* <note>Heraclitus and Democritus were the "weeping" and "laughing" philosophers of antiquity.</note>, and that work by **Leone Leoni**: *I sleep, but my heart is awake.* <note>original: "Ego dormio, & cor meum vigilat."</note>

VII. **Anabasis** <note>original: ἀνάβασις</note> <margin>ascent</margin> or **Ascension** is a musical phrase by which we express exaltation, rising, or high and eminent things, such as that work by **Morales**: (*Christ ascending on high, etc.*) <note>original: "Ascendens Christus in altum." Cristóbal de Morales was a leading Spanish composer.</note>

VIII. **Catabasis** <note>original: κατάβασις</note> <margin>descent</margin> or **Descent** is a musical phrase by which we pronounce the opposite emotions to the former: emotions of servitude, humility, depression, and for expressing the lowest things, such as that work by **Massaino**: *But I have been humbled exceedingly* <note>original: "Ego autem humiliatus sum nimis."</note>, and that work by **Massentio**: *They went down alive into hell.* <note>original: "descenderunt in infernum viuentes."</note>

IX. **Kyklosis** <note>original: Κύκλωσις</note> <margin>circulation</margin> or **Circulation** is a musical phrase in which the voices seem to be driven as if in a circle; it serves words expressing a circular action, such as that work by **Philippe de Monte**: *I will rise and go about the City.* <note>original: "Surgam & circumibo Ciuitatem."</note>

X. **Phuge** <note>original: Φυγὴ</note> <margin>flight</margin> or **Fugue** is a musical phrase suited to words indicating flight, such as: *Flee, my beloved* <note>original: "Fuge dilecte mi."</note>; it also serves to express successive actions, and indeed its use is the most frequent of all.

XI. **Homoiosis** <note>original: Ὁμοίωσις</note> <margin>assimilation</margin> or **Assimilation** is a musical phrase by which the actions of things are properly expressed, as when the phrases of individual voices refer to different things; for example: (*They play the drums, they play the lyre, they strike for us, they shine in robes before the Most High Trinity*) <note>original: "Tympanizant, Cytharizant, pulsant nobis fulgent stolis coram summa Trinitate"</note>. In this song, the **bass** <note>original: "basis"</note> represents a deep drum, while the other voices represent all kinds of instruments.

XII. **Sudden Breaking-off** <note>original: "Repentina abruptio"</note> is a musical phrase by which we express a thing quickly completed; it most often takes place at the end, such as: (*The desire of sinners shall perish.*) <note>original: "Desiderium peccatorum peribit."</note>
Behold, these are the <term>tropes</term> <note>figurative uses of musical language</note> and figures which composers <note>original: "Musurgi," Kircher's term for those skilled in the art of music-making.</note> most commonly use; having explained these, let us now prepare ourselves for practice.

->### EXPLANATION OF THE PLEONASTIC TABLE <note>Pleonastic refers here to a "redundant" or "abundant" table that provides multiple musical options for the same text.</note><-
->Of simple counterpoint for Rhetorical Music-making.<-

This Table has four columns, each series of which is again divided into three parts. The first series of each column contains Musarithms of simple Counterpoint in two, three, four, and five syllables, as the series of each column shows. The second series contains the numbers of polysyllables, both long and short penultimates, and we display the short ones in this way: **III** signifies a trisyllable with a short penultimate; **IV** a quadrisyllable with a short penultimate; **V** a pentasyllable with a short penultimate, and so on for the rest. We display the long penultimates in this way: **III** for a trisyllable with a long penultimate; **IV** for a quadrisyllable with a long penultimate; **V** for a pentasyllable with a long penultimate; **VI** for a hexasyllable with a long penultimate, and so on. The third series contains the musical notes corresponding to each polysyllable, which we call "pleonasms"; this is nothing other than the multiplication of Musarithms represented in notes. We have extended the Musarithms in this Table from trisyllables up to pentasyllables because these four Musarithms are quite sufficient for expressing all possible arrangements of words in songs. Now, let us declare the miraculous use of this Table.

Note, therefore, that composers <note>original: "Melothetas"</note> do not always use the same cadences or intervals, but repeat the same clause in various ways according to a varied mixture of tones, just as was handed down above in the sixth canon. For if anyone were to continually pluck clauses from these and the following Musarithms according to the syllabic quantity of a given theme, he would indeed make a Melody-making complete in all its numbers and adorned with an artful and florid progression, yet it would lack grace and brilliance. He would be doing the same as a novice of Rhetoric who, while he heaps up various "little flowers" and elegances, would compose a speech that is indeed florid, but which lacks the soul of connection and the decorum of harmony. For this reason, more skillful musicians who are powerful in judgment—in order to adorn a song or some motet with an ingenious chaining of periods—are accustomed to mixing clauses of simple Counterpoint with florid and artful periods, repeating them through various intervals, and thus finally a song is made perfect in its numbers.

### Rule I.
### On Musarithmical Pleonasm.

<margin>
What conjoined and disjointed pleonasm is.
</margin>

A Musarithmical <term>Pleonasm|From the Greek for 'excess' or 'superabundance'; here it refers to the technique of adding or multiplying rhythmic values to fit more syllables.</term> is nothing other than the multiplication of any proposed simple musarithm <note>A 'musarithm' is Kircher's term for a mathematical-musical pattern used to set text to music.</note>. Furthermore, this multiplication can be established in two ways, just as we also handed down above in Rule 6: First, through a "broken" or "disjointed" pleonasm—which is the same thing—namely, while the <term>pedometric notes|Rhythmic values used to measure the 'feet' or meter of a poetic line.</term> of some polysyllabic word are divided into different intervals. Second, through a "whole" or "conjoined" pleonasm, namely, while the pedometric notes of some polysyllabic word are established within the same interval. We have shown both in the columns, as the headings teach. These things being proposed, let us now interpret the columns of Musarithms. Thus, the first column has the musarithms for two-syllable words, which strictly speaking do not correspond to anything except two pedometric notes, as was shown in the table of the first arrangement of simple counterpoint. 

But now, so that Rhetorical Music-making—which is a lover of variety—might flourish with greater abundance, we have arranged this table so that the columns of Musarithms do not strictly correspond only to two-syllable, three-syllable, or four-syllable words, but that every one of the said patterns can correspond to every imaginable polysyllable. Thus, the musarithms of the first column can be accommodated to words of 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and however many syllables you finally wish, whether they have a long or short <term>penult|The second-to-last syllable of a word.</term>, through either disjointed or conjoined Pleonasm. The same must be said regarding the musarithms of the 3rd and 4th columns. However, the matter will become clearer by proposing an example.

Suppose, then, there is this two-syllable Musarithm **5 1**, represented in notes as is evident [below]; this Musarithm strictly responds only to two-syllable words. But we assert here that it can be applied to every given polysyllable, which we demonstrate thus: if you first wish to apply it to a three-syllable word, you can carry that into effect by a manifold logic, namely by doubling either number or note, thus:

#### Example I.

# 156 Of the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance

## **NOTE IV.**
### **An explanation of Table II in the Musurgical Chest.**

Table II contains florid <note>ornate or decorative</note> and artistic <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher’s term for the mathematical-musical building blocks used in his system</note> of two, three, and four syllables, as the heading of each column demonstrates. Note, however, that if one were to pluck various Musarithms from this table suited to a theme, he would indeed produce an artistic harmony; yet, because of the same and <term>isochronous</term> <note>original: "isoωrona," meaning equal-timed or rhythmic uniformity</note> intervals, it would appear neither judicious nor particularly pleasing to the ears, unless one were to derive a single Musarithm through various mixtures of tones, as was declared in the preceding sections. For then, the harmony would retain its vigor and beauty. Therefore, this table will serve primarily for artistic and florid <term>clauses</term> <note>musical phrases or cadences</note> to be inserted into a simple counterpoint that has been extensively developed, as is evident in the final period of the paradigm of the first proposition. This florid clause beautifully closes a <term>Melothesia</term> <note>the art of composing a melody</note> derived extensively from a single Musarithm. Such clauses can be inserted anywhere—at the beginning, middle, or end—with this caution: that the numbers of the base 48 and 51 should always be applied to the end; 41, however, to the beginning, middle, and end; and the remaining numbers 65 and 21 only to the beginning and middle.

## **NOTE V.**
### **Showing the practice of Tables III, IV, and V in the Musurgical Chest.**

In this table are contained florid Musarithms especially suited to Ecclesiastical chant and the <term>motet</term> <note>a polyphonic choral composition, usually on a sacred text</note> style. If anyone, therefore, has a mind to produce a musical composition in the Ecclesiastical style, let him make the greatest use of this table. This table has two columns, in each of which the Musarithms are displayed along with their corresponding notes. Let it be as follows:

### **Proposition III.**
#### **Given any sacred text, to arrange a musical composition suitable for the Ecclesiastical style.**

Let the text theme be, for example: *Hail, glorious Virgin, beautiful above all others* <note>original: "Ave Virgo gloriosa super omnes speciosa"</note> and suppose you wish to adorn it with harmonic measures. Do it thus: Having selected, for example, Tone III, let any Musarithms be chosen from the second column of eight-syllable units (for one member of the theme has that many syllables, of which the penultimate is long). These will then be brought to life as musical measures by applying the column of keys to the column of the given tone, using the <term>phonotactic system</term> <note>Kircher's term for his method of organizing sounds into music</note>, in the exact same manner as has always been done until now. (For in the method of operation, no difference at all occurs from simple counterpoint). The resulting harmony will emerge adapted to the Ecclesiastical style. You shall take the greatest care to apply the notes to the corresponding Musarithms of the voices, and omit none of those things that occur, such as the dots attached to notes and the tails of the <term>fusa</term> and <term>semifusa</term> <note>eighth and sixteenth notes</note>; though these things are said for those unskilled in practical music.

## NOTE VII.
### Showing the practice of Tables VIII, IX, and X, which contain the <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher’s term for his "musical numbers" or algorithms used to generate melodies.</note> for polyphonic voices.

Table VIII contains <term>Polyphony</term>, that is, the method by which one can complete musical compositions <note>original: "melothesias"</note> for not just four, but many—indeed any number of—voices. We intended our music-making system to be perfect in every part, so that musicians could not object that an "unmusical" <note>original: "Αμουσον," referring to someone without the inspiration of the Muses.</note> person might compose four-voice pieces but could never reach beyond that. For that reason, we have organized this table of Polyphonics, so that one can compose a song of not just 4, but also 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, or 16 voices, even if they are entirely unskilled in music. This is done with the exact same faculty as the four-voice pieces. If, therefore, someone has the mind to compose a 5-voice song, they can select the appropriate Musarithms for themselves from the column of five-voice sets <note>original: "pentaphoniorum"</note> and bring them to life in the corresponding musical notes, and they will have what they sought. Likewise, if they select the same Musarithms from the columns for seven-voice or six-voice sets, a 6- or 7-voice composition will result. However, since these two polyphonic styles are not as frequently used as those for 4 and 5 voices, we shall omit them and turn our pen to composing 8-voice songs. For an eight-voice piece <note>original: "octicinium"</note> is nothing other than a certain doubled four-voice piece, divided into two choirs; likewise, a 12-voice piece is nothing other than a tripled four-voice piece, divided into three choirs, as we demonstrated in the preceding books regarding the "Musical Knot" <note>original: "Nodo Musico," likely a reference to complex contrapuntal puzzles.</note>. Truly, he who has well understood the manner of proceeding in eight voices will not be able to be ignorant of the others, for the method of proceeding is exactly the same in all of them; but let us declare the matter with a single example.

## Proposition V.
### Given a theme of words, to construct an eight-voice musical composition.

Before we proceed further, Note First: In this table, we have placed Musarithms of multiple voices partly in simple <term>counterpoint</term> and partly in composite or "Florid" style. No one should persuade themselves that an eight-voice composition consists of the whole song being continued in a perpetual sounding of eight voices. Far from it! This would be unpleasant to the ears. Rather, this artifice aims for the two choirs (into which we distribute the four voices) to follow each other skillfully and with alternating choruses. When they have followed each other for a little while, then, according to the requirements of the words, all eight should sound together; this can happen at the beginning or the middle, but at the end, all must always sound together. What we have said regarding eight voices should also be understood for 12 and 16 voices.
Note Second: The divided choirs (or what is the same thing, the four-voice sets) can be in either simple or Florid counterpoint; and therefore, all the tables proposed up to this point can serve this polyphonic musical composition. However, the Musarithms arranged in this present table only...

->**Rules to be observed in Polyphony.**<-

**First:** Total Musarithms for polyphony are to be selected from the appropriate columns; partial ones, however, are taken either from the appropriate columns of this table, or from the previously mentioned tables, yet with this caution: that the first and last numbers of the Musarithms for the two bases must always be the same.
For example, if the last number of the bass Musarithm of the first choir is 8, the first number of the bass Musarithm of the second Choir must likewise be 8, or 1 <note>In Kircher's system, 1 and 8 represent the same note in different octaves, serving as the tonic or "home" note.</note>. If the last number of the first choir is 5, the first of the following must similarly be 5. On the <term>pentagram</term> <note>The five-line musical staff.</note> of the first choir's bass, the notes to which the Musarithms correspond must be arranged so that the first note of the following section on the staff of the second choir's bass is placed precisely under the last note of the prior clause in the same key, as is shown here.

will necessarily coincide with the last of the previous one, as has been said; however, the bass of the first choir rests for three beats <note>Kircher uses "temporibus" (times/beats) to denote duration.</note>, and while the bass of the first choir is sounding, the bass of the second choir likewise rests for three beats. II. In "total" musical algorithms <term>Musarithms; Kircher's term for the numerical sequences that represent musical intervals and rhythms</term>, two basses must be positioned so that they move in contrary motions from an octave into a unison, and vice versa, as the final phrase demonstrates; nor does it matter if two octaves follow each other immediately, for it was shown in the preceding book that this is permitted in this case.

III. If anyone should extract such musical algorithms from the tables <note>original: *pinacibus*</note> of either simple or composite counterpoint, and resolve them in the phonotactic system <term>phonotactico systemate; Kircher's method for translating his numbers into musical notation</term> such that the last number of the first algorithm is one and the same as the first number of the second algorithm, the notes placed upon them will consequently be in unison. Indeed, these musical algorithms, when repeated by alternating choirs, will produce a perfect eight-voice work <term>octicinium</term>. For by varying these two algorithms in different ways—now through a mixture of tones, now by a change of notes, and finally by deducing the phrases of each bass redundantly <term>pleonastice; a technique of stretching a musical idea by adding extra notes</term>—you will be able to produce even a very long song.

IV. In establishing polyphonic composition <term>Melothesia; the art of setting a melody or composing</term>, the exact same rules and canons must be observed which we prescribed at the beginning of this section.

V. The clef signatures of the musical staves in the first choir are the same as the clef signatures of the staves in the second choir. It is, in fact, nothing other than a replicated four-voice work <term>quadricinium</term>. However, if someone wishes to set one choir higher than the other, everyone is free to do so. In that case, the two choirs must be marked as we described on the front of the following Musical Ark <note>The *Arca Musarithmica* was a famous mechanical invention by Kircher—a box containing wooden slats that allowed non-composers to generate music by following mathematical formulas.</note>.

VI. It should also be observed that in the algorithms for polyphonic works, the number 1 in the bass refers to an octave below, while 8 refers to an octave above. All these things must be noted diligently.

VII. A single musical algorithm can serve any variety of multi-syllable words through "pleonasms" <note>Here, "pleonasm" refers to musical ornamentation or dividing a long note into several smaller ones to accommodate more syllables.</note>. For example, let the phrase from the preceding example be: *All nations* <note>original: *Omnes gentes*</note>. This phrase can be adapted to all multi-syllable words through pleonasm. For if you distribute the first and second notes into minims or semiminims <note>Renaissance/Baroque note values: a minim is like a half-note, a semiminim like a quarter-note.</note> while leaving the last two unchanged, you will have all kinds of multi-syllable words with a long penultimate syllable. But if you change the penultimate semibreve into these notes [two diamond-shaped musical notes], and divide the remaining preceding notes according to the number of syllables in the occurring period, you will have all kinds of multi-syllable words with a short penultimate syllable. You will perceive our meaning better in the following example.

-> ### Conclusion <-

In this example it is most clearly evident how even a single <term>Musarithmus</term> <note>A "Musarithmus" is Kircher's term for a musical-mathematical algorithm or a set of numbers that dictates melody and rhythm.</note> can be adaptably applied to all polysyllabic words, even by one unskilled in Music, provided that they perfectly understand the value of the notes. It is also clear from this single example how all <term>Musarithmi</term> of simple or metric counterpoint can be adaptably derived for any periods of words.

**VIII.** The <term>Musarithmi</term> of **Florid counterpoint** <note>Florid counterpoint is a more complex, decorative style of music where multiple notes are played against a single note of the melody.</note> can be adapted to any polysyllabic words in a very similar manner. For if one wishes to set a polysyllabic word with a short second-to-last syllable, the second-to-last note of any phrase must be divided into two equal parts. In other cases, however, you will be able to distribute the simple notes according to the various lengths of the syllables; meanwhile, observing diligently that you do not alter anything in the syncopated <note>notes played off the beat</note> or tied notes. If, however, you wish to change short second-to-last syllables into long second-to-last syllables in polysyllabic words, you will change these notes [musical notation symbols] into [musical notation symbols] and you will have what you seek.

**IX.** In <term>Musarithmi</term> arranged alternately by Choirs, exactly the same thing must be observed as we prescribed in Rule VII. For they can be adaptably applied to any polysyllabic words; yet with this caution: that you also diligently observe what we prescribed in the first rule.

#### On the secret of the harmonic Canon to be perfected with the help of Musarithms.

#### PARADOX I.

I shall add to these another secret of these <term>Musarithms</term> <note>Kircher uses this term to describe his system of musical "building blocks" or mathematical rules for composition.</note>; which, although it is of such a nature that it should not be made common, as it is an exceptional and unique secret, I will nevertheless let it come to light like all the others, lest I seem to have begrudged the public good; Divine goodness will grant even more abundant grace to discover other things. You have seen so far how, from the various <term>metathesis</term> <note>original: "metathesi" — a Greek term meaning the rearrangement or transposition of elements.</note> and transposition of the Musarithmic Columns, innumerable types of different harmonies are born. Lest someone unskilled in music should make a mistake in the placement of words; for indeed, notes are not always applied to individual syllables of words, as is done in <term>simple counterpoint</term><note>A style of music where each note of the melody corresponds to one note in the harmony, usually one note per syllable.</note>; but rather, one syllable is often sustained through various flows of notes, as happens everywhere in <term>Florid counterpoint</term><note>A more complex, decorative style of music where a single syllable of text is stretched across many moving notes.</note>, and finally, after several measures of time, it leaps forward to the next syllable. You can see this done in various places in the <term>recitative style</term><note>A style of singing that imitates the rhythms and cadences of speech.</note> of this composition. 

Hence, so that the <term>beginner</term><note>original: "Tyro"</note> might proceed more safely in this slippery business, you will find points placed beneath the individual notes that are to be pronounced syllable by syllable. However, where a continuous flow of notes corresponds to a single syllable, we have omitted those points. By this, we intended to indicate that after the last distinct point, the pronunciation of that syllable must be continued until the next point, to which the following syllable of the word [is assigned]...

->ON **MECHANICAL MUSIC-MAKING**<-

**Mechanical Music-making** is nothing other than a certain method invented by us, by which anyone—even a person <term>untrained in music<note>original Greek: *amousos*, meaning someone "without the Muses" or lacking musical skill.</note></term>—can compose songs according to the desired artifice through the application of various <term>melody-composing instruments<note>original Latin: *instrumentorum Melotheticorum*. These refer to the physical tools Kircher invented for composition.</note></term>. We will present this mechanical music-making with as much brevity as possible; and so as not to waste time with a preface, we will begin with the construction of the **Musarithmic Chest**.

### *See Illustration XIV, placed at the beginning of this book.*

Kircher's term for the numerical sets used to generate harmonies.</note></term> from the tables onto wooden or paper rods. You shall therefore prepare the Chest with this diligence: Let a certain receptacle be made whose length is equal to its height, namely each being a palm <note>A traditional unit of measurement based on the width of a human hand, roughly 3–4 inches.</note>...

...times, such as four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten times, and we have described each column here only four times. For example, Syntagma I <note>The first major division or "collection" of musical data in the system.</note> has only twelve tablets, each of which contains ten columns. The first tablet contains polysyllables with a long penultimate syllable; the second contains polysyllables with a short penultimate syllable. Therefore, you will write out each column of these tablets several times, together with the rhythmic marks <note>original: "notis metrometris"</note> attached at the bottom of the column. This must be done so that all columns have the most equal division possible—that is, the cells in which the Musarithms <term>Musarithm: Kircher’s term for a mathematical-musical unit or "algorithm" used for composition</term> are to be written must all be equal. If they were unequal, the application of the columns would certainly lead to errors. This equality must be observed not only in the columns of the first Syntagma, but also in the columns of the second and third—in short, in every column whatsoever. ¶ Since the columns of different tablets have an unequal number of cells (some have 9 transverse rows, while some have only 8), I would advise the Music-maker <note>original: "Musurgo"</note> to divide each column into ten cells to keep the device more orderly. Then, in the empty spaces, he should repeat whatever Musarithms he wishes within that same column (nothing is easier). In this way, all columns will obtain an equal number of cells, and the device will turn out more perfect in every respect. Once these small columns have been fashioned from thicker paper or wood, and the Musarithms have been written on them in the order described, you will insert each into its own specific receptacle. For example, in the first cell of the **dodecamorium AC** <note>A twelve-part section of the chest. Kircher uses Greek-derived terms for the divisions: dodecamorium (12 parts) and hectamorium (6 parts).</note> (for this is what we have decided to call that part of the chest divided into 12 cells for simple counterpoint), the wooden rods or slips of paper for the first tablet should be placed. In the second cell, the columns for the second tablet. In the third, the columns for the third tablet, multiplied several times; in the fourth cell, the columns for the fourth tablet, multiplied several times; and so on in order until the last column of the last tablet.

<margin>
The Arrangement
of the Tables
in the musur-
gical chest.
</margin>

In the second **Hectamorio** <note>A six-part division.</note> or six-part space **GHEF**, you will place the columns of the second Syntagma for poetic "florid" counterpoint, written several times on paper or wooden rods. The first cell will serve the Adonic and Dactylic meters; the second will serve the Euripidean Iambics, and so on for the rest, as the description of the chest shows.

In the third **Hectamorio** of the chest, likewise divided into six parts, you will insert all the columns of Syntagma III in order. Inside the lid that closes the chest, you will store the Musarithmic columns for the tones <note>The musical modes.</note>, written separately, along with the two-part summary column. You should attach a specific lid to each receptacle, on the outer surface of which the title of the columns hidden within should be written, the use of which will be made known shortly. And thus you will have a Chest that is perfect in every number; its use follows.

# CHAPTER III.
## On the Use of the Musurgical Chest.

**U**se follows construction; I shall describe this in as few words as possible. Anyone about to compose a song will place the Chest, now equipped with all necessities, before him. ## Section VI.
## *On Armenian Poetry.*

->To the Armenian Fathers of the Society of Jesus and of other Religious Orders:<-

The Armenians follow the Greeks in all things regarding their rules of poetic meter; they have drawn their poetic skills from them just as they have their religious rites. Among their other poets, however, the highest place is deservedly held by Nerses <note>Nerses IV the Gracious (1102–1173), a celebrated Armenian Patriarch, theologian, and poet</note>, the Armenian Patriarch and most famous poet of his nation. From his work, we have taken the theme for our musical setting <term>Melothesia; the art of setting words to melody or the composition itself</term>. It is a three-line verse <term>Tristych; a poem or stanza consisting of three lines</term> of eleven syllables <term>Hendecasyllabic; a line of verse containing eleven syllables</term>, as follows:

*An Armenian Three-Line Eleven-Syllable Verse*

[Three lines of Armenian script]

*Garrachat parraz nuruche smidaz luhs*
*Ansdieziet ariechagan luhs dzachia huchus*
*Pirchiziet puguriz sesa puta pirchel.*

**That is:** *The splendor of glory renews the light of the mind*
*Therefore, let the light of the uncreated sun arise upon this soul*
*O Redeemer of the Universe, hasten to redeem her.*

Whoever, therefore, desires to compose a melody for this three-line, eleven-syllable verse, should select three musical algorithms <term>Musarithms; Kircher's term for numerical sequences used to generate musical harmonies automatically</term> from Table VIII. Let him work in the usual tone according to the prescribed rules, and the following Armenian musical setting will be produced. Let these be the three musical algorithms, and let the tone be the second <note>The "Second Tone" refers to the Hypodorian mode in traditional church music</note>.

->T H E  E N D.<-

Summary of the Imperial Privilege.

By the authority of Emperor FERDINAND III, it is cautioned that no one within the borders of the Holy Empire, and its hereditary Kingdoms and Dominions, shall print or sell, either in whole or in part, the Work entitled *Universal Music-making, or the Great Art of Consonance and Dissonance* <note>original: "Musurgia Universalis, sive Ars Magna Consoni & Dissoni"</note> by Father Athanasius Kircher of the Society of Jesus, for a period of ten years without the Author's permission; under the penalties contained in the Imperial letters. Given at Vienna, the 4th day of the Month of December, in the Year 1649.

Summary of the Catholic King’s Privilege.

By the authority of PHILIP IV, the Catholic King of the Spains, the same Decree is established for the same number of years throughout the Provinces of Belgium subject to Royal dominion, as is more broadly evident from his letters. Given at Brussels, July 10, 1649.

ADMONITION To Bookbinders.

The Illustrations <term>Iconismi: the engraved plates or diagrams.</term> marked (Vol. 2) belong to Volume 2 at the page number indicated there; the other Illustrations, however, in which the Volume is not assigned but only the page is noted, belong to Volume 1. The Frontispiece or Figure which contains the title of the Work with the name of the Author is to be placed before the Title of Volume 1. The Illustration of Apollo marked with Num. XI & XII should be placed before the Title of Volume 2. Finally, the Portrait of the Most Serene Archduke <note>Leopold Wilhelm of Austria, the work's patron.</note> should be placed before the Dedication in Volume 1.
